title: Science, Class 7
subject: Science
description: NCERT Grade 7 Science, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: An Invitation to Science
chapters.summary: In this chapter: science takes flight; thinking like a scientist; materials and their changes; living things, time and shadows.

lessons.title: Science Takes Flight

activities.prompt: How can curiosity help us learn to fly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science Is Everywhere
activities.body: Science covers everything, from tiny objects to distant stars. A science book invites you to ask questions, perform experiments and explore. You might look at cells inside a leaf or study the sun and stars. Curiosity helps learning take flight. A simple paper plane inspired real scientific explorations of flight. Early inventors studied bird wings while modern engineers designed aircraft.
keyPoints: Science covers everything around us.
Questions and experiments help you explore.
Curiosity can make learning take flight.
activities.explanation: Curiosity, experiments and simple ideas can help your learning take flight.

activities.prompt: A paper plane flies poorly. How can a child explore flight?
steps: Look at bird wings because early inventors studied them.
Try small experiments because the flying dream began with observations and experiments.
Ask questions because a science book invites questions and exploration.
The child becomes an explorer because curiosity makes learning take flight.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does science cover?
options: Everything
Only tiny things
Only distant stars
Only living things
activities.explanation: Science covers everything, from tiny objects to distant stars.

activities.prompt: What might you look at inside a leaf?
options: Tiny cells
Bird wings
Aircraft wheels
Distant stars
activities.explanation: Science may involve looking at tiny cells inside a leaf.

activities.prompt: Put the science activities in the order shown in your book.
activities.explanation: Your book lists these science activities in this order.

activities.prompt: What did a simple paper plane do?
options: It inspired real flight explorations.
It replaced careful experiments.
It ended the study of wings.
It stopped aircraft design.
activities.explanation: A simple paper plane inspired real scientific explorations of flight.

activities.prompt: Learning takes flight when ______ leads the way.
activities.hint: Think about asking questions and wanting to discover more.
activities.explanation: Curiosity leads the way when learning takes flight.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its contribution to flight.
activities.explanation: These pairs describe the paper plane, inventors, engineers and the beginning of the flying dream.

activities.prompt: Two paper planes have different wings. Which test is fair?
options: Change one part and keep everything else the same.
Change the wings, paper, and throwing strength together.
Use each different plane once and compare nothing.
Watch many flights without changing any plane part.

why.Change the wings, paper, and throwing st: This mistake changes many ideas, so the cause stays hidden.
why.Use each different plane once and compar: This mistake uses different planes and makes no fair comparison.
why.Watch many flights without changing any: This mistake tests no new design because nothing is changed.

activities.explanation: This changes one idea, so the result can show its effect.

activities.prompt: A child studies leaf cells and distant stars. What does this show?
options: Science covers only very distant things.
Science covers only very tiny things.
Science can cover tiny and distant things.
Science cannot cover both sizes at once.

This mistake limits science to distant things and ignores tiny objects.
This mistake limits science to tiny things and ignores distant stars.
This mistake thinks separate scientific studies cannot belong together.

activities.explanation: Science includes both leaf cells and the movement of stars.

activities.prompt: A child asks questions and tries experiments. What learning is this?
options: Learning that avoids curiosity and exploration.
Learning driven by curiosity and exploration.
Learning that ignores questions and experiments.
Learning that only repeats finished answers.

why.Learning that avoids curiosity and explo: This mistake thinks questions and experiments are not exploration.
why.Learning that ignores questions and expe: This mistake ignores the questions and experiments the child used.
why.Learning that only repeats finished answ: This mistake thinks learning means copying answers without exploring.

activities.explanation: Questions and experiments show curiosity-led learning and exploration.

activities.prompt: A curious child makes small discoveries. What happens next?
options: Curiosity makes learning stop growing.
Learning can continue without curiosity.
Small discoveries end the child's curiosity.
Learning takes flight through curiosity.

This mistake treats curiosity as a barrier to learning.
This mistake thinks curiosity is not needed for learning.
why.Small discoveries end the child's curios: This mistake thinks discoveries stop curiosity instead of growing it.

activities.explanation: Curiosity leads the way when learning takes flight.

activities.prompt: Engineers designed aircraft. Wings were useless. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Engineers ignored every earlier flight idea.
Only paper planes inspired flight explorations.
Bird wings helped guide early flight ideas.
Aircraft designs had no link to wings.

why.Engineers ignored every earlier flight i: This mistake treats early and modern work as completely separate.
why.Only paper planes inspired flight explor: This mistake assumes one inspiration leaves out the bird-wing study.
This mistake separates aircraft design from the study of wings.

activities.explanation: Early inventors studied bird wings, so they were not useless.

lessons.title: Thinking Like a Scientist

activities.prompt: How can curiosity help us discover answers and solve real-world challenges?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What scientists do
activities.body: Scientific thinking starts with curiosity and asks questions. It welcomes the unknown and asks how things work. It also asks why events happen. Scientists learn through activities and experiments. Useful experiences become stepping stones to deeper understanding. Science connects with society, and different fields can inspire each other.
keyPoints: Ask questions and welcome curiosity.
Learn through activities and experiments.
Connect science with society and other fields.
activities.explanation: Scientific thinking helps you explore questions and learn about the world.

activities.prompt: A child sees litter in a stream. Why should people care about nature?
steps: Scientists ask how and why human activities affect nature, so actions matter.
Science can help us study these changes and address environmental challenges.
Science is connected to society, so people and scientists can work together.
Together, people can use science to protect nature.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which action best shows scientific thinking?
options: asking questions and accepting the unknown
ignoring questions and avoiding experiments
assuming how things work without asking why
refusing to learn through activities
activities.explanation: Scientific thinking welcomes curiosity, asks questions, and accepts the unknown.

activities.prompt: Scientists ask ______ things work and why events happen.
activities.hint: This asks about the way something works.
activities.explanation: Scientists ask how things work and why events happen.

activities.prompt: Match each science idea with its connection.
activities.explanation: These connections show how scientific thinking links ideas, activities, society, and nature.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in the learning sequence.
activities.explanation: Activities and experiments help us learn. Useful experiences then become stepping stones to deeper understanding.

activities.prompt: How can scientific ideas in one area lead to discoveries in another?
options: by keeping different fields separate
through connections between science fields
by ignoring useful experiences
by avoiding the unknown
activities.explanation: Different science fields are interconnected. Scientific ideas can inspire discoveries in another area.

activities.prompt: Your class learns that human activities are linked to nature changes. What should it ask next?
options: Ask how and why changes happen
Assume the natural world stays unchanged
Ignore changes and avoid questions
Keep science fields separate from one another
activities.explanation: Human activities are linked to changes in the natural world. Scientists ask how and why changes happen.

activities.prompt: Scientific thinking welcomes curiosity and the unknown. What should a scientist do with an unexpected result?
options: Ask how and why it happened, then plan another experiment.
Accept the unknown and stop asking any further questions.
Call it impossible, because unexpected results have no useful questions.
Change many parts at once, so every possible cause is tested.

why.Accept the unknown and stop asking any f: Welcoming the unknown means continuing to ask and learn.
why.Call it impossible, because unexpected r: Calling it impossible closes off useful curiosity and questions.
why.Change many parts at once, so every poss: Changing many parts hides the cause and does not give clear learning.

activities.explanation: Curiosity and questions help her learn how and why it happened.

activities.prompt: Useful experiences can become stepping stones to deeper understanding. What should the class do after cleaning a stream?
options: Ask deeper questions and use the experience to learn more.
Repeat the cleaning without asking any deeper questions.
Accept the unknown and stop learning from the experience.
Keep ideas separate, because one field cannot help another.

why.Repeat the cleaning without asking any d: Repeating an action without questions does not build deeper understanding.
why.Accept the unknown and stop learning fro: Welcoming the unknown means asking questions, not giving up.
why.Keep ideas separate, because one field c: Science fields are connected and can inspire one another.

activities.explanation: Useful experiences help the class build deeper scientific understanding.

activities.prompt: Human activities are linked to changes in nature. Science can address environmental challenges and is connected to society. How should a town respond?
options: Study the changes, ask why they happen, and test possible solutions.
Choose to ignore changes, because environmental challenges are outside science.
Accept the unknown, and decide that no action can help the town.
Study the changes, but avoid testing any useful possible solutions.

why.Choose to ignore changes, because enviro: This mistake treats science as separate from society and nature.
why.Accept the unknown, and decide that no a: Welcoming the unknown does not mean refusing to act or seek solutions.
why.Study the changes, but avoid testing any: Studying without testing solutions does not use science to address challenges.

activities.explanation: Science can help society study nature and address environmental challenges.

activities.prompt: Science is connected to society. A scientist asks residents about daily activities. Why is this sensible?
options: Daily activities can shape changes in nature, so local knowledge matters.
Daily activities never affect nature, so residents cannot help scientists.
Scientific questions should avoid society, so residents will not confuse them.
Only laboratory work matters, because everyday experiences cannot teach us anything.

why.Daily activities never affect nature, so: This mistake ignores how human activities are linked to changes in nature.
why.Scientific questions should avoid societ: Science is connected to society, so local knowledge can support scientific questions.
why.Only laboratory work matters, because ev: Activities and experiments, including everyday ones, help us learn about the world.

activities.explanation: Human activities change nature, and science is connected to society.

lessons.sceneAlt: Children mix colors in liquid while an adult helps them use droppers during a hands-on science activity.
lessons.sceneCaption: Children explore colors and reactions through a hands-on experiment.

lessons.title: Materials and Their Changes

activities.prompt: Why are some fruits sour, and what happens when haldi stains are washed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Materials Around Us
activities.body: Materials have properties we can examine. It asks why some fruits are sour. It asks what happens when a haldi stain is washed. We will meet metals and non-metals. Some changes can reverse, while others cannot. Heating can speed up some changes. Batteries, lamps and wires help us investigate materials. The Sun’s heat makes water evaporate from seas. Water falls as rain and may trickle down into ground.
keyPoints: Materials can be grouped by their properties.
Some changes can be reversed, while others cannot.
Heating can make some changes happen faster.
A torch battery eventually runs out.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects material properties, changes, investigations and water.

activities.title: See what happens when water is heated or cooled

tasks.say: Move the temperature above 100°C.
tasks.then: The water particles fly apart and water changes into steam.

tasks.say: Move the temperature below 0°C.
tasks.then: The water particles become closely held and water changes into ice.

tasks.say: Warm the water above 20°C and watch the particles.
tasks.then: Heating makes the particles move faster, so the change happens more quickly.

activities.takeaway: Materials can change when heated or cooled, and some changes can be reversed.
activities.explanation: Materials can change when heated or cooled, and some changes can be reversed.

activities.prompt: A torch does not light after its battery has run out. Can changing the wires make it work again?
steps: The battery has run out, because a torch battery cannot be used again after that.
Batteries, lamps and wires can investigate materials, so they are useful test equipment.
Changing the wires does not make this battery usable again, because it has already run out.
Therefore, this torch cannot work again with this battery, even with different wires.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Useful Investigation Tools
activities.prompt: Which items can we use to investigate materials?
options: Fruits, stains, water
Metals, non-metals, changes
Batteries, lamps, wires
Heating, rain, ground
activities.explanation: Batteries, lamps and wires help us investigate materials.

activities.title: The Torch Battery
activities.prompt: A torch battery eventually ______ out and cannot be used again.
activities.hint: Think about what happens when the torch battery cannot work again.
activities.explanation: A torch battery eventually runs out and cannot be used again.

activities.title: Match the Lesson Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each item with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: The book asks why they are sour
The book asks what happens when it is washed
activities.explanation: The lesson examines properties and introduces useful questions and material groups.

activities.title: Changes That Reverse
activities.prompt: Which statement agrees with the lesson?
options: Every change can be reversed.
Some changes can be reversed.
No change can be reversed.
activities.explanation: The lesson says some changes can be reversed, while others cannot.

activities.title: Follow the Water
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: The Sun’s heat makes water evaporate from the seas
Water may trickle down into the ground
activities.explanation: The Sun’s heat makes water evaporate from the seas. The water then falls as rain and may enter the ground.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Idea
activities.prompt: Which statement uses the lesson correctly?
options: Materials have no properties, and every change can be reversed.
Materials are only metals, and torch batteries never run out.
Materials have properties, and some changes cannot be reversed.
Materials change only when heated, and the Sun cools the seas.
activities.explanation: Materials have properties. The Sun heats the seas, and some changes cannot be reversed.

activities.prompt: A learner tests unknown strips using a battery, lamp and wires. Which test is fair?
options: Test each strip the same way and compare the lamp.
Test one strip with wires and compare it with the lamp.
Test each strip, but change the battery each time.
Test each strip only after the battery has run out.

why.Test one strip with wires and compare it: This compares a wire with a lamp, not one material with another.
why.Test each strip, but change the battery: Changing the battery changes the setup, so the comparison is unfair.
why.Test each strip only after the battery h: A run-out battery cannot show whether a material works.

activities.explanation: Using the same setup gives a fair comparison of material properties.

activities.prompt: A learner finds a sour fruit and other fruits. What is the best first step?
options: Compare their properties before placing each fruit in a group.
Connect each fruit to wires and test its lamp.
Use each fruit as a battery for the torch.
Place each fruit in a group before comparing its properties.

why.Connect each fruit to wires and test its: Using wires on fruit confuses a property test with an electrical setup.
why.Use each fruit as a battery for the torc: Using fruit as a battery confuses the material with the test equipment.
why.Place each fruit in a group before compa: Grouping first skips the property comparison needed for classification.

activities.explanation: Materials can be classified by comparing their properties.

activities.prompt: A haldi stain is on cloth. How can we find what washing does to it?
options: Observe the stain before washing and again after washing.
Heat the cloth first and decide without washing it.
Wash the cloth and check only whether the battery runs out.
Compare the stain with a new cloth, but never wash it.

why.Heat the cloth first and decide without: Heating may speed some changes, but it does not answer the washing question.
why.Wash the cloth and check only whether th: A battery running out does not show what washing does to a stain.
why.Compare the stain with a new cloth, but: Never washing the cloth means the effect of washing is not tested.

activities.explanation: Comparing before and after washing shows what washing changes.

activities.prompt: Sea water gets more heat from the Sun. What may happen to it faster?
options: It may evaporate from the sea water faster.
It may freeze into solid ice faster.
It may fall as rain from the sky faster.
It may sink into the ground much faster.

The facts connect the Sun’s heat with evaporation, not freezing.
The fact says water evaporates first, then falls as rain.
Water trickles into the ground after rain, not because heating speeds sinking.

activities.explanation: Heating can make some changes faster, and the Sun’s heat causes evaporation.

activities.prompt: A torch battery has run out. The child tries new wires. What should the child expect?
options: The torch stays off because this battery cannot be used again.
The torch lights because new wires restore the dead battery.
The torch stays off because new wires make the battery run out.
The torch lights because a dead battery still stores enough power.

why.The torch lights because new wires resto: This wrongly thinks new wires can restore a battery that cannot be used again.
why.The torch stays off because new wires ma: This wrongly blames the new wires for making the battery run out.
why.The torch lights because a dead battery: This wrongly assumes a run-out battery can still power a lamp.

activities.explanation: A torch battery that has run out cannot be used again, even with new wires.

activities.prompt: Heating can make some changes happen faster. Why is “every change” too broad?
options: The fact supports faster change for some changes, not all changes.
The fact supports every change, but only some changes need heat.
The fact supports no change, because heat only changes reversible changes.
The fact supports only water changes, so every other change stays still.

why.The fact supports every change, but only: This wrongly turns “some changes” into “every change”.
why.The fact supports no change, because hea: This wrongly says heating has no effect and limits it to reversible changes.
why.The fact supports only water changes, so: This wrongly limits the fact to water and ignores other material changes.

activities.explanation: The word “some” limits the claim and does not cover every change.

lessons.title: Living Things, Time and Shadows

activities.prompt: How do shadows help us understand how living things grow and change over time?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Living Things Change
activities.body: Animals need food and breathing to grow. Blood carries nutrients from food throughout the body. Plants also need food, and may breathe differently from animals. Bodies change as they grow, and can change rapidly during middle-school years. Life on Earth has evolved over a long period. A wall clock or wristwatch shows time passing. Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell time.
keyPoints: Living things need food to grow.
Bodies change during growth.
Clocks and shadows can show time.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect growth, survival and the passing of time.

activities.prompt: A pupil notices their body changing faster and wonders what is happening.
steps: Our bodies change as we grow.
These changes happen rapidly during the middle-school years.
Animals need to eat and breathe to grow because life processes help them survive.
Therefore, the pupil's rapid body changes are part of growth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Time and Change
activities.body: A wall clock or wristwatch tells us the time and how it passes. Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell the time. Living things also change over time. Our bodies change as we grow, and rapidly during middle-school years. Life on Earth has evolved over a long period. These changes happen over time.
keyPoints: Clocks show time passing.
Sun shadows helped tell time.
Growth and evolution show change.
activities.explanation: Clocks and shadows show time, while growth and evolution show change.

activities.title: Bodies During Growth
activities.prompt: What happens to our bodies as we grow?
options: They change.
They stay still.
They stay young.
activities.explanation: Our bodies change as we grow, so change is the correct answer.

activities.title: Animal Growth Needs
activities.prompt: Animals need to eat and breathe in order to grow.
activities.explanation: Animals need both food and breathing to grow.

activities.title: Blood’s Important Job
activities.prompt: Blood carries ______ from food throughout the body.
activities.hint: These parts of food travel around your body.
activities.explanation: Blood carries nutrients from food to every part of the body.

activities.title: Early Time Clues
activities.prompt: Why did early humans use the Sun’s shadows?
options: To tell the time.
To help plants grow.
To carry nutrients.
To change bodies.
activities.explanation: Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell the time.

activities.title: Match the Clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue with what it tells us.
pairs: The time and how it passes
activities.explanation: Sun shadows and clocks tell time. The other pairs show needs, growth and evolution.

activities.title: Different Ways to Breathe
activities.prompt: Plants may breathe in a way that is different from animals.
activities.explanation: The lesson says plants may breathe differently from animals.

activities.title: Join the Ideas Correctly
activities.prompt: Which sentence joins life processes and time clues correctly?
options: Animals need food and breathing; shadows helped plants grow.
Animals need food and breathing; clocks changed animal bodies.
Animals need food and breathing; shadows replaced animal food.
Animals need food and breathing; shadows helped people tell time.
activities.explanation: Animals need food and breathing to grow. Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell time.

activities.prompt: After a meal, nutrients must reach the child's feet. What carries them there?
options: Blood carries them throughout the body.
Air carries them throughout the body.
Water carries them throughout the body.
The stomach carries them to the feet.

This confuses air with the part that carries nutrients.
This confuses water with the part that carries nutrients.
This wrongly keeps all nutrients inside the stomach.

activities.explanation: Blood carries nutrients from food throughout the body.

lessons.sceneCaption: This plant diagram reveals how a leaf is structured.

lessons.title: Light, Space and Hands-On Science

activities.prompt: How does light help us explore space and understand the world around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Light and Science
activities.body: People have developed many ways to generate light. Studying light helps us understand the universe. The Earth and Moon can both cast shadows, and their shadows can lead to eclipses. Day and night depend on light from the Sun. The Earth rotates around its axis, while the Moon goes around the Earth. The chapters use observations, questions and experiments to build your knowledge. Experiments may also create new questions.
keyPoints: People generate light in many ways.
The Earth and Moon can cast shadows.
Observations and experiments build knowledge.
Experiments can create new questions.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects light, space and scientific exploration.

activities.title: Explore Solar and Lunar Eclipses

tasks.say: Move the Moon to 180 degrees and look for the Moon between the Sun and Earth.
tasks.then: You found a solar eclipse, when the Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth.

tasks.say: Move the Moon to 0 degrees and see what happens when it is behind Earth.
tasks.then: You found a lunar eclipse, when Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.

activities.takeaway: Because light travels in straight lines, the Moon can block the Sun’s light and the Earth can block the Sun’s light from reaching the Moon.
activities.explanation: Because light travels in straight lines, the Moon can block the Sun’s light and the Earth can block the Sun’s light from reaching the Moon.

activities.prompt: A child watches daylight change and wonders how day, night, and eclipses are connected.
steps: Day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun, so light explains the daily change.
Earth rotates around its axis, so our position relative to the Sun changes.
The Moon goes around Earth, and Earth goes around the Sun, so their positions change too.
Earth and Moon can cast shadows, and those shadows can cause eclipses.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Ways to Make Light
activities.prompt: Which statement about generating light is true?
options: People make light in many ways.
People make light in one way.
People never make light.
All light comes from the Sun.
activities.explanation: People have developed many ways to generate light. The other choices do not match your lesson.

activities.title: Orbiting the Sun
activities.prompt: The Moon goes around the Earth, and the Earth goes around the ______.
activities.hint: This star gives us light.
activities.explanation: The Earth goes around the Sun, while the Moon goes around the Earth.

activities.title: The Moon's Shadow
activities.prompt: The Moon cannot cast a shadow.
activities.explanation: The Moon can cast a shadow, just like the Earth.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its correct ending.
pairs: depend on light from the Sun
build on what you already know
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important idea from your lesson.

activities.title: Day, Night and Movement
activities.prompt: Which pair of statements is correct?
options: Sunlight affects day and night; Earth rotates.
Moonlight affects day and night; Earth rotates.
Sunlight affects day and night; Moon rotates.
Moonlight affects day and night; Earth stays still.
activities.explanation: Day and night depend on light from the Sun. The Earth also rotates around its axis.

activities.title: Science Helps Us Explore
activities.prompt: Why is studying light useful, and what can experiments do?
options: It helps us understand the universe; they can create new questions.
It helps us understand the universe; they can stop all questions.
It helps us make shadows; they can build chapters.
It helps us rotate the Earth; they can create new questions.
activities.explanation: Studying light helps us understand the universe. Experiments may also create new questions.

activities.prompt: A model uses Earth and Moon as shadow makers. When one shadow covers the other body, what can happen?
options: An eclipse can happen.
Day and night can begin.
A new way to make light can appear.
Earth's axis can change.

This confuses shadows with the Sun's light that controls day and night.
This confuses making light with casting a shadow.
This confuses a shadow with Earth's rotation around its axis.

activities.explanation: Shadows from Earth and Moon can lead to eclipses.

activities.prompt: Day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun. Earth rotates around its axis. What explains the change?
options: Earth's rotation changes our light and dark times.
The Moon makes light to change our daily times.
Earth's shadow causes every day and night.
People invented electric light during daytime.

why.The Moon makes light to change our daily: This wrongly says the Moon makes the light for day and night.
why.Earth's shadow causes every day and nigh: This mistakes eclipses for the cause of ordinary day and night.
why.People invented electric light during da: This mistakes a human-made light for the cause of day and night.

activities.explanation: Earth's rotation changes our position, and our light changes between day and night.

activities.prompt: A child draws the Moon on several clear evenings. The Moon goes around Earth. What should the drawings show?
options: The Moon can have different positions around Earth.
The Moon can always stay above the same tree.
The Sun can move around Earth between drawings.
The Earth can stay still beside the Sun.

why.The Moon can always stay above the same: This treats going around as if the Moon stayed still.
why.The Sun can move around Earth between dr: This reverses which body goes around the Sun.
This ignores that Earth goes around the Sun.

activities.explanation: Going around means the Moon can have different positions around Earth.

activities.prompt: Children test why day and night change. Which plan is fairest?
options: Record light and dark times at the same place.
Record light and dark times at many places.
Test a Moon shadow at midday.
Change the Sun's light every hour.

why.Record light and dark times at many plac: Changing places at one time does not show one place changing.
A Moon shadow is used for eclipses, not ordinary day and night.
Changing the light source stops us checking the real Sun's light.

activities.explanation: Keeping one place shows that same place changing from light to dark.

activities.prompt: A child says, "Every dark patch is an eclipse." Earth and Moon cast shadows. What is wrong?
options: Some dark patches are not shadows from Earth or Moon.
Shadows from Earth or Moon never cause eclipses.
An eclipse happens whenever people make light.
The Moon always casts a shadow on the Sun.

why.Shadows from Earth or Moon never cause e: This denies that Earth and Moon shadows can cause eclipses.
why.An eclipse happens whenever people make: This confuses making light with the shadows that cause eclipses.
why.The Moon always casts a shadow on the Su: This treats a possible shadow as one that always happens.

activities.explanation: An eclipse needs a shadow from Earth or Moon, not just any dark patch.

activities.prompt: Activities encourage us to ask, explore, and experiment. An experiment confirms an idea and raises a new question. What should happen next?
options: Explore the new question with another experiment.
Stop testing because the first idea worked.
Change the fact so the idea looks perfect.
Only repeat the same test without thinking.

why.Stop testing because the first idea work: This mistakes one confirmed idea for the end of exploration.
why.Change the fact so the idea looks perfec: This thinks evidence should be changed instead of explored.
why.Only repeat the same test without thinki: This mistakes repetition without new thinking for scientific exploration.

activities.explanation: New questions can lead to more experiments and new ideas.

lessons.title: Question the Answer

activities.prompt: What curious questions could turn an ordinary answer into a surprising discovery?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Questions and Answers
activities.body: In school and tests, we usually receive questions and are expected to answer them. Finding answers matters, but asking interesting questions matters too. Great scientists both ask and answer amazing questions. There are no wrong questions when curiosity leads the way. We can imagine questions about life, the universe and everything.
keyPoints: We usually receive questions in school and tests.
Great scientists ask questions and answer them.
Curiosity makes interesting questions welcome.
activities.explanation: Curiosity makes asking interesting questions as important as answering them.

activities.prompt: Someone says, “Just make it half!” What problem do they mean?
steps: An answer can fit many problems, because it can hide different questions.
For cake, it could mean equal shares, because the cake is shared.
For an essay, it means shorter, because the essay is too long.
We ask more because each problem may hide a different question.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: One Answer, Many Questions
activities.body: An answer can lead to many possible questions. For example, “Just make it half!” could answer how to get equal shares of cake. It could also answer a problem involving a too-long essay or a too-small envelope. It could also answer a problem involving dancing to a long song. We should ask interesting questions instead of obvious ones.
keyPoints: One answer can have many possible questions.
“Make it half” can answer different problems.
Interesting questions are better than obvious ones.
activities.explanation: One answer can have many possible questions.

activities.title: What Tests Give Us
activities.prompt: What are we usually given in school and tests?
options: Recipes
Stories
Questions
Marks
activities.explanation: The lesson says that school and tests usually give us questions.

activities.title: Great Questioners
activities.prompt: Great scientists only answer questions and never ask them.
activities.explanation: Great scientists ask amazing questions as well as answering them.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Can guide questions about life and the universe
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how curiosity, scientists, interesting questions and imagination are linked.

activities.title: Sharing Cake
activities.prompt: Someone asks, “How can we get equal shares of cake?” Which answer fits?
options: Just make it half!
Make it much bigger!
Make it perfectly round!
Make it a different colour!
activities.explanation: The lesson says that “make it half” can answer how to get equal shares of cake.

activities.title: More Than One Question
activities.prompt: An answer such as “Just make it half!” can have only one possible question.
activities.explanation: The answer can have many possible questions, including how to get equal shares of cake.

activities.title: A Curious Learner
activities.prompt: Which learner follows the lesson's advice?
options: Answering without curiosity
Asking only obvious questions
Asking interesting and imaginative questions
Avoiding every uncertain question
activities.explanation: The lesson tells us to ask interesting questions and use imagination.

activities.context: While exploring a science book, a student noticed a paper plane resting near a leaf. The book invited questions, experiments, and close looking. The student wondered how wings could help flight, so she compared the plane with the wings of birds and imagined how engineers might design aircraft. She also began observing the sun and stars and considered how tiny cells inside a leaf fit into the wide world of science. Her curiosity led to small discoveries.
activities.prompt: The student wants to turn her question about flight into a small discovery. What should she do next?
options: Test a paper plane with one changed feature and record what she observes.
Look at a paper plane once and decide that flight has already been fully explained.
Study only the bird wings and avoid performing any experiment.
Observe the sun and stars and treat them as part of the flight experiment.

why.Look at a paper plane once and decide th: One observation cannot fully explore the idea of flight.
why.Study only the bird wings and avoid perf: Studying wings is useful, but this does not test her question.
why.Observe the sun and stars and treat them: Observing stars is worthwhile, but it is a different question.

activities.explanation: This turns her question into an experiment.

activities.context: While exploring a science book, a student noticed a paper plane resting near a leaf. The book invited questions, experiments, and close looking. The student wondered how wings could help flight, so she compared the plane with the wings of birds and imagined how engineers might design aircraft. She also began observing the sun and stars and considered how tiny cells inside a leaf fit into the wide world of science. Her curiosity led to small discoveries.
activities.prompt: Why did the paper plane help the student begin exploring flight?
options: It gave her a question she could explore through observations and experiments.
It showed her that flight could be explored by watching birds alone.
It meant she no longer needed experiments or new observations.
It directed her only toward distant stars rather than toward flight.

why.It showed her that flight could be explo: Watching birds was not the only way she began exploring.
why.It meant she no longer needed experiment: A paper plane can inspire experiments rather than remove the need for them.
why.It directed her only toward distant star: The plane encouraged her interest in wings, aircraft, and flight.

activities.explanation: The plane prompted a question about flight.

activities.context: While exploring a science book, a student noticed a paper plane resting near a leaf. The book invited questions, experiments, and close looking. The student wondered how wings could help flight, so she compared the plane with the wings of birds and imagined how engineers might design aircraft. She also began observing the sun and stars and considered how tiny cells inside a leaf fit into the wide world of science. Her curiosity led to small discoveries.
activities.prompt: If the student changed her focus from the paper plane to the sun and stars, what should she do?
options: Observe their movement and ask questions about what she notices.
Continue folding paper planes because stars cannot be explored scientifically.
Study leaf cells and record them as observations of the stars.
Stop exploring because science covers only one topic at a time.

why.Continue folding paper planes because st: Stars can belong to scientific exploration.
why.Study leaf cells and record them as obse: Leaf cells and stars are different subjects.
why.Stop exploring because science covers on: Science includes tiny objects and distant stars.

activities.explanation: Studying the movement of stars can involve questions and observation.

activities.prompt: Explain why a paper plane can be a starting point for exploring flight.
activities.answer: A paper plane can be a starting point because the simple paper plane inspired real scientific explorations of flight. It encourages a learner to ask questions, perform experiments, and explore. The idea also connects with the work of early inventors, who studied bird wings, and modern engineers, who designed aircraft.
points: A simple paper plane inspired real explorations.
Scientific exploration involves questions and experiments.
Early inventors studied bird wings.
Modern engineers designed aircraft.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community notices that human activities are changing the natural world. Students are unsure what caused the change, so they begin asking questions and planning activities to investigate it. Their experiments help them understand the process and build on useful experiences. They also consider how the change affects society and how science might help address the environmental challenge. They compare ideas from different science fields and see how one idea can support work in another.
activities.prompt: After noticing the change but not knowing its cause, what should the students do next?
options: Ask questions and plan activities or experiments to investigate how and why it happens.
Accept the unknown and stop gathering information because no cause has been found yet.
Choose an answer immediately so the investigation does not remain open to the unknown.
Study only the effect on society and leave the change in the natural world unexplained.

why.Accept the unknown and stop gathering in: Accepting the unknown does not mean refusing to investigate it.
why.Choose an answer immediately so the inve: Scientific thinking stays open to questions rather than deciding too soon.
why.Study only the effect on society and lea: Understanding the case requires considering both the natural world and society.

activities.explanation: This uses curiosity and investigation to learn about the change.

activities.context: A community notices that human activities are changing the natural world. Students are unsure what caused the change, so they begin asking questions and planning activities to investigate it. Their experiments help them understand the process and build on useful experiences. They also consider how the change affects society and how science might help address the environmental challenge. They compare ideas from different science fields and see how one idea can support work in another.
activities.prompt: What should the students do with what they learn about human activities and the natural world?
options: Consider how science can help society address the environmental challenge.
Keep learning separate from society because science and society are unrelated.
Treat every human activity as having no connection to natural-world changes.
Use the learning only to repeat the activity without considering its effects.

why.Keep learning separate from society beca: Science is connected to the society in which people live.
why.Treat every human activity as having no: Human activities are linked to changes in the natural world.
why.Use the learning only to repeat the acti: Scientific understanding should lead to thoughtful questions and action.

activities.explanation: This connects science with society and the environmental challenge.

activities.prompt: Explain why scientific thinking is useful when students do not know what caused a change in the natural world.
activities.answer: Scientific thinking welcomes curiosity and accepts the unknown, so not knowing the cause is a starting point rather than a reason to stop. It helps students ask how the change happens and why it occurs. Activities and experiments then provide useful experiences that lead to deeper understanding.
points: Curiosity and questions begin the investigation.
The unknown is accepted rather than treated as a reason to stop.
Students ask how and why the change occurred.
Activities and experiments lead to deeper understanding.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a materials lesson, a student notices that a fruit tastes sour. The student also sees a haldi stain on a sleeve and wonders what happens when it is washed. The group uses a battery, lamp and wires to investigate materials, then sorts them according to their properties. Their torch battery eventually runs out. Later, they discuss water changing in sunlight: it evaporates from the seas because of the Sun’s heat, falls as rain, and may trickle down into the ground.
activities.prompt: If the Sun’s heat increased, what would happen to the first step in water’s journey shown in the case?
options: Water would fall as rain before evaporating.
Water would evaporate from the seas at a faster rate.
Water would trickle into the ground without evaporating.
Evaporation from the seas would become slower.

why.Water would fall as rain before evaporat: Rain forms after water evaporates from the seas.
why.Water would trickle into the ground with: The water first evaporates and may later trickle into the ground.
why.Evaporation from the seas would become s: Increased heat would not make evaporation slower.

activities.explanation: Heating can make changes happen faster, including evaporation.

activities.context: During a materials lesson, a student notices that a fruit tastes sour. The student also sees a haldi stain on a sleeve and wonders what happens when it is washed. The group uses a battery, lamp and wires to investigate materials, then sorts them according to their properties. Their torch battery eventually runs out. Later, they discuss water changing in sunlight: it evaporates from the seas because of the Sun’s heat, falls as rain, and may trickle down into the ground.
activities.prompt: How should the group organize the materials before the book introduces metals and non-metals?
options: Sort them only by the places where they were found.
Treat every sample as a metal because metals will be introduced.
Separate the samples randomly and ignore their properties.
Compare their properties and identify which are metals and which are non-metals.

why.Sort them only by the places where they: The place where a material is found is not the stated basis for classification.
why.Treat every sample as a metal because me: Mentioning metals later does not make every material a metal.
why.Separate the samples randomly and ignore: Random sorting would not classify materials by their properties.

activities.explanation: Materials can be classified by their properties before distinguishing metals from non-metals.

activities.prompt: Explain why the torch battery cannot be used again and how this is different from a reversible change.
activities.answer: The torch battery eventually runs out, and that change cannot be reversed, so the battery cannot be used again. A reversible change is different because it can be undone, returning the material to its earlier condition. Therefore, a run-out battery represents an irreversible change, while an undoable change is reversible.
points: Explains that the battery eventually runs out.
States that running out cannot be reversed.
Describes a reversible change as one that can be undone.
Distinguishes reversible and irreversible changes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student notices that the position of a stick’s shadow changes across the ground. The student also notices that their body is changing as it grows. At school, the student learns that animals need food and breathing to grow and that blood carries nutrients from food throughout the body. Later, the student watches a plant grow and learns that plants may breathe differently from animals. The student thinks about how early humans could tell time without a clock.
activities.prompt: If the student wanted to use the method early humans used to tell time, what should they do?
options: Track how the Sun’s shadow changes.
Read the time on a wall clock.
Use a wristwatch to follow the passing time.
Use the shadow of the plant instead of the Sun’s shadow.

A wall clock tells time, but it was not the method early humans used.
why.Use a wristwatch to follow the passing t: A wristwatch is also a clock-like device, not the early method.
why.Use the shadow of the plant instead of t: The shadow must come from the Sun, not from a plant.

activities.explanation: Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell time.

activities.context: A student notices that the position of a stick’s shadow changes across the ground. The student also notices that their body is changing as it grows. At school, the student learns that animals need food and breathing to grow and that blood carries nutrients from food throughout the body. Later, the student watches a plant grow and learns that plants may breathe differently from animals. The student thinks about how early humans could tell time without a clock.
activities.prompt: What should the student do to help the plant continue growing?
options: Give the plant food so it can grow.
Make the plant breathe in exactly the same way as an animal.
Keep food away because the plant already breathes.
Give food to the student instead of the plant.

why.Make the plant breathe in exactly the sa: Plants may breathe differently from animals.
why.Keep food away because the plant already: Breathing does not remove the plant’s need for food.
why.Give food to the student instead of the: Food for the plant must be given to the plant itself.

activities.explanation: Plants need food to grow.

activities.prompt: Explain how telling time with a clock differs from telling time with the Sun’s shadows.
activities.answer: Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell the time. A wall clock or wristwatch also tells the time and how it passes. The difference is that the shadow method follows the Sun’s shadow, while the clock method uses a device made to tell time.
points: Early humans used the Sun’s shadows.
A shadow can be used to tell the time.
A wall clock or wristwatch tells the time.
The two methods use different sources.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class is preparing a hands-on display about light and space. One table uses a round ball as Earth and a smaller round object as Moon, while a lamp represents the Sun. The student moves the Moon around Earth and notices that a shadow can sometimes fall across Earth. Another student rotates Earth and observes that one side receives light while the other side is dark. The display also includes shadow drawings and questions for visitors.
activities.prompt: If the lamp, smaller ball, and larger ball become aligned in the model, what might happen next?
options: An eclipse could occur when the smaller ball's shadow reaches the larger ball.
Day and night would occur wherever the larger ball is placed.
The smaller ball would stop receiving light and disappear from the model.
The shadow would vanish because the lamp's light passes through both balls.

why.Day and night would occur wherever the l: Day and night depend on light from the Sun and Earth's rotation, not the alignment itself.
why.The smaller ball would stop receiving li: A shadow can block the lamp's light without making the smaller ball disappear.
why.The shadow would vanish because the lamp: The model shows a shadow crossing the larger ball rather than disappearing.

activities.explanation: A shadow falling across the larger ball can lead to an eclipse.

activities.context: A class is preparing a hands-on display about light and space. One table uses a round ball as Earth and a smaller round object as Moon, while a lamp represents the Sun. The student moves the Moon around Earth and notices that a shadow can sometimes fall across Earth. Another student rotates Earth and observes that one side receives light while the other side is dark. The display also includes shadow drawings and questions for visitors.
activities.prompt: If the larger ball stopped rotating, what would happen to its light and dark areas?
options: One side could remain lit while the opposite side stayed dark.
Both sides would become fully lit at the same time.
Both sides would become completely dark.
The lit side would move quickly to the opposite side.

why.Both sides would become fully lit at the: Rotation, rather than stopping it, moves a place from light into darkness.
Some light from the lamp would still reach the side facing it.
why.The lit side would move quickly to the o: A moving light-and-dark pattern requires the larger ball to keep rotating.

activities.explanation: Without rotation, the side facing the lamp could stay lit while the other side stayed dark.

activities.context: A class is preparing a hands-on display about light and space. One table uses a round ball as Earth and a smaller round object as Moon, while a lamp represents the Sun. The student moves the Moon around Earth and notices that a shadow can sometimes fall across Earth. Another student rotates Earth and observes that one side receives light while the other side is dark. The display also includes shadow drawings and questions for visitors.
activities.prompt: After an experiment confirms that a shadow can cause an eclipse in the model, what should the student do next?
options: Write down a new question suggested by the result and investigate it.
Remove the model because the result leaves no further questions.
Change the display to show only ideas that have already been confirmed.
Stop experimenting because confirmation ends the investigation.

why.Remove the model because the result leav: A confirmed result can still lead to further exploration and experiments.
why.Change the display to show only ideas th: The activities are meant to encourage asking, exploring, experimenting and thinking scientifically.
why.Stop experimenting because confirmation: New questions can guide further investigations even after an idea is confirmed.

activities.explanation: Experiments that confirm an idea may also create new questions.

activities.prompt: Explain why day and night happen on Earth.
activities.answer: Day and night happen because different parts of Earth receive light from the Sun at different times. Earth rotates around its axis, so places move into and out of the light. This rotation gives a place daylight and then darkness.
points: Day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun.
Earth rotates around its axis.
The rotation moves places into and out of the light.
A place experiences light and then darkness.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science lesson, a student was asked to explain why a piece of cake had been shared unevenly. The student expected to find the correct answer, but instead asked, “How could we get equal shares of cake?” The teacher smiled and invited the class to suggest possible answers. The class soon began asking imaginative questions instead of accepting the first obvious response.
activities.prompt: After hearing the student's question, what should the teacher do next?
options: Invite students to explore the question and suggest possible answers.
Give only the expected answer and end the discussion.
Tell the student that the question is wrong because no answer was supplied.
Ask students to repeat the obvious response without considering other questions.

why.Give only the expected answer and end th: This gives an answer but ignores the student's curiosity.
why.Tell the student that the question is wr: This contradicts the idea that curious questions are not wrong.
why.Ask students to repeat the obvious respo: This discourages imaginative exploration of the question.

activities.explanation: This encourages both answering and asking interesting questions.

chapters.title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral
chapters.summary: In this chapter: litmus and the nature of substances; red rose as an indicator; turmeric as an indicator; odour as an indicator.

lessons.title: Litmus and the Nature of Substances

activities.prompt: Could a tiny splash reveal whether a substance is acidic or basic?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Litmus Shows Us
activities.body: Litmus is a natural substance obtained from lichens. Litmus paper is available in blue and red colours. It shows different colours in acidic or basic substances. Blue litmus paper turns red in acid. Red litmus paper turns blue in a base. This colour change makes litmus an acid-base indicator.
keyPoints: Litmus is obtained from lichens.
Blue and red litmus paper are available.
Different colours show acidic and basic substances.
Litmus is an acid-base indicator.
activities.explanation: Litmus helps us recognise some substances by their colour changes.

activities.prompt: Lemon juice and soap solution touch litmus paper. What colour changes happen?
steps: Soap solution is basic, so red litmus paper turns blue.
Lemon juice is acidic, so blue litmus paper turns red.
These two colours show that litmus is an acid-base indicator.
So litmus helps identify acidic and basic substances.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Spray Surprise
activities.prompt: What appeared after liquid was sprayed on their papers?
options: A colour pattern
A welcome message
A litmus strip
A hidden picture
activities.explanation: The liquid spray made a welcome message appear on their papers.

activities.prompt: The litmus activity should use red litmus paper as well as blue.
activities.explanation: Good, the activity should be repeated with both litmus colours.

activities.title: Why Use Litmus?
activities.prompt: Why is litmus called an acid-base indicator?
options: It shows different colours.
It gives a sour taste.
It feels slippery.
It forms three groups.
activities.explanation: Litmus shows different colours, so it acts as an acid-base indicator.

activities.title: Match Litmus and Groups
activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Blue paper turns red with acidic substances. Red paper turns blue with basic substances.

activities.title: Recognising Acidic Substances
activities.prompt: A substance that turns blue litmus paper red is called ______.
activities.hint: This substance gives blue litmus paper a red colour.
activities.explanation: Substances that turn blue litmus paper red are acidic.

activities.prompt: Group C includes soap solution and lime water.
activities.explanation: Soap solution and lime water belong to Group B, not Group C.

activities.prompt: Red litmus paper touches soap solution. What colour should appear?
options: The paper should turn blue.
The paper should turn red.
The paper should stay red.
The paper should lose its colour.

This confuses the two directions of the litmus colour change.
This assumes a basic substance does not change red paper.
This assumes soap solution washes the colour from paper.

activities.explanation: Soap solution is basic, so it turns red litmus paper blue.

activities.prompt: Lemon juice touches blue litmus paper. What colour should most likely appear?
options: The paper should turn red.
The paper should turn blue.
The paper should stay blue.
The paper should lose its colour.

This assumes every liquid turns litmus paper blue.
This assumes Group A liquids leave litmus paper unchanged.
This assumes the liquid washes colour from the paper.

activities.explanation: Lemon juice is acidic, so it turns blue litmus paper red.

activities.prompt: A child touches a basic substance. What feeling is most likely?
options: The substance should feel slippery to touch.
The substance should feel rough to touch.
The substance should taste sour immediately.
The substance should feel completely dry.

why.The substance should feel rough to touch: This confuses a basic property with the sour taste of acids.
why.The substance should taste sour immediat: This confuses a basic property with a rough texture.
why.The substance should feel completely dry: This confuses touch with a basic substance's colour change.

activities.explanation: Basic substances generally feel slippery, so this is the likely feeling.

activities.prompt: An unknown liquid tastes sour. What should most likely happen to blue litmus?
options: The paper should probably turn red.
The paper should probably turn blue.
The paper should probably stay red.
The paper should probably lose its colour.

This thinks sour tastes must mean the liquid is basic.
This swaps the expected colours of the two papers.
why.The paper should probably lose its colou: This thinks sour tastes wash colour from litmus paper.

activities.explanation: Sour-tasting substances tend to be acidic, and acids turn blue paper red.

lessons.title: Red Rose as an Indicator

activities.prompt: Can a red rose reveal which substances are acidic, basic, or neutral?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making Red Rose Extract
activities.body: Fallen red rose petals can make an indicator. Crush the petals with a mortar and pestle. Pour hot water over them. Leave the water until it becomes coloured. The liquid left after filtration is the required flower extract. Add lemon juice to red rose extract in test tube A. Red rose extract can test whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral.
keyPoints: Fallen red rose petals can make an indicator.
Hot water is poured over crushed rose petals.
Red rose extract can test acidic, basic and neutral substances.
activities.explanation: You can follow these steps to prepare and use red rose extract.

activities.prompt: How can fallen red rose petals help test an unknown liquid?
steps: Collect fallen red rose petals, because they can become an indicator.
Crush them first, because hot water goes over the crushed petals.
Wait for colour, because the water must become coloured before filtering.
Keep it, because it can test acidic, basic, or neutral samples.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which petals can be collected to make an indicator?
options: Fallen petals of red roses
Fresh petals of blue flowers
Green leaves from rose plants
Roots from rose plants
activities.explanation: Fallen petals of red roses can be collected to make an indicator.

activities.prompt: The rose petals are crushed with a mortar and pestle.
activities.explanation: A mortar and pestle are used to crush the rose petals.

activities.prompt: Hot ______ is poured over the crushed petals.
activities.hint: It is poured over the crushed petals.
activities.explanation: Hot water is poured over the crushed petals.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its partner.
activities.explanation: The petals are crushed, hot water is added, and filtration gives the flower extract.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes the required flower extract?
options: Liquid left after filtration.
Petals left after crushing.
Water left before colouring.
Juice left before adding.
activities.explanation: The liquid left after filtration is the required flower extract.

activities.prompt: Red rose extract can test only whether a substance is acidic.
activities.explanation: It can also test whether a substance is basic or neutral.

activities.prompt: What can red rose extract test?
options: Whether it is acidic, basic or neutral
Whether it is hot, cold or coloured
Whether it is sweet, salty or bitter
Whether it is hard, soft or smooth
activities.explanation: Red rose extract can test whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral.

activities.prompt: The petals are crushed. What should happen next to prepare the extract?
options: Pour hot water, wait for colour, then filter the liquid.
Filter the liquid, wait for colour, then pour hot water.
Wait for colour, pour hot water, then filter the liquid.
Pour hot water, filter the liquid, then wait for colour.

why.Filter the liquid, wait for colour, then: This wrongly filters before the water has become coloured.
why.Wait for colour, pour hot water, then fi: The water must become coloured before the liquid is filtered.
why.Pour hot water, filter the liquid, then: Filtering must wait until the water has become coloured.

activities.explanation: This order pours, colours, and filters the extract correctly.

activities.prompt: A gardener wants another natural indicator. What could she try?
options: A fruit or vegetable that can act as an indicator.
More fallen red rose petals from the same tree.
Hot water poured over the crushed petals.
The mortar used to crush the rose petals.

why.More fallen red rose petals from the sam: This repeats the red rose indicator instead of trying another natural one.
why.Hot water poured over the crushed petals: Hot water helps prepare the rose extract, but is not another natural source.
why.The mortar used to crush the rose petals: The mortar crushes petals, but it does not act as an indicator.

activities.explanation: Many fruits, vegetables, and flowers can act as indicators.

lessons.title: Turmeric as an Indicator

activities.prompt: Could turmeric paper help us discover which solutions are basic?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making and Using Turmeric Paper
activities.body: Turmeric is mixed with a little water to make a paste. The turmeric-coated paper is taken out and dried. The dried yellow paper is cut into turmeric strips. Put a drop of each tested sample on the paper. Turmeric turns red in a basic solution, so turmeric paper can identify basic substances. It stays unchanged in acidic and neutral solutions.
keyPoints: Turmeric paste coats paper before it is dried.
Dry yellow paper is cut into strips.
Red turmeric indicates a basic solution.
activities.explanation: This links preparing turmeric paper with using it to find basic substances.

activities.prompt: A child tests an unknown liquid and wants to know whether it is basic.
steps: Mix turmeric with a little water because this makes the paste.
Dry the coated paper because the dried yellow paper is cut next.
Cut strips because each tested sample is placed on turmeric paper.
A red strip shows basic because turmeric turns red in basic solution.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Reading the Colour Change
activities.body: Turmeric paper shows a clear change when a tested sample is basic. In a basic solution, turmeric turns red. In acidic and neutral solutions, turmeric stays unchanged. This colour change helps identify basic substances. It helps you use turmeric paper as an indicator.
keyPoints: Basic solution: turmeric turns red.
Acidic solution: turmeric stays unchanged.
Neutral solution: turmeric stays unchanged.
activities.explanation: A red colour change is the clue to a basic solution.

activities.title: The First Step
activities.prompt: What is the first step in making turmeric paper?
options: Dry the turmeric strips.
Make a turmeric paste.
Cut the yellow paper.
Place a sample on the paper.
activities.explanation: Turmeric is first mixed with a little water to make a paste.

activities.title: Making Turmeric Strips
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Mix turmeric with a little water.
Take out the turmeric-coated paper and dry it.
Cut the dried yellow paper into turmeric strips.
activities.explanation: The paste comes before drying, and the dried paper is cut into strips.

activities.title: The Colour Change
activities.prompt: In a basic solution, turmeric turns ______.
activities.hint: Think about the colour change in a basic solution.
activities.explanation: Turmeric turns red when it meets a basic solution.

activities.title: Placing a Sample
activities.prompt: A drop of each tested sample is placed on turmeric paper.
activities.explanation: Each tested sample is placed on the turmeric paper as a drop.

activities.title: Solutions and Colour Changes
activities.prompt: Match each solution with its turmeric paper result.
activities.explanation: Turmeric turns red only in a basic solution. It stays unchanged otherwise.

activities.title: The Red Result
activities.prompt: The turmeric paper turns red. Which solution was tested?
options: Acidic solution
Neutral solution
Basic solution
activities.explanation: Turmeric turns red in a basic solution, so the tested solution was basic.

activities.prompt: A sample leaves the turmeric indicator unchanged. What can the sample be?
options: The sample may be acidic or neutral.
The sample must be basic.
The sample must be basic and acidic.
The sample cannot be acidic or neutral.

This mistake treats basic solution as if it stayed unchanged.
This mistake says acidic solution changes turmeric, but it does not.
This mistake rules out both solutions that can stay unchanged.

activities.explanation: Turmeric stays unchanged in both acidic and neutral solutions.

activities.prompt: Which order correctly prepares turmeric paper for testing samples?
options: Mix the paste, coat the paper, dry it, then cut strips.
Mix the paste, cut the paper, coat it, then dry it.
Coat the paper, mix the paste, dry it, then cut strips.
Dry the paste, mix it, coat the paper, then cut strips.

why.Mix the paste, cut the paper, coat it, t: Cutting must happen after drying, not before coating.
why.Coat the paper, mix the paste, dry it, t: The paste must be mixed before the paper is coated.
why.Dry the paste, mix it, coat the paper, t: The paper must be coated before it is dried.

activities.explanation: This follows mixing, coating, drying, and cutting in the right order.

activities.prompt: Basic and acidic samples are placed on separate turmeric strips. What happens?
options: The basic strip turns red; the acidic strip stays yellow.
The basic strip stays yellow; the acidic strip turns red.
The basic strip turns red; the acidic strip also turns red.
The basic strip stays yellow; the acidic strip also stays yellow.

why.The basic strip stays yellow; the acidic: This swaps the results for basic and acidic samples.
why.The basic strip turns red; the acidic st: This wrongly treats the acidic sample as basic.
why.The basic strip stays yellow; the acidic: This wrongly treats the basic sample as acidic or neutral.

activities.explanation: Basic turns the turmeric red, while acidic leaves it unchanged.

activities.prompt: Several unlabelled samples may be acidic, neutral, or basic. What is the fairest test?
options: Place each sample drop on a separate turmeric strip.
Place all sample drops on one turmeric strip.
Place only one sample drop on a turmeric strip.
Place no sample drops on the turmeric strips.

why.Place all sample drops on one turmeric s: This mistake mixes all tested samples on one piece of paper.
why.Place only one sample drop on a turmeric: This mistake leaves most samples untested.
why.Place no sample drops on the turmeric st: This mistake tests no samples, so no result can be seen.

activities.explanation: Each sample gets its own strip, so every tested sample can be checked.

activities.prompt: Could a smell help us spot a hidden chemical change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changing odours
activities.body: Some substances change their odour in acidic or basic conditions. Substances with changing odours are called olfactory indicators. Tamarind water goes on one onion strip. Baking soda solution goes on the other strip. The container is closed tightly and left overnight. Then, the odour is checked again after the drops spread.
keyPoints: Some substances change their odour in acidic or basic conditions.
Substances with changing odours are called olfactory indicators.
The odour is checked again after the drops spread.
activities.explanation: This activity shows how to observe changing odours.

activities.title: Watch an indicator show acid or base

tasks.say: Use more acid than base and add another acid drop.
tasks.then: The litmus turns red, showing that the mixture is acidic.

tasks.say: Make the numbers of acid and base drops equal.
tasks.then: The litmus shows a neutral colour when equal strengths mix.

tasks.say: Use more base than acid and add another base drop.
tasks.then: The litmus turns blue, showing that the mixture is basic.

activities.takeaway: An indicator, including an olfactory indicator, can reveal whether a substance is acidic or basic.
activities.explanation: An indicator, including an olfactory indicator, can reveal whether a substance is acidic or basic.

activities.prompt: How can a child test two liquids on onion strips?
steps: Tightly close the container and leave it overnight, allowing possible odour changes.
Put tamarind water on one onion strip, which receives one liquid.
Use baking soda solution on the other strip for the comparison.
Check the odours after the drops spread; changed odours show olfactory indicators.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Some substances change their odour in acidic or basic conditions.

activities.prompt: What are substances with changing odours called?
options: Olfactory indicators
Closed containers
Baking soda
Tamarind water

activities.prompt: Substances with changing odours are called ______ indicators.
activities.hint: This word means relating to the sense of smell.
activities.explanation: The full name is olfactory indicators.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its description in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Tamarind water and baking soda solution go on separate onion strips.

activities.prompt: Which liquid is placed on one onion strip?
options: Tamarind water
Baking soda solution
Tamarind solution
Onion strip liquid
activities.explanation: Tamarind water is placed on one onion strip.

activities.prompt: After the drops spread, what observation does the lesson ask you to make?
options: The odour is checked again
The container is closed again
The strips are dried again
The drops are covered again
activities.explanation: The lesson asks you to check the odour again after the drops spread.

activities.prompt: One onion strip has tamarind water. What should happen next?
options: Put baking soda solution on the other onion strip.
Put baking soda solution on the same onion strip.
Close only the container holding the tamarind strip.
Add both liquids before checking either onion strip.

why.Put baking soda solution on the same oni: Both liquids go on one strip, so the two strips cannot be compared.
why.Close only the container holding the tam: Closing one container does not give the other strip baking soda solution.
why.Add both liquids before checking either: This skips the separate-strip method and changes both strips at once.

activities.explanation: This is right because each strip receives one of the two liquids.

activities.prompt: The container stays closed overnight. Why do this before checking the odour?
options: To give the substances time to change their odour.
To make the tamarind water and baking soda solution mix.
To make the onion strips receive equal amounts of liquid.
To replace checking the odour after the drops spread.

why.To make the tamarind water and baking so: This wrongly treats closing the container as a way to mix the liquids.
why.To make the onion strips receive equal a: Closing the container cannot equalise the liquid amounts.
why.To replace checking the odour after the: The odour must still be checked after the drops spread.

activities.explanation: This is right because the overnight wait allows a possible odour change.

activities.prompt: Which test can show that a substance is an olfactory indicator?
options: Check its odour in acidic and basic conditions.
Check its colour in acidic and basic conditions.
Check its taste in acidic and basic conditions.
Check its texture in acidic and basic conditions.

why.Check its colour in acidic and basic con: This confuses the sense of smell with the sense of sight.
why.Check its taste in acidic and basic cond: This confuses the sense of smell with the sense of taste.
why.Check its texture in acidic and basic co: This confuses the sense of smell with the sense of touch.

activities.explanation: This is right because olfactory indicators change their odour in these conditions.

activities.prompt: Both onion strips get tamarind water. What is wrong with the test?
options: The other strip does not get baking soda solution.
The first strip does not get tamarind water.
The container is not closed tightly enough.
The odour is checked before the drops spread.

why.The first strip does not get tamarind wa: This ignores that both strips already receive tamarind water.
why.The container is not closed tightly enou: This mistakes the liquid choice for a problem with closing the container.
why.The odour is checked before the drops sp: This is only a problem if the odour is checked too early.

activities.explanation: This is right because the other strip should receive baking soda solution.
