lessons.title: Mixing Acids and Bases

activities.prompt: What happens when lemon juice meets lime water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mixing Acids and Bases
activities.body: Lemon juice is diluted with about twenty drops of water. A drop of blue litmus solution is added, and the solution turns red. Lime water is then added slowly while the solution is swirled. The colour changes from red to blue. The solution is no longer acidic because lime water has neutralised the acid's effect. This is called a neutralisation reaction. Salt and water form while heat is released.
keyPoints: Blue litmus solution turns red in diluted lemon juice.
Lime water neutralises the effect of the acid.
Salt and water form while heat is released.
activities.explanation: You can spot the reaction through its colour changes.

activities.title: Neutralise an acid

tasks.say: Add base until it is neutral.
tasks.then: Acid and base have cancelled each other out.

tasks.say: Add one more drop of base.
tasks.then: Now it is basic.

activities.takeaway: An acid and a base can neutralise each other.
activities.explanation: An acid and a base can neutralise each other.

activities.prompt: What happens when lime water is added to diluted lemon juice?
steps: Diluted lemon juice turns blue litmus red, showing an acid effect.
Lime water is swirled in slowly so it mixes with the acid.
The colour changes from red to blue as the acid is neutralised.
This neutralisation reaction forms salt and water while releasing heat.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What colour does the diluted lemon juice turn after blue litmus solution is added?
options: Red
Blue
Green
Clear
activities.explanation: Great choice! The solution turns red after blue litmus solution is added.

activities.prompt: Lime water is added all at once to the solution.
activities.explanation: Good try. Lime water is added slowly while the solution is swirled.

activities.prompt: In a neutralisation reaction, acid plus base gives salt, ______ and heat.
activities.hint: This liquid is also added to the lemon juice solution.
activities.explanation: Well done! Acid plus base gives salt, water and heat.

activities.prompt: Match each action with what happens next.
pairs: The colour changes from red to blue
activities.explanation: Excellent matching! Each colour change helps show what happens during the reaction.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in the correct order.
items: Add lime water slowly while swirling
Watch the colour change from red to blue
activities.explanation: Perfect order! You followed the whole reaction from the first colour change to the last.

activities.prompt: Why is the solution no longer acidic after lime water is added?
options: Lime water neutralises the acid's effect.
Blue litmus neutralises the acid's effect.
Swirling neutralises the acid's effect.
Salt neutralises the acid's effect.
activities.explanation: Exactly right! Lime water has neutralised the effect of the acid.

activities.prompt: The solution remains acidic after lime water is added.
activities.explanation: Good thinking! The solution is no longer acidic after lime water is added.

activities.prompt: Which equation matches the neutralisation reaction?
options: Acid plus base gives salt and water.
Acid plus base gives salt, water, heat.
Acid plus base gives water and heat.
Acid plus base gives salt and heat.
activities.explanation: You got it! Acid plus base gives salt, water and heat.

activities.prompt: A child adds blue litmus to diluted lemon juice. What colour should appear?
options: It will turn red because the liquid shows an acid effect.
It will turn blue because the litmus solution starts blue.
It will turn green because water changes the litmus colour.
It will stay blue because dilution removes the acidic effect.

why.It will turn blue because the litmus sol: This assumes the starting litmus colour must remain.
why.It will turn green because water changes: This confuses dilution with a green colour change.
why.It will stay blue because dilution remov: This wrongly thinks dilution removes the acidic effect.

activities.explanation: Blue litmus turns red in the diluted lemon juice.

activities.prompt: Four children test lime water on diluted lemon juice. Which test best shows neutralisation?
options: Add lime water slowly, swirl, and watch the litmus colour change.
Add lime water quickly, hide the colour, and do not swirl.
Add only water, swirl, and watch the litmus colour change.
Add lime water before litmus, then guess the final colour.

why.Add lime water quickly, hide the colour,: Hiding the colour and skipping swirling remove fair observations.
why.Add only water, swirl, and watch the lit: Adding only water cannot test the effect of lime water.
why.Add lime water before litmus, then guess: Guessing the final colour gives no real test.

activities.explanation: Slow addition, swirling, and watching give a clear neutralisation test.

lessons.title: Neutralisation in Daily Life

activities.prompt: How can baking soda help an itchy ant bite?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is neutralisation?
activities.body: An acid and a base neutralise each other. They form salt and water, and heat is produced. This helps in daily life. Neutralisation can help with problems involving ant bites, acidic soil and industrial waste. Baking soda and lime are bases. Substances can be acidic, basic or neutral. Natural extracts act as indicators, showing different colours in acidic and basic solutions.
keyPoints: An acid and a base neutralise each other.
Salt and water form, and heat is produced.
Neutralisation helps with bites, soil and waste.
activities.explanation: Neutralisation connects acids and bases with useful changes in everyday life.

activities.title: Neutralise an acid

tasks.say: Add base until it is neutral.
tasks.then: Acid and base have cancelled each other out.

tasks.say: Add one more drop of base.
tasks.then: Now it is basic.

activities.takeaway: An acid and a base can neutralise each other.
activities.explanation: An acid and a base can neutralise each other.

activities.prompt: A child gets an ant bite. Can baking soda help, and what will happen?
steps: An ant bite injects formic acid, so the bite is acidic.
Baking soda is a base, so it can neutralise the acid.
The acid and base react, so salt and water form with heat.
Therefore, neutralisation can help manage the ant bite.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does baking soda act as?
options: A base
An acid
An indicator
A natural extract
activities.explanation: Baking soda is a base. A base can neutralise an acid.

activities.prompt: An ant bite injects formic acid into the skin.
activities.explanation: An ant bite injects an acidic liquid called formic acid into the skin.

activities.prompt: Lime is a ______.
activities.hint: What is lime used to treat acidic soil?
activities.explanation: Lime is a base. It can neutralise acidic soil.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its matching nature or result.
activities.explanation: These pairs show each substance's nature or result. An ant bite involves formic acid, while neutralisation forms salt and water.

activities.prompt: What happens when organic matter releases acids in soil?
options: They neutralise the soil's basic nature.
They increase the soil's basic nature.
They create salt and water in soil.
They make all plants grow well in soil.
activities.explanation: Organic matter releases acids that neutralise the basic nature of soil.

activities.prompt: Natural extracts show the same colour in acidic and basic solutions.
activities.explanation: An indicator shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions.

activities.prompt: Put the neutralisation change in order.
items: An acid and a base react
Salt and water form with heat
activities.explanation: An acid reacts with a base. They neutralise each other, and salt and water form with heat.

activities.prompt: Why are natural extracts useful as indicators?
options: They show colours for acidic and basic solutions.
They make every solution into a neutral substance.
They create salt and water in natural extracts.
They change acidic soil into basic soil.
activities.explanation: Natural extracts can act as indicators. An indicator shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions.

activities.prompt: An ant bite puts formic acid in the skin. What forms when baking soda neutralises it?
options: Salt and water form together with heat.
More formic acid forms together with cold water.
Baking soda stays alone, and the formic acid disappears.
Salt forms with the acid, but no water or heat appears.

why.More formic acid forms together with col: This mistake thinks neutralisation makes more acid instead of neutralising it.
why.Baking soda stays alone, and the formic: This mistake thinks the base is not changed during neutralisation.
why.Salt forms with the acid, but no water o: This mistake forgets that water and heat also form.

activities.explanation: This is what happens when an acid and a base neutralise.

activities.prompt: Acidic factory waste must enter a lake. What should happen before it is released?
options: The waste should be heated, because heat turns acid into salt.
The waste should get more basic, so no neutralisation can occur.
The waste should be neutralised, so less acid enters the lake.
The waste should be made acidic, so the lake stays unchanged.

why.The waste should be heated, because heat: This mistake treats heat as the substance that changes acid into salt.
why.The waste should get more basic, so no n: This mistake confuses making waste basic with neutralising its acid.
why.The waste should be made acidic, so the: This mistake thinks adding acid helps when acid already causes the problem.

activities.explanation: Neutralisation reduces the acid before the waste enters the lake.

activities.context: Ashwin and Keerthi tested lemon juice from Group A and soap solution from Group B. Lemon juice sprayed on blue litmus paper turned it red. When soap solution was sprayed on red litmus paper, it turned blue. Keerthi noticed that each paper changed to the colour of the other. Their teacher asked them to repeat the litmus activity with both red and blue papers and explain what the colour changes showed.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best fits the result when lemon juice was sprayed on blue litmus paper?
options: The sample is basic because it turned blue litmus paper red.
The sample is acidic because it turned red litmus paper blue.
The sample is acidic because it turned blue litmus paper red.
The sample is neither acidic nor basic because litmus changed colour.

why.The sample is basic because it turned bl: A change from blue to red identifies an acidic substance, not a basic one.
why.The sample is acidic because it turned r: That explanation describes the soap solution's result on red litmus paper, not the lemon juice test.
why.The sample is neither acidic nor basic b: A colour change shows that litmus is responding, not that the substance is neither acidic nor basic.

activities.context: Ashwin and Keerthi tested lemon juice from Group A and soap solution from Group B. Lemon juice sprayed on blue litmus paper turned it red. When soap solution was sprayed on red litmus paper, it turned blue. Keerthi noticed that each paper changed to the colour of the other. Their teacher asked them to repeat the litmus activity with both red and blue papers and explain what the colour changes showed.
activities.prompt: Why can litmus be called an acid-base indicator?
options: Its natural source in lichens makes it an indicator.
Its two available colours identify every substance without testing.
It shows the same colour whether the substance is acidic or basic.
Its different colours reveal whether a substance is acidic or basic.

why.Its natural source in lichens makes it a: Being obtained from lichens does not by itself explain its indicator role.
why.Its two available colours identify every: The two colours are useful only when their changes are observed during testing.
why.It shows the same colour whether the sub: Litmus shows different colours, so it does not give the same result for acidic and basic substances.

activities.explanation: Colour changes distinguish acidic substances from basic substances, which is the purpose of an indicator.

activities.prompt: How does litmus show whether a substance is acidic or basic?
activities.answer: Litmus is an acid-base indicator because it shows different colours. If a substance turns blue litmus paper red, the substance is acidic. If a substance turns red litmus paper blue, the substance is basic. The observed colour change therefore identifies the type of substance.
points: Litmus shows different colours.
Blue litmus paper turning red indicates an acidic substance.
Red litmus paper turning blue indicates a basic substance.
Litmus is therefore an acid-base indicator.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class activity, a student collected fallen petals from red roses. She crushed them with a mortar and pestle, then poured hot water over the crushed petals. She left the mixture until the water became coloured. Next, she must separate the liquid from the petals. She plans to put some red rose extract into test tube A and add lemon juice, then use the extract to test the lemon juice.
activities.prompt: What should the student do next to obtain the flower extract?
options: Filter the mixture and collect the coloured liquid.
Leave the mixture longer without separating the petals.
Crush the petals again and add the mixture to test tube A.
Pour away the water and keep only the petals.

why.Leave the mixture longer without separat: Leaving it longer does not perform the required separation.
why.Crush the petals again and add the mixtu: Crushing again does not produce the liquid extract needed for the test.
why.Pour away the water and keep only the pe: Keeping the petals discards the coloured liquid needed for the test.

activities.explanation: Filtration separates the liquid from the crushed petals.

activities.context: During a class activity, a student collected fallen petals from red roses. She crushed them with a mortar and pestle, then poured hot water over the crushed petals. She left the mixture until the water became coloured. Next, she must separate the liquid from the petals. She plans to put some red rose extract into test tube A and add lemon juice, then use the extract to test the lemon juice.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the student skipped filtration?
options: She would not obtain the required flower extract.
She would obtain the extract without another step.
She could use the crushed petals as the prepared extract.
She would need only to add more hot water.

why.She would obtain the extract without ano: Skipping filtration leaves the petals and liquid together.
why.She could use the crushed petals as the: Crushed petals are not the liquid flower extract.
why.She would need only to add more hot wate: More hot water would not perform the missing filtration step.

activities.explanation: The extract is the liquid remaining after filtration.

activities.prompt: Explain how to prepare flower extract from fallen red rose petals.
activities.answer: First, collect fallen petals of red roses. Crush them with a mortar and pestle, then pour hot water over the crushed petals. Leave the water until it becomes coloured. Finally, filter the mixture. The liquid left after filtration is the required flower extract and can be used for tests.
points: Fallen red rose petals are collected and crushed.
Hot water is poured over the crushed petals.
The water is left until it becomes coloured.
The liquid left after filtration is the required extract.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner mixes turmeric with a little water to make a paste. The coated paper is taken out and dried, and the dried yellow paper is cut into turmeric strips. A drop from each tested sample is placed on a strip. The tested samples are basic, acidic, and neutral. The learner observes the colours and decides which sample is basic.
activities.prompt: What would happen when the drop of the basic sample is placed on the turmeric strip?
options: The turmeric strip turns red.
The turmeric strip stays yellow.
The turmeric strip turns blue.
The turmeric strip becomes colourless.

An unchanged strip would not show the expected basic reaction.
Blue is not the indicated colour for a basic solution.
Colourlessness is not the indicated result for a basic solution.

activities.explanation: Turmeric turns red in a basic solution.

activities.context: A learner mixes turmeric with a little water to make a paste. The coated paper is taken out and dried, and the dried yellow paper is cut into turmeric strips. A drop from each tested sample is placed on a strip. The tested samples are basic, acidic, and neutral. The learner observes the colours and decides which sample is basic.
activities.prompt: After seeing one red strip and two unchanged strips, what should the learner conclude?
options: The test identifies the basic sample but does not distinguish the acidic and neutral samples.
The unchanged strips prove that both samples are basic.
The red strip proves that the sample is acidic.
The learner can identify the acidic sample from its unchanged colour.

why.The unchanged strips prove that both sam: Unchanged turmeric does not separate acidic and neutral solutions.
why.The red strip proves that the sample is: Red indicates basic behaviour, not acidic behaviour.
why.The learner can identify the acidic samp: Acid and neutral solutions can both leave turmeric unchanged.

activities.explanation: Red identifies the basic sample.

activities.prompt: Explain how turmeric paper is prepared and used to identify a basic solution.
activities.answer: Turmeric is mixed with a little water to make a paste, which coats the paper. After the paper dries and is cut into strips, a drop of each tested solution is placed on a strip. Red turmeric indicates a basic solution, while an unchanged strip indicates an acidic or neutral solution.
points: Turmeric is mixed with a little water.
The coated paper is dried and cut into strips.
A drop of the tested solution is placed on a strip.
Turmeric turns red in a basic solution.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Two onion strips are placed in a container. Tamarind water is placed on one onion strip, and baking soda solution is placed on the other strip. The container is closed tightly and left overnight. After the drops have spread, the odour of each strip is checked again to find out whether either one has changed.
activities.prompt: After the overnight wait, the student notices that the drops have spread. What is the correct next step?
options: Compare the odour of the two onion strips again.
Close the container again without examining the strips.
Replace each treated strip before checking anything.
Add more drops and leave without checking.

why.Replace each treated strip before checki: This removes the evidence being tested.
why.Add more drops and leave without checkin: This delays the needed odour check.

activities.explanation: This follows the second odour check.

activities.context: Two onion strips are placed in a container. Tamarind water is placed on one onion strip, and baking soda solution is placed on the other strip. The container is closed tightly and left overnight. After the drops have spread, the odour of each strip is checked again to find out whether either one has changed.
activities.prompt: If one strip still has the same odour after the second check, what conclusion is safest?
options: This test has not shown an odour change on that strip.
That strip must be an olfactory indicator.
Both solutions must have had the same effect.
The strip must have changed in an acidic condition.

why.That strip must be an olfactory indicato: An olfactory indicator is defined by an odour change.
why.Both solutions must have had the same ef: One result cannot establish the effect on both solutions.
why.The strip must have changed in an acidic: No odour change means an acidic change is not demonstrated.

activities.explanation: Only a changed odour would show the effect described.

activities.prompt: Why is the odour checked again after the drops have spread?
activities.answer: The second odour check shows whether tamarind water or baking soda solution changed the onion strip’s smell. This helps connect the result with the lesson: substances with changing odours are called olfactory indicators, and some change their odour in acidic or basic conditions.
points: A second odour check is made.
It tests whether the odour changed.
The result connects with acidic or basic conditions.
The lesson identifies changing-odour substances as olfactory indicators.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is investigating a sample of lemon juice. First, the student dilutes it with about twenty drops of water and adds a drop of blue litmus solution. The solution turns red. The student then adds lime water slowly while swirling the mixture. The colour eventually changes from red to blue, showing that the solution is no longer acidic.
activities.prompt: What does the red colour after blue litmus solution is added show about the diluted lemon juice?
options: The solution still behaves as an acid.
The lime water has already neutralised the acid.
The neutralisation reaction has produced salt and water.
The solution is basic and will remain red.

why.The lime water has already neutralised t: Lime water had not yet been added at that stage.
why.The neutralisation reaction has produced: Salt and water form during neutralisation, which happens later.
why.The solution is basic and will remain re: The final solution is no longer acidic, so red is not its final colour.

activities.explanation: The blue litmus turning red shows that the solution is acidic.

activities.context: A student is investigating a sample of lemon juice. First, the student dilutes it with about twenty drops of water and adds a drop of blue litmus solution. The solution turns red. The student then adds lime water slowly while swirling the mixture. The colour eventually changes from red to blue, showing that the solution is no longer acidic.
activities.prompt: What occurs during the reaction between the acid in the lemon juice and the lime water?
options: Salt and water form while heat is released.
Salt forms while water and heat disappear.
Water forms while salt is absorbed and heat is released.
Heat is absorbed while salt and water remain unchanged.

why.Salt forms while water and heat disappea: Neutralisation does not remove the water or release heat in the opposite way.
why.Water forms while salt is absorbed and h: The reaction produces both salt and water.
why.Heat is absorbed while salt and water re: Neutralisation releases heat rather than absorbing it.

activities.explanation: A neutralisation reaction produces salt and water and releases heat.

activities.prompt: Explain why the solution changes from red to blue when lime water is added.
activities.answer: Blue litmus turns red in the diluted lemon juice, showing that the solution is acidic. Adding lime water neutralises the acid's effect. As the acid is neutralised, the colour changes from red to blue, so the final solution is no longer acidic.
points: Blue litmus turns red in the acidic solution.
Lime water neutralises the acid's effect.
The colour changes from red to blue.
The final solution is no longer acidic.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student gets an ant bite, and an acidic liquid called formic acid enters the skin. The student knows that baking soda is a base and has learned that an acid and a base neutralise each other. At the school garden, acidic soil is harming plant growth, so it will be treated with lime, which is a base. Another group has acidic factory waste that must not be released into a lake unchanged.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the formic acid from the ant bite mixed with baking soda?
options: The acid and base would neutralise each other, forming salt and water while releasing heat.
The acid and base would remain unchanged because they would not react together.
The acid and base would react to form salt only, without producing water or heat.
The acid and base would neutralise each other but would absorb heat instead of releasing it.

why.The acid and base would remain unchanged: An acid and a base do react during neutralisation, so they would not remain unchanged.
why.The acid and base would react to form sa: Neutralisation forms both salt and water, not only salt.
why.The acid and base would neutralise each: Heat is released during neutralisation rather than absorbed.

activities.explanation: Formic acid is acidic, while baking soda is a base, so they neutralise each other.

activities.context: A student gets an ant bite, and an acidic liquid called formic acid enters the skin. The student knows that baking soda is a base and has learned that an acid and a base neutralise each other. At the school garden, acidic soil is harming plant growth, so it will be treated with lime, which is a base. Another group has acidic factory waste that must not be released into a lake unchanged.
activities.prompt: What should the other group do with the acidic factory waste before releasing it into the lake?
options: They should neutralise the waste before releasing it into the lake.
They should make the waste more acidic before releasing it into the lake.
They should release the waste first and neutralise it after it reaches the lake.
They should mix the waste with acid so that it remains acidic during release.

why.They should make the waste more acidic b: Making the waste more acidic would increase its acidity rather than neutralise it.
why.They should release the waste first and: The waste needs to be neutralised before release, not after reaching the lake.
why.They should mix the waste with acid so t: Adding acid would not neutralise the acidity already present in the waste.

activities.explanation: Acidic factory waste can be neutralised before it is released into a lake.

activities.prompt: Explain why the formic acid in an ant bite can be neutralised with baking soda.
activities.answer: Formic acid injected by an ant bite is acidic, while baking soda is a base. When they react, the acid and base neutralise each other. The products are salt and water, and heat is released during the reaction.
points: Formic acid is identified as an acidic substance.
Baking soda is identified as a base.
An acid and a base neutralise each other.
Neutralisation forms salt and water while releasing heat.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What happens to red litmus paper in a basic substance?
options: It turns blue
It turns red
It stays red
It turns yellow

Soap solution

items: Add about twenty drops of water to lemon juice

chapters.title: Electricity: Circuits and Their Components
chapters.summary: In this chapter: electricity around us and safety; electric cell and battery; electric lamps; electrical circuits and leds.

lessons.title: Electricity around us and safety

activities.prompt: How does electricity travel from nature to our homes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Electricity and safety
activities.body: Electricity can be generated in several ways. Falling water can generate it at a hydroelectric power house. It reaches homes and factories through wires. We connect devices to sockets in our homes. Danger signs tell us to handle electricity carefully. Never experiment with the power supply at home or school. For experiments, use only batteries or cells. A portable source is useful for learning electricity. Portable generators can be dangerous.
keyPoints: Falling water can generate electricity.
Electricity reaches homes and factories through wires.
Use only batteries or cells for experiments.
activities.explanation: These key ideas cover electricity, connections, and safe experiments.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test electricity at school with a portable generator.
steps: The generator is tempting because a portable source is useful for learning.
It is unsafe because electricity from portable generators can still be dangerous.
The power supply is banned because school experiments must never use it.
The child should use a battery or cell, the allowed experiment source.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How electricity travels
activities.prompt: How does electricity reach our homes and factories?
options: Through wires
Through sockets
Using batteries
Near danger signs
activities.explanation: Electricity from different sources reaches our homes and factories through wires.

activities.title: Connecting a device
activities.prompt: We connect electrical devices to sockets in the walls of our homes.
activities.explanation: Electrical devices connect to sockets in the walls of our homes.

activities.title: Choosing an experiment source
activities.prompt: For experiments, use only ______ or cells.
activities.hint: Think of the allowed source for experiments.
activities.explanation: Only batteries or cells should be used for experiments.

activities.title: Safety matching
activities.prompt: Match each thing with its safety advice.
pairs: Connect it to a wall socket
activities.explanation: Each pair links an item with the correct safety advice.

activities.title: The electricity route
activities.prompt: Put the electricity route in order.
activities.explanation: Falling water generates electricity at the power house. Wires carry it to homes and factories.

activities.title: Choosing an experiment source
activities.prompt: Which source should you use for experiments?
options: The power supply
A portable generator
Batteries or cells
A wall socket
activities.explanation: Only batteries or cells should be used for experiments. Portable generators can still be dangerous.

activities.title: Portable generator safety
activities.prompt: A portable generator can never be dangerous.
activities.explanation: Even electricity from portable generators can be dangerous.

activities.title: Responding to danger
activities.prompt: A danger sign is visible. What should you do?
options: Experiment with the power supply
Ignore the warning sign
Use a portable generator
Handle electricity carefully
activities.explanation: Danger signs warn us that electricity must be handled carefully. Never experiment with the power supply.

activities.prompt: A factory loses its only wire path. Can electricity still reach it?
options: No, electricity reaches through wires.
Yes, it can travel through wall sockets.
Yes, it can travel through falling water.
Yes, it can become a danger sign.

The child confuses wall sockets with the wires that carry electricity.
why.Yes, it can travel through falling water: The child confuses falling water, a source, with electricity's route.
The child mistakes a danger sign for something that carries electricity.

activities.explanation: Electricity from different sources reaches homes and factories through wires.

lessons.title: Electric cell and battery

activities.prompt: How does a tiny cell make your torch shine?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Electric cells and batteries
activities.body: An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy. Its two ends are terminals: one positive and one negative. The metal cap is the positive terminal, while the flat metal disc is the negative terminal. A battery is two or more cells joined together. The positive terminal of one cell connects to the negative terminal of another. Joining more cells can provide energy for longer or give more energy.
keyPoints: An electric cell has positive and negative terminals.
The metal cap is positive, and the flat metal disc is negative.
Two or more joined cells form a battery.
activities.explanation: A battery joins cells to provide electrical energy to a circuit.

activities.title: Build a battery-powered circuit

tasks.say: Close the switch with one cell and one bulb.
tasks.then: The bulb lights because the circuit is closed.

tasks.say: Close the switch with three cells and one bulb.
tasks.then: More cells provide more energy to the circuit.

tasks.say: Open the switch with three cells and one bulb.
tasks.then: The bulb goes out because the circuit is open.

activities.takeaway: A battery is made from cells joined together, and its cells provide electrical energy when the circuit is closed.
activities.explanation: A battery is made from cells joined together, and its cells provide electrical energy when the circuit is closed.

activities.prompt: Two cells are ready. How should they be joined for a torch?
steps: Check signs because each cell has one positive and one negative terminal.
Join a positive terminal to a negative terminal because their signs differ.
They form a battery because two or more cells are joined.
The torch can then work for longer or receive more energy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the positive terminal
activities.prompt: Which part is the positive terminal of an electric cell?
options: Metal cap
Plastic cover
Cell terminal
Rubber strip
activities.explanation: The metal cap is the positive terminal. It carries the cell's positive sign.

activities.title: One of each sign
activities.prompt: Every electric cell has one positive terminal and one negative terminal.
activities.explanation: Every cell has two terminals. One is positive, and the other is negative.

activities.title: Name the terminal
activities.prompt: The flat metal disc is the ______ terminal.
activities.hint: Check which sign is marked on the flat metal disc.
activities.explanation: The flat metal disc carries the negative sign and is the negative terminal.

activities.title: Match each part
activities.prompt: Match each item on the left with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each cell has marked positive and negative terminals. Two or more joined cells are called a battery.

activities.title: Name the joined cells
activities.prompt: What are two or more cells joined together called?
options: Battery
Terminal
Circuit
Sign
activities.explanation: Two or more cells joined together are called a battery.

activities.title: One word, two uses
activities.prompt: Which statement about the word battery is correct?
options: It can mean a single cell.
It can only mean many cells.
It means the metal cap.
It means a negative terminal.
activities.explanation: The word battery may also be used for a single cell.

activities.title: More cells and energy
activities.prompt: Joining more cells leaves the energy for a circuit unchanged.
activities.explanation: Joining more cells provides energy for a circuit for longer or gives more energy.

activities.prompt: A working torch gets another cell. What energy change should be expected?
options: The torch can work for longer or receive more energy.
The torch must lose energy because one more cell was joined.
The torch will stop working because more cells were joined.
The new cell will have two positive terminals after joining.

why.The torch must lose energy because one m: This mistake thinks joining cells reduces the energy available.
why.The torch will stop working because more: This mistake thinks joined cells cannot provide energy to a circuit.
why.The new cell will have two positive term: This mistake forgets that every cell has only one positive terminal.

activities.explanation: Joining more cells provides energy for longer or gives more energy.

activities.prompt: Some mobile phones are powered by one cell. How can this work?
options: One cell can supply electrical energy without joining other cells.
One cell works only because batteries need two or more cells.
One cell works only when its positive and negative ends touch.
One cell cannot work because only a battery gives electrical energy.

why.One cell works only because batteries ne: This mistake mixes up one cell with a battery of joined cells.
why.One cell works only when its positive an: This mistake thinks a cell needs its own terminals joined together.
why.One cell cannot work because only a batt: This mistake thinks only a joined battery can give electrical energy.

activities.explanation: A cell is a portable energy source, and some phones use one.

lessons.title: Electric lamps

activities.prompt: What makes a lamp shine brightly inside a torch?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Parts of electric lamps
activities.body: An incandescent lamp has a thin wire fixed inside its glass bulb. The glowing wire is called the filament. Two thicker wires support it and form the terminals. The terminals do not touch. The filament gets hot and glows to give light. Many old torchlights use incandescent lamps. Many torches use Light Emitting Diode lamps, or LEDs. LEDs have no filaments. An LED's negative terminal joins its shorter wire.
keyPoints: The glowing thin wire is called the filament.
Two thicker wires support the filament and form the terminals.
Many torches use LEDs, which have no filaments.
activities.explanation: These are the main parts and uses of electric lamps.

activities.prompt: An old torchlight has a thin glowing wire. A new torch has differently shaped LEDs. Why are their lamps different?
steps: The old torchlight uses an incandescent lamp.
Its thin wire is the filament because it glows and gives light.
Many torches today use LEDs, which do not have filaments.
Thus, old lamps use filaments, while new torches can use shaped LEDs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which part is the filament in an incandescent lamp?
options: A thicker support wire
The glass bulb
The glowing thin wire
An LED's shorter wire
activities.explanation: The filament is the glowing thin wire inside an incandescent lamp.

activities.prompt: The thin glowing wire inside an incandescent lamp is its ______.
activities.hint: Find the name of the glowing wire.
activities.explanation: The glowing thin wire inside an incandescent lamp is its filament.

activities.prompt: Match each lamp part or fact to its name or result.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a lamp part with the matching fact.

activities.prompt: Why does an incandescent lamp give light?
options: The glass bulb gets hot and glows.
The terminals join and glow.
The filament gets hot and glows.
The LED filament gets hot.
activities.explanation: The filament gets hot and glows. This glowing filament gives light.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order that light appears.
items: Fix the thin wire inside the glass bulb.
Let two thicker wires support the filament.
The filament glows and gives light.
activities.explanation: The filament gets hot after it is supported. It then glows and gives light.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the two lamp types?
options: An incandescent lamp has no filament.
Both lamp types have filaments.
Neither lamp type has a filament.
An LED has no filament.
activities.explanation: LEDs have no filaments. Incandescent lamps have a glowing filament.

activities.prompt: A lamp maker joins the two thick wires together. Which rule for an incandescent lamp is now broken?
options: Its filament should stay thin inside the glass.
Its filament should become hot and glow.
Its two terminals should not touch each other.
Its thick wires should hold the filament in place.

why.Its filament should stay thin inside the: This mistakes the filament's thinness for the rule about touching terminals.
This mistakes the filament's light action for the rule about touching terminals.
why.Its thick wires should hold the filament: This mistakes the support role for the rule about touching terminals.

activities.explanation: The two thick wires form terminals, and those terminals do not touch.

activities.prompt: A torch contains two lamps, and each lamp has a different shape. What can the torch contain?
options: One incandescent filament inside each lamp.
One or more LEDs without any filaments.
One filament shared by both torch lamps.
Two touching terminals inside each lamp.

why.One incandescent filament inside each la: This wrongly treats the different-shaped torch lamps as incandescent lamps.
This invents a filament, but LEDs do not have filaments.
This confuses support wires with separate terminals inside a lamp.

activities.explanation: A torch may use one or more LEDs of different shapes.

activities.prompt: LED A has its short wire attached to the negative terminal. LED B has its long wire attached there. Which LED is correct?
options: Both LEDs are connected correctly.
LED B is connected correctly.
Neither LED is connected correctly.
LED A is connected correctly.

Only LED A follows the shorter-wire rule for the negative terminal.
The negative terminal uses the shorter wire, not the longer one.
LED A follows the rule, so this claim is wrong.

activities.explanation: An LED's negative terminal is attached to its shorter wire.

activities.prompt: A modern torch uses an LED lamp. An old torchlight uses an incandescent lamp. Which observation best shows their light-giving parts differ?
options: The old lamp has two thick wires; the new one does not.
The old lamp has shorter wires; the new one does not.
The old lamp has a glowing thin wire; the new one does not.
The old lamp has touching terminals; the new one does not.

why.The old lamp has two thick wires; the ne: Thick wires are supports, so this does not show the glowing part.
why.The old lamp has shorter wires; the new: Shorter wires belong to an LED's negative terminal, not its light-giving part.
why.The old lamp has touching terminals; the: Incandescent terminals do not touch, so this cannot describe the old lamp.

activities.explanation: The old filament glows, while the LED has no filament.

activities.prompt: A child claims every torch lamp has a thin filament that glows. Which lamp shows the claim is wrong?
options: A torch lamp with a glowing thin wire.
A torch lamp made with an LED.
An old torchlight with an incandescent lamp.
A torch lamp held by two thick wires.

A glowing thin wire is a filament, so it supports the claim.
why.An old torchlight with an incandescent l: An incandescent lamp does have a filament, so it supports the claim.
Two thick wires support a filament in an incandescent lamp.

activities.explanation: LEDs have no filaments, so this lamp breaks the claim.

lessons.title: Electrical circuits and LEDs

activities.prompt: How can we make an LED glow in a simple circuit?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How circuits make lamps glow
activities.body: An electrical circuit gives electric current a complete path. Current can flow when a lamp’s two terminals connect to a cell. The incandescent lamp then glows. Current travels from the positive terminal to the negative terminal. An LED works differently. Current passes through it in one direction only, so its terminals must connect correctly.
keyPoints: An electrical circuit gives current a complete path.
An incandescent lamp glows when both terminals connect to a cell.
An LED lets current pass in one direction only.
activities.explanation: A complete path lets current reach the lamp.

activities.title: Light the bulb

tasks.say: Close the switch.
tasks.then: With no gap, current can flow and the bulb lights.

tasks.say: Open it again.
tasks.when: closed == 0 and cells >= 1 and bulbs >= 2 or closed == 0 and cells == 2
tasks.then: A gap anywhere stops the current.

activities.takeaway: Current flows only around a closed path.
activities.explanation: Current flows only around a closed path.

activities.prompt: A lamp is joined to a cell, but it stays dark. What should we check first?
steps: A complete path is needed because current must pass through the circuit.
A broken filament stops current, so the lamp cannot glow.
Checking the filament is useful because a break would stop the current.
The dark lamp may have a broken filament, so check it first.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What makes an incandescent lamp glow?
options: Both terminals connect to a cell.
One terminal connects to a cell.
A filament connects to a cell.
A battery joins two cells.
activities.explanation: The lamp glows when both of its terminals connect to a cell.

activities.prompt: An electrical circuit gives electric current a complete path.
activities.explanation: A complete path allows current to flow through the circuit.

activities.prompt: An LED must be connected correctly. It must keep ______.
activities.hint: Think about what a correctly connected LED does.
activities.explanation: Correct LED connections allow current to pass in the allowed direction.

activities.prompt: Match each circuit idea with its correct meaning.
pairs: Two terminals connected to a cell
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a key idea from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the current’s path through the LED in order.
activities.explanation: Current moves from the cell’s positive terminal through the LED.

activities.prompt: If a filament breaks, the lamp can still glow because current continues.
activities.explanation: A broken filament stops the current and prevents the lamp from glowing.

activities.prompt: Why does a broken filament prevent a lamp from glowing?
options: It stops the current in the circuit.
It gives current another complete path.
It changes current to one direction only.
It joins the cell’s positive and negative terminals.
activities.explanation: The broken filament stops current, so the lamp cannot glow.

activities.prompt: An incandescent lamp is connected to a cell. Its two lamp terminals are swapped at the cell. What happens?
options: It still glows, because either lamp terminal can join the positive terminal.
It stops glowing, because current must enter one fixed lamp terminal.
It stops glowing, because swapping the wires breaks the complete path.
It glows dimmer, because current now moves through it less strongly.

why.It stops glowing, because current must e: This mistake assumes an incandescent lamp has one fixed positive terminal.
why.It stops glowing, because swapping the w: This mistake assumes swapping the wires breaks the complete circuit path.
why.It glows dimmer, because current now mov: This mistake assumes reversed current makes the lamp glow less strongly.

activities.explanation: Right: either lamp terminal can be joined to the positive terminal.

activities.prompt: A lamp is connected to a cell. Its filament breaks while the wires stay joined. What happens?
options: The lamp stops glowing, because the broken filament stops current.
The lamp keeps glowing, because the cell still sends current.
The lamp stops glowing, because its terminals lose their connections.
The lamp flashes once, then the broken filament repairs itself.

why.The lamp keeps glowing, because the cell: This mistake assumes current can pass through a broken filament.
why.The lamp stops glowing, because its term: This mistake thinks the lamp’s wires have become disconnected.
why.The lamp flashes once, then the broken f: This mistake imagines the filament can repair itself after breaking.

activities.explanation: Right: a broken filament stops current, so the lamp cannot glow.

lessons.title: Switches and circuit diagrams

activities.prompt: How can one tiny switch control a whole circuit?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How switches and symbols work
activities.body: In the ON position, the circuit is closed. In the OFF position, a gap stops current. A switch can go anywhere in a circuit. Circuit diagrams use symbols, which make circuits easier to draw and understand. A cell's long line marks its positive end. Its short line marks its negative end. An LED's triangle points along current flow. Its two arrows show that it gives out light.
keyPoints: ON gives a closed circuit.
OFF leaves a gap that stops current.
A switch can go anywhere in a circuit.
Symbols make circuit diagrams easier to draw and understand.
Long and short cell lines mark positive and negative ends.
An LED's arrows show that it gives out light.
activities.explanation: Switch positions and circuit symbols help us understand circuits.

activities.title: Change the circuit

tasks.say: Close the switch.
tasks.then: The bulb lights.

tasks.say: Add a second bulb.
tasks.then: Two bulbs share one cell, so they glow less.

tasks.say: Add another cell.
tasks.then: More cells make them brighter.

activities.takeaway: A switch opens or closes the path for current.
activities.explanation: A switch opens or closes the path for current.

activities.prompt: Where should a switch go to control a lamp in another room?
steps: The lamp should stop when the switch is OFF.
An OFF switch leaves a gap, so current cannot flow.
A switch can be placed anywhere, so its room does not matter.
The switch can therefore be elsewhere and still control the lamp.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Reading circuit symbols
activities.body: Electrical parts can be shown using symbols. The long line in a cell's symbol marks its positive end. The short line marks its negative end. In an LED's symbol, the triangle points along the direction of current flow. Its two arrows show that the LED gives out light. These symbol clues help you read a circuit diagram.
keyPoints: Electrical components can be shown using symbols.
A cell's long line marks its positive end.
A cell's short line marks its negative end.
An LED's triangle points along current flow.
An LED's two arrows show that it gives out light.
activities.explanation: Symbols make circuits easier to draw and understand.

activities.prompt: What happens when a switch is in the ON position?
options: The circuit becomes closed.
A gap breaks the circuit.
The switch leaves the circuit.
Current is blocked by a gap.
activities.explanation: The ON position has a closed circuit.

activities.prompt: A switch can be placed ______ in a circuit.
activities.hint: Choose the word that means at any place.
activities.explanation: The switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit.

activities.prompt: Match each circuit clue to what it shows.
activities.explanation: ON gives a closed circuit. OFF leaves a gap.

activities.prompt: What does a circuit diagram show?
options: An electrical circuit using symbols
An electrical circuit without symbols
An electrical circuit using pictures
An electrical circuit using numbers
activities.explanation: A circuit diagram shows an electrical circuit using symbols.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order when a switch is turned OFF.
items: The switch is in the OFF position.
activities.explanation: The gap prevents current from flowing.

activities.prompt: Which statement about an LED's symbol is correct?
options: Triangle: current direction; arrows: light output
Triangle: light output; arrows: current direction
Triangle: circuit gap; arrows: light output
Triangle: current direction; arrows: circuit gap
activities.explanation: The triangle points in the current direction. The two arrows show that the LED gives out light.

activities.prompt: A working circuit has an OFF switch. What happens to the lamp?
options: The lamp stays on because the circuit remains closed.
The lamp goes off because a gap stops current.
The lamp flashes because current passes through the gap.
The lamp stays dim because some current still passes.

why.The lamp stays on because the circuit re: This mistakes OFF for ON, which has a closed circuit.
why.The lamp flashes because current passes: This mistakes a gap for a path that lets current through.
why.The lamp stays dim because some current: This wrongly assumes some current can pass through a gap.

activities.explanation: This is right because OFF leaves a gap that prevents current.

activities.prompt: An ON switch sits beside a lamp, not a cell. What happens?
options: The circuit works because the switch can be anywhere.
The circuit fails because the switch must stay beside the cell.
The lamp stays off because a switch away from the cell leaves a gap.
The lamp changes because the switch has a different job there.

why.The circuit fails because the switch mus: This wrongly assumes a switch works only beside a cell.
why.The lamp stays off because a switch away: This wrongly assumes a gap remains when the switch is elsewhere.
why.The lamp changes because the switch has: This wrongly assumes moving a switch gives it a new job.

activities.explanation: This is right because a switch can be placed anywhere in the circuit.

activities.prompt: An LED triangle points backwards. How should a child fix it?
options: Point the triangle in the direction of current flow.
Point the triangle against the direction of current flow.
Replace the triangle with the cell's long positive line.
Replace the triangle with a gap from an OFF switch.

why.Point the triangle against the direction: This reverses the meaning of the triangle's pointing direction.
why.Replace the triangle with the cell's lon: This confuses the LED triangle with the cell's terminal symbol.
why.Replace the triangle with a gap from an: This confuses the LED triangle with the OFF switch symbol.

activities.explanation: This is right because the triangle points in the direction of current flow.

activities.prompt: A child says LED arrows show current. Which correction explains the symbol?
options: The arrows show light, while the triangle shows current.
The arrows show current, while the triangle shows light.
Both show light, because an LED gives out light.
Neither shows meaning, because symbols hide what they mean.

why.The arrows show current, while the trian: This confuses the arrows with the triangle and swaps their meanings.
why.Both show light, because an LED gives ou: This wrongly assumes the triangle also shows light.
why.Neither shows meaning, because symbols h: This wrongly assumes symbols hide what they mean.

activities.explanation: This is right because the arrows show light and the triangle shows current.

lessons.title: Conductors, insulators and types of current

activities.prompt: What makes some materials carry electricity while others stop it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Materials that carry or block current
activities.body: Electric current passes easily through some materials but not through others. A conductor is a material that allows electric current to flow easily. An insulator does not allow current to pass through. Metals, such as silver, copper and gold, are conductors. Plastic, rubber and ceramics are insulators. Wires use metals, while coverings use insulators.
keyPoints: Conductors allow electric current to flow easily.
Insulators do not allow current to pass through.
Metals make wires, while insulators cover them.
activities.explanation: These words help you describe which materials carry current and which block it.

activities.prompt: Why is a plastic-covered wire safer to touch than a bare wire?
steps: Metal wires allow electric current because metals are conductors.
The body conducts too, so touching a bare wire can cause shock.
Plastic covers wires because it does not allow current through.
This insulation protects people from electric shocks.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Safe coverings and types of current
activities.body: Insulators cover wires, plug tops and switches. These coverings protect people from electric shocks. The human body is a conductor of electricity. Electricity from batteries is called Direct Current. Electricity from power plants is called Alternating Current. These two kinds of current come from different sources.
keyPoints: Insulating coverings protect people from electric shocks.
The human body conducts electricity.
Batteries provide Direct Current, while power plants provide Alternating Current.
activities.explanation: Insulators keep people safer, and current sources have different current types.

activities.prompt: Which material allows electric current to flow easily?
options: Plastic
Copper
Rubber
Ceramics
activities.explanation: Copper is one of the best electrical conductors.

activities.prompt: Metals are used for making wires because they conduct electricity.
activities.explanation: Metals are conductors, so they are used for making wires.

activities.prompt: Materials that do not allow current to pass through are called ______.
activities.hint: This word begins with the letter i.
activities.explanation: Insulators stop current from passing through them.

activities.prompt: Electricity from power plants is called what?
options: Direct Current
Alternating Current
Conductor
Insulator
activities.explanation: Power plants provide Alternating Current.

activities.prompt: Which covering helps protect people from electric shocks at a switch?
options: Metal
Plastic
Copper
Silver
activities.explanation: Switch coverings use insulators, which protect people from electric shocks.

activities.prompt: A child touches a bare metal wire on a powered cable. What is most likely to happen?
options: The child may receive an electric shock.
The child is safe because the body cannot conduct current.
The child is safe because metal keeps current from flowing.
The child is safe because the wire is not covered.

why.The child is safe because the body canno: This mistake treats the human body as an insulator.
why.The child is safe because metal keeps cu: This mistake treats metal as an insulator.
why.The child is safe because the wire is no: This mistake assumes bare metal is safer than a covered wire.

activities.explanation: Both metal and the body conduct current, so a shock is possible.

activities.prompt: A bulb is joined in a battery circuit. Which test best checks whether a material allows current?
options: Replace a wire gap with the material, then watch the bulb.
Touch the material to one battery end and watch the bulb.
Place the material near the battery and watch the bulb.
Wrap the material around the battery and watch the bulb.

why.Touch the material to one battery end an: One connection does not test the material in the full path.
why.Place the material near the battery and: The material stays outside the path, so current cannot pass through it.
why.Wrap the material around the battery and: A battery connection alone does not test the material between wire ends.

activities.explanation: The material is placed in the path where current can flow.

activities.prompt: A switch has metal inside and plastic outside. Why does the switch need both materials?
options: Metal carries current, while plastic blocks it and protects people.
Metal blocks current, while plastic carries it to the switch.
Both materials carry current, so the switch works safely.
Both materials block current, so the switch needs no wires.

why.Metal blocks current, while plastic carr: This mistake swaps the jobs of conductors and insulators.
why.Both materials carry current, so the swi: This mistake assumes plastic also carries current.
why.Both materials block current, so the swi: This mistake treats the metal part as an insulator.

activities.explanation: Metal conducts current, while plastic insulates and protects people.

activities.prompt: A child holds a metal tool touching a live wire. Why might the child receive an electric shock?
options: Current can pass through the metal and the body.
The body blocks current, so the tool cannot shock.
The metal stops current before it reaches the hand.
Current passes through the tool but not the body.

why.The body blocks current, so the tool can: This mistake treats the human body as an insulator.
why.The metal stops current before it reache: This mistake assumes metal blocks electric current.
why.Current passes through the tool but not: This mistake allows current through metal but blocks it through the body.

activities.explanation: Metal and the body both conduct current, so current can reach the child.

activities.prompt: Someone says a metal cover can protect a plug top from shocks. Why is this claim unsafe?
options: Metal conducts current, so it cannot safely cover a plug.
Metal blocks current, so it can safely cover a plug.
Metal protects better than plastic, so it can cover a plug.
Metal only carries battery current, so it can cover a plug.

why.Metal blocks current, so it can safely c: This mistake treats metal as an insulator.
why.Metal protects better than plastic, so i: This mistake assumes metal insulates better than plastic.
why.Metal only carries battery current, so i: This mistake thinks metal carries only battery current.

activities.explanation: Metal conducts current, while plug covers need insulating plastic.
