activities.context: During a school visit to a hydroelectric power house, a student sees falling water being used to generate electricity. The electricity reaches homes and factories through wires. The student also carries a portable generator for learning about electricity. Near the power house, a danger sign warns that electricity must be handled carefully. The student wonders whether the portable generator is safe and plans an experiment after returning home.
activities.prompt: After returning home, what should the student do before conducting the planned experiment?
options: Use batteries or cells for the experiment.
Connect the portable generator to wall sockets at home.
Test the portable generator using the school power supply.
Begin the generator experiment without reading any danger signs.

why.Connect the portable generator to wall s: Wrong: involves using the home power supply.
why.Test the portable generator using the sc: Wrong: power supplies must not be used.
why.Begin the generator experiment without r: Wrong: ignores the warning about careful handling.

activities.explanation: Correct: batteries or cells are permitted.

activities.context: During a school visit to a hydroelectric power house, a student sees falling water being used to generate electricity. The electricity reaches homes and factories through wires. The student also carries a portable generator for learning about electricity. Near the power house, a danger sign warns that electricity must be handled carefully. The student wonders whether the portable generator is safe and plans an experiment after returning home.
activities.prompt: If the student replaces the portable generator with batteries or cells for the experiment, what is true?
options: The experiment follows the rule for permitted experiments.
The student must use the home power supply instead.
The danger sign no longer has any meaning.
The portable generator becomes safer than batteries or cells.

why.The student must use the home power supp: Wrong: home power supplies are not allowed.
why.The danger sign no longer has any meanin: Wrong: the warning still concerns electricity.
why.The portable generator becomes safer tha: Wrong: the generator can still be dangerous.

activities.explanation: Correct: batteries or cells are allowed.

activities.prompt: Why must experiments at home or school use batteries or cells rather than the power supply?
activities.answer: Electricity from portable generators can also be dangerous, so using one at home would not make the experiment safe. Danger signs remind us to handle electricity carefully. Batteries or cells are the only sources allowed for experiments, so they are the appropriate choice for learning safely.
points: Power supplies must not be used for experiments.
Portable generators can also be dangerous.
Danger signs warn us to handle electricity carefully.
Only batteries or cells are allowed.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A torch has stopped working. A student opens it and finds two cells joined inside. The positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the other, so the cells form a battery. The student checks the metal caps and flat metal discs. The caps are marked positive, while the discs are marked negative. The student wonders whether adding another cell would make the torch work for longer.
activities.prompt: If the student joins another cell correctly, what result should the student expect?
options: The joined cells could give the circuit more energy or keep it supplied for longer.
The torch would have less energy because the new cell takes energy away from the existing cells.
Only the newly added cell would supply energy, and the original cells would stop working.
The torch's energy would not change because joining more cells makes no difference.

why.The torch would have less energy because: Joining more cells provides more energy.
why.Only the newly added cell would supply e: It can also provide energy to the circuit for longer.
why.The torch's energy would not change beca: The other choices suggest that extra cells reduce or do not affect the energy.

activities.explanation: The new cell is joined to the existing cells.

activities.context: A torch has stopped working. A student opens it and finds two cells joined inside. The positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the other, so the cells form a battery. The student checks the metal caps and flat metal discs. The caps are marked positive, while the discs are marked negative. The student wonders whether adding another cell would make the torch work for longer.
activities.prompt: If the student used only one of the cells, which statement would be correct?
options: The single cell could still be called a battery, and some mobile phones are powered by a single cell.
The single cell could not be called a battery because a battery must have at least two cells.
The single cell could power only a torch and could never power a mobile phone.
The single cell would no longer be a portable source of electrical energy.

why.The single cell could not be called a ba: Some mobile phones are powered by one cell.
why.The single cell could power only a torch: A cell remains a portable source of electrical energy.
why.The single cell would no longer be a por: The other choices confuse the meaning of battery or deny facts about cells.

activities.explanation: The word battery may also be used for a single cell.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an electric cell and a battery.
activities.answer: An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy and has one positive terminal and one negative terminal. A battery is made when two or more cells are joined together. However, the word battery may also be used for one cell.
points: A cell is a portable source of electrical energy.
A cell has one positive and one negative terminal.
A battery can mean two or more joined cells.
The word battery may also refer to a single cell.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Riya’s old torchlight uses an incandescent lamp. Inside its glass bulb, a thin wire is fixed in place, while two thicker wires support it. The thin wire produces light after becoming hot. The thick wires form the lamp’s terminals, and they do not touch each other. At the shop, Riya sees a torch that uses LEDs. One LED on display has a shorter wire.
activities.prompt: Riya switches on the old torchlight. Why does its lamp give light?
options: Its filament gets hot and glows.
Its two thicker support wires get hot and glow.
Its glass bulb gets hot and glows.
Its terminals touch each other and glow.

why.Its two thicker support wires get hot an: The thicker wires support the filament rather than provide the light.
The glass bulb contains the lamp’s parts but does not provide the light.
The two terminals do not touch each other.

activities.explanation: The filament is the thin wire that becomes hot and glows.

activities.context: Riya’s old torchlight uses an incandescent lamp. Inside its glass bulb, a thin wire is fixed in place, while two thicker wires support it. The thin wire produces light after becoming hot. The thick wires form the lamp’s terminals, and they do not touch each other. At the shop, Riya sees a torch that uses LEDs. One LED on display has a shorter wire.
activities.prompt: The shop worker must connect the negative terminal of the LED. Which connection should the worker choose?
options: Connect it to the shorter wire of the LED.
Connect it to the filament of the LED.
Connect it to the glass bulb of the LED.
Connect it to a thicker supporting wire of the LED.

An LED does not have a filament.
The negative terminal is not attached to the glass bulb.
why.Connect it to a thicker supporting wire: The thicker supporting wires belong to an incandescent lamp.

activities.explanation: The negative terminal of an LED is attached to its shorter wire.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an incandescent lamp and an LED lamp.
activities.answer: An incandescent lamp contains a thin wire called a filament, held by two thicker wires. Its filament becomes hot and glows to provide light. An LED lamp does not have a filament. Therefore, an LED does not provide light by heating and glowing a filament like an incandescent lamp.
points: An incandescent lamp has a thin filament.
Two thicker wires support the filament.
The filament becomes hot and glows.
LEDs do not have filaments.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner makes a circuit with a cell and an incandescent lamp. The LED then replaces the lamp, joining the LED’s positive terminal to the cell’s positive terminal and the LED’s negative terminal to the cell’s negative terminal. The LED glows. Later, the learner looks at a battery with a metal strip joining the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next. The learner wonders whether the LED would still glow if these connections were reversed.
activities.prompt: If the learner reverses both LED connections, what would happen next?
options: It would not glow because current could not pass through the LED in the reversed direction.
It would keep glowing because reversing the connection still gives current a complete path.
It would glow with the same result because either LED terminal can be joined to the positive terminal.
It would continue to glow because the circuit is complete.

why.It would keep glowing because reversing: A complete path does not make current direction irrelevant.
why.It would glow with the same result becau: The either-terminal rule applies to the lamp, not the LED.
why.It would continue to glow because the ci: The LED also needs the correct terminal orientation.

activities.explanation: Correct: reversed current cannot pass through the LED.

activities.context: A learner makes a circuit with a cell and an incandescent lamp. The LED then replaces the lamp, joining the LED’s positive terminal to the cell’s positive terminal and the LED’s negative terminal to the cell’s negative terminal. The LED glows. Later, the learner looks at a battery with a metal strip joining the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next. The learner wonders whether the LED would still glow if these connections were reversed.
activities.prompt: When the learner checks the metal strip in the battery, which observation matches its role?
options: It links the first cell’s positive terminal with the next cell’s negative terminal.
It links the first cell’s negative terminal with the next cell’s positive terminal.
It links the first cell’s positive terminal with the next cell’s positive terminal.
It links the first cell’s negative terminal with the next cell’s negative terminal.

why.It links the first cell’s negative termi: This reverses the stated positive-to-negative connection.
why.It links the first cell’s positive termi: The described strip does not join positive to positive.
why.It links the first cell’s negative termi: The described strip does not join negative to negative.

activities.explanation: Correct: the strip joins positive to the next negative.

activities.prompt: Explain why reversing the LED’s connections would stop it glowing.
activities.answer: Reversing the LED’s connections would stop it glowing. Current passes through an LED in one direction only. Its positive terminal must join the cell’s positive terminal, and its negative terminal must join the cell’s negative terminal. The reversed arrangement therefore does not allow current through the LED.
points: The LED would not glow.
Current passes through an LED in one direction only.
The LED’s positive terminal must join the cell’s positive terminal.
The LED’s negative terminal must join the cell’s negative terminal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Riya draws a circuit diagram for a circuit containing a cell, a switch, and an LED. She uses symbols for each component. The switch is placed near the middle of the circuit. Its symbol is shown in the ON position, so the circuit is closed. The LED's triangle points in the direction of current flow, and the two arrows show that it gives out light.
activities.prompt: Riya changes the switch from ON to OFF. What will happen next?
options: The LED will no longer give out light.
Current will continue to flow through the gap.
The LED will continue to give out light.
The switch will still make the circuit closed.

why.Current will continue to flow through th: A gap prevents current from flowing.
Without current flowing, the LED does not give out light.
why.The switch will still make the circuit c: The OFF position does not have a closed circuit.

activities.explanation: The OFF position creates a gap, so current cannot flow.

activities.context: Riya draws a circuit diagram for a circuit containing a cell, a switch, and an LED. She uses symbols for each component. The switch is placed near the middle of the circuit. Its symbol is shown in the ON position, so the circuit is closed. The LED's triangle points in the direction of current flow, and the two arrows show that it gives out light.
activities.prompt: Riya notices that the triangle in the LED's symbol faces away from the direction of current flow. How should she correct the symbol?
options: Face the triangle toward the direction in which current flows.
Face the triangle in the opposite direction.
Replace the triangle with the long line used in a cell's symbol.
Use the two arrows in place of the triangle.

why.Face the triangle in the opposite direct: Pointing it the opposite way would contradict the rule for the symbol.
why.Replace the triangle with the long line: The long line shows a cell's positive terminal, not the LED's current direction.
why.Use the two arrows in place of the trian: The two arrows show that the LED gives out light, while the triangle shows current direction.

activities.explanation: The triangle in an LED's symbol points in the direction of current flow.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a switch in the ON position and a switch in the OFF position.
activities.answer: In the ON position, the switch has a closed circuit, so current can flow. In the OFF position, there is a gap in the circuit, so current cannot flow.
points: ON means a closed circuit.
Current can flow in a closed circuit.
OFF means there is a gap.
A gap prevents current from flowing.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A person was replacing the covering around a copper wire and checking a plug top and switch. The plastic and rubber coverings stopped electricity from passing through and protected the person from electric shocks. The copper wire carried electricity because copper is a conductor. Later, the person tested a device powered by a battery and compared it with a system powered by a power plant.
activities.prompt: If the person removed the plastic covering before checking the switch, what would be the likely result?
options: The person would be more likely to receive an electric shock.
The copper wire would carry electric current less easily.
The plastic covering would allow electric current to pass through it.
The person would be protected better than before.

why.The copper wire would carry electric cur: Removing a covering does not change copper into a poor conductor.
why.The plastic covering would allow electri: Plastic remains an insulator even when it is removed.
why.The person would be protected better tha: Removing the insulating covering reduces protection.

activities.explanation: Removing the covering removes protection against shocks.

activities.context: A person was replacing the covering around a copper wire and checking a plug top and switch. The plastic and rubber coverings stopped electricity from passing through and protected the person from electric shocks. The copper wire carried electricity because copper is a conductor. Later, the person tested a device powered by a battery and compared it with a system powered by a power plant.
activities.prompt: If the battery-powered system were replaced by a system powered by a power plant, what change would occur in the type of electricity?
options: It would change from Direct Current to Alternating Current.
It would change from Alternating Current to Direct Current.
It would remain Direct Current because the copper wire carries electricity.
It would remain Alternating Current because the power plant supplies electricity.

why.It would remain Direct Current because t: The copper wire does not determine the type of electricity.
why.It would remain Alternating Current beca: The source changes, so the type of electricity also changes.

activities.explanation: Battery electricity is Direct Current.

activities.prompt: Explain why metals are used for making wires and why plastic, rubber and ceramics are used around wires, plug tops and switches.
activities.answer: Metals are used for making wires because they are conductors and allow electric current to flow easily. Plastic, rubber and ceramics are insulators, so they are used to cover wires, plug tops and switches. These coverings do not allow current to pass through and help protect people from electric shocks.
points: Metals allow electric current to flow easily.
Metals are therefore used for making wires.
Plastic, rubber and ceramics are insulators.
Insulating coverings help protect people from electric shocks.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Electricity: Circuits and Their Components

activities.prompt: For experiments, we should use only batteries or cells.
activities.explanation: Batteries and cells are safe sources for the experiments in your lesson.

activities.prompt: Match each part to its correct name or function.
pairs: Thin wire inside a glass bulb
activities.explanation: Each part has a clear role in a cell or an incandescent lamp.

activities.prompt: How must an LED be joined so that it receives current?
options: Both terminals to the positive terminal
Both terminals to the negative terminal
Positive to positive, negative to negative
Positive to negative, negative to positive
activities.explanation: Current passes through an LED in one direction only. Its terminals must be joined correctly.

activities.prompt: Materials that allow electric current to flow easily are called ______.
activities.hint: Metals belong to this group.
activities.explanation: Conductors let current pass easily. Metals are conductors and are used for making wires.

activities.prompt: The OFF position of a switch has a gap that prevents current from flowing.
activities.explanation: The gap in the OFF position breaks the path for current.

activities.prompt: What does the long line in a cell's symbol show?
options: Its negative terminal
Its positive terminal
Its filament
Its switch position
activities.explanation: The long line shows the positive terminal. The short line shows the negative terminal.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order to show how an incandescent lamp glows.
items: Connect the lamp's terminals to a cell
The filament gets hot and glows
activities.explanation: Connecting the lamp forms a circuit. Current then passes through it and heats the filament.

activities.prompt: A broken ______ stops the current and prevents an incandescent lamp from glowing.
activities.hint: It is the glowing thin wire inside the glass bulb.
activities.explanation: The filament is the thin wire inside the lamp. If it breaks, current cannot pass through it.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct item.
pairs: The two arrows in an LED's symbol
activities.explanation: These pairs connect safety, circuit symbols and lamp parts with their correct meanings.

chapters.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals
chapters.summary: In this chapter: metals at the ironsmith’s workshop; malleability, ductility and sonority; metals as heat and electricity conductors; how iron rusts.

lessons.title: Metals at the Ironsmith’s Workshop

activities.prompt: How does an ironsmith turn iron into everyday tools?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Sudarshan Shapes Metal
activities.body: Sudarshan makes items like pans and buckets. He uses iron metal for these items. Wood prepares handles when needed. Coal heats iron inside a furnace. A furnace is a place where metal is heated. The hot iron becomes red hot. The ironsmith beats it with a hammer to shape an axe. Copper, aluminium and iron are metals. They are lustrous and hard. Lustrous means shiny.
keyPoints: Iron is used to make pans and buckets.
Coal heats iron inside a furnace.
The ironsmith beats red-hot iron with a hammer.
activities.explanation: Metals are heated, beaten and shaped into useful objects.

activities.prompt: Sudarshan is making an axe from iron. Why must he heat and beat the iron?
steps: Coal heats the iron in the furnace, because coal provides the heat.
The iron turns red hot because the furnace heats it.
The ironsmith beats the hot iron because hammering gives it a shape.
The beaten iron becomes an axe, so both heating and beating are needed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sudarshan’s Useful Items
activities.prompt: Which metal does Sudarshan use to make pans and buckets?
options: Wood
Iron
Coal
Copper
activities.explanation: Sudarshan uses iron metal to make everyday items like pans and buckets.

activities.title: The Fuel for the Furnace
activities.prompt: ______ is used in furnaces to heat iron.
activities.hint: This material helps heat the iron.
activities.explanation: Coal is used in furnaces to heat iron before it is beaten.

activities.title: Match Each Material
activities.prompt: Match each material with its use in the workshop.
pairs: Used to make pans and buckets
Used in furnaces to heat iron
activities.explanation: Each material has a special job in making the workshop’s items.

activities.title: When Iron Turns Red Hot
activities.prompt: When does the iron block become red hot?
options: Before it enters the furnace
After a handle is attached
When it is heated
After the axe is finished
activities.explanation: The iron block becomes red hot when it is heated.

activities.title: The Ironsmith’s Steps
activities.prompt: Put the ironsmith’s steps in the correct order.
items: Coal heats iron in a furnace
The ironsmith beats the iron with a hammer
The iron takes the shape of an axe
activities.explanation: The iron is heated first. Then it is beaten until it becomes an axe.

activities.title: Shiny and Hard Metals
activities.prompt: Which set contains only metals that are lustrous and hard?
options: Copper, aluminium and iron
Coal, sulfur and wood
Sodium and potassium
activities.explanation: Copper, aluminium and iron are lustrous and hard. The other materials are softer.

activities.prompt: An iron block is heated in Sudarshan's coal furnace. What happens next if he is making an axe?
options: He beats the red-hot iron to give it shape.
He beats the cold iron to give it shape.
He beats the hot coal to give it shape.
He beats the hot wood to give it shape.

Heating makes the iron red hot before the beating.
Coal heats the iron, but coal is not beaten into an axe.
Wood is used for handles, while iron is used for the axe.

activities.explanation: The hot iron is beaten so it takes the shape of an axe.

activities.prompt: A child says heating alone gives iron its axe shape. What observation shows that the claim misses a step?
options: The iron block turns red hot in the furnace.
The coal is used to heat the iron block.
The hot iron is beaten with a hammer.
The wooden handle is prepared for the axe.

why.The iron block turns red hot in the furn: Red heat shows heating, but it does not show shaping.
Coal provides heat, but it does not show the shaping step.
why.The wooden handle is prepared for the ax: Preparing a handle does not shape the iron into an axe.

activities.explanation: Beating the hot iron gives it the shape of an axe.

activities.prompt: A child needs a hard, lustrous metal for an item. Which pair both fit?
options: Copper and aluminium
Coal and sulfur
Wood and sodium
Mercury and coal

why.Coal and sulfur: Coal and sulfur are not as hard as metals.
why.Wood and sodium: Wood is not as hard as metals, and sodium is soft.
why.Mercury and coal: Mercury is liquid, and coal is not as hard as metals.

activities.explanation: Copper and aluminium are both lustrous and hard.

activities.prompt: Which prediction is correct if a knife touches sodium and potassium?
options: Both can be cut because both are soft.
Both can be cut because both are lustrous.
Neither can be cut because both are hard.
Only sodium can be cut because potassium is hard.

why.Both can be cut because both are lustrou: Lustre does not show that a material can be cut.
why.Neither can be cut because both are hard: This wrongly treats sodium and potassium as hard.
why.Only sodium can be cut because potassium: This wrongly treats potassium as hard, though both are soft.

activities.explanation: Sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife.

activities.prompt: Coal becomes the axe in the furnace. Why is this wrong?
options: Coal heats the iron; the iron is beaten into shape.
Coal is beaten with a hammer to make the axe.
Coal is used to prepare the wooden axe handle.
Coal becomes red hot and is shaped into the axe.

why.Coal is beaten with a hammer to make the: The ironsmith beats the iron, not coal, with a hammer.
why.Coal is used to prepare the wooden axe h: Wood is used for handles, while coal is used for heat.
why.Coal becomes red hot and is shaped into: Red heat belongs to the heated iron, not the coal.

activities.explanation: Coal heats the iron, and the beaten iron becomes the axe.

lessons.sceneAlt: A blacksmith in period clothing hammers a piece of hot iron.
lessons.sceneCaption: A blacksmith in period clothing hammers a piece of hot iron.

lessons.title: Malleability, Ductility and Sonority

activities.prompt: What makes metals flatten, stretch into wires, and ring when struck?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Properties of Metals
activities.body: Metals can show different properties. Malleability is the ability to be beaten into thin sheets. Ductility is the ability to be drawn into wires. Sonority means making a ringing sound. A metal spoon and coin ring, while coal and wood make dull sounds. Brittle materials break into pieces when hammered. Wood is neither malleable nor brittle.
keyPoints: Malleability means being beaten into thin sheets.
Ductility means being drawn into wires.
Sonority means making a ringing sound.
activities.explanation: These properties describe how materials change or sound.

activities.prompt: A child hammers an iron nail and coal. What will happen?
steps: An iron nail becomes flat when it is beaten.
This shows malleability because the nail becomes a thin sheet.
Coal does not flatten because it cannot become a thin sheet.
So the nail is malleable, but coal is not.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is an example of a metal sheet?
options: Thin silver foil
An iron nail
A lump of coal
A wooden block
activities.explanation: Thin silver foil is one of the metal sheet examples.

activities.prompt: The ability to be beaten into thin sheets is called ______.
activities.hint: This property is used when metal is beaten flat.
activities.explanation: This property is called malleability.

activities.prompt: Match each material with what happens when it is beaten.
activities.explanation: Iron nails and aluminium flatten, but coal and sulfur do not.

activities.prompt: Which description fits a brittle material?
options: It breaks into pieces when hammered.
It becomes a thin sheet when beaten.
It can be drawn into a wire.
It produces a ringing sound.
activities.explanation: A brittle material breaks into pieces when hammered.

activities.prompt: Put these stages in order for the gold wire.
activities.explanation: One gram of gold can become a wire two kilometres long.

activities.prompt: Which property is shown when gold becomes a long, thin wire?
options: Ductility
Malleability
Brittleness
Sonority
activities.explanation: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into wires.

activities.prompt: A child hammers an iron nail and a piece of coal. What should happen?
options: The nail flattens, but the coal does not.
The coal flattens, but the iron nail does not.
Both the iron nail and coal become flat.
Neither the iron nail nor coal becomes flat.

why.The coal flattens, but the iron nail doe: This reverses the known results for iron and coal.
This wrongly assumes that coal can become a sheet.
why.Neither the iron nail nor coal becomes f: This wrongly assumes that iron cannot become flat.

activities.explanation: Iron nails become flat, while coal does not become flat.

activities.prompt: A child taps two spoons, one metal and one wood. What happens?
options: The wooden spoon rings, but the metal spoon sounds dull.
Both spoons make a dull, quiet sound.
Both spoons make a clear, ringing sound.
The metal spoon rings, but the wooden spoon sounds dull.

why.The wooden spoon rings, but the metal sp: This reverses the sounds made by metal and wood.
This wrongly assumes that metal makes a dull sound.
This wrongly assumes that wood makes a ringing sound.

activities.explanation: A metal spoon rings, while wood produces a dull sound.

activities.prompt: Gold, silver, coal, and sulfur are beaten. Which pair becomes flat?
options: Coal and sulfur
Gold and silver
Gold and coal
Silver and sulfur

why.Coal and sulfur: Coal and sulfur do not become flat when beaten.
why.Gold and coal: This wrongly assumes that coal can become a thin sheet.
why.Silver and sulfur: This wrongly assumes that sulfur can become a thin sheet.

activities.explanation: Gold and silver are the most malleable metals.

activities.prompt: Everything flattens when beaten. Which result shows this claim is wrong?
options: An iron nail becomes flat when beaten.
A metal spoon makes a ringing sound.
Coal does not become flat when beaten.
Gold and silver become flat when beaten.

This supports the claim rather than showing that it is wrong.
This tests sound, not the claim about flattening.
This supports the claim rather than showing that it is wrong.

activities.explanation: Coal is a counterexample because it does not become flat.

lessons.sceneAlt: Three pieces of aluminium foil are placed on a sheet of paper.
lessons.sceneCaption: Thin aluminium foil demonstrates the malleability of metals.

sceneCredit.text: A sample of aluminium foil on a piece of paper by Vitaium, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Vitaium

lessons.title: Metals as Heat and Electricity Conductors

activities.prompt: Why does a metal spoon feel warmer than a wooden spoon?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Heat and Electricity Conductors
activities.body: Heat can travel through some materials. The metal spoon becomes hotter than the wooden spoon. Heat travels through the metal spoon and makes it hotter. Wood transfers heat poorly. Materials that transfer heat are called conductors. Metals are good conductors, while wood is a poor conductor. Aluminium, iron and copper make an electric bulb glow. Good electrical conductors allow electricity to flow easily.
keyPoints: Metals are good conductors of heat.
Wood is a poor conductor of heat.
Good electrical conductors allow electricity to flow easily.
activities.explanation: Metals transfer heat well, and good electrical conductors let electricity flow easily.

activities.prompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are placed in warm food. What will happen, and why?
steps: Heat travels through the metal spoon because metals conduct heat well.
Wood transfers heat poorly, so the wooden spoon gets less heat.
Therefore, the metal spoon becomes hotter than the wooden spoon.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Hotter Spoon
activities.prompt: Which spoon becomes hotter in the lesson?
options: The metal spoon
The wooden spoon
Both spoons equally
Neither spoon
activities.explanation: Heat travels through the metal spoon and makes it hotter.

activities.title: Heat Transfer Word
activities.prompt: Materials that transfer heat are called ______.
activities.hint: These materials carry heat from one point to another.
activities.explanation: Materials that transfer heat are called conductors.

activities.title: Meaning of Conduction
activities.prompt: Materials that transfer heat are called conductors.
activities.explanation: This is the lesson's meaning of a heat conductor.

activities.title: Cooking Materials
activities.prompt: Match each item with what the lesson says.
activities.explanation: Metals conduct heat, so they are useful for cooking vessels.

activities.title: Metals in an Electric Bulb
activities.prompt: Which three materials make an electric bulb glow?
options: Aluminium, iron and copper
Wood, plastic and rubber
Aluminium, wood and plastic
Iron, copper and rubber
activities.explanation: Aluminium, iron and copper make an electric bulb glow.

activities.title: Heat and Electricity Together
activities.prompt: A cooking vessel has a handle that does not conduct heat. Another metal makes a bulb glow. Which explanation fits?
options: The handle reduces heat transfer, and the metal carries electricity.
The handle conducts heat, and the metal stops electricity.
Both parts transfer heat poorly, and the bulb stays dark.
The handle carries electricity, and the metal transfers no heat.
activities.explanation: A non-conducting handle reduces heat transfer, while a metal carries electricity.

activities.prompt: A cooking vessel has a metal body and a wooden handle. Why use this design?
options: The metal body passes heat, while the wooden handle slows it.
The wooden body passes heat, while the metal handle slows it.
The metal body blocks heat, while the wooden handle passes it.
Both parts pass heat at the same speed to the cook.

why.The wooden body passes heat, while the m: This swaps the heat-transfer roles of metal and wood.
why.The metal body blocks heat, while the wo: This wrongly treats metal as blocking heat and wood as conducting it.
why.Both parts pass heat at the same speed t: It ignores that wood transfers heat poorly.

activities.explanation: Metal conducts heat well, while wood is a poor conductor.

activities.prompt: A hot cooking vessel needs a handle. Which material is most suitable?
options: Wood
Copper
Iron
Aluminium

why.Copper: Copper is a metal, so it conducts heat well.
why.Iron: Iron is a metal, so it conducts heat well.
why.Aluminium: Aluminium is a metal, so it conducts heat well.

activities.explanation: Wood is a poor heat conductor, so the handle stays cooler.

activities.prompt: The tested bulb-glow materials were all metals. A student says every metal must make a bulb glow. Is the student right?
options: The test does not show that every metal makes a bulb glow.
The test shows that every metal must make a bulb glow.
The test shows that only wood can make a bulb glow.
The test shows that metals never help electricity flow.

why.The test shows that every metal must mak: This turns a one-way test result into a claim about every metal.
why.The test shows that only wood can make a: This swaps metals for wood, which the facts do not name.
why.The test shows that metals never help el: Aluminium, iron, and copper make bulbs glow, so this is opposite.

activities.explanation: The test says glow materials are metals, not that every metal glows.

lessons.sceneCaption: A captain demonstrates heat conduction using a heat-pipe experiment for elementary students.

lessons.title: How Iron Rusts

activities.prompt: What does iron look like after spending time outdoors?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Iron and Rust
activities.body: Iron objects can develop brown deposits when they are left in the open. The brown deposit is called rust, and its formation is called rusting. Dry air alone does not cause rust. Both water and air are needed, so moist air is responsible for rust forming. Painting, oiling and greasing can prevent iron from rusting. Galvanisation protects iron with a layer of zinc metal.
keyPoints: Rust is a brown deposit on iron.
Water and air are needed for rusting.
Paint, oil, grease and zinc can protect iron.
activities.explanation: You have learned the causes of rust and ways to protect iron.

activities.prompt: Why does an iron key rust outside in moist air, but not in dry air?
steps: Iron needs both water and air because brown deposits need both.
Moist air provides water, so it helps rusting begin.
The brown deposit is called rust, and its formation is rusting.
Therefore, the key rusts in moist air, while dry air alone cannot rust it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the brown deposit on iron called?
options: Rust
Zinc
Paint
Corrosion
activities.explanation: Rust is the brown deposit that forms on iron. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Iron develops brown deposits in dry air alone.
activities.explanation: Dry air alone does not make iron develop brown deposits. Water is also needed.

activities.prompt: Both ______ and air are needed for brown deposits to develop on iron.
activities.hint: Think about the moisture in moist air.
activities.explanation: Water and air are both needed for rusting.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: Gradual deterioration of a metal surface
Protection with a layer of zinc metal
activities.explanation: You matched each metal term with its correct meaning.

activities.prompt: What does moist air do to iron?
options: Helps rust form
Stops rust forming
Keeps iron dry
Makes iron green
activities.explanation: Moist air is responsible for brown deposits forming on iron. Great choice!

activities.prompt: Galvanisation protects iron with a layer of zinc metal.
activities.explanation: Correct. Galvanisation uses a layer of zinc metal to protect iron.

activities.prompt: What is corrosion?
options: Metal surface gradually worsening
Brown deposit on iron
Layer of zinc metal
Coating on copper
activities.explanation: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal surface. You found the exact meaning.

activities.prompt: Put these stages in the order described for rusting.
items: Iron is left in the open
The brown deposit is called rust
activities.explanation: Iron needs water and air, and moist air helps brown deposits form. The deposit is called rust.

activities.prompt: An iron nail is left outside in moist air. What will most likely happen?
options: The nail will develop a brown deposit.
The nail will stay unchanged in dry air.
The nail will develop a green coating.
The nail will develop a black coating.

Dry air is not the situation described outside.
This confuses iron rust with copper's green coating.
This confuses iron rust with silver's black coating.

activities.explanation: The nail has water and air, so rust can form.

activities.prompt: Which pair best tests whether water is needed for rusting?
options: Dry air and moist air
Dry air and oily metal
Moist air and painted metal
Greased metal and wet metal

why.Dry air and oily metal: This changes both moisture and the oil covering.
why.Moist air and painted metal: This changes both moisture and the paint covering.
why.Greased metal and wet metal: This changes both the grease covering and the water.

activities.explanation: This changes only moisture while both samples still have air.

lessons.sceneAlt: A rusted cast-iron gear assembly once used to operate gates at Garga Dam in Jharkhand, India.
lessons.sceneCaption: A rusted gear assembly at Garga Dam shows how exposed iron develops brown rust deposits.

funFacts: The Iron Pillar of Delhi was made in the time of Chandragupta II more than 1600 years ago. It is about 8 metres high and weighs more than 6000 kilograms.

lessons.title: Other Metals and Non-metals in Air and Water

activities.prompt: What happens when metals and non-metals meet air and water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Metals and Non-metals in Air and Water
activities.body: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame. It becomes magnesium oxide when it reacts with oxygen in air. This oxide turns red litmus paper blue, so its solution is basic. Sodium is stored in kerosene because it reacts with oxygen and water. Sulfur forms sulfur dioxide in air, which makes sulfurous acid in water. Non-metal oxides are acidic, and non-metals are not malleable, ductile or sonorous.
keyPoints: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame.
Magnesium oxide has a basic solution.
Sulfur dioxide makes sulfurous acid in water.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how metals and non-metals react with air and water.

activities.prompt: Magnesium burns in air. Its white powder makes a basic solution. What does red litmus do?
steps: Magnesium reacts with air's oxygen, so magnesium oxide forms.
The white powder is magnesium oxide, so its solution is basic.
Red litmus turns blue, which confirms that the solution is basic.
This fits the rule that metal oxides are generally basic.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens when magnesium burns?
options: A dazzling white flame appears.
A dull red flame appears.
A yellow flame appears.
The metal stays unchanged.
activities.explanation: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame and becomes white powder.

activities.prompt: Magnesium oxide turns red litmus paper blue.
activities.explanation: Yes. Magnesium oxide turns red litmus paper blue, so its solution is basic.

activities.prompt: The solution of magnesium oxide is ______ in nature.
activities.hint: Think about the litmus-paper clue.
activities.explanation: The solution of magnesium oxide is basic in nature.

activities.prompt: What forms when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water?
options: Sulfurous acid
Magnesium oxide
Sodium
Sulfur
activities.explanation: Sulfurous acid forms when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water.

activities.prompt: Sulfur reacts when it is placed in water.
activities.explanation: There is no reaction when sulfur is placed in water.

activities.prompt: Match each substance with what happens or what it is like.
pairs: burns with a dazzling white flame
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a property or reaction described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the changes involving sulfur in order.
activities.explanation: Burning sulfur forms sulfur dioxide, which then dissolves in water.

activities.prompt: Which statement about oxides is correct?
options: Metal oxides are generally basic.
Metal oxides are generally acidic.
Non-metal oxides are generally basic.
activities.explanation: Metal oxides are generally basic. Oxides of non-metals are acidic in nature.

activities.prompt: Magnesium burns in air and leaves white powder. What will its solution do to red litmus paper?
options: It will turn the paper blue.
It will turn the paper red.
It will leave the paper unchanged.
It will burn the paper instead.

This confuses a basic magnesium oxide solution with an acidic one.
This assumes the white powder does not form a solution.
This thinks the white powder is still burning after the flame stops.

activities.explanation: Magnesium oxide forms a basic solution, so red litmus turns blue.

activities.prompt: Burning sulfur in air forms sulfur dioxide gas. The gas is bubbled through water. What kind of solution forms?
options: An acidic solution will form in the water.
A basic solution will form in the water.
A neutral solution will form in the water.
No liquid solution will form in the water.

This confuses a non-metal oxide with the usual basic metal oxides.
why.A neutral solution will form in the wate: This assumes no acid forms when sulfur dioxide dissolves.
why.No liquid solution will form in the wate: This thinks sulfur dioxide stays unchanged instead of reacting with water.

activities.explanation: Sulfur dioxide makes sulfurous acid, and this solution is acidic.

lessons.sceneAlt: Ignited magnesium burns in air with a brilliant flame.
lessons.sceneCaption: Magnesium burns brightly in air, matching the lesson’s key experiment.

sceneCredit.text: Magburn1 by Yannickcosta1, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Yannickcosta1

lessons.title: Metals and Non-metals in Everyday Life

activities.prompt: How do metals and non-metals quietly shape the things around us every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Metals, Non-metals and Alloys
activities.body: Metals and non-metals have different properties. Metals are generally lustrous, which means shiny. They are malleable, so they can be shaped. They are ductile, so they can be pulled. They also conduct heat and electricity well. Most non-metals do not shine and are generally poor conductors. Alloys are mixtures of metals, or a metal and a non-metal. Oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, chlorine and iodine have useful everyday roles.
keyPoints: Metals are generally shiny, malleable and ductile.
Metals conduct heat and electricity well.
Alloys contain metals, sometimes with a non-metal.
activities.explanation: These properties help you spot metals and understand useful mixtures.

activities.prompt: A metal wire carries electricity. A non-metal piece replaces it. Will electricity pass as easily?
steps: Metals conduct electricity well, so the metal wire carries it easily.
Non-metals are generally poor conductors, so they carry electricity less easily.
The non-metal piece would slow the flow because it conducts electricity poorly.
Therefore, the metal wire is better for carrying electricity.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Non-metal You Need
activities.prompt: Which non-metal do humans need for survival?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Chlorine
Iodine
activities.explanation: Oxygen is a non-metal that humans need for survival.

activities.title: What Is an Alloy?
activities.prompt: Which sentence describes an alloy correctly?
options: An alloy mixes metals or metal and non-metal.
An alloy mixes only non-metals with others.
An alloy stays pure and has no mixture.
An alloy is only a nutrient for plants.
activities.explanation: An alloy is a mixture of metals or of a metal and a non-metal.

activities.title: Carbon and Life
activities.prompt: Carbon is the building ______ of all life forms.
activities.hint: Carbon helps form the basis of living things.
activities.explanation: Carbon is the building block of all life forms.

activities.title: Elements and Their Uses
activities.prompt: Match each element with its correct use.
pairs: Building block of all life forms
Applied on wounds as an antiseptic
activities.explanation: Each element has a useful role in life, farming or cleaning.

activities.title: The Conductor Test
activities.prompt: Which property shows that a metal is a good conductor?
options: It passes heat and electricity well.
It is usually shiny.
It can be shaped into sheets.
It can be pulled into wires.
activities.explanation: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Shining, shaping and pulling show other metal properties.

activities.title: Carbon's Many Roles
activities.prompt: Which statement about carbon is correct?
options: It is part of proteins, fats and carbohydrates.
It is used in water purification.
It helps make fertilisers and chemicals.
It is placed on wounds as antiseptic.
activities.explanation: Carbon is an important part of proteins, fats and carbohydrates.

activities.prompt: Humans need oxygen for survival. Room A has oxygen. Room B does not. Which room is safer for a person?
options: Room A, because humans need oxygen to survive.
Room B, because people need less oxygen indoors.
Room A, because oxygen makes metals more shiny.
Room B, because carbon can replace oxygen for people.

why.Room B, because people need less oxygen: This confuses needing less oxygen indoors with not needing any.
why.Room A, because oxygen makes metals more: This mistakes a metal property for a human survival need.
why.Room B, because carbon can replace oxyge: This confuses carbon's life-building role with oxygen's survival role.

activities.explanation: Humans need oxygen for survival, so Room A is safer.

activities.prompt: Carbon is the building block of all life forms. Is carbon important only in proteins?
options: No. Carbon is also an important part of fats and carbohydrates.
No. Carbon is an important part only of proteins.
No. Carbon is an important part only of fertilisers.
No. Carbon has no important part in any living thing.

why.No. Carbon is an important part only of: This narrows carbon's role to proteins and ignores fats and carbohydrates.
This confuses carbon with nitrogen's role in making fertilisers.
why.No. Carbon has no important part in any: This wrongly ignores carbon's role in proteins and all life forms.

activities.explanation: Carbon is also important in fats and carbohydrates, not only proteins.

activities.prompt: Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth. Nitrogen is used to make fertilisers. What should nitrogen fertiliser do to plants?
options: Plants should grow better because nitrogen supports their growth.
Plants should grow less because nitrogen removes nutrients from soil.
Plants should stay the same because fertilisers do not supply nutrients.
Plants should stop growing because nitrogen is not useful to plants.

why.Plants should grow less because nitrogen: This wrongly treats nitrogen as something that removes plant nutrients.
why.Plants should stay the same because fert: This wrongly assumes that fertilisers do not supply needed nutrients.
why.Plants should stop growing because nitro: This contradicts nitrogen's essential role in plant growth.

activities.explanation: Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth.

activities.prompt: Chlorine is used in water purification. Iodine solution is applied on wounds as an antiseptic. What should be used for dirty drinking water?
options: Use chlorine, because it is used in water purification.
Use iodine solution, because it is used on wounds.
Use iodine solution, because every liquid can purify water.
Use chlorine, because it is used on wounds.

why.Use iodine solution, because it is used: This confuses an antiseptic for wounds with a water purifier.
why.Use iodine solution, because every liqui: This wrongly assumes that any liquid can purify water.
why.Use chlorine, because it is used on woun: This swaps chlorine's water use with iodine's wound use.

activities.explanation: Chlorine is used in water purification, so it fits this need.

activities.prompt: An alloy can contain two metals or a metal and a non-metal. Sample A has two metals. Sample B has a metal and a non-metal. Which statement fits both?
options: Both are alloys, and both are important for modern technologies.
Only Sample A is an alloy, so only it helps modern technologies.
Only Sample B is an alloy, so only it helps modern industries.
Neither is an alloy, so neither helps modern technologies.

why.Only Sample A is an alloy, so only it he: This wrongly thinks two metals cannot form an alloy.
why.Only Sample B is an alloy, so only it he: This wrongly thinks a metal and a non-metal cannot form an alloy.
why.Neither is an alloy, so neither helps mo: This wrongly treats both allowed mixtures as not being alloys.

activities.explanation: Both match the alloy rule, and alloys are important for modern technologies.

activities.prompt: Metals are lustrous, malleable, and good electrical conductors. Which plan tests these properties fairly?
options: Compare shine, hammer flat, and test each wire for electricity.
Compare shine, pull gently, and test each wire for heat.
Compare shine, heat water, and hammer each strip into shape.
Pull each strip, compare heat, and test each strip for shine.

why.Compare shine, pull gently, and test eac: It checks heat and ductility instead of malleability and electricity.
why.Compare shine, heat water, and hammer ea: It checks shine and malleability, but not electrical conduction.
why.Pull each strip, compare heat, and test: It checks ductility and shine, but not malleability or electricity.

activities.explanation: Its three actions check shine, malleability, and electrical conduction.

lessons.sceneAlt: A blacksmith in period clothing hammers a piece of hot iron.
lessons.sceneCaption: A blacksmith in period clothing hammers a piece of hot iron.

activities.prompt: Explain why coal is used at the ironsmith’s workshop and how the iron is changed into an axe.
activities.answer: Coal is used in the furnace to heat the iron. As the iron block is heated, it becomes red hot. The ironsmith then beats the hot iron with a hammer. This beating gives the iron the shape of an axe.
points: Coal is used in the furnace.
Heating makes the iron block red hot.
The hot iron is beaten with a hammer.
Beating gives the iron the shape of an axe.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While cooking in a kitchen, a cook uses a metal spoon and a metal cooking vessel. The spoon soon becomes hotter than a wooden spoon placed nearby because heat travels through the metal. The cook chooses a vessel handle that does not conduct heat. Elsewhere, an electrician prepares to handle a bulb. Aluminium, iron, and copper make the bulb glow, showing that electricity flows easily through them.
activities.prompt: If the two spoons remain in the cooking vessel for the same time, what would happen next?
options: The wooden one would warm more slowly than the metal one.
The wooden one would warm faster because wood is a good conductor.
Both would reach the same temperature because they are in the same vessel.
The metal one would cool faster because heat leaves it quickly.

why.The wooden one would warm faster because: Wood is a poor conductor, not a good one.
why.Both would reach the same temperature be: Sharing a vessel does not remove the difference in heat transfer.
why.The metal one would cool faster because: Metals conduct heat well; this does not mean that they cool faster.

activities.explanation: Wood transfers heat poorly, so it warms more slowly.

activities.context: While cooking in a kitchen, a cook uses a metal spoon and a metal cooking vessel. The spoon soon becomes hotter than a wooden spoon placed nearby because heat travels through the metal. The cook chooses a vessel handle that does not conduct heat. Elsewhere, an electrician prepares to handle a bulb. Aluminium, iron, and copper make the bulb glow, showing that electricity flows easily through them.
activities.prompt: Before handling the bulb, what should the electrician do?
options: Use a plastic cover and rubber gloves before handling the bulb.
Touch the bulb with bare hands because the tested materials are all metals.
Use a metal cover but no gloves because metals conduct electricity.
Remove the cover and handle only the glowing metal with bare hands.

why.Touch the bulb with bare hands because t: Bare-handed contact with conducting metal can expose the electrician to shock.
why.Use a metal cover but no gloves because: A metal cover can conduct electricity and is not safe like a plastic cover.
why.Remove the cover and handle only the glo: Removing the protective cover and working bare-handed removes protection from shock.

activities.explanation: Plastic covers and rubber gloves protect electricians from electric shock.

activities.prompt: Explain why a metal spoon becomes hotter than a wooden spoon.
activities.answer: Conduction is the transfer of heat from one point to another. Materials that transfer heat are called conductors. Metals are good conductors, so heat passes through a metal spoon and makes it hot. Wood is a poor conductor, so it transfers heat poorly and stays cooler.
points: Defines conduction.
Explains that metals conduct heat well.
Explains that wood transfers heat poorly.
Connects conduction to the different spoon temperatures.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After rain, a child leaves an iron gate outdoors. The gate is exposed to moist air, and brown deposits later appear on its surface. A similar gate kept in dry air does not develop brown deposits. The child wants to protect the outdoor gate and is considering painting it or coating it with zinc metal.
activities.prompt: If the gate were kept in dry air instead of outdoors, what would happen to it?
options: The iron would remain free of rust.
Brown deposits would begin forming even without moisture.
It would rust faster than it does in moist air.
It would develop a green coating instead.

why.Brown deposits would begin forming even: This wrongly assumes that moisture is unnecessary.
why.It would rust faster than it does in moi: This gets the effect of moisture wrong.
why.It would develop a green coating instead: This confuses iron with the possible coating on copper objects.

activities.explanation: Dry air alone does not cause brown deposits or rust.

activities.context: After rain, a child leaves an iron gate outdoors. The gate is exposed to moist air, and brown deposits later appear on its surface. A similar gate kept in dry air does not develop brown deposits. The child wants to protect the outdoor gate and is considering painting it or coating it with zinc metal.
activities.prompt: The child chooses galvanisation to protect the gate. What will protect the iron?
options: A layer of zinc metal.
A layer of copper metal.
A layer of silver metal.
A layer of moist air.

Copper objects may develop green coatings, but zinc is used for galvanisation.
Silver objects may develop black coatings, but zinc is used for galvanisation.
Moist air is responsible for rust forming on iron.

activities.explanation: Galvanisation protects iron with a layer of zinc metal.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between rusting and rust.
activities.answer: Rusting is the process by which iron develops a brown deposit. That brown deposit is called rust. The two words therefore describe different parts of the same change: rusting is the formation process, while rust is the material that forms on the iron.
points: Rusting is the formation process.
Rust is the brown deposit formed on iron.
Rusting and rust are related but are not the same thing.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At an air-and-water activity, a student burned magnesium in air. A dazzling white flame appeared, leaving white powder, which the student identified as magnesium oxide. When some powder was dissolved in water, its solution turned red litmus paper blue. The student placed sulfur in water and observed no reaction, then burned sulfur in air. The student also showed a piece of sodium kept in kerosene.
activities.prompt: Why did the solution made from magnesium oxide turn the red litmus paper blue?
options: The solution was basic in nature.
The solution was acidic in nature.
The magnesium oxide had turned into sulfur dioxide.
The sulfur in the water had changed the solution's nature.

The solution of magnesium oxide is basic, not acidic.
why.The magnesium oxide had turned into sulf: Sulfur dioxide is formed by burning sulfur, not by magnesium oxide.
why.The sulfur in the water had changed the: Sulfur did not react with the water, so it did not change the solution.

activities.explanation: A basic solution turns red litmus paper blue.

activities.context: At an air-and-water activity, a student burned magnesium in air. A dazzling white flame appeared, leaving white powder, which the student identified as magnesium oxide. When some powder was dissolved in water, its solution turned red litmus paper blue. The student placed sulfur in water and observed no reaction, then burned sulfur in air. The student also showed a piece of sodium kept in kerosene.
activities.prompt: What should the student expect if sodium is removed from kerosene and exposed to both air and water?
options: It will react strongly with both oxygen and water.
It will react only with oxygen and remain unaffected by water.
It will react only with water and remain unaffected by oxygen.
It will not react with either oxygen or water.

why.It will react only with oxygen and remai: Sodium also reacts with water, so an oxygen-only reaction is incorrect.
why.It will react only with water and remain: Sodium also reacts with oxygen, so a water-only reaction is incorrect.
why.It will not react with either oxygen or: Sodium does react with oxygen and water, which is why it is stored in kerosene.

activities.explanation: Sodium reacts strongly with both oxygen and water.

activities.prompt: Explain how burning magnesium in air produces magnesium oxide and why its solution is basic.
activities.answer: Magnesium burns in air with a dazzling white flame. The white powder left after burning is magnesium oxide, which forms when magnesium reacts with oxygen in air. Magnesium oxide turns red litmus paper blue, showing that its solution is basic in nature.
points: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame.
The white powder formed is magnesium oxide.
Magnesium reacts with oxygen in air.
The solution of magnesium oxide is basic.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community gardener checks soil where vegetables are growing. Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth, and nitrogen is used to manufacture fertilisers and other chemicals. At a clinic, a worker handles water purification using chlorine, while a nurse applies an iodine solution to a wound as an antiseptic. Nearby, a metal sheet is shaped for a machine part because metals are generally malleable and ductile.
activities.prompt: If the fertiliser supplied to the gardener contained no nitrogen, what effect should the gardener expect?
options: Plants would receive less of the nutrient needed for growth.
Plants would receive more of the nutrient needed for growth.
Plants would receive the same amount of the nutrient needed for growth.
Plants would no longer need the nutrient for growth.

why.Plants would receive more of the nutrien: Nitrogen is not added to the plants in this changed situation.
why.Plants would receive the same amount of: Changing the fertiliser to contain no nitrogen does not increase its supply.
why.Plants would no longer need the nutrient: An essential nutrient remains necessary for plant growth.

activities.explanation: Nitrogen is essential for plant growth, so removing it reduces the nutrient supplied.

activities.context: A community gardener checks soil where vegetables are growing. Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth, and nitrogen is used to manufacture fertilisers and other chemicals. At a clinic, a worker handles water purification using chlorine, while a nurse applies an iodine solution to a wound as an antiseptic. Nearby, a metal sheet is shaped for a machine part because metals are generally malleable and ductile.
activities.prompt: If the metal sheet were replaced by a typical non-metal, what would most likely happen when shaping it?
options: It would generally be less able to be beaten into shape or drawn out.
It would generally be more able to be beaten into shape or drawn out.
It would generally be equally easy to beat into shape and draw out.
It would generally be easy to beat into shape but difficult to draw out.

why.It would generally be more able to be be: Most non-metals are not ductile, so drawing them out is generally difficult.
why.It would generally be equally easy to be: Metals are generally both malleable and ductile, unlike most non-metals.
why.It would generally be easy to beat into: Most non-metals are generally neither malleable nor ductile, so both abilities would be limited.

activities.explanation: Most non-metals are not malleable, so beating them into shape is generally difficult.

activities.prompt: Explain how metals and most non-metals differ in appearance, shaping, and conduction.
activities.answer: Metals are generally lustrous, malleable and ductile, and they are good conductors of heat and electricity. Most non-metals are not lustrous, are not malleable or ductile, and are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
points: Compares lustre
Compares malleability
Compares ductility
Compares heat and electrical conduction
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The World of Metals and Non-metals

activities.prompt: What is true about copper, aluminium and iron?
options: They are lustrous and hard
They are soft enough for a knife
They are liquid at room temperature
They transfer heat poorly
activities.explanation: Copper, aluminium and iron are metals. They are lustrous and hard.

activities.prompt: Iron nails become flat when they are beaten.
activities.explanation: Iron nails become flat when beaten. This shows the property called malleability.

activities.prompt: The ability to be drawn into wires is called ______.
activities.hint: This property helps metals make wires.
activities.explanation: Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn into wires.

activities.prompt: Match each property or clue with the correct material.
activities.explanation: Each match shows a property, change or use described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for making an axe in the correct order.
items: Coal is used to heat iron
The iron block becomes red hot
The ironsmith beats the hot iron
The iron is beaten into an axe
activities.explanation: Coal heats the iron until it becomes red hot. The ironsmith then beats it into an axe.

activities.prompt: Which handle can stay cooler because it transfers heat poorly?
options: Wood
Iron
Copper
Aluminium
activities.explanation: Wood transfers heat poorly, so a wooden handle can stay cooler.

activities.prompt: All tested materials that make an electric bulb glow are metals.
activities.explanation: The tested materials that make an electric bulb glow are metals.

activities.prompt: Match each material with its correct property, change or use.
pairs: burns with a dazzling white flame
activities.explanation: Each material matches the change or use described in the lesson.

chapters.title: Changes Around Us
chapters.summary: In this chapter: seeing changes around us; changes in appearance only; changes that form new substances; rusting and combustion.

lessons.title: Seeing Changes Around Us

activities.prompt: What surprising changes can we notice around us today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Noticing Changes
activities.body: Changes happen around us and can be noticed in many ways. An ice cube can change into water. A banana can develop more brown spots and a strong smell. A rose plant can show a bud. Changes can affect the size of an object or substance. Using our senses helps us observe these changes around us.
keyPoints: An ice cube can change into water.
Changes can affect the size of an object or substance.
Our senses help us observe changes.
activities.explanation: Looking closely helps you notice many changes around you.

activities.title: Explore water as its temperature changes

tasks.say: Set the temperature to -10°C.
tasks.then: The water particles stay in place, showing that water has become solid ice.

tasks.say: Set the temperature to 50°C.
tasks.then: The particles slide past each other, showing that water is liquid.

tasks.say: Set the temperature to 110°C.
tasks.then: The particles fly apart, showing that water has become steam.

activities.takeaway: Heating or cooling water changes how its particles move and the state of the water.
activities.explanation: Heating or cooling water changes how its particles move and the state of the water.

activities.prompt: A banana has more brown spots and a strong smell. What changes can we notice?
steps: The banana has more brown spots now, so its appearance has changed.
We can see this change because our senses observe changes around us.
The strong smell is another sign because smell can observe changes.
Therefore, the banana has changed in ways that our senses can observe.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What had been placed there earlier?
options: A bud on the rose plant
A cube of ice
More brown spots on the banana
Cold water in the bottle
activities.explanation: Well spotted! A cube of ice had been placed there earlier.

activities.prompt: I had noticed a ______ on the rose plant the previous day.
activities.hint: Choose the word from the rose plant observation.
activities.explanation: Great! A bud had been noticed on the rose plant.

activities.prompt: Which two changes had happened to the banana?
options: Brown spots and a strong smell
A rose bud and a strong smell
Brown spots and cold water
An ice cube and a rose bud
activities.explanation: Good choice! The banana had more brown spots and a strong smell.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Excellent! Each pair shows a change or observation from the lesson.

activities.prompt: According to the lesson, what can changes affect?
options: The speed of an object
The size of an object
The weight of a substance
The age of a substance
activities.explanation: Exactly! Changes can affect the size of an object or substance.

activities.prompt: A banana has developed more brown spots. Which statement about this same banana is also true?
options: A cube had been placed.
It had changed into water.
It had a strong smell.
A rose bud had appeared.
activities.explanation: Well done! The same banana had developed more brown spots and now had a strong smell.

activities.prompt: A child finds water where a cube had been. Which earlier action best explains the water?
options: The child had placed a rose bud there.
The child had placed a banana there.
The child had placed an ice cube there.
The child had placed cold water there.

A rose bud explains a bud on a rose, not water.
A banana can explain brown spots, but not water from ice.
Cold water was already water, so it does not explain the change.

activities.explanation: The ice cube changed into water, which explains what was found.

activities.prompt: The water in a bottle was cold earlier. It is no longer cold now. A student says nothing changed. What is wrong?
options: Water always changes colour when its coldness changes.
Coldness can change even when water still looks the same.
Every visible sign must show a change in coldness.
Water can never change after entering a bottle.

why.Water always changes colour when its col: This wrongly assumes every coldness change also changes colour.
why.Every visible sign must show a change in: This wrongly treats every visible sign as evidence of coldness change.
why.Water can never change after entering a: This wrongly assumes water cannot change in a bottle.

activities.explanation: The water is no longer cold, so a real change occurred.

activities.prompt: The water in a bottle was cold earlier. Students want to check whether it is still cold. Which method is fair?
options: Feel the water with the sense of touch.
Smell the water with the sense of smell.
Hear the water with the sense of hearing.
See the water with the sense of sight.

Smell can notice a strong smell, but not coldness.
why.Hear the water with the sense of hearing: Hearing does not tell whether the water feels cold.
Sight can show the water, but not whether it feels cold.

activities.explanation: Touch can show whether the water feels cold or not.
