lessons.title: Changes in Appearance Only

activities.prompt: Can materials look completely different and still be the same?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Looking Different, Staying the Same
activities.body: Physical changes can alter how a material looks without making a new substance. Folding paper, inflating a balloon and crushing chalk can change shape or size. Letting air out can return the balloon to its earlier state. Water can also change between solid, liquid and gas. These changes affect physical properties such as shape, size and state.
keyPoints: Physical changes can change a material's appearance.
The material stays the same during a physical change.
Shape, size and state are physical properties.
activities.explanation: A material may look different without becoming a new substance.

activities.title: Explore how water changes

tasks.say: Set the temperature below 0°C.
tasks.then: The water becomes solid ice, but it is still water.

tasks.say: Set the temperature above 100°C.
tasks.then: The water becomes a gas, but no new substance is formed.

activities.takeaway: Heating or cooling changes water's state and appearance without making a new substance.
activities.explanation: Heating or cooling changes water's state and appearance without making a new substance.

activities.prompt: Crushing chalk changes its look. Why is it still a physical change?
steps: Its shape and size change because crushing breaks it into smaller pieces.
The chalk's material stays the same because the pieces are still chalk.
No new substance forms, so this is a physical change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why the Material Stays the Same
activities.body: Physical changes do not create a new substance. The material stays the same, even when its appearance changes. A change in shape, size or state can look very different. Water can be solid, liquid or gas, and it can change from one state to another. The same material may therefore look different after a physical change.
keyPoints: No new substance forms during a physical change.
Shape, size and state can change.
Water can exist in three states.
activities.explanation: Physical changes change physical properties, not the material itself.

activities.prompt: What can paper do during a physical change?
options: Fold into a new object
Become a new substance
Turn into chalk
Disappear completely
activities.explanation: Paper can be folded to make new objects. Its material stays the same.

activities.prompt: A balloon can be inflated and then allowed to lose its ______.
activities.hint: This gas fills the balloon.
activities.explanation: The balloon can first gain air and then lose it.

activities.prompt: Match each change with the material used.
activities.explanation: Each material can show a physical change in a different way.

activities.prompt: What can water do during a physical change?
options: Change from one state to another
Form a completely new substance
Become only a solid
Stop existing
activities.explanation: Water can change between solid, liquid and gas. It remains water.

activities.prompt: A piece of chalk is crushed into powder. Which statement best explains the change?
options: The chalk became a new substance.
The chalk changed its identity.
The chalk stayed the same material.
The chalk was no longer present.
activities.explanation: Crushing changes the chalk's appearance. No new substance is formed.

activities.prompt: Put the balloon changes in order.
items: Allow the balloon to lose its air
activities.explanation: Inflating makes the balloon larger. Letting the air out then makes it smaller.

activities.prompt: A child folds a sheet of paper into a boat. What changes?
options: The paper's shape changes, but its material stays the same.
The paper's material changes when the paper is folded.
The paper's state changes when the paper is folded.
The paper's size must change when the paper is folded.

why.The paper's material changes when the pa: It wrongly thinks any shape change creates a new material.
why.The paper's state changes when the paper: It wrongly thinks folding changes the paper's state.
why.The paper's size must change when the pa: It wrongly thinks folding must change the paper's size.

activities.explanation: Right: folding changes the paper's shape, not its material.

activities.prompt: A balloon is filled, then emptied. What happens to its size?
options: It becomes smaller because the balloon loses air.
It becomes larger because the balloon loses air.
It stays the same because the balloon loses air.
It becomes solid because the balloon loses air.

why.It becomes larger because the balloon lo: It wrongly connects losing air with becoming larger.
why.It stays the same because the balloon lo: It wrongly ignores the air leaving the balloon.
why.It becomes solid because the balloon los: It wrongly thinks losing air makes the balloon solid.

activities.explanation: Right: the balloon becomes smaller as it loses air.

activities.prompt: Chalk is crushed into powder. What changes during this change?
options: The chalk's shape and size change.
The chalk's material and state change.
The chalk's shape and material change.
The chalk's size and substance change.

It wrongly says both material and state change.
It wrongly says the material changes with the shape.
It wrongly says crushing creates a new substance.

activities.explanation: Right: crushing changes the chalk's shape and size.

activities.prompt: Ice changes into liquid water. What stays the same during this change?
options: The water stays water, and no new substance forms.
The water becomes a new substance during the change.
The water stays water, but its state stays the same.
The water becomes a solid substance during the change.

why.The water becomes a new substance during: It wrongly says the state change creates a new substance.
why.The water stays water, but its state sta: It wrongly says the state must remain unchanged.
why.The water becomes a solid substance duri: It wrongly predicts a change into a solid state.

activities.explanation: Right: the state changes, but the water stays water.

activities.prompt: Crushing chalk makes powder. Which observation shows a physical change happened?
options: The shape and size changed, while the material stayed the same.
The shape and size changed, so the material also changed.
The state changed, while the material stayed the same.
The state stayed the same, so the material also changed.

why.The shape and size changed, so the mater: It wrongly says a shape and size change also changes the material.
why.The state changed, while the material st: It wrongly treats a state change as proof that chalk changed.
why.The state stayed the same, so the materi: It wrongly says the material changed when the state did not.

activities.explanation: Right: shape and size changed, while the material stayed the same.

activities.prompt: Someone says folding paper makes a new substance. What is wrong?
options: Folding changes shape, but it does not form a new substance.
Folding changes shape, so it always forms a new substance.
New substances cannot change shape when objects are folded.
Physical changes always replace the original material.

why.Folding changes shape, so it always form: It wrongly believes every shape change makes a new substance.
why.New substances cannot change shape when: It wrongly believes new substances cannot change shape.
why.Physical changes always replace the orig: It wrongly believes physical changes always replace the material.

activities.explanation: Right: a new shape does not create a new substance.

lessons.title: Changes That Form New Substances

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered what happens when we blow into a glass?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How New Substances Form
activities.body: When you blow into tap water, bubbles form, but its appearance stays the same. When you blow into lime water, bubbles form and it turns milky. Milky means cloudy and white. A new white substance settles below. It is called calcium carbonate. This is a chemical change because new substances form. A chemical reaction is the process that forms them.
keyPoints: Blowing air into tap water produces bubbles only.
Blowing air into lime water makes it milky.
A chemical change forms one or more new substances.
A chemical reaction forms new substances.
activities.explanation: The lime water formed a new white-coloured substance called calcium carbonate.

activities.prompt: A child blows air into two cups. One has tap water. One has lime water. What happens, and why?
steps: Blowing air into tap water makes bubbles, because air enters it.
The tap water keeps its appearance, so the change is not visible.
Exhaled carbon dioxide reacts with lime water, making bubbles and milky water.
White calcium carbonate settles, so a chemical change occurs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happened when air was blown into lime water?
options: Only bubbles appeared
New white substance formed
The water stayed unchanged
A fizzing sound occurred
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide from exhaled air reacted with lime water. The water became milky, and a white substance formed.

activities.prompt: A chemical reaction is the process through which ______ substances form.
activities.hint: A reaction makes something that was not there before.
activities.explanation: A chemical reaction forms one or more new substances.

activities.prompt: Match each material with the result described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Only bubbles appeared in tap water. Lime water became milky, and a white substance settled. Vinegar and baking soda produced a fizzing sound.

activities.prompt: Why did lime water turn milky after air was blown into it?
options: Air bubbles mixed with it
Carbon dioxide reacted with it
Tap water mixed with it
White substance settled in it
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide from exhaled air reacted with lime water. The reaction formed new substances.

activities.prompt: Put the vinegar and baking soda events in the order described.
activities.explanation: Mixing produced a fizzing sound and gas bubbles. The gas formed was carbon dioxide.

activities.prompt: Which new substance formed when lime water reacted with carbon dioxide?
options: Carbon dioxide
Baking soda
Calcium carbonate
Exhaled air
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide from exhaled air reacted with lime water. Calcium carbonate, a new white-coloured substance, formed.

activities.prompt: Vinegar and baking soda are mixed. Which result shows that new substances formed?
options: Fizzing sounds and gas bubbles appear together.
Only bubbles form, with no fizzing sound heard.
Fizzing sounds occur, but no new gas forms.
Only fizzing sounds occur, with no bubbles seen.

why.Only bubbles form, with no fizzing sound: This treats bubbles as ordinary air rather than newly formed carbon dioxide.
why.Fizzing sounds occur, but no new gas for: This thinks fizzing can happen without a new gas forming.
why.Only fizzing sounds occur, with no bubbl: This misses the gas bubbles that appear with the fizzing sound.

activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide gas forms, causing the fizzing sounds and bubbles.

activities.prompt: Bubbles appear during an experiment. A child says bubbles always prove a chemical change. Why is the claim flawed?
options: Tap water makes bubbles, but its appearance does not change.
Lime water makes bubbles, but no new substance forms.
Air bubbles contain carbon dioxide in every experiment.
Gas bubbles always make the liquid look milky.

why.Lime water makes bubbles, but no new sub: This denies the calcium carbonate that forms in lime water.
why.Air bubbles contain carbon dioxide in ev: This assumes every bubble comes from exhaled carbon dioxide.
why.Gas bubbles always make the liquid look: This confuses milky lime water with the result of every bubble.

activities.explanation: This gives a counterexample because bubbles alone do not prove a chemical change.

activities.prompt: Blowing air into lime water makes it milky. Why does this happen?
options: Carbon dioxide reacts, making white calcium carbonate.
Air bubbles remain, making white calcium carbonate.
Carbon dioxide escapes, making white calcium carbonate.
Lime water settles, making white calcium carbonate.

why.Air bubbles remain, making white calcium: This treats the bubbles as unchanged air, not reacting carbon dioxide.
why.Carbon dioxide escapes, making white cal: This says carbon dioxide leaves instead of reacting with lime water.
why.Lime water settles, making white calcium: This blames lime water settling instead of carbon dioxide reacting.

activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide from the air reacts, forming calcium carbonate.

activities.prompt: One cup has tap water. Another has lime water. Which test best shows the change?
options: Compare tap water and lime water before and after blowing.
Compare the bubble sizes in both liquids after blowing.
Compare the amounts of air blown into each liquid.
Compare the cup sizes before blowing air into them.

why.Compare the bubble sizes in both liquids: Bubble size does not show whether a new substance forms.
why.Compare the amounts of air blown into ea: Different air amounts do not show what changed in each liquid.
why.Compare the cup sizes before blowing air: Cup size does not show whether a new substance forms.

activities.explanation: This compares an unchanged appearance with milky water and a white substance.

lessons.title: Rusting and Combustion

activities.prompt: What happens when iron meets air and magnesium meets fire?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Happens During Rusting and Combustion?
activities.body: Rusting forms a new brown-coloured substance called rust. It is a chemical change because a new substance forms. This brown substance is iron oxide. Burning magnesium ribbon forms magnesium oxide, and produces heat and light. Combustion is a reaction with oxygen that produces heat and/or light. Combustible substances undergo combustion. The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its ignition temperature. Fuel needs heat to reach ignition temperature.
keyPoints: Rusting forms iron oxide, a new brown-coloured substance.
Rusting is a chemical change because a new substance forms.
Magnesium burning forms magnesium oxide, with heat and light.
Combustion is a chemical reaction with oxygen that produces heat and/or light.
Wood, paper, cotton and kerosene are combustible substances.
The covered candle stopped burning after some time.
Oxygen is the component of air that supports combustion.
Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature where a substance catches fire.
activities.explanation: These changes show how new substances form during rusting and combustion.

activities.prompt: Why does a covered candle stop burning after some time?
steps: The candle was burning, so heat and light showed combustion.
Combustion is a reaction with oxygen from the air.
The covered candle stopped burning after some time.
Therefore, the cover blocked oxygen needed by the flame.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Combustible Substances
activities.prompt: Which one is listed as a combustible substance?
options: rust
iron oxide
wood
magnesium oxide
activities.explanation: Wood is one of the combustible substances named in the lesson.

activities.title: A New Substance
activities.prompt: Rusting forms a new brown-coloured substance.
activities.explanation: The new brown-coloured substance formed during rusting is called rust.

activities.title: Match Each Event
activities.prompt: Match each event with its substance or result.
activities.explanation: Each event is matched with the substance formed or the result recorded.

activities.title: Burning Magnesium Ribbon
activities.prompt: What happened when the magnesium ribbon burned?
options: New iron oxide formed with heat and light.
New magnesium oxide formed with heat and light.
New rust formed with heat and light.
No new substance formed with heat and light.
activities.explanation: Burning the ribbon formed magnesium oxide. Heat and light were also produced.

activities.title: Steps of Combustion
activities.prompt: Put these steps of combustion in order.
activities.explanation: The fuel first reaches ignition temperature. It then reacts with oxygen, producing heat and/or light.

activities.prompt: A magnesium ribbon burns and gives off light. Which observation best shows that a chemical change occurred?
options: A new substance forms together with heat and light.
Only heat and light appear, but no new substance forms.
The ribbon only changes shape while heat and light appear.
Brown rust forms while the ribbon produces heat.

why.Only heat and light appear, but no new s: Heat and light alone do not show that a new substance formed.
why.The ribbon only changes shape while heat: This wrongly treats a shape change as evidence of a chemical change.
why.Brown rust forms while the ribbon produc: This wrongly mixes rusting with burning magnesium ribbon.

activities.explanation: Magnesium oxide formed with heat and light, showing a new substance.

activities.prompt: An iron surface becomes covered with brown rust. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Only the iron's colour changed, so no new substance formed.
The iron became magnesium oxide, so combustion occurred.
A chemical change formed the new substance iron oxide.
The iron only changed shape, but its substance stayed the same.

why.Only the iron's colour changed, so no ne: Rust is a new substance, not just a different colour.
why.The iron became magnesium oxide, so comb: Magnesium oxide comes from burning magnesium, not rusting iron.
why.The iron only changed shape, but its sub: Rusting changes the substance, not merely the iron's shape.

activities.explanation: Rusting forms brown rust, and rust is iron oxide.

activities.prompt: A student wants to test whether paper can burn. What should the student do first?
options: Cover the paper and wait for it to burn.
Light the paper before it reaches its ignition temperature.
Cool the paper until it reaches its ignition temperature.
Heat the paper until it reaches its ignition temperature.

Covering the paper limits oxygen instead of testing needed heat.
why.Light the paper before it reaches its ig: This wrongly assumes paper can burn before reaching ignition temperature.
why.Cool the paper until it reaches its igni: This wrongly assumes cooling can bring paper to its ignition temperature.

activities.explanation: Combustion needs enough heat for the fuel to reach ignition temperature.

activities.prompt: A burning substance has enough heat, but no oxygen reaches it. What should happen next?
options: It cannot keep burning because combustion needs oxygen.
It will burn more strongly because heat is enough.
It will turn into rust because oxygen is missing.
It will keep burning because light replaces oxygen.

why.It will burn more strongly because heat: This wrongly assumes heat alone is enough for combustion.
why.It will turn into rust because oxygen is: This wrongly assumes missing oxygen makes rust form.
why.It will keep burning because light repla: This wrongly assumes light can replace oxygen in combustion.

activities.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, so heat alone cannot keep it going.

activities.prompt: An iron nail forms brown rust. A paper sheet burns with heat and light. Which change shows combustion?
options: The rusting, because a new substance also forms.
The paper, because rust is another name for combustion.
The paper, because combustion produces heat and light.
The rusting, because combustible substances always form rust.

why.The rusting, because a new substance als: This wrongly treats every new substance formation as combustion.
why.The paper, because rust is another name: This wrongly treats rusting and combustion as the same process.
why.The rusting, because combustible substan: This wrongly assumes all combustible substances form rust.

activities.explanation: The paper burns with heat and light, which show combustion.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes Together

activities.prompt: What changes can happen together as a candle burns?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changes in wax and other materials
activities.body: When a candle burns, melted wax moves up the wick. Heat from the flame makes the wax evaporate. Melting, solidifying and evaporating wax are physical changes. Burning wax vapour is a chemical change. A reversible change lets us get the original form back. Ice can be refrozen after melting, and water vapour can become liquid water. Chopped vegetables and popcorn cannot return to their original forms.
keyPoints: Melting, solidifying and evaporating wax are physical changes.
Burning wax vapour is a chemical change.
Reversible changes can bring back the original form.
activities.explanation: These examples help you recognise different kinds of change.

activities.prompt: A candle burns. Which wax changes are physical, and which are chemical?
steps: Melted wax moves up the wick.
Heat from the flame makes the wax evaporate.
Melting and evaporating wax are physical changes.
Burning wax vapour is a chemical change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which wax change is chemical?
options: Melting wax
Burning wax vapour
Solidifying wax
Evaporating wax
activities.explanation: Burning wax vapour is a chemical change. The other wax changes are physical.

activities.prompt: Burning wax vapour is a ______ change.
activities.hint: This change happens when wax vapour burns.
activities.explanation: Burning wax vapour is a chemical change. Well done!

activities.prompt: What does a reversible change let us do?
options: Make the change permanent
Keep the form unchanged
Get the original form back
Stop the change happening
activities.explanation: A reversible change lets us get the original form back. You’ve got it!

activities.prompt: Match each change with its result.
pairs: Original size and shape are lost
activities.explanation: Melting and refreezing ice returns its original form. Condensing water vapour gives liquid water. Chopping vegetables and popping popcorn cannot restore the original forms.

activities.prompt: Which change cannot be reversed?
options: Chopping vegetables
Melting ice
Condensing water vapour
Refreezing ice
activities.explanation: Chopped vegetables cannot return to their original size and shape. The other changes can be reversed.

activities.prompt: Put these wax changes in the correct order.
items: Melted wax moves up the wick
activities.explanation: Melted wax moves up the wick. Heat makes it evaporate. The wax vapour then burns.

activities.prompt: A candle's wax melts and moves up the wick. What happens next?
options: It evaporates, and its vapour can burn.
It stays liquid, and its vapour can burn.
It evaporates, but its vapour cannot burn.
It solidifies, and then its vapour burns.

why.It stays liquid, and its vapour can burn: This confuses evaporation with melting, so the wax never becomes vapour.
why.It evaporates, but its vapour cannot bur: This mistakes a physical change for the later chemical change.
why.It solidifies, and then its vapour burns: This reverses the heating step, so wax becomes solid before burning.

activities.explanation: Flame heat evaporates wax; burning wax vapour is a chemical change.

activities.prompt: The wax melts and evaporates. Then its vapour burns. Why are these different changes?
options: Melting and evaporating wax are physical changes; burning its vapour is chemical.
Melting and evaporating wax are chemical changes; burning its vapour is physical.
All three wax changes are physical because the flame only heats them.
All three wax changes are chemical because the flame burns them.

why.Melting and evaporating wax are chemical: This swaps the physical and chemical changes.
why.All three wax changes are physical becau: This treats every heated change as physical, even burning wax vapour.
why.All three wax changes are chemical becau: This treats every heated change as chemical, even melting and evaporating.

activities.explanation: Melting and evaporating wax are physical changes, while burning vapour is chemical.

activities.prompt: An ice cube melts in a cup. It is later refrozen. What can we say about the change?
options: The change is reversible because the original ice can return.
The change is not reversible because the ice melted.
The change is reversible because the ice became water.
The change is not reversible because water cannot freeze.

why.The change is not reversible because the: This confuses melting with the later freezing step.
why.The change is reversible because the ice: This gives the wrong reason; refreezing, not melting, restores ice.
why.The change is not reversible because wat: This confuses refreezing with being unable to freeze.

activities.explanation: Ice can be refrozen after melting, so the original form can return.

activities.prompt: Water vapour becomes liquid drops on a cool lid. Can this change be reversed?
options: Yes, because water vapour can be condensed back into liquid water.
No, because water vapour can never become a liquid.
No, because liquid water cannot become water vapour again.
Yes, because every change involving water is reversible.

why.No, because water vapour can never becom: This wrongly says condensation cannot happen.
why.No, because liquid water cannot become w: This confuses condensation with the change in the other direction.
why.Yes, because every change involving wate: This wrongly treats all water changes as reversible.

activities.explanation: Water vapour can become liquid water again, so this change is reversible.

activities.prompt: A child says chopped vegetables can be mixed back together. Can they regain their first shape?
options: No, because chopping cannot restore their original size and shape.
Yes, because mixing the pieces reverses the chopping.
Yes, because the pieces are still the same vegetables.
No, because only melted substances can return to their form.

why.Yes, because mixing the pieces reverses: This confuses putting pieces together with restoring their first form.
why.Yes, because the pieces are still the sa: This assumes unchanged pieces must have an unchanged shape.
why.No, because only melted substances can r: This wrongly limits reversal to melted substances.

activities.explanation: Chopped vegetables cannot return to their original size and shape.

activities.prompt: A child says popcorn and melting ice are both reversible. Is that claim correct?
options: No. Ice can refreeze, but popcorn cannot return to its original form.
Yes. Both can return to their original forms after changing.
No. Popcorn can return, but ice cannot refreeze.
Yes. Every change that affects size can be reversed.

why.Yes. Both can return to their original f: This wrongly assumes both changes can bring back the first form.
why.No. Popcorn can return, but ice cannot r: This swaps what can return: popcorn cannot, but ice can.
why.Yes. Every change that affects size can: This wrongly assumes every size change can be undone.

activities.explanation: Ice can be refrozen after melting. Popcorn cannot return to its original form.

lessons.title: Useful, Harmful and Natural Changes

activities.prompt: Which everyday changes are helpful, harmful, or surprisingly useful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changes Can Be Useful or Harmful
activities.body: Some changes are useful, while others are harmful in a particular situation. A change may be useful or harmful, depending on the situation. Making curd, ripening fruits, cutting fruits and cooking food are desirable changes. Rusting iron and decay of stored food are undesirable changes. Decomposing food can help make compost. Physical and chemical changes in rocks are called weathering. Erosion breaks down and moves rock and soil.
keyPoints: Useful and harmful depend on the situation.
Some food changes are desirable.
Weathering changes rocks and eventually forms soil.
activities.explanation: This lesson sorts changes and shows how rocks change.

activities.prompt: Why is decay bad for stored food but good for leftover scraps?
steps: Grandma stores bread, and the stored food decays.
This is undesirable because the family cannot use that food.
She uses other scraps for compost, which decay can make.
So decay is harmful in storage, but useful for compost.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which food change is desirable?
options: Making curd
Decay of stored food
Drying paint
Rusting iron
activities.explanation: Making curd is a desirable change. The other options are not desirable food changes.

activities.prompt: Match each change with a suitable description.
activities.explanation: Making curd and ripening fruits are desirable. Rusting iron and decay of stored food are undesirable.

activities.prompt: Decomposing food can turn food waste into ______.
activities.hint: This useful product comes from decomposing food waste.
activities.explanation: Decomposing food waste can be useful because it helps make compost.

activities.prompt: How does using fuels in vehicles affect the atmosphere?
options: It increases carbon dioxide.
It decreases carbon dioxide.
It removes carbon dioxide.
It changes air into soil.
activities.explanation: Using fuels in vehicles increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in the rock-changing process.
items: Large rocks are broken into smaller pieces.
Physical and chemical changes occur in rocks.
activities.explanation: Large rocks become smaller through rock changes. These changes are weathering, which eventually leads to soil.

activities.prompt: Which event is erosion during a physical change?
options: A landslide
Making curd
Ripening fruits
Drying paint
activities.explanation: Erosion during a landslide breaks down and moves rock and soil. It is a physical change.

activities.prompt: A van burns fuel beside a newly painted gate. Which change comes from the van's fuel use?
options: It adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
It dries the gate's paint and causes pollution.
It decays food stored near the vehicle.
It grows tree roots inside nearby rocks.

why.It dries the gate's paint and causes pol: This wrongly links fuel use to paint drying.
This wrongly links fuel use to stored-food decay.
This wrongly links fuel use to growing tree roots.

activities.explanation: Right: using fuels in vehicles increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

activities.prompt: A learner says temperature changes can break rocks. Which test is fairest?
options: Use similar rocks, change only temperature, and compare cracks.
Use different rocks, change temperature and paint, then compare cracks.
Use one rock, change nothing, and guess if cracks appear.
Use food scraps, change their containers, and compare decay.

why.Use different rocks, change temperature: Changing temperature and paint gives two causes, so the test is unfair.
why.Use one rock, change nothing, and guess: No change is made, so the test cannot show what caused cracks.
why.Use food scraps, change their containers: This tests food decay, so it cannot show the effect of temperature.

activities.explanation: Right: temperature changes can break rocks, so this tests the cause.

activities.prompt: Tree roots are only one cause of rock cracks during weathering. What observation weakens this claim?
options: Water froze inside a crack and split the rock.
A tree root grew inside the crack and split it.
Stored food decayed just beside the cracked rock.
Vehicle fuel burned just beside the cracked rock.

why.A tree root grew inside the crack and sp: This observation supports tree roots, so it does not weaken the claim.
why.Stored food decayed just beside the crac: This wrongly links nearby food decay to cracking the rock.
why.Vehicle fuel burned just beside the crac: This wrongly links nearby fuel burning to cracking the rock.

activities.explanation: Right: freezing water breaks rocks, so roots are not the only cause.

lessons.sceneCaption: Food waste is turned into compost, a useful natural change.

activities.context: I had placed a cube of ice there earlier. The ice cube had changed into water. I had noticed a bud on the rose plant the previous day. The cold water in the bottle was no longer cold. The banana had developed more brown spots. The banana now had a strong smell. The students were describing different kinds of changes.
activities.prompt: Why does the ice cube's change show that a change can affect a substance?
options: The original cube was replaced by water.
The cube stayed in exactly the same form.
Only the place of the cube changed.
The water became colder than before.

A change in location is described.
It describes a temperature change instead.

activities.explanation: The cube changed into water.

activities.context: I had placed a cube of ice there earlier. The ice cube had changed into water. I had noticed a bud on the rose plant the previous day. The cold water in the bottle was no longer cold. The banana had developed more brown spots. The banana now had a strong smell. The students were describing different kinds of changes.
activities.prompt: Which observations support the claim that the banana underwent a change?
options: More brown areas can be seen, and a strong smell can be detected.
The banana is colder than before.
The banana has stayed completely unchanged.
Its strong smell is the only change that occurred.

A change in coldness is not described.
why.Its strong smell is the only change that: It ignores the additional brown spots.

activities.explanation: Both appearance and smell changed.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the change shown by the ice and the change shown by the banana?
activities.answer: The ice cube changed into water. The banana changed by developing more brown spots and having a strong smell. Thus, both changes can be noticed with the senses, but the ice change is shown by its change into water, while the banana change is shown by its appearance and smell.
points: The ice cube changed into water.
The banana developed more brown spots.
The banana had a strong smell.
Both changes were observed with the senses.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Paper was folded to make a new object. A balloon was inflated and then allowed to lose its air. A piece of chalk was crushed into powder. The materials remained the same during each change, and no new substance formed. Their appearance changed because their shape or size changed. Water was also changed from one state to another.
activities.prompt: If the inflated balloon is allowed to lose its air, what should happen next in this physical change?
options: The balloon will become smaller without changing into another material.
The balloon will become smaller and form a new substance inside.
The balloon will keep its size but change into another material.
The balloon will remain unchanged because physical changes affect only state.

why.The balloon will become smaller and form: A physical change does not form a new substance.
why.The balloon will keep its size but chang: The change can affect size, and the material does not become another material.
why.The balloon will remain unchanged becaus: Physical changes can affect shape, size and state, so the balloon need not remain unchanged.

activities.explanation: Losing air can reduce the balloon's size while its material remains the same.

activities.context: Paper was folded to make a new object. A balloon was inflated and then allowed to lose its air. A piece of chalk was crushed into powder. The materials remained the same during each change, and no new substance formed. Their appearance changed because their shape or size changed. Water was also changed from one state to another.
activities.prompt: Why can crushed chalk look different from the original piece while still being the same material?
options: Crushing altered the chalk's shape and size without changing its material.
Crushing created a new powder substance from the chalk.
Crushing changed only the state of the chalk and left its shape unchanged.
Crushing replaced the original chalk with another material.

why.Crushing created a new powder substance: The powder is the crushed chalk, not a newly formed substance.
why.Crushing changed only the state of the c: The stated change is in shape and size, not merely state.
why.Crushing replaced the original chalk wit: Crushing does not replace the chalk with another material.

activities.explanation: Crushing changes shape and size while keeping the same material.

activities.prompt: Explain why folding paper, allowing a balloon to lose its air, and crushing chalk are physical changes.
activities.answer: These changes are physical changes because they affect properties such as shape or size without forming a new substance. Folding changes the paper's shape, inflating or deflating the balloon changes its size, and crushing chalk changes the chalk's shape and size. The material involved remains the same in each case.
points: Identifies the examples as physical changes
Explains the changes in shape or size
States that no new substance forms
Notes that each material remains the same
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student blew air into a glass of tap water and then into a glass of lime water. The tap water produced bubbles only, and its appearance did not change. The lime water produced bubbles and became milky or cloudy. A new white substance settled at the bottom of the tumbler. Later, the student mixed vinegar and baking soda. They heard a fizzing sound and saw gas bubbles.
activities.prompt: Why did the tap water and lime water look different after air was blown into them?
options: Carbon dioxide from exhaled air reacted with lime water, forming new substances.
The air bubbles made the lime water cloudy because the bubbles stayed in it.
Calcium carbonate formed in the tap water and made it look milky.
Both glasses became cloudy because bubbles in exhaled air formed calcium carbonate in each.

why.The air bubbles made the lime water clou: This mistakes trapped bubbles for the cause of the cloudiness.
why.Calcium carbonate formed in the tap wate: This places calcium carbonate in the wrong glass.
why.Both glasses became cloudy because bubbl: This wrongly suggests that calcium carbonate formed in both glasses.

activities.explanation: This correctly identifies the reaction and the formation of new substances.

activities.context: A student blew air into a glass of tap water and then into a glass of lime water. The tap water produced bubbles only, and its appearance did not change. The lime water produced bubbles and became milky or cloudy. A new white substance settled at the bottom of the tumbler. Later, the student mixed vinegar and baking soda. They heard a fizzing sound and saw gas bubbles.
activities.prompt: If the gas from the vinegar-and-baking-soda mixture is passed into lime water, what should happen next?
options: The lime water should become milky as calcium carbonate forms.
The lime water should stay clear because carbon dioxide does not react with it.
The lime water should fizz and produce only bubbles, like tap water.
A white substance should form in the tap water instead of the lime water.

why.The lime water should stay clear because: This wrongly denies the stated reaction between carbon dioxide and lime water.
why.The lime water should fizz and produce o: This confuses the vinegar-and-baking-soda reaction with blowing air into tap water.
why.A white substance should form in the tap: This identifies the wrong liquid in which the new substance would form.

activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form milky calcium carbonate.

activities.context: A student blew air into a glass of tap water and then into a glass of lime water. The tap water produced bubbles only, and its appearance did not change. The lime water produced bubbles and became milky or cloudy. A new white substance settled at the bottom of the tumbler. Later, the student mixed vinegar and baking soda. They heard a fizzing sound and saw gas bubbles.
activities.prompt: Which conclusion about the activities in the passage is best supported?
options: Mixing vinegar and baking soda was a chemical reaction because carbon dioxide formed.
Blowing air into tap water was a chemical change because bubbles formed.
Making lime water cloudy was only a physical change because the bubbles caused it.
The vinegar-and-baking-soda mixture was unchanged because only a sound was produced.

why.Blowing air into tap water was a chemica: Bubbles alone do not show that a new substance formed in tap water.
why.Making lime water cloudy was only a phys: A new white substance formed in the lime water.
why.The vinegar-and-baking-soda mixture was: The mixture also produced gas bubbles, not only a fizzing sound.

activities.explanation: A new gas formed, so the mixture showed a chemical reaction.

activities.prompt: Explain why blowing air into tap water and lime water produced different results.
activities.answer: Blowing into tap water produced bubbles only, with no change in appearance. In lime water, carbon dioxide from exhaled air reacted, forming calcium carbonate and a small amount of water. The new white-coloured substance made the lime water milky and settled at the bottom, so new substances formed.
points: Only bubbles appeared in the tap water, with no appearance change.
Carbon dioxide from exhaled air reacted with the lime water.
Calcium carbonate and a small amount of water formed.
The lime water became milky, and the white substance settled.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An iron article left in air develops a brown coating over time. A student identifies the coating as rust and says a new substance has formed. Later, a magnesium ribbon is burned. During the burning, magnesium oxide forms, and heat and light are seen. The student also places a lid over a burning candle. After some time, the candle stops burning.
activities.prompt: Why should the student classify the formation of rust as a chemical change?
options: A different substance is produced.
The brown coating shows only a change in appearance.
The iron has changed shape instead of forming a new substance.
Heat and light were released as the rust formed.

why.The brown coating shows only a change in: A change in colour alone does not show that a new substance formed.
why.The iron has changed shape instead of fo: The change concerns a new substance, not merely the shape of the iron.
why.Heat and light were released as the rust: Heat and light are linked with the burning of magnesium, not the given description of rusting.

activities.explanation: Rusting forms rust, which is iron oxide.

activities.context: An iron article left in air develops a brown coating over time. A student identifies the coating as rust and says a new substance has formed. Later, a magnesium ribbon is burned. During the burning, magnesium oxide forms, and heat and light are seen. The student also places a lid over a burning candle. After some time, the candle stops burning.
activities.prompt: What should the student do after the covered candle stops burning?
options: Remove the cover so oxygen can reach the flame.
Leave it covered and wait for more heat.
Add another layer of covering.
Wait for the candle to recover by itself.

The covered candle stopped because it could no longer burn normally.
More covering would not restore the oxygen needed for combustion.
why.Wait for the candle to recover by itself: Waiting alone would not change the lack of oxygen.

activities.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion.

activities.prompt: Explain why rusting and burning magnesium are chemical changes.
activities.answer: Rusting is a chemical change because it forms rust, and rust is iron oxide. Burning magnesium also forms a new substance called magnesium oxide, with heat and light produced. Both are chemical changes because a new substance is formed during the process.
points: Rust is a new brown substance.
Rust is iron oxide.
Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide.
Heat and light are produced during combustion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A candle is burning, and melted wax is carried up the wick. Heat from the flame makes the wax evaporate, and the wax vapour then burns. The students classify melting, solidifying, and evaporating wax as physical changes, while burning wax vapour is a chemical change. They also think about whether the changes involved can be reversed.
activities.prompt: At what point does the burning of the wax vapour happen in the candle's sequence of changes?
options: Evaporation occurs before burning.
Burning occurs while the wax is still melted.
Solidifying occurs before evaporation.
Burning occurs before the wax evaporates.

why.Burning occurs while the wax is still me: The burning step involves wax vapour rather than melted wax.
The case describes evaporation before burning.
why.Burning occurs before the wax evaporates: The wax must evaporate before its vapour can burn.

activities.explanation: Heat causes the wax to evaporate before the vapour burns.

activities.context: A candle is burning, and melted wax is carried up the wick. Heat from the flame makes the wax evaporate, and the wax vapour then burns. The students classify melting, solidifying, and evaporating wax as physical changes, while burning wax vapour is a chemical change. They also think about whether the changes involved can be reversed.
activities.prompt: Which stage in the case should be recorded as a chemical change?
options: The burning stage
The melting stage
The solidifying stage
The evaporation stage

why.The melting stage: Melting wax is a physical change.
why.The solidifying stage: Solidifying wax is a physical change.
why.The evaporation stage: Evaporating wax is a physical change.

activities.explanation: Burning wax vapour is a chemical change.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the evaporation of wax and the burning of wax vapour.
activities.answer: Melting, solidifying, and evaporating wax are physical changes because they involve changes in the wax's form or state without burning it. Burning wax vapour is a chemical change. This shows that physical and chemical changes can occur together in the same candle-burning process.
points: Melting, solidifying, and evaporating wax are physical changes.
Burning wax vapour is a chemical change.
Physical and chemical changes occur together.
The change in form is different from burning.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why some changes in the kitchen are desirable while others are undesirable.
activities.answer: Cutting fruit and cooking food are desirable changes because they prepare food for eating. Leaving milk to become curd is desirable. Rusting iron and food decay are undesirable changes. A change that is undesirable in one situation may be useful in another, such as food decomposing to form compost.
points: Cutting fruit and cooking food are desirable.
Making curd is desirable.
Rusting iron and food decay are undesirable.
A change may be useful in a different situation.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Changes Around Us

activities.prompt: Which action is a physical change?
options: Folding paper
Burning paper
Making curd
Rusting iron
activities.explanation: Folding changes the paper's shape. Its material stays the same.

activities.prompt: We can observe changes around us using our senses.
activities.explanation: Our senses help us notice changes in objects and substances.

activities.prompt: Put the changes involving candle wax in order.
items: Melted wax is carried up the wick.
The wax evaporates because of the flame's heat.
activities.explanation: The wax melts, evaporates and then burns. The last step is chemical.

activities.prompt: What happened when air was blown into lime water?
options: It became milky with bubbles.
It stayed clear with bubbles only.
It stayed clear without bubbles.
It turned milky without bubbles.
activities.explanation: Lime water produced bubbles and became milky or cloudy.

activities.prompt: A chemical change forms one or more new ______.
activities.hint: These are made during a chemical reaction.
activities.explanation: A chemical reaction is a process that forms new substances.

activities.prompt: Why did the covered candle stop burning?
options: It lost all its oxygen.
It became too shiny.
It could not get enough oxygen.
It gained more heat.
activities.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion. The cover stopped oxygen from reaching the flame.

activities.prompt: Combustion needs enough heat for fuel to reach its ignition temperature.
activities.explanation: A substance must reach its ignition temperature before it catches fire.

activities.prompt: Chopped vegetables can return to their original size and shape.
activities.explanation: Chopped vegetables cannot return to their original form. This change is not reversible.

activities.prompt: Match each example with its correct description.
pairs: physical and chemical changes in rocks
breaks down and moves rock and soil
activities.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks and can lead to soil. Erosion moves rock and soil.

boss.sceneCaption: An ice cube melts on a hot stone.

chapters.title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change
chapters.summary: In this chapter: life stages and growing up; reproductive changes and puberty; emotions and behaviour; food and personal hygiene.

lessons.title: Life Stages and Growing Up

activities.prompt: What changes can happen to your body as you grow up?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Growing Through Life
activities.body: People pass through infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age. Each person passes through these stages at a different pace. Adolescence comes between childhood and adulthood. It is a period of rapid growth and development between ages 10 and 19. During this time, the body prepares for adulthood. Height changes become more noticeable. Adolescent boys may get a hoarse voice. Both boys and girls grow hair in different body parts.
keyPoints: People pass through the same life stages at different paces.
Adolescence is rapid growth and development between ages 10 and 19.
During adolescence, the body prepares for adulthood.
activities.explanation: Adolescence is the changing stage between childhood and adulthood.

activities.prompt: Sam and Lee have the same age. Their heights change at different speeds. Why can this happen?
steps: People pass through life stages at different paces.
This explains why their bodies change at different times.
Sam's faster height change fits adolescence.
So the same age does not mean the same growth pace.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Middle Stage
activities.prompt: Which stage comes between childhood and adulthood?
options: Infancy
Adolescence
Old age
Childhood
activities.explanation: Adolescence is the stage between childhood and adulthood.

activities.title: Different Paces
activities.prompt: Each person passes through life's stages at the same pace.
activities.explanation: Each person passes through the stages at a different pace.

activities.title: Rapid Development
activities.prompt: Adolescence is a period of rapid ______ and development between ages 10 and 19.
activities.hint: This change can make people taller.
activities.explanation: Adolescence includes rapid growth and development.

activities.title: Preparing for Adulthood
activities.prompt: What does the body prepare for during adolescence?
options: It prepares for infancy.
It remains fully in childhood.
It prepares for old age.
It prepares for adulthood.
activities.explanation: The body prepares for adulthood during adolescence.

activities.title: Life Stage Order
activities.prompt: Put the human life stages in the order people pass through them.
activities.explanation: These stages are listed from the start of life to old age.

activities.title: A Hoarse Voice
activities.prompt: Which growth can give adolescent boys a hoarse voice?
options: Faster height growth
Body hair growth
Voice box growth
Weight growth
activities.explanation: Growth of the voice box can cause a hoarse voice in adolescent boys.

activities.prompt: Adolescence is a period of rapid growth. What change should be expected?
options: Height increase becomes more noticeable.
Height increase completely stops.
Height increase becomes less noticeable.
Height increase stays exactly the same.

This wrongly treats adolescence as a time of no growth.
This wrongly suggests growth becomes less noticeable.
This wrongly suggests the growth pattern stays unchanged.

activities.explanation: Height growth becomes more noticeable during adolescence.

activities.prompt: An adolescent boy has a hoarse voice. What likely caused this?
options: The voice box is growing.
The throat has stopped growing.
The body has finished adulthood.
Height growth has completely stopped.

This wrongly assumes that a boy's throat stops growing.
This wrongly treats adolescence as fully completed adulthood.
This wrongly assumes that height growth stops when the voice changes.

activities.explanation: A growing voice box can make an adolescent boy's voice hoarse.

activities.prompt: Two classmates begin changing at different times. What explains this best?
options: They pass through stages at different paces.
They pass through every stage together.
They pass through stages at one fixed pace.
They never change during adolescence.

Thinking they grow together wrongly assumes one shared pace.
why.They pass through stages at one fixed pa: Thinking one pace is fixed wrongly ignores individual differences.
Thinking no changes happen confuses adolescence with no growth.

activities.explanation: This matches the fact that people grow at different paces.

activities.prompt: Which activity fairly checks whether girls change height and weight?
options: Record girls' height and weight at two times.
Record only boys' height and weight once.
Ask girls about their future height changes.
Record girls' height once and guess weight.

why.Record only boys' height and weight once: Recording boys alone cannot show changes in girls.
why.Ask girls about their future height chan: Future reports do not show actual height and weight changes.
why.Record girls' height once and guess weig: Guessing weight does not provide a real weight record.

activities.explanation: Two records can show whether height and weight changed.

activities.prompt: A poster says everyone reaches adulthood at the same time. Two classmates reach adulthood at different times. What should its writer change?
options: Each person passes through stages at their own pace.
Adulthood comes before childhood for every person.
Old age begins before adulthood for every person.
Everyone must pass through stages at one pace.

why.Adulthood comes before childhood for eve: Putting adulthood first wrongly reverses childhood and adulthood.
why.Old age begins before adulthood for ever: Putting old age first wrongly reverses adulthood and old age.
why.Everyone must pass through stages at one: One shared pace wrongly ignores different growth speeds.

activities.explanation: Different times fit the fact that people pass through stages at different paces.

lessons.sceneCaption: An adolescent boy leaps energetically across a park parapet in Allahabad.

lessons.title: Reproductive Changes and Puberty

activities.prompt: What surprising changes can happen to your body as you grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Body Changes During Puberty
activities.body: Puberty brings changes inside and outside your body. These changes prepare it for adult reproduction. Boys often grow facial hair, which can become a moustache and beard. Acne is a skin condition with small reddish pimples. Secondary sexual characteristics are features that distinguish males from females. They are not directly involved in reproduction. Each person changes at a different pace.
keyPoints: Puberty prepares the body for adult reproduction.
Secondary sexual characteristics distinguish males from females.
Each person changes at a different pace.
activities.explanation: Puberty affects everyone, but the timing and nature of changes differ.

activities.prompt: Friends notice that their bodies are changing at different times. A friend worries that something is wrong.
steps: Puberty changes the body because it prepares it for adult reproduction.
The timing, nature, and extent of changes differ between people.
This occurs because each person experiences adolescence at a different pace.
So their different timing is normal and does not show a problem.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Change During Puberty
activities.prompt: The lesson says that boys often grow what?
options: Facial hair
A menstrual cycle
A period
A skin condition
activities.explanation: Boys often grow facial hair. This hair can later become a moustache and beard.

activities.title: How Long Can Menstruation Last?
activities.prompt: Menstruation may last for three to ______ days.
activities.hint: Use the longest duration given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Menstruation may last for three to seven days.

activities.prompt: Differences in the timing and amount of hair growth are normal.
activities.explanation: These differences are normal. People grow hair at different times and in different amounts.

activities.title: Match Each Change
activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each change has a clear meaning. Remember that acne is a skin condition.

activities.title: Different Cycle Lengths
activities.prompt: Which statement about menstrual cycle lengths is correct?
options: Some girls have cycles from 21–35 days.
Every cycle lasts exactly seven days.
Every cycle repeats after three days.
No cycle lasts longer than seven days.
activities.explanation: Some girls have menstrual cycles that range from 21–35 days. The other statements confuse cycle and period lengths.

activities.title: Order the Time Spans
activities.prompt: Put these time spans from shortest to longest.
activities.explanation: Menstruation may last three to seven days. Cycle lengths include 21, 28 and 30 days.

activities.prompt: Boys often grow facial hair. This hair can later become a moustache and a beard. His friend has less facial hair at the same age. Which conclusion is most likely?
options: Their facial hair can grow at different times and in different amounts.
Their facial hair must grow at exactly the same time and amount.
Less facial hair means his friend will never become an adult.
Their facial hair must grow together because all boys are alike.

why.Their facial hair must grow at exactly t: This mistake assumes that all boys grow facial hair at one pace.
why.Less facial hair means his friend will n: This mistake treats less facial hair as proof that adulthood cannot happen.
why.Their facial hair must grow together bec: This mistake assumes that being boys makes every change happen together.

activities.explanation: This is right because timing and amount of hair growth can differ normally.

activities.prompt: Puberty brings external and internal body changes. These changes prepare the body for adult reproduction. Friends begin noticing these changes at different times. What should they understand?
options: The differences are normal because each person changes at a different pace.
The differences mean one body is failing to prepare for adulthood.
The friends must have the same changes at the same time.
Only external changes matter because internal changes are not part of puberty.

why.The differences mean one body is failing: This mistake treats normal differences as signs that a body is failing.
why.The friends must have the same changes a: This mistake wrongly assumes that everyone changes at the same pace.
why.Only external changes matter because int: This mistake thinks that only outside changes count during puberty.

activities.explanation: This is right because each person experiences adolescence at a different pace.

activities.prompt: The menstrual cycle generally recurs every 28–30 days. It is more commonly called the period. A girl's cycle follows the usual 28-day pattern. When should her next period start?
options: About 28 days later, because this matches her usual cycle.
About 21 days later, because this is the shortest cycle.
About 30 days later, because this is another usual length.
About 35 days later, because every cycle must grow longer.

why.About 21 days later, because this is the: This mistake uses the shortest possible cycle instead of her usual pattern.
why.About 30 days later, because this is ano: This mistake overlooks the specific 28-day pattern she follows.
why.About 35 days later, because every cycle: This mistake assumes that each cycle must always become longer.

activities.explanation: This is right because 28 days matches the cycle she usually follows.

activities.prompt: Menstruation may last for three to seven days. A girl says her period lasted three days and must be wrong. What is the best response?
options: Three days fits the range, so it does not show a problem.
Three days is too short, because every period must last seven days.
Three days is outside the range, because the range starts after it.
Three days proves every later period must also last three days.

why.Three days is too short, because every p: This mistake assumes that every period lasts the longest possible time.
why.Three days is outside the range, because: This mistake treats the starting point of the range as outside it.
why.Three days proves every later period mus: This mistake treats one duration as a rule for every later period.

activities.explanation: This is right because three days is included in the stated range.

lessons.sceneAlt: A series of photographs tracks the same girl's pubic hair and breast development across successive ages.
lessons.sceneCaption: The Tanner scale illustrates female pubertal development through pubic hair and breast growth.

lessons.title: Emotions and Behaviour

activities.prompt: Why can growing up feel so wonderfully confusing and exciting?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Growing and changing
activities.body: Adolescence brings emotional and behavioural changes as well as physical changes. Emotions may feel exciting, confusing, or both. Many young people feel stronger emotions than they did as children. Mood swings can spark music, dance, or sports. Curiosity and excitement may give you a new viewpoint. You may also try social initiatives or explore new interests. Understanding emotions helps you make better choices and respond thoughtfully.
keyPoints: Adolescence includes emotional and behavioural changes.
Strong emotions may feel exciting or confusing.
Curiosity and excitement can give a new viewpoint.
Understanding emotions supports better choices.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how emotions, curiosity and new interests shape adolescence.

activities.prompt: A teenager feels very happy, then suddenly confused. What might the teenager do, and why?
steps: Strong emotions can make a day feel exciting or confusing, because adolescence may bring stronger feelings.
Mood swings can encourage music, dance or sports, because changing moods may lead to varied activities.
Understanding emotions helps make better choices, because it supports thoughtful responses.
The teenager can accept changing feelings and use them to guide thoughtful choices.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Kinds of change
activities.prompt: Which kinds of change does adolescence involve?
options: school, emotional and behavioural
physical, emotional and behavioural
physical, family and behavioural
school, family and emotional
activities.explanation: Adolescence involves emotional and behavioural changes as well as physical changes.

activities.title: Connect the ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its result.
activities.explanation: The lesson links each idea with its matching result.

activities.title: Exciting or confusing?
activities.prompt: Emotional changes during adolescence may be exciting, but never confusing.
activities.explanation: Emotional changes during adolescence may be exciting, confusing, or both.

activities.title: Strong feelings
activities.prompt: Adolescents often experience stronger ______ than children do.
activities.hint: Think about what feelings can feel like during adolescence.
activities.explanation: Adolescents often experience stronger emotions than children do.

activities.title: Why understand emotions?
activities.prompt: Why is understanding emotions helpful?
options: to join social initiatives supporting others
to choose and respond thoughtfully
to feel stronger and more confusing emotions
to explore new areas with real curiosity
activities.explanation: Understanding emotions helps us make better choices and respond thoughtfully.

activities.title: A thoughtful result
activities.prompt: Which result follows from understanding your emotions?
options: always feel only excitement more often
avoid every feeling that confuses you
lose interest in every new area
make better choices and respond thoughtfully
activities.explanation: Understanding emotions helps us make better choices and respond thoughtfully.

activities.prompt: A teenager feels excited one moment and confused the next. Which activity may this mood encourage?
options: Listening to music, dancing, or playing sports.
Buying school supplies and paying school bills.
Finishing homework and following every classroom rule.
Choosing books and sitting quietly all day.

why.Buying school supplies and paying school: This mistake connects mood changes only to school supplies.
why.Finishing homework and following every c: This mistake connects mood changes only to school rules.
why.Choosing books and sitting quietly all d: This mistake assumes mood changes always lead to quiet activities.

activities.explanation: Correct: Mood swings can encourage varied activities such as music, dance or sports.

activities.prompt: A school group wants to support people who need help. What may an adolescent do?
options: Join a social initiative supporting needy people.
Keep all support work to themselves.
Ask the group to stop helping people.
Wait for adults to do every helping task.

This mistake wrongly assumes adolescents avoid helping work.
This mistake wrongly assumes adolescents discourage helping work.
why.Wait for adults to do every helping task: This mistake wrongly assumes adolescents never join support work.

activities.explanation: Correct: Adolescents may join social initiatives that support needy and disadvantaged people.

activities.prompt: A teenager wants to act when angry. What can understanding emotions help the teenager do?
options: Pause and respond thoughtfully to the situation.
Respond angrily without thinking about feelings.
Make a choice without noticing any emotions.
Wait for the feeling to make every decision.

why.Respond angrily without thinking about f: This mistake treats strong feelings as a reason for thoughtless action.
why.Make a choice without noticing any emoti: This mistake ignores the help that understanding emotions gives.
why.Wait for the feeling to make every decis: This mistake gives emotions all control over choices.

activities.explanation: Correct: Understanding emotions helps us make better choices and respond thoughtfully.

activities.prompt: Claim: Every adolescent feels and acts in exactly the same way. Why is this claim flawed?
options: Each person's adolescence is a unique journey.
Every adolescent must join social initiatives.
Every adolescent must feel stronger emotions.
Every adolescent must choose the same activities.

why.Every adolescent must join social initia: This mistake turns one possible activity into a rule for everyone.
why.Every adolescent must feel stronger emot: This mistake turns one common change into identical feelings for everyone.
why.Every adolescent must choose the same ac: This mistake assumes everyone chooses the same activities.

activities.explanation: Correct: Adolescence is a unique journey for every person.

lessons.sceneAlt: A teenager skates in Enugu State, Nigeria as a fun way to exercise and for recreation.
lessons.sceneCaption: A teenager enjoys recreational skating in Enugu, Nigeria.

lessons.title: Food and Personal Hygiene

activities.prompt: Why does your body need special care as you grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Food, Cleanliness and Care
activities.body: Your body changes during adolescence. A nutritious diet helps you grow. Proteins and carbohydrates help growth and performance. Your body also needs fats, vitamins and minerals. A deficiency means not getting enough of something needed. Body hygiene means keeping clean and can protect you from infections. Menstrual hygiene means care during menstruation. Use sanitary pads and dispose of them safely. Support menstrual hygiene and reduce stigma, or shame.
keyPoints: Good food supports growth and performance.
Keeping clean can protect you from infections.
Sanitary pads help maintain menstrual hygiene.
activities.explanation: Good food, body care and menstrual hygiene work together for your health.

activities.prompt: An adolescent's diet is missing iron and vitamin B12. What should they do, and why?
steps: Their body changes during adolescence, so good nutrition matters.
Proper growth and good performance need proteins and carbohydrates.
The body also needs adequate fats, vitamins and minerals.
Missing iron or vitamin B12 can cause blood-related problems, so a nutritious diet is needed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why is a nutritious diet very important during adolescence?
options: The body changes
Growth needs finish
Vitamin needs vanish
Mineral needs stop
activities.explanation: The body changes during adolescence, so a nutritious diet is very important.

activities.prompt: Proper growth and good performance need proteins and carbohydrates.
activities.explanation: Proteins and carbohydrates help with proper growth and good performance.

activities.prompt: The body also needs adequate fats, ______ and minerals.
activities.hint: Name one thing needed along with fats and minerals.
activities.explanation: The body needs fats, vitamins and minerals in adequate amounts.

activities.prompt: What can a deficiency of iron or vitamin B12 cause?
options: Greater need for hygiene
Less need for vitamins
More need for minerals
Blood-related health problems
activities.explanation: A deficiency of iron or vitamin B12 can cause blood-related health problems.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct use or purpose.
pairs: Wrap in newspaper and put inside a dustbin
Provide pads free or at a reduced price
Improve adolescent health, including menstrual health and hygiene
Provide affordable biodegradable pads through Jan Aushadhi Kendras
activities.explanation: Each item has a clear use or purpose in supporting menstrual hygiene.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for disposing of a used sanitary pad in order.
activities.explanation: Used sanitary pads should be wrapped in newspaper and put inside a dustbin.

activities.prompt: We should feel ashamed to talk about using sanitary pads.
activities.explanation: We should reduce stigma and support menstrual hygiene.

activities.prompt: Which statement about menstrual hygiene support is correct?
options: RKSK supplies biodegradable pads at Jan Aushadhi Kendras.
Suvidha gives pads free or at a reduced price.
Menstrual Hygiene Scheme gives free or reduced-price pads.
Suvidha mainly aims to improve adolescent health.
activities.explanation: The Menstrual Hygiene Scheme provides pads free or at a reduced price.

activities.prompt: An adolescent is growing, but their diet lacks proteins and carbohydrates. What may happen?
options: Proper growth and good performance may not get full support.
Proper growth may get support, but good performance may not.
Good performance may get support, but proper growth may not.
Both may get support, because proteins and carbohydrates are optional.

why.Proper growth may get support, but good: This mistake thinks growth needs support but performance does not.
why.Good performance may get support, but pr: This mistake thinks performance needs support but growth does not.
why.Both may get support, because proteins a: This mistake thinks proteins and carbohydrates are not needed.

activities.explanation: This is right because growth and performance need proteins and carbohydrates.

activities.prompt: A student maintains proper body hygiene. What may be the result?
options: Potential infections may be less likely.
Potential infections will certainly disappear.
Only menstrual comfort may improve.
Blood-related problems may occur.

why.Potential infections will certainly disa: This mistake thinks protection means every infection must disappear.
This mistake thinks body hygiene only affects menstrual comfort.
This mistake mixes up hygiene with iron and vitamin B12 deficiency.

activities.explanation: This is right because body hygiene can protect against potential infections.
