lessons.title: Fitness, Friends and Safe Choices

activities.prompt: How can we stay fit, choose wisely, and help our friends online?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making Wise Choices
activities.body: Exercise keeps your body and mind healthy. Physical activity builds stamina, helping you keep active, and boosts your mood. Be polite and respect others. Adolescents, or young people, may feel attracted to peers and copy their behaviour. Use online platforms responsibly. Ask parents and teachers for guidance. Do not join cyberbullying. People being bullied should seek help. Be careful with pictures and personal information. Say ‘NO’ firmly to harmful substances.
keyPoints: Exercise keeps the body and mind healthy.
Online platforms need responsible use and guidance.
Refuse harmful substances firmly and confidently.
activities.explanation: Good choices support your health, respect and well-being.

activities.prompt: A student receives hurtful messages online and is asked to keep them secret. What should the student do, and why?
steps: The messages use digital devices to harass the student, so this is cyberbullying.
The student should handle it wisely because online harassment can harm well-being.
The student should seek help from parents or teachers because their guidance is useful.
Therefore, the student should tell a parent or teacher instead of keeping the messages secret.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Healthy Habit
activities.prompt: Which habit keeps your body and mind fit and healthy?
options: Regular exercise
Careful sharing
Polite behaviour
Responsible platform use
activities.explanation: Regular exercise keeps your body and mind fit and healthy. You chose a healthy habit.

activities.title: Positive Platform Use
activities.prompt: Which action can help you use online platforms positively?
options: Give personal information to strangers
Post pictures carelessly
Ask for guidance
Harass someone online
activities.explanation: Guidance from elders and teachers helps you use online platforms positively.

activities.title: Energy for Activity
activities.prompt: Physical activity builds ______ and boosts your mood.
activities.hint: Energy for keeping active.
activities.explanation: Physical activity builds stamina. It also boosts your mood.

activities.title: Match the Safety Choices
activities.prompt: Match each safety choice with the correct idea.
pairs: Seek help from parents and teachers
Be careful when sharing with strangers
activities.explanation: Cyberbullying happens online. Bullied people should seek help and share information carefully.

activities.title: Help for a Bullied Person
activities.prompt: A classmate sends harmful messages online. What should the bullied person do?
options: Join the messages
Ask for help
Share personal details
Keep it secret
activities.explanation: Cyberbullying uses digital devices or platforms to harass. Handle it wisely and seek help.

activities.title: Harmful Substances
activities.prompt: Which set contains only harmful substances?
options: Polite, respectful and confident
Guidance, elders and teachers
Tobacco, gutka and alcohol
Physical activity, stamina and mood
activities.explanation: Tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedi, alcohol and illegal drugs harm health. They can also be addictive.

activities.prompt: A student exercises regularly instead of sitting still all day. What will likely happen?
options: The body and mind stay fit and healthy.
The student gets tired more easily during daily activity.
The student needs less physical activity after exercising.
The student feels worse after every active lesson.

why.The student gets tired more easily durin: This wrongly assumes that exercise reduces stamina instead of building it.
why.The student needs less physical activity: This wrongly assumes that exercise removes the need for future activity.
why.The student feels worse after every acti: This wrongly assumes that exercise harms the body and mind.

activities.explanation: This is right because regular exercise keeps the body and mind healthy.

activities.prompt: A student changes an answer because a liked classmate changed it. Why might this happen?
options: The student wants to copy the liked classmate's behaviour.
The student wants to disagree with the liked classmate.
The student learned the answer from a teacher instead.
The student wants the classmate to change the answer again.

why.The student wants to disagree with the l: This mistakes peer attraction for wanting to oppose the classmate.
why.The student learned the answer from a te: This wrongly credits a teacher although the scenario shows peer influence.
why.The student wants the classmate to chang: This wrongly assumes the student wants another change instead of copying.

activities.explanation: Peer attraction can make an adolescent mimic the behaviour of a liked classmate.

activities.prompt: An online stranger asks for your school name and daily routine. What should you do?
options: Keep details private and ask an adult for help.
Share details because the stranger seems friendly.
Share only your school name as a fair test.
Post details so the stranger can contact you.

why.Share details because the stranger seems: This mistakes a friendly stranger for a safe person.
why.Share only your school name as a fair te: This wrongly assumes that sharing only some personal information is safe.
why.Post details so the stranger can contact: This wrongly thinks posting details will protect you from strangers.

activities.explanation: Being careful with personal information protects you when talking with strangers.

activities.prompt: You keep receiving insulting messages from an online classmate. What is the wisest choice?
options: Tell a parent or teacher and handle it wisely.
Insult the classmate back for every message.
Keep every message secret and hope it stops.
Ask the classmate to insult you less kindly.

why.Insult the classmate back for every mess: This mistakes fighting back for handling cyberbullying wisely.
why.Keep every message secret and hope it st: This avoids the help that parents and teachers can provide.
why.Ask the classmate to insult you less kin: This tries to fix harassment by joking with the harasser.

activities.explanation: The messages use online tools to harass you, so they are cyberbullying.

activities.prompt: You want to join an online platform but feel unsure. What should you do?
options: Ask an elder or teacher before using the platform.
Join it at once without asking anyone.
Follow every prompt, even harmful ones.
Invite strangers to join you there.

This wrongly assumes that no guidance is needed.
This mistakes following others for using a platform responsibly.
This ignores strangers and the need for responsible platform use.

activities.explanation: This is right because elder and teacher guidance helps use platforms positively.

activities.prompt: At a gathering, someone offers you alcohol and laughs when you refuse. What should you do?
options: Say no firmly, even if the person laughs.
Try it once so the person stops asking.
Accept it to stay with the group.
Ask for it again to make a better choice.

This wrongly assumes that trying it once will make it safe.
This wrongly treats group acceptance as more important than health.
why.Ask for it again to make a better choice: This wrongly assumes that asking again can make a harmful substance safe.

activities.explanation: This is right because firm refusal helps you avoid harmful and addictive substances.

lessons.title: Hormones and Responsible Growing

activities.prompt: What are hormones secretly helping your body do as you grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Hormones Help Your Body
activities.body: Hormones are chemicals produced inside your body. They work in different body parts. The brain sends signals, and hormones are released when needed. They help control growth and development. Some also affect mood and behaviour. Puberty changes prepare your body for adult reproduction. During adolescence, seeking support and making healthy choices help you face the future.
keyPoints: Hormones are chemicals produced inside the body.
They help regulate growth and development.
Support and healthy decisions help during adolescence.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects body changes with support and healthy choices.

activities.prompt: A young person feels upset and argues with friends during adolescence. Why might this happen, and what can help?
steps: Adolescence brings physical, biological, and emotional changes.
Hormones are released at suitable times because the brain sends signals.
Some hormones influence mood and behaviour, so the feelings may change.
They should seek support and guidance when making healthy choices.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Growing Through Adolescence
activities.body: Adolescence is the period when you change from childhood to adulthood. It generally begins around age 10 and usually lasts until age 19. During this time, significant physical, biological and emotional changes occur. Puberty includes external and internal changes. These changes prepare your body for adult reproduction. Asking for support and making healthy decisions help you face the future.
keyPoints: Adolescence is a period of change.
Puberty includes internal and external changes.
Support and healthy decisions help you face the future.
activities.explanation: Adolescence brings physical, biological and emotional changes.

activities.prompt: Hormones are chemicals produced inside our bodies.
activities.explanation: Hormones are chemicals made inside the body.

activities.prompt: What mainly causes menstruation and other signs of puberty?
options: Hormones
Body signals only
Brain signals only
Growth charts
activities.explanation: Hormones mainly cause menstruation and other signs of puberty.

activities.prompt: Hormones are chemicals that are produced ______ our bodies.
activities.hint: Where are they produced?
activities.explanation: Hormones are produced inside the body.

activities.prompt: Which action can help you during adolescence?
options: Seeking support and guidance
Keeping all changes to yourself
Making only convenient decisions
Waiting for adulthood to begin
activities.explanation: Support and guidance, together with healthy decisions, help you face the future.

activities.prompt: Put these life stages in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Adolescence is the period of change from childhood to adulthood.

activities.prompt: Puberty has only external changes and prepares the body for reproduction.
activities.explanation: Puberty includes internal changes as well as external changes. It prepares the body for adult reproduction.

activities.prompt: Some hormones influence mood and behaviour. A child suddenly cries and argues. What may explain this?
options: Hormone changes may be affecting the child's feelings.
The brain has stopped sending suitable signals.
The body has finished all childhood changes.
Only physical changes can affect a person's feelings.

why.The brain has stopped sending suitable s: This wrongly assumes the brain no longer sends release signals.
why.The body has finished all childhood chan: This wrongly treats the end of adolescence as the end of all body changes.
why.Only physical changes can affect a perso: This wrongly rules out hormone effects on feelings.

activities.explanation: This is right because some hormones influence mood and behaviour.

activities.prompt: Hormones are chemicals made inside our bodies. The brain sends a signal before release. Why does this happen?
options: The signal helps release it at a suitable time.
The signal makes it release at any time.
The signal stops it from ever being released.
The signal removes all other hormones.

This wrongly ignores the need for a suitable release time.
why.The signal stops it from ever being rele: This wrongly thinks a brain signal can block every release.
This wrongly assumes one signal removes all other hormones.

activities.explanation: This is right because hormones are released at suitable times after brain signals.

activities.prompt: Menstruation and other puberty signs are mainly caused by hormones. Puberty includes internal and external changes. What explains both ideas?
options: Hormones inside the body cause signs and regulate development.
Hormones outside the body cause signs and regulate development.
Only external changes cause signs inside the body.
Internal changes happen without any hormone effects.

why.Hormones outside the body cause signs an: This wrongly places hormone production outside the body.
why.Only external changes cause signs inside: This wrongly ignores that hormones also affect internal changes.
why.Internal changes happen without any horm: This wrongly treats internal changes as unrelated to hormones.

activities.explanation: This fits because hormones are produced inside the body and regulate development.

activities.prompt: Hormones regulate growth, and some influence mood. During adolescence, a young person grows and feels moody. What explains this?
options: Hormones regulate growth and can influence mood.
Hormones regulate growth but never influence mood.
Hormones influence mood but do not regulate growth.
Only physical changes can influence a person's mood.

why.Hormones regulate growth but never influ: This wrongly assumes hormones never affect mood.
why.Hormones influence mood but do not regul: This wrongly assumes hormones do not regulate growth.
why.Only physical changes can influence a pe: This wrongly says physical changes are the only cause of mood.

activities.explanation: This is right because hormones regulate growth and some influence mood.

lessons.sceneCaption: An adolescent boy leaps energetically across a park parapet in Allahabad.

activities.context: A student is in adolescence, the period between childhood and adulthood. The student is growing rapidly, and an increase in height has become more noticeable. Because the body is preparing for adulthood, the student knows that development may continue at a pace that is different from other people. The student notices hair growing in different parts of the body. For an adolescent boy in the same situation, growth of the voice box may make his voice hoarse.
activities.prompt: Why has the student's increase in height become more noticeable?
options: The student is passing through a stage of rapid growth and development.
The student has already completed the stage between childhood and adulthood.
The student's voice box has recently grown.
The student's hair is growing in different body areas.

why.The student has already completed the st: Adolescence comes before adulthood, not after it.
why.The student's voice box has recently gro: Voice-box growth relates mainly to changes in a boy's voice.
why.The student's hair is growing in differe: Hair growth does not directly explain a more noticeable increase in height.

activities.explanation: Adolescence involves rapid growth and development.

activities.context: A student is in adolescence, the period between childhood and adulthood. The student is growing rapidly, and an increase in height has become more noticeable. Because the body is preparing for adulthood, the student knows that development may continue at a pace that is different from other people. The student notices hair growing in different parts of the body. For an adolescent boy in the same situation, growth of the voice box may make his voice hoarse.
activities.prompt: If an adolescent boy's voice box did not grow, which change would be less likely to happen because of that change?
options: His voice becoming hoarse
His height increasing
His body preparing for adulthood
His hair growing in different body areas

why.His height increasing: Height can become more noticeable during adolescence.
why.His body preparing for adulthood: The body prepares for adulthood during adolescence.
why.His hair growing in different body areas: Boys and girls grow hair in different body areas.

activities.explanation: Voice-box growth can give adolescent boys a hoarse voice.

activities.prompt: Explain why adolescence is considered a period of rapid growth and development.
activities.answer: Adolescence is the stage between childhood and adulthood, lasting from 10 to 19 years of age. During this period, the body prepares for adulthood. Height growth becomes especially noticeable, while changes in height, weight, and hair growth also occur. These changes show why adolescence is a time of rapid growth and development.
points: Adolescence comes between childhood and adulthood.
It lasts from 10 to 19 years of age.
The body prepares for adulthood during this stage.
Height, weight, and hair growth undergo changes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During adolescence, a boy notices that facial hair is beginning to grow, while small reddish pimples appear on his skin. A girl in the same class finds that her menstrual cycle generally comes around every 28–30 days, although some girls have cycles lasting 21–35 days. Their bodily changes are happening at different rates, and both are preparing for adult reproduction.
activities.prompt: What is most likely to happen as the boy’s facial hair continues to develop?
options: His facial hair may later form a moustache and beard.
His facial hair will probably vanish before adulthood.
The new pimples will be replaced by a moustache and beard.
His facial hair will develop at precisely the same time as the girl’s menstruation.

why.His facial hair will probably vanish bef: Facial hair does not normally disappear.
why.The new pimples will be replaced by a mo: Pimples and hair growth are separate changes.
why.His facial hair will develop at precisel: Different changes can occur at different times.

activities.explanation: Facial hair often develops further in this way.

activities.context: During adolescence, a boy notices that facial hair is beginning to grow, while small reddish pimples appear on his skin. A girl in the same class finds that her menstrual cycle generally comes around every 28–30 days, although some girls have cycles lasting 21–35 days. Their bodily changes are happening at different rates, and both are preparing for adult reproduction.
activities.prompt: If the boy’s changes appear earlier than the girl’s, what is the best conclusion?
options: Both can be experiencing normal adolescence at different paces.
The earlier changes show that the boy is not experiencing adolescence normally.
Both must have exactly the same amount and timing of changes.
The girl must not be experiencing puberty until the boy finishes.

why.The earlier changes show that the boy is: Different timing does not mean the boy is abnormal.
why.Both must have exactly the same amount a: Changes in timing and amount can differ.
why.The girl must not be experiencing pubert: One person need not finish before another begins.

activities.explanation: Each person experiences adolescence at a different pace.

activities.prompt: Explain why the timing, nature, and extent of adolescence changes can differ between people.
activities.answer: Adolescence does not follow one timetable for everybody. Its timing, nature, and extent can differ from person to person, and each person goes through it at a different pace. That is why one classmate may notice puberty changes earlier, later, or in a different amount from another.
points: Changes can differ in timing.
Changes can differ in nature.
Changes can differ in extent.
Each person has a different pace.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An adolescent notices that feelings change quickly and can be exciting, confusing, or both. The adolescent enjoys music and dance, sometimes joins social initiatives helping people who are needy or disadvantaged, and becomes deeply interested in a new area. Curiosity and excitement open a different way of looking at things. Before acting, the adolescent tries to understand the emotions involved, while remembering that every person's journey is unique.
activities.prompt: If the adolescent understands their emotions before responding to a difficult situation, what is the most likely result?
options: The adolescent will choose more wisely and respond with care.
The adolescent will choose less wisely because the feelings become confusing.
The adolescent will lose interest in exploring new areas.
The adolescent will have exactly the same emotional journey as everyone else.

why.The adolescent will choose less wisely b: Confusing feelings do not necessarily make choices worse.
why.The adolescent will lose interest in exp: Understanding emotions does not remove interest in new areas.
why.The adolescent will have exactly the sam: Adolescence is unique for every person, not identical for everyone.

activities.explanation: Understanding emotions supports better choices and thoughtful responses.

activities.context: An adolescent notices that feelings change quickly and can be exciting, confusing, or both. The adolescent enjoys music and dance, sometimes joins social initiatives helping people who are needy or disadvantaged, and becomes deeply interested in a new area. Curiosity and excitement open a different way of looking at things. Before acting, the adolescent tries to understand the emotions involved, while remembering that every person's journey is unique.
activities.prompt: After becoming deeply interested in a new area, what is a likely development for the adolescent?
options: Heightened curiosity and excitement may provide a new viewpoint.
The adolescent's viewpoint will remain unchanged because the interest is temporary.
The adolescent will lose curiosity because every journey is unique.
Stronger emotions will always cause confusion about the new area.

why.The adolescent's viewpoint will remain u: A deeper interest can develop alongside a changed viewpoint.
why.The adolescent will lose curiosity becau: Uniqueness does not prevent curiosity or interest.
why.Stronger emotions will always cause conf: Strong emotions may be exciting, confusing, or both.

activities.explanation: Heightened curiosity and excitement give adolescents a new viewpoint.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between emotional changes during adolescence and mood swings.
activities.answer: Emotional changes during adolescence may be exciting, confusing, or both, and adolescents often experience stronger emotions than children do. Mood swings are changes in feelings that can encourage varied activities such as music, dance, or sports.
points: Emotional changes may be exciting or confusing.
Adolescents often experience stronger emotions.
Mood swings can encourage varied activities.
Examples include music, dance, and sports.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An adolescent girl is growing and wants to do well in school. Her meals include protein and carbohydrate foods, but she wonders whether her diet needs other nutrients. She uses sanitary pads and feels uncomfortable when people joke about them. After using a pad, she wants to know the correct disposal method and how she can encourage others to support menstrual hygiene.
activities.prompt: What should she do next with her diet?
options: Add adequate fats, vitamins and minerals to the protein and carbohydrate foods in her diet.
Replace her protein and carbohydrate foods with fats, vitamins and minerals only.
Add more protein and carbohydrates, but treat fats, vitamins and minerals as unnecessary.
Keep only iron or vitamin B12 and regard all other nutrients as unnecessary.

why.Replace her protein and carbohydrate foo: This wrongly removes nutrients needed for growth and performance.
why.Add more protein and carbohydrates, but: Growth and performance need proteins and carbohydrates, while other nutrients are also necessary.
why.Keep only iron or vitamin B12 and regard: Iron and vitamin B12 do not replace the other needed nutrients.

activities.explanation: This gives her all the nutrient groups her body needs.

activities.context: An adolescent girl is growing and wants to do well in school. Her meals include protein and carbohydrate foods, but she wonders whether her diet needs other nutrients. She uses sanitary pads and feels uncomfortable when people joke about them. After using a pad, she wants to know the correct disposal method and how she can encourage others to support menstrual hygiene.
activities.prompt: After using a sanitary pad at home, what should she do next?
options: Wrap the used pad in newspaper and put it inside a dustbin.
Put the used pad directly into the dustbin without wrapping it.
Keep the used pad wrapped in newspaper for reuse.
Leave the used pad in the bathroom for someone else to handle.

why.Put the used pad directly into the dustb: Wrapping the pad in newspaper is required before disposal.
why.Keep the used pad wrapped in newspaper f: A used pad should be disposed of rather than reused.
why.Leave the used pad in the bathroom for s: The correct method is to wrap the pad and place it inside a dustbin.

activities.explanation: This is the correct method for disposing of used pads.

activities.prompt: Explain why a nutritious diet is important during adolescence, and what could happen if iron or vitamin B12 is lacking.
activities.answer: A nutritious diet is important because the body changes during adolescence. Proteins and carbohydrates support proper growth and good performance, while the body also needs adequate fats, vitamins and minerals. If iron or vitamin B12 is lacking, adolescents can develop blood-related health problems. Thus, a nutritious diet must include all these needed nutrients.
points: The body changes during adolescence.
Proteins and carbohydrates support growth and performance.
Adequate fats, vitamins and minerals are also needed.
An iron or vitamin B12 deficiency can cause blood-related health problems.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student began exercising regularly with classmates. Soon, she felt fitter, had more stamina and felt happier. When peers asked her to post a personal picture online to strangers, she remembered her parents’ advice to be careful and refused. Later, a classmate posted an insulting message about her. She sought help from her parents and teacher instead of staying silent.
activities.prompt: Why did the student become fitter, gain stamina, and feel happier after beginning regular exercise?
options: The exercise routine improved her physical fitness and boosted her mood because activity supports both body and mind.
Her classmates’ encouragement, rather than exercise, produced her stamina and happiness.
The online picture request made her physically fit by giving her more energy.
Her parents’ advice about online pictures improved her physical endurance.

why.Her classmates’ encouragement, rather th: Physical activity builds stamina and boosts mood.
why.The online picture request made her phys: Peers’ encouragement is not stated to cause these benefits.
why.Her parents’ advice about online picture: Advice about pictures does not improve physical fitness or stamina.

activities.explanation: Regular exercise keeps the body and mind fit and healthy.

activities.context: A student began exercising regularly with classmates. Soon, she felt fitter, had more stamina and felt happier. When peers asked her to post a personal picture online to strangers, she remembered her parents’ advice to be careful and refused. Later, a classmate posted an insulting message about her. She sought help from her parents and teacher instead of staying silent.
activities.prompt: After receiving an insulting message online, what is the wisest action for the student to take?
options: Tell her parents and teacher about the harassment so that they can help her handle it wisely.
Keep the message secret because adults cannot help with online bullying.
Insult the classmate back because cyberbullying requires an equal response.
Forward the message to a wider group so that the incident appears more serious.

why.Keep the message secret because adults c: Parents and teachers can provide guidance and help.
why.Insult the classmate back because cyberb: Support is available, so secrecy is not the best response.
why.Forward the message to a wider group so: Insulting or spreading the message continues the harmful behaviour.

activities.explanation: The message is cyberbullying because it uses an online platform to harass her.

activities.prompt: How does regular physical activity affect a person’s fitness, stamina, and mood?
activities.answer: Regular exercise keeps the body and mind fit and healthy. Physical activity builds stamina and boosts mood. Therefore, exercise supports the body’s fitness, improves physical endurance, and helps the mind feel positive. These benefits show why regular activity supports both physical and mental well-being.
points: Keeps the body and mind fit and healthy
Builds physical stamina
Boosts mood
Supports overall well-being
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student notices that menstruation has started and that her body and feelings are changing. She wonders what is causing these changes and whether she should try to handle everything alone. A teacher explains that hormones are chemicals produced inside the body and that they help regulate growth and development. The student talks with a trusted adult about making healthy decisions and preparing for the future.
activities.prompt: If signals from the brain reached the body at unsuitable times, what could happen?
options: Some hormones might be released at unsuitable times.
Hormones would no longer be chemicals produced inside the body.
Hormones would immediately stop regulating growth and development.
All body changes caused by hormones would stop forever.

why.Hormones would no longer be chemicals pr: Changing the timing of signals would not change what hormones are.
why.Hormones would immediately stop regulati: Hormones help regulate growth and development.
why.All body changes caused by hormones woul: Unsuitable signals would not necessarily stop every hormonal effect.

activities.explanation: Hormones are released at suitable times in response to brain signals.

activities.context: A student notices that menstruation has started and that her body and feelings are changing. She wonders what is causing these changes and whether she should try to handle everything alone. A teacher explains that hormones are chemicals produced inside the body and that they help regulate growth and development. The student talks with a trusted adult about making healthy decisions and preparing for the future.
activities.prompt: What should the student do when changes make her feel unsure about the future?
options: Talking with someone for support can help her make healthy choices and face what lies ahead.
She should keep all decisions private because asking for help can stop healthy choices.
She needs support only after adolescence has ended.
Support is useful for physical changes but not for emotional changes.

why.She should keep all decisions private be: Private decision-making may leave her without needed guidance.
why.She needs support only after adolescence: Adolescence involves significant changes, so support can be useful during it.
why.Support is useful for physical changes b: Support can help with physical, biological and emotional changes.

activities.explanation: Seeking support and guidance helps with healthy decision-making.

activities.context: A student notices that menstruation has started and that her body and feelings are changing. She wonders what is causing these changes and whether she should try to handle everything alone. A teacher explains that hormones are chemicals produced inside the body and that they help regulate growth and development. The student talks with a trusted adult about making healthy decisions and preparing for the future.
activities.prompt: Why are menstruation and other signs of puberty connected with preparing for adult reproduction?
options: Puberty brings external and internal changes that prepare the body for adult reproduction.
Puberty changes only outward appearance because internal changes are unimportant.
Puberty prepares the body by ending all physical and emotional changes.
Puberty prepares the body for adult life but has no connection with adult reproduction.

why.Puberty changes only outward appearance: Puberty involves significant physical and biological changes.
why.Puberty prepares the body by ending all: Puberty does not end all physical and emotional changes.
why.Puberty prepares the body for adult life: The stated purpose of puberty includes preparation for adult reproduction.

activities.explanation: Puberty prepares the body through external and internal changes.

activities.title: Place in the life cycle
activities.prompt: Which stage comes directly before adolescence?
options: Infancy
Childhood
Adulthood
Old age
activities.explanation: Adolescence is the stage between childhood and adulthood.

activities.title: A different pace
activities.prompt: Everyone passes through adolescence at exactly the same age.
activities.explanation: Each person passes through life stages and experiences adolescence at a different pace.

activities.title: Changing emotions
activities.prompt: What may emotions feel like during adolescence?
options: Always calm and predictable
Exciting, confusing, or both
Only pleasant and unchanging
Boring and very predictable
activities.explanation: Adolescent emotions may be exciting, confusing, or both.

activities.title: Connect the terms
activities.prompt: Match each description with its correct lesson term.
pairs: tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedi, alcohol and illegal drugs
activities.explanation: Each pair links a description to the correct lesson term.

activities.title: The menstrual cycle
activities.prompt: The menstrual cycle generally recurs every ______ days.
activities.hint: Recall the usual length of the menstrual cycle.
activities.explanation: It is also commonly called the period.

activities.title: Stages of human life
activities.prompt: Put the stages of human life in order.
activities.explanation: The given order shows how people move through the stages of human life.

activities.title: Puberty and reproduction
activities.prompt: Secondary sexual characteristics are directly involved in reproduction.

chapters.title: Heat Transfer in Nature
chapters.summary: In this chapter: heat, climate and the start of conduction; conduction, insulators and warm homes; convection and land and sea breezes; radiation and heat transfer together.

lessons.title: Heat, Climate and the Start of Conduction

activities.prompt: Why can two places feel so different in the same winter?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Heat Around Us
activities.body: The Sun is the main source of heat and light for us on Earth. Kerala is nearer the equator than Sikkim. The climate near the equator is generally hot. Heat moves from hotter parts to colder parts by conduction. A heated particle passes heat to its neighbour. Particles keep their positions. Heat mainly travels by conduction in solids. Metals conduct heat well, so they are used for cooking utensils.
keyPoints: Heat moves from hotter to colder parts.
A heated particle passes heat to its neighbour.
Particles stay in their positions.
activities.explanation: You have learnt how heat travels through solids.

activities.prompt: A metal cooking utensil sits in hot food. Why does its cooler handle become warm?
steps: Metals are good conductors of heat, so cooking utensils use them.
Conduction moves heat from the hotter food to the colder handle.
Heated particles pass heat to their neighbours without changing positions.
Therefore, the handle warms as heat travels through the metal.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Winter in Kerala
activities.prompt: How is winter in Kerala different from winter in Gangtok?
options: Kerala is warmer and more humid.
Gangtok is warmer and more humid.
Kerala is colder and drier.
Gangtok is colder and drier.
activities.explanation: Winter in Kerala is comparatively warm and humid compared with Gangtok.

activities.title: Join Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct answer.
pairs: Main source of heat and light
activities.explanation: Great matching! These ideas are all about heat and climate.

activities.title: What Is Conduction?
activities.prompt: In which direction does heat move during conduction?
options: From a hotter part to a colder part.
From a colder part to a hotter part.
From a heavier part to a lighter part.
From a larger part to a smaller part.
activities.explanation: Conduction moves heat from a hotter part of an object to a colder part.

activities.title: Heat Travelling Through Neighbours
activities.prompt: Put these steps of conduction in the correct order.
items: It passes heat to its neighbour
Heat passes to the next neighbour
activities.explanation: Heat keeps moving between neighbours while the particles stay in place.

activities.title: Why Use Metal Utensils?
activities.prompt: Why are metals used for cooking utensils?
options: Because they conduct heat well.
Because they keep food away from heat.
Because they move heat away from all food.
Because they stay at one fixed temperature.
activities.explanation: Metals are good conductors of heat, so they are used for cooking utensils.

activities.prompt: Kerala is nearer the equator than Sikkim. What climate is generally expected near Kerala?
options: Kerala will generally have a hot climate.
Sikkim will generally have a hot climate.
Both places will always have the same climate.
Kerala will always have a cold climate.

why.Sikkim will generally have a hot climate: This puts the equatorial place in the wrong location.
why.Both places will always have the same cl: This treats similar climates as proof of identical climates.
This turns a generally hot climate into always cold.

activities.explanation: Climates near the equator are generally hot.

activities.prompt: A metal cooking utensil touches hot food. What happens to heat in the utensil?
options: Heat moves from the hot food towards the cooler part.
Heat moves from the cool part towards the hot food.
Heat stays only in the food and enters no utensil.
Cold moves from the utensil into the hot food.

why.Heat moves from the cool part towards th: This reverses the direction of heat during conduction.
why.Heat stays only in the food and enters n: This ignores that metals conduct heat and allow heating.
why.Cold moves from the utensil into the hot: This confuses heat moving with cold moving.

activities.explanation: Conduction carries heat from hotter parts to colder parts.

activities.prompt: Ravi says particles must move to carry heat. Which observation shows his claim is wrong?
options: Heat passes while every particle keeps its position.
Heat passes while every particle moves to a new position.
Cold particles move towards the hotter part of the metal.
The hot part moves completely into the colder part.

why.Heat passes while every particle moves t: This wrongly assumes particles must move during conduction.
why.Cold particles move towards the hotter p: This confuses heat transfer with movement of cold particles.
why.The hot part moves completely into the c: This confuses heat transfer with movement of a hot part.

activities.explanation: Particles pass heat to neighbours without changing positions.

activities.prompt: One metal utensil is tested for heat conduction. Which test is best?
options: Heat one end, then check whether the other end warms.
Place both ends in hot food, then check the middle.
Leave it in sunlight, then check whether the middle warms.
Put cold food beside it, then check whether it cools.

why.Place both ends in hot food, then check: Heating both ends hides whether heat travels along the solid.
why.Leave it in sunlight, then check whether: This tests sunlight's heating, not conduction along the solid.
why.Put cold food beside it, then check whet: This tests cooling, not heat travelling through the solid.

activities.explanation: This directly tests conduction along a solid metal.

lessons.title: Conduction, Insulators and Warm Homes

activities.prompt: Why do some homes feel cozier than others?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Heat, Conductors and Insulators
activities.body: Heat can move through metals easily. Materials that allow this are called conductors. Glass and wood stop heat passing easily, so they are insulators. Air also slows heat moving through it. Woollen fabric traps air, and layers of blankets trap air too. Trapped air reduces heat loss. Hollow bricks trap air. Wood-and-mud layers prevent heat loss and keep houses warm.
keyPoints: Metals conduct heat easily.
Glass, wood and trapped air slow heat transfer.
Air is trapped in fabrics, blankets and hollow bricks.
Wood and mud layers reduce heat loss.
activities.explanation: Trapped air and insulating materials help homes stay comfortable.

activities.prompt: Four pins are fixed to a metal strip. What happens when it is heated?
steps: The end nearest the candle gets heat first.
Heat travels along the metal strip from that heated end.
The nearest pin's wax melts first because it receives heat first.
Melted wax releases each pin, giving the order I, II, III, IV.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which material lets heat pass through it easily?
options: Glass
Metal
Woollen fabric
Mud
activities.explanation: Metals allow heat to pass through them easily, so they are good conductors.

activities.prompt: Why does the nearest pin fall first?
options: Heat melts the wax
Heat moves the candle
Heat makes metal hollow
Heat fills the strip
activities.explanation: The nearest pin falls first because heat melts the wax holding it.

activities.prompt: Why do two thin blankets keep more warmth than one thick blanket?
options: Air is trapped between them
Metal is trapped between them
Glass is trapped between them
Wax is trapped between them
activities.explanation: Two thin blankets trap air between them. This keeps more warmth.

activities.prompt: Why do hollow bricks help houses in very hot and cold climates?
options: They trap air
They trap metal
They trap wax
They trap glass
activities.explanation: Hollow bricks trap air, which helps houses stay warm in winter and cool in summer.

activities.prompt: Match each material or part to its role.
pairs: Carries heat from its heated end
activities.explanation: Each choice describes a material or layer that moves heat or reduces heat loss.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for the nearest pin in order.
items: The wax holding the pin melts
activities.explanation: Heat moves from the heated end. It melts the wax, so the nearest pin falls first.

activities.prompt: A hot drink has glass and metal lids. Which is the better heat insulator?
options: The glass lid, because heat does not pass through it easily.
The metal lid, because heat does not pass through it easily.
The glass lid, because it makes more heat inside the drink.
The metal lid, because it traps air between thin layers.

why.The metal lid, because heat does not pas: Metal allows heat through easily, so it is the better conductor.
why.The glass lid, because it makes more hea: A better insulator reduces heat loss instead of making more heat.
why.The metal lid, because it traps air betw: This wrongly uses the trapped-air idea from clothing to explain metal.

activities.explanation: Glass does not allow heat through easily, so it is the better insulator.

activities.prompt: How can hollow bricks help a house in a very hot climate?
options: They trap air, which is a poor conductor.
They trap air, which passes heat easily.
They make the house produce more cool air.
They stop all heat from reaching the walls.

Air is a poor conductor, so it does not pass heat easily.
why.They make the house produce more cool ai: Houses use heat transfer; hollow bricks do not make cool air.
why.They stop all heat from reaching the wal: Hollow bricks slow heat transfer, but they do not stop all heat.

activities.explanation: Trapped air slows heat transfer, so the house stays cooler.

activities.prompt: A child says the farthest pin falls first. What is the best reply?
options: Farther pins fall later because heat travels along the metal strip.
Farther pins fall first because heat travels along the metal strip.
Farther pins never fall because heat cannot travel through metal.
Farther pins fall together because all the wax melts at once.

why.Farther pins fall first because heat tra: This child has reversed the direction of heat travel.
why.Farther pins never fall because heat can: Heat passes through metal, so the far pin's wax can melt.
why.Farther pins fall together because all t: Each pin's wax melts at a different time along the strip.

activities.explanation: Heat travels from the heated end, so farther pins receive it later.

lessons.title: Convection and Land and Sea Breezes

activities.prompt: What secrets hide in the way air and water move?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How heat moves
activities.body: Smoke contains hot gases and tiny solid pieces called particles. Air around a candle becomes heated. Air in a cup expands, becomes lighter and rises. The cup rises. Heated water expands, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler water comes down to replace it. This movement of particles transfers heat and is called convection. At night, cooler air moves from land to sea, making a land breeze.
keyPoints: Smoke contains hot gases and tiny solid pieces called particles.
Heated air and water expand, become lighter and rise.
Convection transfers heat through moving particles.
At night, cooler air moves from land to sea.
activities.explanation: Convection transfers heat through the movement of particles.

activities.prompt: Why does a paper cup above a burning candle rise?
steps: Air around the candle flame becomes heated.
Heated air in the cup expands and occupies more space.
The warmed air becomes lighter and rises.
Therefore, the paper cup above the candle rises.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Air near a flame
activities.prompt: What happens to air around a candle flame?
options: It becomes heated
It becomes cooler
It becomes heavier
It stays unchanged
activities.explanation: The air around a candle flame becomes heated.

activities.prompt: Warmed air becomes lighter and rises.
activities.explanation: Warmed air becomes lighter and rises.

activities.title: Air in the cup
activities.prompt: When air warms inside the cup, it ______ and occupies more space.
activities.hint: Warm air takes up more room.
activities.explanation: Heated air expands and occupies more space inside the cup.

activities.prompt: At night, cooler air moves from the sea towards the land.
activities.explanation: At night, cooler air moves from the land towards the sea. This makes a land breeze.

activities.title: Match the heating clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue with its matching result.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows what happens during heating or convection.

activities.title: Convection in water
activities.prompt: Which movement shows convection in heated water?
options: Cooler water rises while warm water stays still.
Warm water rises while cooler water comes down.
Water moves sideways without any heating.
All particles stay still during heating.
activities.explanation: Heated water expands and rises. Cooler water comes down to replace it.

activities.title: Water-heating steps
activities.prompt: Put the water-heating steps in order.
items: Heated water expands and becomes lighter.
Cooler water at the sides comes down.
activities.explanation: Heated water rises first, then cooler water comes down to replace it.

activities.title: Direction of a land breeze
activities.prompt: At night, which way does cooler air move?
options: From the sea towards the land
From the soil into the sky
From the sea into deep water
From the land towards the sea
activities.explanation: Cooler air moves from land towards sea at night. This makes a land breeze.

activities.prompt: A paper cup is placed above a burning candle. What will happen next?
options: The cup will rise because warmed air rises.
The cup will sink because heated air becomes heavier.
The cup will stay still because warmed air stays below.
The cup will fall because the flame makes it heavier.

why.The cup will sink because heated air bec: Heated air becomes lighter, not heavier, so this is wrong.
why.The cup will stay still because warmed a: Warmed air rises instead of staying below the cup.
why.The cup will fall because the flame make: This mistake assumes that the flame makes the cup heavier.

activities.explanation: Warmed air becomes lighter and rises, so the cup rises.

activities.prompt: A pan of water is heated from below. What observation would show convection happening?
options: Warm water rises while cooler water moves down at the sides.
Water becomes one flat layer with no particles moving.
The whole container becomes warm without any water moving.
Only the water surface changes while all water stays still.

why.Water becomes one flat layer with no par: This mistake thinks heating happens without particle movement.
why.The whole container becomes warm without: Convection transfers heat through movement, not without it.
why.Only the water surface changes while all: This mistake thinks only the surface can show convection.

activities.explanation: Convection needs actual particle movement, and this shows it.

lessons.title: Radiation and Heat Transfer Together

activities.prompt: How does the Sun’s warmth travel all the way to Earth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three Ways Heat Moves
activities.body: Heat can move in three ways. A medium is a material through which heat moves. Radiation transfers heat without needing a material medium. Conduction passes heat through a material. Convection moves heat through water. All objects radiate heat. A hot utensil cools by radiating heat to its surroundings. Light-coloured clothes reflect most of the heat falling on them. Dark surfaces absorb more heat than light surfaces.
keyPoints: Radiation transfers heat without a material medium
Conduction and convection need a medium
All objects radiate heat
activities.explanation: Radiation, conduction and convection are the lesson's three heat-transfer processes.

activities.prompt: A dark shirt warms in sunlight; a hot utensil cools indoors. Why?
steps: The Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation, which needs no material medium.
The dark shirt warms more because dark surfaces absorb more heat.
The hot utensil cools because it radiates heat to its surroundings.
Thus, radiation warms the shirt but cools the utensil.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Heat Transfer in a Bukhari
activities.body: Heat can travel in three ways: radiation, conduction and convection. Radiation needs no material medium, while conduction and convection do. Radiation carries the Sun's heat to Earth. Convection heats water in a utensil. A bukhari brings all three processes together. Hot utensils cool by radiation. Dark surfaces absorb more heat than light surfaces.
keyPoints: Conduction and convection need a medium
Radiation needs no material medium
A bukhari uses all three heat-transfer processes
activities.explanation: A bukhari brings together all three ways of transferring heat.

activities.title: Heat from the Sun
activities.prompt: How does the heat of the Sun reach Earth?
options: Radiation
Convection
Conduction
Reflection
activities.explanation: The Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation.

activities.title: Complete the Sentence
activities.prompt: The heat of the Sun reaches Earth by ______.
activities.hint: Think of the process that needs no material medium.
activities.explanation: Radiation carries the Sun's heat to Earth.

activities.title: Does Radiation Need a Medium?
activities.prompt: Radiation needs a material medium to transfer heat.
activities.explanation: Radiation can transfer heat without needing a material medium.

activities.title: Match the Examples
activities.prompt: Match each example with its heat-transfer idea.
pairs: Water in a utensil being heated
activities.explanation: Radiation carries the Sun's heat to Earth. Convection heats water, and a bukhari uses all three processes.

activities.title: Which Surface Absorbs More?
activities.prompt: Which surface absorbs more heat?
options: A light surface
A dark surface
Both equally
Neither absorbs heat
activities.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb more heat than light surfaces.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Pair
activities.prompt: Which pair of statements is correct?
options: Radiation needs a medium; water heats by conduction.
Convection needs no medium; dark surfaces reflect most heat.
Radiation needs no medium; water heats by convection.
Conduction needs no medium; hot utensils reflect heat.
activities.explanation: Radiation can transfer heat without a material medium. Water in a utensil is heated by convection.

activities.prompt: Sunlight warms Earth's surface. Which explanation of the heat's journey is correct?
options: The heat crosses space by radiation, without a material medium.
The heat travels through air currents between the Sun and Earth.
Heat moves through Earth's solid ground from the Sun.
Heat needs a continuous solid path to reach Earth.

why.The heat travels through air currents be: This mistake treats radiation as if it travelled through air.
why.Heat moves through Earth's solid ground: This mistake treats radiation as if it travelled through solid ground.
why.Heat needs a continuous solid path to re: This mistake believes radiation needs a continuous material path.

activities.explanation: Radiation transfers heat without needing a material medium.

activities.prompt: Light and dark shirts hang in sunlight. Which should warm more?
options: The dark shirt, because dark surfaces absorb more heat.
The light shirt, because reflected heat makes it warmer.
Both equally, because light surfaces absorb all incoming heat.
Neither, because radiation cannot heat clothes outdoors.

why.The light shirt, because reflected heat: This mistake treats reflected heat as absorbed warming.
why.Both equally, because light surfaces abs: This mistake thinks light surfaces absorb all the incoming heat.
why.Neither, because radiation cannot heat c: This mistake believes radiation cannot warm clothes without contact.

activities.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb more heat than light surfaces.

activities.prompt: A hot utensil is left in a room. What should happen next?
options: It should cool by radiating heat to its surroundings.
It should cool only because warm air rises away.
It should cool as heat travels through its metal handle.
It should stay hot because radiation needs a material medium.

why.It should cool only because warm air ris: This mistake says convection alone causes the utensil to cool.
why.It should cool as heat travels through i: This mistake says conduction through the handle causes the cooling.
why.It should stay hot because radiation nee: This mistake treats radiation as if it needed a material medium.

activities.explanation: A hot utensil cools by radiating heat to its surroundings.

activities.prompt: A cold spoon rests in a cold room. Which prediction is fair?
options: The spoon still radiates heat to its surroundings.
The spoon cannot radiate because it is already cold.
The spoon radiates only after sunlight warms it first.
The spoon radiates heat only through its metal handle.

why.The spoon cannot radiate because it is a: This mistake thinks only hot objects can radiate heat.
why.The spoon radiates only after sunlight w: This mistake thinks radiation must start after sunlight warms an object.
why.The spoon radiates heat only through its: This mistake thinks radiation can use only one solid path.

activities.explanation: All objects radiate heat, even when they are cold.

lessons.title: The Water Cycle

activities.prompt: How does water travel around Earth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water Goes Round and Round
activities.body: Water moves around Earth in a repeating cycle. The Sun heats water in oceans, rivers and lakes. Evaporation means this liquid water changes into water vapour. When vapour cools, it condenses to form clouds. Clouds bring rain, snow and hail. This falling water is called precipitation. Sunlight can turn snow and ice into water. The cycle redistributes and replenishes water. It also conserves Earth's total amount of water.
keyPoints: Liquid water fills oceans, rivers and lakes.
Solid water forms snow, ice sheets and mountain glaciers.
Water vapour cools to make clouds.
activities.explanation: This cycle keeps water moving while conserving Earth's total water.

activities.title: Follow a drop of water

tasks.say: Go to the clouds.
tasks.then: Vapour cools high up and condenses.

tasks.say: Make it rain.
tasks.then: Heavy drops fall.

tasks.say: Bring it back to the sea.
tasks.then: Then the cycle begins again.

activities.takeaway: Water keeps moving between the sea, the air and the land.
activities.explanation: Water keeps moving between the sea, the air and the land.

activities.prompt: Why does a lake lose water faster on a sunny day?
steps: A lake holds liquid water, which can be heated by the Sun.
The Sun’s heat makes the water evaporate faster.
The evaporated water enters the atmosphere as water vapour.
So, a sunny day makes the lake lose water faster.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens when the Sun heats water in oceans, rivers and lakes?
options: It changes into vapour.
It changes into ice.
It turns into clouds.
It sinks deeper.
activities.explanation: The Sun's heat makes liquid water evaporate into water vapour.

activities.prompt: When water vapour cools, it ______ to form clouds.
activities.hint: Think about what happens when vapour cools.
activities.explanation: Cooling makes water vapour condense, and this forms clouds.

activities.prompt: What can Sunlight's radiation do to snow and ice?
options: Turn them into water.
Cover them with clouds.
Fill rivers with water.
Make them evaporate.
activities.explanation: Sunlight's radiation can turn snow and ice into water.

activities.prompt: Match each form of water with where it is found.
pairs: Snow, ice sheets and mountain glaciers
activities.explanation: These pairs show the three forms of water on Earth.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the water cycle in order.
activities.explanation: The Sun starts the process. Cooling forms clouds, which bring precipitation.

activities.prompt: What does the water cycle do besides conserving Earth's total water?
options: It redistributes and replenishes water.
It creates more water on Earth.
It keeps water in one place.
It removes water from Earth.
activities.explanation: The cycle redistributes and replenishes water in rivers, lakes and oceans.

activities.prompt: A child leaves one wet cloth in sunlight and one in shade. Which cloth dries first?
options: Sunlight makes the cloth dry first.
Shade makes the cloth dry first.
Both cloths dry at the same speed.
Neither cloth dries because cold stops evaporation.

This mistake thinks shade heats water more than sunlight.
This mistake ignores sunlight’s faster evaporation.
why.Neither cloth dries because cold stops e: This mistake thinks cold prevents all evaporation.

activities.explanation: This is right because sunlight makes water evaporate faster.

activities.prompt: Sun heats a lake, and water vapour cools. What should form next?
options: Clouds should form in the air.
Rain should fall into the lake.
Snow should settle on the lake.
Hail should fall onto the lake.

This mistake jumps ahead to precipitation.
This mistake jumps ahead to precipitation.
This mistake jumps ahead to precipitation.

activities.explanation: Cooling water vapour makes it condense and form clouds.

activities.prompt: Which test best shows whether sunlight makes water evaporate faster?
options: Put equal water amounts in sunlight and shade.
Put equal water amounts in two sunny places.
Put unequal water amounts in sunlight and shade.
Put empty cups in sunlight and shade.

why.Put equal water amounts in two sunny pla: This mistake keeps sunlight the same in both places.
why.Put unequal water amounts in sunlight an: This mistake changes both sunlight and water amounts.
This mistake tests empty cups instead of water.

activities.explanation: This changes sunlight while keeping the water amounts equal.

activities.prompt: Rain reaches a dry river. What does this show about water on Earth?
options: Water moves to new places and fills rivers.
A new supply of water forms from rain.
All water on Earth moves into rivers.
The total amount of water on Earth changes.

This mistake thinks rain creates new water.
This mistake thinks the whole supply enters one river.
why.The total amount of water on Earth chang: This mistake confuses redistribution with changing the total.

activities.explanation: The cycle redistributes water and replenishes rivers.

activities.prompt: Why can Earth’s total amount of water stay the same during the cycle?
options: Water moves between different forms and places.
Clouds make new water during the cycle.
Rivers remove water from the cycle.
Water vanishes when it reaches the ocean.

This mistake thinks clouds create extra water.
This mistake thinks rivers destroy water.
why.Water vanishes when it reaches the ocean: This mistake thinks reaching the ocean ends the cycle.

activities.explanation: The cycle moves and conserves Earth’s total water.

lessons.title: Seepage, Groundwater and Water Conservation

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered where rainwater goes after it soaks into the ground?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water moves underground
activities.body: Water drawn from wells can seep into the ground. Water seeps fastest through gravel, then sand, and slowest through clay. This seeping of surface water through soil and rocks is infiltration. Groundwater fills spaces in sediments and openings in rocks. Layers storing groundwater are aquifers. More concrete surfaces reduce infiltration, while rainwater harvesting and recharge pits help replenish groundwater. Ice stupas melt slowly in spring and supply farming water.
keyPoints: Water seeps fastest through gravel and slowest through clay.
Groundwater is stored in sediments and rocks.
Water conservation helps replenish groundwater.
activities.explanation: This card introduces important ideas about water moving underground.

activities.prompt: A gardener pours equal water onto gravel, sand, and clay in three boxes. Where should water reach a tray first?
steps: Gravel has wider spaces between particles, so water seeps through easily.
Water moves faster through gravel than sand because gravel spaces are wider.
Water moves slowest through clay, so clay holds back the water.
Therefore, water should reach the tray first through the gravel.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Through which material does water seep fastest?
options: gravel
sand
clay
activities.explanation: Gravel has wider spaces between its particles, so water seeps through it easily.

activities.prompt: Water drawn from wells has ______ into the ground.
activities.hint: This word describes water moving down into the ground.
activities.explanation: Water drawn from wells seeps into the ground.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct description.
activities.explanation: These pairs connect materials and layers with the way they store or let through water.

activities.prompt: Where may groundwater lie?
options: From a few metres to hundreds of metres above ground
From a few metres to hundreds of metres below ground
Only at the ground surface without any depth
Only inside concrete surfaces in towns
activities.explanation: Groundwater may lie from a few metres to hundreds of metres below the ground.

activities.prompt: Put these materials in order from fastest to slowest for water to seep through.
activities.explanation: Water seeps fastest through gravel, more slowly through sand and slowest through clay.

activities.prompt: Which pair of practices helps replenish groundwater?
options: Rainwater harvesting and recharge pits
Concrete surfaces and sealed drains
Clay layers and frozen water
Rock openings and sediment spaces
activities.explanation: Rainwater harvesting and recharge pits help replenish groundwater.

activities.prompt: Three equal boxes hold gravel, sand, and clay. The gardener pours equal water into each. Which lets water reach a tray first?
options: Gravel, because its wider spaces let water seep easily.
Sand, because gravel spaces are too wide for water.
Clay, because water moves fastest through tight spaces.
Clay, because all soil lets water seep at once.

why.Sand, because gravel spaces are too wide: This reverses the comparison by calling gravel's wide spaces a problem.
why.Clay, because water moves fastest throug: This mistakes tight spaces for faster movement, but clay is slowest.
why.Clay, because all soil lets water seep a: This assumes every soil passes water at the same speed.

activities.explanation: This is right because gravel's wider spaces let water seep fastest.

activities.prompt: Rain falls on a town with many concrete surfaces and a nearby field. Where will more water soak into the ground?
options: In the town, because concrete lets water soak in quickly.
In the field, because soil lets more water infiltrate.
In both places, because concrete cannot stop infiltration.
In the town, because concrete surfaces make water rise.

why.In the town, because concrete lets water: This wrongly treats concrete as helping water enter the ground.
why.In both places, because concrete cannot: This wrongly assumes concrete surfaces do not reduce infiltration.
why.In the town, because concrete surfaces m: This wrongly thinks concrete pushes water upward into the ground.

activities.explanation: This is right because more concrete reduces water infiltration.

activities.prompt: Rainwater soaks through soil and rocks beside a well. What may happen next, and why?
options: Some water may seep down and later be drawn from the well.
The water stays on top and cannot enter the well.
The water freezes into an ice stupa above the well.
The concrete surface pushes the water into the well.

why.The water stays on top and cannot enter: This wrongly thinks surface water cannot soak into the ground.
why.The water freezes into an ice stupa abov: This confuses infiltration with freezing water in an ice stupa.
why.The concrete surface pushes the water in: This wrongly treats concrete as a way to draw water downward.

activities.explanation: This is right because seeping water can become groundwater drawn from wells.

activities.prompt: Groundwater fills spaces in an underground layer hundreds of metres below ground. What does this show?
options: An aquifer can store groundwater at this depth.
An aquifer can only store water at the surface.
An ice stupa can store groundwater in sediment.
Concrete can store groundwater in rock openings.

why.An aquifer can only store water at the s: This wrongly assumes groundwater cannot lie deep underground.
why.An ice stupa can store groundwater in se: This confuses an ice stupa with an underground water layer.
why.Concrete can store groundwater in rock o: This confuses concrete with sediments and rock openings.

activities.explanation: This is right because aquifers store groundwater at possible depths.

activities.prompt: A town makes recharge pits and collects rainwater. What should happen to groundwater over time?
options: Groundwater should be replenished as more water soaks down.
Groundwater should vanish because recharge pits block all seeping.
Groundwater should rise faster because clay is the fastest soil.
Groundwater should freeze because pits always hold ice.

why.Groundwater should vanish because rechar: This wrongly thinks recharge pits stop water from seeping down.
why.Groundwater should rise faster because c: This reverses the seepage order by calling clay faster than gravel.
why.Groundwater should freeze because pits a: This confuses groundwater recharge with frozen water in an ice stupa.

activities.explanation: This is right because rainwater harvesting and recharge pits replenish groundwater.

activities.prompt: Frozen water forms a tall ice stupa. It melts slowly in spring. How can it help a farm?
options: It can supply water for farming as it melts slowly.
It can make concrete surfaces soak up more rain.
It can fill aquifer spaces with frozen water.
It can speed water through clay and gravel alike.

why.It can make concrete surfaces soak up mo: This wrongly treats an ice stupa as a way to increase infiltration.
why.It can fill aquifer spaces with frozen w: This confuses an ice stupa with an underground water store.
why.It can speed water through clay and grav: This wrongly thinks frozen water increases seepage through soil.

activities.explanation: This is right because a melting ice stupa slowly supplies water for farming.
