activities.context: A family in Gangtok used a metal cooking utensil for hot food. The part touching the food became hot, while the handle also warmed as heat moved through the metal. In Kerala, the winter weather is comparatively warm and humid because it is nearer the equator and has a long coastline that helps make its weather warmer and more humid.
activities.prompt: The family is choosing between two coastal places for a comparatively warm and humid winter. Which place best fits the facts in the case?
options: The nearer-to-equator place with the long coastline
The farther-from-equator place with the long coastline
The nearer-to-equator place with the short coastline
The farther-from-equator place with the short coastline

why.The farther-from-equator place with the: The long coastline helps, but being farther from the equator does not give the warmer climate found near the equator.
why.The nearer-to-equator place with the sho: Being near the equator helps, but a short coastline does not provide the stated coastline effect.
why.The farther-from-equator place with the: This choice has neither the nearer-to-equator condition nor the long-coastline condition.

activities.explanation: The climate near the equator is generally hot, and the long coastline helps make the weather warmer and more humid.

activities.context: A family in Gangtok used a metal cooking utensil for hot food. The part touching the food became hot, while the handle also warmed as heat moved through the metal. In Kerala, the winter weather is comparatively warm and humid because it is nearer the equator and has a long coastline that helps make its weather warmer and more humid.
activities.prompt: The family wants heat to pass from the hot food to the cooler handle of the cooking utensil. What should it choose?
options: A metal utensil, because heat can pass through it by conduction.
A non-metal utensil, because it will be a better conductor of heat.
A metal utensil, but only if its particles move toward the hot food.
A non-metal utensil, because cooking utensils should stop heat from reaching the handle.

why.A non-metal utensil, because it will be: The case identifies metals, rather than non-metals, as good conductors.
why.A metal utensil, but only if its particl: Particles do not change their positions during conduction.
why.A non-metal utensil, because cooking ute: The aim is to transfer heat through the utensil, not prevent it from reaching the handle.

activities.explanation: Metals are good conductors of heat, so they are used for cooking utensils.

activities.prompt: Explain why Kerala has comparatively warm and humid winters compared with Gangtok.
activities.answer: Kerala is nearer the equator, where the climate is generally hot. Its long coastline also helps make the weather warmer and more humid. Together, these facts explain why Kerala's winter is comparatively warm and humid compared with Gangtok.
points: Kerala is nearer the equator than Sikkim.
The climate near the equator is generally hot.
Kerala has a long coastline.
The long coastline helps make the weather warmer and more humid.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A candle is placed under one end of a metal strip, and pins labelled I, II, III and IV are fixed along it with wax, beginning nearest the candle. The flame heats the metal end, and the strip shows how heat moves. In another part of the house, two thin blankets are put on a bed because trapped air can reduce heat loss from the body.
activities.prompt: After the candle is placed under the strip, what order will the pins fall in?
options: I, II, III, IV
II, I, III, IV
III, II, I, IV
IV, III, II, I

why.II, I, III, IV: The pin nearest the candle should not fall second.
why.III, II, I, IV: The third pin should not fall before the first two.
why.IV, III, II, I: The farthest pin should not fall first.

activities.explanation: Heat reaches the nearest pin first and melts its wax.

activities.context: A candle is placed under one end of a metal strip, and pins labelled I, II, III and IV are fixed along it with wax, beginning nearest the candle. The flame heats the metal end, and the strip shows how heat moves. In another part of the house, two thin blankets are put on a bed because trapped air can reduce heat loss from the body.
activities.prompt: A person in the house can choose between one thick blanket and two thin blankets. Which choice keeps more warmth?
options: Two thin blankets, because more air is trapped between their layers.
Two thin blankets, because heat passes more easily through the space between them.
One thick blanket, because trapped air occurs only between separate layers.
One thick blanket, because woollen fabric traps no air in its pores.

why.Two thin blankets, because heat passes m: Trapped air reduces heat loss rather than allowing heat to pass easily.
why.One thick blanket, because trapped air o: Woollen fabric also traps air in its pores.
why.One thick blanket, because woollen fabri: A thick blanket does not keep more warmth than two thin blankets with air trapped between them.

activities.explanation: Two thin blankets trap air between them, and trapped air is a poor conductor.

activities.prompt: Explain why a metal strip makes the pins fall, but a glass strip would make them remain longer.
activities.answer: Heat travels easily through a metal strip, so it reaches the wax at different points and melts it. Glass does not allow heat to pass through easily, so replacing the metal with glass would slow the warming. The pins would therefore remain in place longer.
points: Heat travels along the metal strip.
Heat melts the wax holding the pins.
Glass does not allow heat to pass through easily.
The pins remain longer because the wax warms more slowly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student watches a paper cup rise above a burning candle. Air around the flame becomes heated, so the air in the cup expands, becomes lighter, and rises. Nearby, heated water expands and rises while cooler water at the sides comes down to replace it. At night, cooler air moves from the land towards the sea. The student also notices smoke made of hot gases and tiny solid particles.
activities.prompt: Which result is most likely if the air around the candle flame stays cool instead of becoming heated?
options: The cup would be less likely to rise.
The cup would rise more quickly.
The cup would move downward.
The cup would stay at the same height.

Stronger warming makes air expand and rise.
Warmed air rises rather than moving downward.
Cool air would not provide the warming that made the cup rise.

activities.explanation: Less warming would mean less expansion and rising inside the cup.

activities.context: A student watches a paper cup rise above a burning candle. Air around the flame becomes heated, so the air in the cup expands, becomes lighter, and rises. Nearby, heated water expands and rises while cooler water at the sides comes down to replace it. At night, cooler air moves from the land towards the sea. The student also notices smoke made of hot gases and tiny solid particles.
activities.prompt: If the rising heated water stopped moving upward, what movement of cooler water would help continue the movement of water in the case?
options: Cooler water would rise from the sides.
Cooler water would travel downward along the sides.
Cooler water would move sideways towards the heated water.
Cooler water would move upward through the centre.

Cooler water does not rise like heated water.
why.Cooler water would move sideways towards: The replacement movement is downward, not sideways.
why.Cooler water would move upward through t: Rising heated water occupies the central upward movement.

activities.explanation: Cooler water comes down at the sides to replace rising water.

activities.prompt: Explain why the paper cup rises above the burning candle.
activities.answer: The air close to the candle flame becomes warm. This warmth makes the air inside the cup expand, so it occupies more space and becomes lighter. The lighter warm air rises, and the cup rises with the rising air.
points: Air around the flame is heated.
Heated air inside the cup expands.
The expanded warm air becomes lighter and rises.
The cup rises with the rising air.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the day, the Sun's heat reaches Earth without any material medium. A student wearing light-coloured clothes stands in sunlight, so most of the heat falling on the clothes is reflected. The student heats water in a utensil on a bukhari. Convection heats the water, while the hot utensil loses heat to its surroundings without touching them directly. Using the bukhari involves all three processes of heat transfer.
activities.prompt: If the student replaced the light-coloured clothes with dark ones, what change would be expected?
options: The clothes would absorb more heat than the light surface did.
The clothes would reflect most of the heat falling on them.
The clothes would absorb less heat than the light surface did.
The clothes would radiate no heat at all.

why.The clothes would reflect most of the he: This describes light-coloured clothes, not dark ones.
why.The clothes would absorb less heat than: Dark surfaces absorb more, not less, heat than light surfaces.
why.The clothes would radiate no heat at all: All objects radiate heat, including clothes.

activities.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb more heat than light surfaces.

activities.context: During the day, the Sun's heat reaches Earth without any material medium. A student wearing light-coloured clothes stands in sunlight, so most of the heat falling on the clothes is reflected. The student heats water in a utensil on a bukhari. Convection heats the water, while the hot utensil loses heat to its surroundings without touching them directly. Using the bukhari involves all three processes of heat transfer.
activities.prompt: If only the heat-transfer process that does not need a material medium were considered, which process could still move heat in the bukhari?
options: Radiation could still move the heat.
Conduction could still move the heat without a medium.
Convection could still move the heat without a medium.
No process could move heat without a medium.

why.No process could move heat without a med: Radiation does not need a material medium.

activities.explanation: Radiation can transfer heat without a material medium.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Sun's heat can reach Earth and why a hot utensil can cool without direct contact.
activities.answer: Heat from the Sun reaches Earth by radiation, so it can cross without a material medium. In contrast, conduction and convection both need a medium. The hot utensil cools by radiating heat to its surroundings, and all objects radiate heat.
points: The Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation.
Radiation does not need a material medium.
Conduction and convection need a medium.
A hot utensil cools by radiation.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Sunlight warms a mountain glacier. Some snow and ice turn into liquid water, which flows into a river. Heat from the Sun causes some river water to evaporate. The water vapour cools and condenses to form a cloud. Later, the cloud releases precipitation, replenishing water in the river and nearby lake.
activities.prompt: If the Sun’s heat on the river becomes stronger, what should happen next?
options: The river should lose water more quickly through evaporation.
The river should gain liquid water because of the stronger heating.
The river should remain unchanged because evaporation only affects water vapour.
The river’s water should turn directly into snow and hail.

why.The river should gain liquid water becau: Wrong: heating does not add liquid water to the river.
why.The river should remain unchanged becaus: Wrong: liquid river water can evaporate when heated.
why.The river’s water should turn directly i: Wrong: this confuses evaporation with the formation of solid precipitation.

activities.explanation: Correct: stronger heating makes river water evaporate more quickly.

activities.context: Sunlight warms a mountain glacier. Some snow and ice turn into liquid water, which flows into a river. Heat from the Sun causes some river water to evaporate. The water vapour cools and condenses to form a cloud. Later, the cloud releases precipitation, replenishing water in the river and nearby lake.
activities.prompt: After the cloud releases precipitation, what should happen to the river and lake?
options: The river and lake should gain water from precipitation.
The river and lake should lose water to the cloud.
The river and lake should turn completely solid.
The river and lake should stay unchanged because precipitation does not reach them.

why.The river and lake should lose water to: Wrong: precipitation comes from the cloud rather than taking water from them.
why.The river and lake should turn completel: Wrong: precipitation does not necessarily make the water bodies completely solid.
why.The river and lake should stay unchanged: Wrong: precipitation falls from clouds and can reach rivers and lakes.

activities.explanation: Correct: precipitation replenishes water in rivers and lakes.

activities.prompt: How does the water cycle conserve the total amount of water on Earth?
activities.answer: The water cycle redistributes and replenishes water across Earth. Water changes between solid, liquid and gas, moving from ice and snow to liquid water, then into vapour and clouds. Precipitation returns water to rivers, lakes and oceans. This repeated movement conserves the total amount of water on Earth.
points: Water moves among oceans, rivers, lakes, ice, snow and glaciers.
Evaporation, condensation and precipitation link the cycle.
Precipitation replenishes rivers, lakes and oceans.
The total amount of water on Earth is conserved.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A town has many concrete paths, so less rainwater enters the ground. Residents collect rainwater and direct it into recharge pits to replenish groundwater stored in aquifers. At a nearby farm, frozen water has built a tall, cone-shaped ice stupa. During spring, it melts slowly and supplies water for farming. Nearby wells draw groundwater that has seeped through layers of gravel, sand, and clay.
activities.prompt: If the gravel layer below the wells were changed to clay, what would happen to seepage?
options: It would become slower because clay is the slowest seepage material.
It would become faster because clay has wider spaces between its particles.
It would remain unchanged because groundwater is already stored below.
It would become faster because the wells pull water through the layers.

why.It would become faster because clay has: Gravel has wider spaces between its particles.
why.It would remain unchanged because ground: Stored groundwater does not prevent seepage from changing.
why.It would become faster because the wells: Drawing water from wells does not make clay allow faster seepage.

activities.explanation: Water moves through clay more slowly than through gravel or sand.

activities.context: A town has many concrete paths, so less rainwater enters the ground. Residents collect rainwater and direct it into recharge pits to replenish groundwater stored in aquifers. At a nearby farm, frozen water has built a tall, cone-shaped ice stupa. During spring, it melts slowly and supplies water for farming. Nearby wells draw groundwater that has seeped through layers of gravel, sand, and clay.
activities.prompt: Why is the slowly melting ice stupa useful to the nearby farm?
options: Its slow melting releases water for the farm to use in spring.
It gives the farm its whole water supply at once.
It prevents the farm from receiving water in spring.
It provides water only after the frozen structure has completely melted.

why.It gives the farm its whole water supply: Its melting supplies water that the farm can use.
why.It prevents the farm from receiving wate: Slow melting provides water over time rather than all at once.
why.It provides water only after the frozen: Water is supplied as the ice stupa melts, not only after it has completely melted.

activities.explanation: The ice stupa melts slowly during spring.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between infiltration and groundwater, and what are aquifers?
activities.answer: Infiltration is the seeping of surface water through soil and rocks. Groundwater is stored in spaces between sediments and openings in rocks. Aquifers are the underground layers in which groundwater is stored.
points: Defines infiltration as surface water seeping through soil and rocks.
Describes where groundwater is stored.
Explains that aquifers are underground water-storing layers.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Measurement of Time and Motion
chapters.summary: In this chapter: measuring time in earlier times; ancient indian clocks and mechanical timekeepers; the simple pendulum and its time period; modern clocks and units of time.

lessons.title: Measuring Time in Earlier Times

activities.prompt: How did people tell time before clocks?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Natural cycles and time devices
activities.body: People noticed that many events in nature repeated after definite intervals. They used these natural cycles to keep time. The Sun rising and setting helped define a day. They also made devices for measuring smaller parts of a day. A sundial used a changing shadow. Water clocks used flowing water. An hourglass used flowing sand. A candle clock used markings to show time passing as it burned.
keyPoints: Natural cycles helped people keep time.
The Sun's cycle helped define a day.
Different devices measured smaller time intervals.
activities.explanation: Nature gave people patterns for keeping and measuring time.

activities.prompt: A child needs to measure a day and a shorter part. What can help?
steps: The Sun's rising and setting can define a day because the cycle repeats.
Natural cycles helped people keep time through repeated events.
For a shorter interval, a sundial works because its shadow changes position.
Use the Sun's cycle for days and a sundial for shorter times.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which natural cycle was used to define a day?
options: Water flowing from a vessel
The Sun rising and setting
Sand flowing between two bulbs
A candle burning with markings
activities.explanation: The Sun rising and setting formed a natural cycle. People used this cycle to define a day.

activities.prompt: Match each time device with the method it uses.
activities.explanation: Each device uses a different method. Shadows, water, sand and burning all helped show time.

activities.prompt: A ______ uses the changing position of a shadow to tell the time.
activities.hint: Look for the device that uses a shadow.
activities.explanation: A sundial uses the changing position of a shadow to tell the time.

activities.prompt: How does a water clock measure time?
options: Using a changing shadow
Using candle markings
Using flowing water
Using flowing sand
activities.explanation: Water clocks measure time using water flowing out of or into a vessel.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in the order that led to measuring time.
items: The Sun's cycle defines a day
activities.explanation: Repeated events helped people notice natural cycles. The Sun's cycle defined a day, and devices measured smaller intervals.

activities.prompt: Which device can measure intervals as short as two seconds?
options: Sundial
Hourglass
Water clock
Samrat Yantra
activities.explanation: The Samrat Yantra can measure intervals as short as two seconds. It is 27 metres high.

activities.prompt: A shadow changes position while its object stays still. What can the shadow do?
options: It can tell the time.
It can hold water for later.
It can measure sand between two bulbs.
It can rise and set each day.

This mistake treats a shadow as a water container.
This mistake mixes a sundial with an hourglass.
This mistake treats the shadow like the Sun's cycle.

activities.explanation: A sundial tells time from changing shadow positions.

activities.prompt: Sand moves between two bulbs. What does this device measure?
options: Time, through the flowing sand.
Time, through the rising water.
Time, through the moving shadow.
Time, through the burning marks.

This mistake uses water instead of sand for an hourglass.
This mistake uses a shadow instead of sand for an hourglass.
This mistake uses candle marks instead of sand for an hourglass.

activities.explanation: Sand flows between the two bulbs, so the device measures time.

activities.prompt: A task needs a tool that can measure an interval as short as two seconds. Which tool should be chosen?
options: The 27-metre Samrat Yantra
The Sun's rising and setting
The candle clock's burn marks
The water clock's flowing water

why.The Sun's rising and setting: This mistake treats a whole-day cycle as a two-second measure.
why.The candle clock's burn marks: This mistake assumes candle marks can measure two-second intervals.
why.The water clock's flowing water: This mistake assumes flowing water can measure two-second intervals.

activities.explanation: The Samrat Yantra can measure intervals as short as two seconds.

activities.prompt: A child says people could measure only whole days with nature's cycles. Why is this claim flawed?
options: People made devices for smaller intervals within a day.
People stopped using repeated natural events.
People made devices only for measuring whole days.
People believed that days had no smaller parts.

why.People stopped using repeated natural ev: This mistake says people ignored repeating natural events.
why.People made devices only for measuring w: This mistake says their devices could measure only whole days.
why.People believed that days had no smaller: This mistake says they believed days had no smaller parts.

activities.explanation: They made devices specifically for smaller intervals within a day.

lessons.title: Ancient Indian Clocks and Mechanical Timekeepers

activities.prompt: How did ancient India turn shadows, water, and drums into ways to tell time?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Time Was Measured
activities.body: Ancient Indians measured time with shadows and water clocks. The earliest shadow reference appears in the Arthasastra, an ancient Indian text. Water clocks became less accurate as their levels fell. The sinking bowl clock improved timekeeping. A Ghatika-yantra used a sinking bowl. Its sinking was announced with drums, conch shells or a gong. Pendulum clocks later replaced it. People continued using the Ghatika-yantra at religious places.
keyPoints: Shadows and water clocks were used for measuring time.
The sinking bowl clock improved timekeeping.
Pendulum clocks later replaced the Ghatika-yantra.
activities.explanation: These details show early ways to keep time and a later mechanical breakthrough.

activities.prompt: A water clock becomes less accurate during the day. Why might a sinking bowl help?
steps: Water clocks lose accuracy when their water levels fall.
The sinking bowl clock was developed to improve timekeeping.
It is meant to improve timing as the water level drops.
So it can help a clock that loses accuracy during use.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Two Ways to Measure Time
activities.prompt: Which two methods did ancient Indians use to measure time?
options: Shadows and water clocks
Stars and musical drums
Pendulums and steam engines
Candles and metal rings
activities.explanation: Shadows and water clocks were both used for measuring time in ancient India.

activities.title: A Shadow Formula

lessons.title: The Simple Pendulum and Its Time Period

activities.prompt: Why does a swinging ball keep its own special rhythm?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How a Pendulum Moves
activities.body: A simple pendulum has a heavy ball called the bob. The bob hangs from a rigid support by a long thread. When it swings, the bob repeats its path after a fixed interval. This motion is periodic. One oscillation is completed when the bob moves from an extreme position and returns. The time taken for one oscillation is called the time period.
keyPoints: The bob is the heavy ball.
One oscillation ends when the bob returns.
The time period measures one complete oscillation.
activities.explanation: This is the key idea of pendulum motion.

activities.title: Change the length

tasks.say: Make the string 100 cm long.
tasks.then: A long pendulum takes about 2 seconds for each swing.

tasks.say: Make it 25 cm long.
tasks.then: A shorter pendulum swings faster.

activities.takeaway: The time period depends on the length of the pendulum.
activities.explanation: The time period depends on the length of the pendulum.

activities.prompt: Two pendulums have equal string lengths, but different bob masses. Will their time periods be different?
steps: Use the same length because only bob mass should change.
The time period depends on length, not bob mass.
Because the lengths are equal, both time periods will be equal.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Affects the Time Period?
activities.body: The time period is the time needed for one complete oscillation. An oscillation is complete when the bob leaves an extreme position and returns. The time period depends on the pendulum’s length, but not on the bob’s mass. Pendulums of the same length have the same time period at a given place.
keyPoints: The time period measures one oscillation.
Length affects the time period.
The bob’s mass does not affect the time period.
activities.explanation: These rules help you compare pendulums.

activities.title: Name the Heavy Ball
activities.prompt: What is the heavy ball of a simple pendulum called?
options: bob
thread
support
period
activities.explanation: The bob is the heavy ball that hangs from the support.

activities.explanation: Galileo noticed this steady timing while watching the swinging lamp.

activities.hint: It connects the bob to the support.
activities.explanation: A long thread connects the bob to its rigid support.

activities.prompt: Match each pendulum part or idea with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the correct meaning of a pendulum word.

activities.title: Find the Time Period
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Divide the total time by ten
activities.explanation: The time period equals the time for ten oscillations divided by ten.

activities.title: Compare Two Pendulums
activities.prompt: Two pendulums have the same length at a given place. What can you say?
options: They have the same time period.
The first has a longer time period.
The second has a shorter time period.
They have different time periods.
activities.explanation: Pendulums of the same length have the same time period at a given place.

activities.title: Change the Bob's Mass
activities.prompt: A heavier bob is used. The length stays the same. What happens to its period?
options: It stays the same.
It becomes longer.
It becomes shorter.
It stops swinging.
activities.explanation: The time period depends on the pendulum’s length, but not on the bob’s mass.

activities.prompt: Two pendulums have equal string lengths, but different bob masses. How will their time periods compare?
options: Heavier bob gives a longer time period.
Lighter bob gives a shorter time period.
Both give the same time period.
Heavier bob gives no time period.

This wrongly thinks a heavier bob makes the period longer.
This wrongly thinks a lighter bob makes the period shorter.
Every completed oscillation has a time period.

activities.explanation: The period depends on length, not bob mass.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test whether bob mass changes the time period. Which setup gives the fairest test?
options: Change the mass and keep the length equal.
Change the length and keep the mass equal.
Change both mass and length each time.
Use equal lengths at two different places.

why.Change the length and keep the mass equa: This changes length instead of testing bob mass.
Changing both hides the effect of each change.
why.Use equal lengths at two different place: Using two places adds another change besides mass.

activities.explanation: Only bob mass changes, so the test checks mass alone.

lessons.title: Modern Clocks and Units of Time

activities.prompt: How do modern clocks keep time so precisely?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Clocks Keep Time
activities.body: Clocks keep time through a process that repeats again and again. Quartz clocks use tiny, rapid vibrations from a quartz crystal. Atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years. The SI unit of time is the second, written s. A minute has 60 seconds, and an hour has 60 minutes. The Ghatika-yantra measured a time unit called ghatika or ghati. A day had 60 equal ghatis.
keyPoints: Clocks use a continuously repeating process.
Quartz clocks use tiny, rapid vibrations from a quartz crystal.
The second is the SI unit of time.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects clocks with seconds, minutes, hours, and ghatis.

activities.prompt: A school experiment lasts for a very long time. Which clock should be chosen, and why?
steps: All clocks use a continuously repeating process, because repeating motion helps them keep time.
Quartz clocks use tiny, rapid crystal vibrations, so those movements provide their repeating process.
Atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years, so they suit a very long experiment.
Choose an atomic clock, because it stays accurate for much longer than a quartz clock.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which unit is the SI unit of time?
options: second
minute
hour
ghatika
activities.explanation: The second is the SI unit of time, and its symbol is s.

activities.prompt: One minute contains 60 seconds.
activities.explanation: Yes, there are 60 seconds in one minute.

activities.prompt: There are ______ seconds in one minute.
activities.hint: Remember the lesson’s time conversion.
activities.explanation: A minute contains 60 seconds.

activities.prompt: Match each time term with its description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a unit or period and its description from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these time units from smallest to largest.
activities.explanation: A minute contains seconds, and an hour contains minutes.

activities.prompt: A day was divided into 60 equal ghatis.
activities.explanation: Yes, a day was divided into 60 equal ghatis.

activities.prompt: Which clocks lose only one second in millions of years?
options: quartz clocks
atomic clocks
the Ghatika-yantra
clocks using a repeating process
activities.explanation: Today’s atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years.

activities.prompt: The Ghatika-yantra divides a day into equal ghatis. An hour has 60 minutes. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both divisions contain 60 equal parts
Both divisions contain 60 seconds
Both divisions contain 60 hours
Both divisions contain 60 ghatis

why.Both divisions contain 60 seconds: This mistake confuses the counted parts with seconds.
why.Both divisions contain 60 hours: This mistake confuses the counted parts with hours.
why.Both divisions contain 60 ghatis: This mistake assigns ghatis to an hour instead of minutes.

activities.explanation: This is right because a day has 60 ghatis and an hour has 60 minutes.

lessons.title: Slow, Fast and Speed

activities.prompt: How can we tell which runner is moving faster?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Speed
activities.body: Speed tells you how much distance an object covers in one unit of time. An object covering more distance in the same time moves faster. Speed can be written as metre per second or kilometres per hour. The speed for a whole journey is its average speed.
keyPoints: More distance in the same time means faster movement.
Speed equals distance divided by time.
Speed units include m/s and km/h.
Whole-journey speed is average speed.
activities.explanation: Speed links distance and time.

activities.title: Race two cars

tasks.say: Make the two cars level.
tasks.then: Same speed, same distance in the same time.

tasks.say: Make red twice as fast as blue.
tasks.then: In the same time, red goes twice as far.

activities.takeaway: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time.
activities.explanation: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time.

activities.prompt: Two friends run for the same time. Which friend is running faster?
steps: Compare each distance, because distance shows speed when time is equal.
The times are equal, so the friend covering more distance is faster.
That friend is faster, because more distance in equal time means faster movement.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: At the same instant, which runner is running faster?
options: The runner behind the others
The runner ahead of the others
All runners at the same speed
No runner is moving
activities.explanation: A runner ahead of others at the same instant is running faster.

activities.prompt: Objects covering more distance in the same time are moving faster.
activities.explanation: More distance covered in the same time means faster movement.

activities.prompt: The time taken by an object can be found from its distance and ______.
activities.hint: Think about what measures how fast an object moves.
activities.explanation: Distance and speed are used to find the time taken.

activities.prompt: Match each speed word to its meaning.
pairs: Distance covered in one unit of time
Speed calculated for the whole journey
activities.explanation: These pairs show what speed, average speed and speed units mean.

activities.prompt: Which train has the highest speed?
options: Covers the smallest distance in unit time
Covers no distance in unit time
Covers the greatest distance in unit time
Covers equal distances in unit time
activities.explanation: The train covering the greatest distance in unit time has the highest speed.

activities.prompt: How is speed calculated for a whole journey?
options: Total time divided by total distance
Total distance multiplied by total time
Total distance added to total time
Total distance divided by total time
activities.explanation: Speed equals total distance divided by total time.

activities.prompt: At one instant, one runner is ahead of another. What does this show?
options: The ahead runner is faster, because both appear at the same instant.
The behind runner is faster, because being behind shows quicker movement.
Both runners are equally fast, because they appear at the same instant.
The ahead runner is slower, because a visible lead means slower speed.

why.The behind runner is faster, because bei: This confuses being behind with faster movement.
why.Both runners are equally fast, because t: This mistakes appearing together for having equal speeds.
why.The ahead runner is slower, because a vi: This confuses having a lead with moving slowly.

activities.explanation: This is right because the runner ahead is faster at the same instant.

activities.prompt: Two scooters travel for the same time. One covers more distance. Which scooter is faster?
options: The scooter covering more distance is faster, because both times are equal.
The scooter covering less distance is faster, because less distance feels quicker.
Both scooters are equally fast, because they travel for the same time.
The scooter covering more distance is slower, because more distance means slower speed.

why.The scooter covering less distance is fa: This confuses less distance with faster movement.
why.Both scooters are equally fast, because: This assumes equal times always mean equal speeds.
why.The scooter covering more distance is sl: This confuses greater distance with slower movement.

activities.explanation: This is right because more distance in equal time means faster movement.

activities.prompt: Trains travel for one unit of time. One covers the greatest distance. Which train has the highest speed?
options: The train covering the greatest distance has the highest speed.
The train covering the least distance has the highest speed.
Every train has equal speed because their travel times are equal.
The train covering the greatest distance has the lowest speed.

why.The train covering the least distance ha: This mistakes the smallest distance for the highest speed.
why.Every train has equal speed because thei: This ignores the different distances covered in equal times.
why.The train covering the greatest distance: This confuses the greatest distance with the lowest speed.

activities.explanation: This is right because the greatest distance in unit time means the highest speed.

activities.prompt: A car finishes a journey with fast and slow parts. Which speed best describes the whole journey?
options: The average speed, because it uses the total distance and total time.
The highest speed, because the fastest part describes the whole journey.
The lowest speed, because the slowest part describes the whole journey.
The final part's speed, because it happens at the end of the journey.

why.The highest speed, because the fastest p: This mistakes the fastest part for the speed of the whole journey.
why.The lowest speed, because the slowest pa: This mistakes the slowest part for the speed of the whole journey.
why.The final part's speed, because it happe: This uses only the final part instead of the whole journey.

activities.explanation: This is right because average speed is calculated for the whole journey.

activities.prompt: A walker knows the distance and speed of a trip. How can the walker find the time taken?
options: Use the distance and speed to calculate the time taken.
Use the distance alone, because distance always shows the time.
Use the speed alone, because speed always shows the time.
Guess the time, because distance and speed cannot show time.

why.Use the distance alone, because distance: This wrongly assumes distance alone can show time.
why.Use the speed alone, because speed alway: This wrongly assumes speed alone can show time.
why.Guess the time, because distance and spe: This wrongly claims distance and speed cannot show time.

activities.explanation: This is right because time can be found from distance and speed.

activities.prompt: A car keeps the same speed but travels for longer. What happens to its total distance?
options: It increases, because total distance is speed multiplied by total time.
It decreases, because a longer time makes the distance smaller.
It stays the same, because the speed does not change.
It cannot be known, because distance does not depend on time.

why.It decreases, because a longer time make: This wrongly treats a longer time as making distance smaller.
why.It stays the same, because the speed doe: This ignores that total distance also depends on time.
why.It cannot be known, because distance doe: This wrongly claims distance does not depend on time.

activities.explanation: This is right because total distance equals speed multiplied by total time.

lessons.title: Linear, Uniform and Non-uniform Motion

activities.prompt: How can we tell if something always moves at the same speed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different kinds of motion
activities.body: Motion along a straight line is called linear motion. When its speed stays constant, it is uniform linear motion. The object covers equal distances in equal time intervals. When speed changes, it is non-uniform linear motion. It covers unequal distances in equal time intervals. A speedometer shows speed, while an odometer shows distance travelled.
keyPoints: Linear motion happens along a straight line.
Uniform motion has constant speed.
Non-uniform motion has changing speed.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you recognise how motion changes over equal time intervals.

activities.title: Race two cars

tasks.say: Make the two cars level.
tasks.then: Same speed, same distance in the same time.

tasks.say: Make red twice as fast as blue.
tasks.then: In the same time, red goes twice as far.

activities.takeaway: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time.
activities.explanation: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time.

activities.prompt: A cyclist rides straight. Equal time intervals show equal distances. What motion is this?
steps: Because the cyclist rides straight, the motion is linear.
Equal distances in equal times show that the speed stays constant.
Straight-line motion at a constant speed is called uniform linear motion.
So this cyclist has uniform linear motion.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: An odometer measures a vehicle’s speed in km/h.
activities.explanation: An odometer measures distance travelled, not a vehicle’s speed.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct description.
activities.explanation: The speedometer shows speed. The odometer shows distance. Train X has uniform motion.

activities.prompt: A vehicle on a straight road covers equal distances in equal time intervals. Its motion is:
options: Average speed
Distance measurement
Uniform linear motion
Non-uniform linear motion
activities.explanation: Equal distances in equal time intervals show uniform linear motion.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to identify uniform linear motion.
items: Check that the motion is along a straight line.
Check that the speed stays constant.
Confirm that equal distances are covered in equal time intervals.
activities.explanation: Uniform linear motion is straight-line motion with constant speed and equal distances in equal times.

activities.prompt: Why are average speeds needed?
options: Because all distances are equal.
Because speed is always uniform.
Because motion is rarely uniform.
Because odometers show average speed.
activities.explanation: Average speeds are needed because motion is rarely uniform.

activities.prompt: A car travels on a straight road. Its speedometer shows the same reading throughout the journey. What does this show?
options: The car has uniform linear motion.
The car has non-uniform linear motion.
The car has travelled a greater distance.
The car has changed its speed.

This mistake ignores the straight road and unchanged speedometer reading.
why.The car has travelled a greater distance: The speedometer shows speed, not the total distance travelled.
An unchanged speedometer reading does not show a speed change.

activities.explanation: The same speedometer reading shows that the speed stays constant.

activities.prompt: A scooter moves on a straight path. In equal time intervals, it covers unequal distances. What can be said about the next interval?
options: Its distance could be different from the earlier ones.
Its distance must equal the first interval's distance.
Its distance must be greater than every earlier distance.
Its distance must be smaller than every earlier distance.

why.Its distance must equal the first interv: Changing speed does not mean returning to the first interval's distance.
why.Its distance must be greater than every: Changing speed does not always make each later distance greater.
why.Its distance must be smaller than every: Changing speed does not always make each later distance smaller.

activities.explanation: Unequal distances show changing speed, so the next distance could differ.

activities.prompt: A child's journey includes faster and slower parts. The child wants one speed value for the whole journey. Which value is useful?
options: The average speed for the whole journey.
The speedometer reading at the end.
The odometer reading at the start.
The distance covered in the last part.

A final speedometer reading shows only the speed at that moment.
An odometer reading measures distance, not speed.
A distance reading alone does not provide one whole-journey speed.

activities.explanation: Average speeds are useful because motion is rarely uniform.

activities.prompt: Someone says, "Every real journey has perfectly constant speed on a straight road." What is wrong with this claim?
options: Uniform linear motion is ideal, while real motion is rarely uniform.
Uniform linear motion needs changing speed along a straight road.
Real journeys cannot be straight because uniform motion needs curves.
The odometer cannot show whether a journey has constant speed.

why.Uniform linear motion needs changing spe: Uniform linear motion needs constant speed, not changing speed.
why.Real journeys cannot be straight because: Uniform linear motion can occur along a straight line.
why.The odometer cannot show whether a journ: This mistake focuses on measuring instruments instead of the claim.

activities.explanation: Uniform linear motion is ideal, while real motion is rarely uniform.

activities.prompt: A cart moves on a straight track. Which fair test can show whether its motion is uniform?
options: Measure its distances over equal time intervals.
Measure its distance once during the whole test.
Measure its speed at one moment during the test.
Measure its distances over different time intervals.

why.Measure its distance once during the who: One distance cannot show whether equal distances repeat in equal times.
why.Measure its speed at one moment during t: One speed reading cannot show whether the speed stays constant.
why.Measure its distances over different tim: Different time intervals do not make equal time comparisons fair.

activities.explanation: Equal distances in equal time intervals show uniform linear motion.

activities.context: Long ago, people noticed that many events in nature repeated after definite intervals, so they began using natural cycles for keeping time. The rising and setting Sun defined a day, while smaller intervals were measured with special devices. At a learning centre, a visitor uses a sundial, checks a water clock, watches sand fall in an hourglass, and observes a burning candle clock. The centre also has a tall Samrat Yantra for measuring very short intervals.
activities.prompt: As the Sun moves, what will happen to the shadow used by the visitor's sundial?
options: Its position will change.
Its position will remain fixed.
Water will begin flowing from it.
Sand will move between two bulbs.

A fixed shadow would not show changing time.
Water flow is a feature of a water clock.
Sand movement belongs to an hourglass.

activities.explanation: A sundial uses the changing position of a shadow.

activities.context: Long ago, people noticed that many events in nature repeated after definite intervals, so they began using natural cycles for keeping time. The rising and setting Sun defined a day, while smaller intervals were measured with special devices. At a learning centre, a visitor uses a sundial, checks a water clock, watches sand fall in an hourglass, and observes a burning candle clock. The centre also has a tall Samrat Yantra for measuring very short intervals.
activities.prompt: Why is the sundial able to show different times during the day?
options: Its shadow changes position.
Water flows from a marked vessel.
Sand falls between two bulbs.
Its wax shortens as it burns.

Water flow is used by a water clock.
Sand flow is used by an hourglass.
Burning marks the passage of time on a candle clock.

activities.explanation: The changing shadow is used to tell the time.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a sundial and a candle clock?
activities.answer: A sundial tells time by using the changing position of a shadow. A candle clock has markings that show the passage of time as the candle burns. Thus, both measure time, but they show it in different ways.
points: Sundial uses a shadow's changing position.
Candle clock shows time through markings.
Candle markings show passage while it burns.
Both are devices for measuring time.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a temple ritual, a caretaker watches a Ghatika-yantra bowl while visitors wait for the right moment. When the bowl sinks, he announces the event by beating a gong. The bowl is a water-based timekeeper. A student asks why a sinking bowl works better than an ordinary water clock, and why the Ghatika-yantra remained important even after pendulum clocks arrived.
activities.prompt: If the caretaker used an ordinary water clock instead of the sinking bowl, what change should he expect as the water level falls?
options: Its accuracy would become less reliable, which is why the sinking-bowl design was developed.
It would become more accurate because the falling water would move more quickly.
It would remain equally accurate because water level has no effect on water clocks.
It would stop marking time immediately because any falling water makes a clock unusable.

why.It would become more accurate because th: Falling water does not automatically make a clock more accurate.
why.It would remain equally accurate because: Water level does affect the accuracy of a water clock.
why.It would stop marking time immediately b: A water clock does not necessarily stop working as soon as water begins to fall.

activities.explanation: Water clocks became less accurate as their water levels fell.

activities.context: At a temple ritual, a caretaker watches a Ghatika-yantra bowl while visitors wait for the right moment. When the bowl sinks, he announces the event by beating a gong. The bowl is a water-based timekeeper. A student asks why a sinking bowl works better than an ordinary water clock, and why the Ghatika-yantra remained important even after pendulum clocks arrived.
activities.prompt: The visitor wants to recommend a shadow-based method instead of using the water bowl. Which statement gives the strongest historical support?
options: The Arthasastra has the earliest reference to shadow-based measurement, and Varahamihira gave an accurate shadow-based expression around 530 CE.
The Ghatika-yantra has the earliest reference to shadow-based measurement, because its bowl sank during rituals.
Varahamihira's expression around 530 CE described a sinking water clock rather than a shadow.
Christiaan Huygens based his 1657 pendulum-clock patent on the Arthasastra's shadow method.

why.The Ghatika-yantra has the earliest refe: The Ghatika-yantra was a water clock, not a reference to shadow measurement.
why.Christiaan Huygens based his 1657 pendul: Huygens patented the pendulum clock; no link to the Arthasastra's shadow method is given.

activities.explanation: The Arthasastra records the earliest reference to shadow-based measurement.

activities.prompt: Explain why an ordinary water clock could become less accurate and how the sinking bowl addressed this problem.
activities.answer: Ancient water clocks became less accurate as their water levels fell. The sinking bowl water clock was developed to improve timekeeping. Its sinking movement provided an improved way of showing time compared with an ordinary water clock whose accuracy declined as the water level dropped.
points: Water-clock accuracy declined as water levels fell.
The sinking bowl was developed to improve timekeeping.
The design addressed the weakness of ordinary water clocks.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between one oscillation and the time period of a pendulum?
activities.answer: An oscillation is one complete movement of the bob from an extreme position and back again. The time period is the time taken to complete this one oscillation. Thus, the time period measures how long one complete back-and-forth movement takes.
points: An oscillation begins at an extreme position.
The bob returns to the starting extreme position.
The time period is the duration of one oscillation.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how the quartz and atomic clocks relate to keeping time, and how the ghatika-yantra’s unit was related to a day.
activities.answer: Every clock uses a continuously repeating process to keep time. The quartz clock uses tiny, rapid vibrations of a quartz crystal. The atomic clock loses only one second in millions of years. The Ghatika-yantra’s unit is called ghatika or ghati, and a day has 60 equal ghatis.
points: All clocks use a continuously repeating process.
Quartz clocks use tiny, rapid crystal vibrations.
Atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years.
A day was divided into 60 equal ghatis.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Three runners are moving along a track during a race. At one instant, the first runner is ahead of the other two. During the next equal interval of time, the first runner covers the greatest distance. A finish line is farther ahead, and the runners continue at the same speeds for the same length of time.
activities.prompt: At the same instant, one runner is farther ahead than the other runners. Which statement must be correct?
options: That runner is moving faster than the others.
That runner must have the highest average speed for the whole race.
That runner must cover the greatest distance over any future period.
That runner must reach the finish line before the others.

why.That runner must have the highest averag: One instant does not show the average speed for the whole race.
why.That runner must cover the greatest dist: Future distances depend on whether the runners change their speeds.
why.That runner must reach the finish line b: Current speed does not guarantee being first if later speeds change.

activities.explanation: Being ahead at the same instant shows a higher speed.

activities.context: Three runners are moving along a track during a race. At one instant, the first runner is ahead of the other two. During the next equal interval of time, the first runner covers the greatest distance. A finish line is farther ahead, and the runners continue at the same speeds for the same length of time.
activities.prompt: During one unit of time, one runner covers a greater distance than each other runner. What does this show?
options: That runner has the higher speed.
That runner will always have a higher average speed for the whole race.
That runner must remain ahead at every later instant.
That runner will reach the finish line first, no matter what happens next.

why.That runner will always have a higher av: One interval does not determine the average speed for the whole race.
why.That runner must remain ahead at every l: Later positions depend on whether speeds change.
why.That runner will reach the finish line f: A later result is not guaranteed if speeds change.

activities.explanation: More distance in the same time means a higher speed.

activities.prompt: How does knowing that one runner is ahead at the same instant show which runner is moving faster?
activities.answer: At the same instant, the runner who is ahead must be moving faster than the others. This comparison uses their positions at one moment. It does not by itself show the average speed for the whole race or guarantee that the same runner will stay ahead if speeds change.
points: Compares runners at the same instant.
Identifies the runner ahead as faster.
Does not establish whole-race average speed.
Does not guarantee the same result after speed changes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A driver is travelling in Train X on a straight route. The speedometer shows the train’s speed, while the odometer shows how far it has travelled. Train X maintains a steady speed, so each equal period contains the same length of travel. Later, the speedometer reading changes and the odometer reading keeps increasing. The driver wants one speed value to describe the whole journey.
activities.prompt: Why can Train X be described as being in uniform linear motion during the first part of the journey?
options: The train travels at a constant speed and covers equal distances in equal time intervals.
The train travels at a changing speed and covers unequal distances in equal time intervals.
The odometer measures the train’s speed, so its reading proves that the motion is uniform.
The train follows a straight route, so its motion must always remain uniform.

why.The train travels at a changing speed an: Changing speed would indicate non-uniform linear motion.
why.The odometer measures the train’s speed,: An odometer measures distance travelled, not speed.
why.The train follows a straight route, so i: Straight-line motion can be either uniform or non-uniform.

activities.explanation: Constant speed and equal distances in equal times both indicate uniform linear motion.

activities.context: A driver is travelling in Train X on a straight route. The speedometer shows the train’s speed, while the odometer shows how far it has travelled. Train X maintains a steady speed, so each equal period contains the same length of travel. Later, the speedometer reading changes and the odometer reading keeps increasing. The driver wants one speed value to describe the whole journey.
activities.prompt: After the speedometer reading changes, what should the driver expect when comparing the train’s distances in equal time intervals?
options: The distances will be unequal because the train’s speed is changing.
The distances will be equal because the train is still moving along a straight route.
The distances will be equal because the odometer reading is increasing.
The distances will be equal because the train was previously moving uniformly.

why.The distances will be equal because the: Straight-line motion alone does not guarantee equal distances.
An increasing odometer reading does not show that speed is constant.
Earlier uniform motion does not determine what happens after the speed changes.

activities.explanation: Changing speed means the motion is non-uniform.

activities.context: A driver is travelling in Train X on a straight route. The speedometer shows the train’s speed, while the odometer shows how far it has travelled. Train X maintains a steady speed, so each equal period contains the same length of travel. Later, the speedometer reading changes and the odometer reading keeps increasing. The driver wants one speed value to describe the whole journey.
activities.prompt: What should the driver use to describe the whole journey with one speed value?
options: The driver should use average speed, since the train does not remain at one speed for the entire trip.
The driver should use the first speedometer reading, since it represents every part of the journey.
The driver should use the odometer reading, since it provides the average speed.
The driver should use a constant speed, since every journey is uniform.

why.The driver should use the first speedome: The first reading does not describe the whole journey after the speed changes.
why.The driver should use the odometer readi: An odometer measures distance travelled rather than average speed.
why.The driver should use a constant speed,: A journey with changing speed is not uniform.

activities.explanation: Average speeds are useful when motion is rarely uniform.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between uniform linear motion and non-uniform linear motion.
activities.answer: Uniform linear motion is straight-line movement at a constant speed, so equal distances are covered in equal time intervals. Non-uniform linear motion is also movement along a straight line, but the speed changes. Therefore, unequal distances are covered in equal time intervals.
points: Both types involve motion along a straight line.
Uniform motion has a constant speed.
Uniform motion covers equal distances in equal times.
Non-uniform motion covers unequal distances in equal times.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Measurement of Time and Motion

activities.prompt: Which clock uses the changing position of a shadow?
options: Sundial
Water clock
Hourglass
Candle clock
activities.explanation: A sundial uses the changing position of a shadow to tell time.

activities.prompt: A day was defined using water flowing between two bulbs.
activities.explanation: The Sun rising and setting defined a day. An hourglass uses flowing sand.

activities.prompt: Match each timekeeper with its working feature.

activities.prompt: The SI unit of time has the symbol ______.
activities.hint: It is one letter.
activities.explanation: The SI unit of time is the second, whose symbol is s.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to find a pendulum’s time period.
items: Measure the time for ten oscillations
Divide the total time by ten
activities.explanation: The time period is found by dividing the time for ten oscillations by ten.

activities.prompt: Why was the sinking bowl water clock developed?
options: To improve timekeeping.
To measure longer distances.
To measure vehicle speed.
To define the SI unit.
activities.explanation: Water clocks became less accurate as their water levels fell. The sinking bowl improved timekeeping.

activities.prompt: Galileo found that each oscillation of a given pendulum took the same time.
activities.explanation: Galileo found that each oscillation of a given pendulum took the same time.

activities.prompt: How is an object's average speed calculated?
options: Total distance ÷ total time
Total time ÷ total distance
Total distance × total time
Total distance − total time
activities.explanation: The speed calculated for the whole journey is its average speed.

activities.prompt: Which instrument measures and displays a vehicle's speed?
options: Speedometer
Odometer
Pendulum
Sundial

chapters.title: Life Processes in Animals
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: food and digestion begin; lesson 2: food passes through the oesophagus and stomach; lesson 3: absorption, waste removal and other digestive systems; lesson 4: how humans breathe.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Food and Digestion Begin

activities.prompt: What happens to your food as it travels through your body?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Food and Digestion
activities.body: Animals get energy from the food they eat. Food contains complex parts called carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Digestion means breaking these parts into simpler forms. It starts in your mouth and ends at the anus. It happens inside the alimentary canal, a long tube in your body. Mechanical digestion is the first breakdown of food. Teeth crush and chew food into fine pieces.
keyPoints: Food gives animals energy.
Complex food parts break into simpler forms.
Digestion starts in the mouth and ends at the anus.
The alimentary canal is a long tube inside the body.
Teeth crush and chew food into fine pieces.
activities.explanation: Digestion breaks complex food parts into simpler forms.

activities.prompt: A child chews starchy food while recalling a favourite meal. What happens in the mouth?
steps: Teeth crush and chew food, so the pieces become smaller.
This first breakdown is called mechanical digestion.
Recalling the favourite food releases more saliva.
Saliva helps change starch, a carbohydrate, into sugar.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Complex Food Components
activities.prompt: What must happen to complex food components?
options: Stay exactly the same
Break into simpler forms
Turn into salts only
Become larger and harder
activities.explanation: Complex components such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats must break down.

activities.title: Match the Partners
activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a food source, an action or the alimentary canal.

activities.title: Starch and Carbohydrates
activities.prompt: Starch is a type of ______.
activities.hint: Saliva helps break this food component into sugar.
activities.explanation: Starch is a type of carbohydrate.

activities.title: The Journey of Digestion
activities.prompt: Where does digestion start and end?
options: In the mouth and at the anus
In the nose and at the feet
In the stomach and at the hands
In the throat and at the knees
activities.explanation: Digestion starts in the mouth and ends at the anus.

activities.title: The Digestive Juice
activities.prompt: Saliva contains a digestive ______ that helps break starch into sugar.
activities.hint: This liquid helps starch change into sugar.
activities.explanation: Saliva contains a digestive juice that helps break starch into sugar.

activities.title: Mechanical Digestion Begins
activities.prompt: Put the steps and description in order.
items: Teeth crush and chew the food
This creates the first breakdown of food
activities.explanation: Teeth crush and chew food, creating the first breakdown called mechanical digestion.

activities.prompt: A child chews food into many tiny pieces. What has happened first?
options: Mechanical digestion has broken the food smaller.
Saliva has changed all the food into sugar.
The body has gained energy from the food.
Digestion has ended and reached the anus.

why.Saliva has changed all the food into sug: Saliva helps break starch into sugar, not all food.
why.The body has gained energy from the food: Food gives energy, but that is not the first breakdown.
why.Digestion has ended and reached the anus: Digestion ends at the anus only after passing through the canal.

activities.explanation: Crushing and chewing make smaller pieces, which is mechanical digestion.

activities.prompt: A child recalls a favourite meal. Why does more saliva appear?
options: To help break starch into sugar.
To crush food into smaller pieces.
To give energy to the body.
To carry food to the anus.

Teeth, not saliva, crush and chew food.
Food gives the body energy, but saliva does not.
Digestion runs through the canal, while saliva helps break starch.

activities.explanation: Saliva contains a juice that helps break starch into sugar.

activities.prompt: A child has eaten breakfast. Which statement explains why the child can keep playing?
options: The food gives the child’s body energy.
The food breaks into smaller forms inside the body.
The food forms teeth that help with chewing.
The food starts digestion at the child’s mouth.

why.The food breaks into smaller forms insid: Breaking food into simpler forms is part of digestion.
why.The food forms teeth that help with chew: Teeth break food; food does not form new teeth.
why.The food starts digestion at the child’s: Digestion begins in the mouth, but that is not the energy source.

activities.explanation: Animals obtain energy from the food they eat.

activities.prompt: Bees and sunbirds suck nectar. Animal infants drink mother’s milk. What does this comparison show?
options: Animals can get food in different ways.
All animals need mother’s milk.
All animals chew solid food.
Only bees and sunbirds need food.

The examples do not show every animal drinking mother’s milk.
Bees and sunbirds suck nectar rather than chew solid food.
Animals need food to obtain energy, so these animals need it too.

activities.explanation: Nectar feeding and milk feeding show different ways to get food.

activities.prompt: A child thinks starch needs no breakdown. Why is this claim wrong?
options: Starch must break down into simpler forms.
Starch is not a carbohydrate at all.
Starch can stay unchanged after it is eaten.
Teeth alone can break starch into sugar.

Starch is a type of carbohydrate.
why.Starch can stay unchanged after it is ea: Complex food components must be broken into simpler forms.
Teeth make smaller pieces, while saliva helps break starch into sugar.

activities.explanation: Starch is a complex carbohydrate, so digestion must simplify it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Food Passes Through the Oesophagus and Stomach

activities.prompt: How does your food travel from your mouth to your stomach?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Food Moves Through Your Body
activities.body: Your food travels through a tube from your mouth to your stomach. This tube is called the oesophagus, or food pipe. The tongue mixes chewed food with saliva and pushes it onwards. The pipe walls contract and relax in waves. These movements push food into the stomach. The stomach churns food and releases juice, acid and mucus. The juice breaks proteins into simpler parts. Acid kills many harmful bacteria, while mucus protects the stomach lining. The stomach changes partly digested food into a semi-liquid mass. The small intestine is almost 6 metres long. It is also the longest part of the alimentary canal.
keyPoints: The oesophagus carries food from the mouth to the stomach.
The stomach churns food and helps break down proteins.
Mucus protects the stomach lining from acid.
activities.explanation: This card shows how food moves and is protected inside your body.

activities.prompt: A child chews a bite of food. How does it reach the stomach and change there?
steps: The tongue mixes food with saliva and pushes it towards the oesophagus.
Waves from the food pipe walls push food down into the stomach.
The stomach walls contract and relax, so they churn the food.
Churning helps turn the food into a partly digested semi-liquid mass.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Food Pipe
activities.prompt: What is the food pipe?
options: A passage from the mouth to the stomach
A tube inside the small intestine
A part that stores digestive juice
A layer that protects the stomach
activities.explanation: The food pipe is a passage from the mouth to the stomach.

activities.title: The Tongue Helps
activities.prompt: The tongue pushes chewed food towards the ______.
activities.hint: This is another name for the food pipe.
activities.explanation: The tongue mixes food with saliva and pushes it towards the oesophagus.

activities.title: Pipe Movements
activities.prompt: The food pipe walls contract and relax in a wave-like motion.
activities.explanation: These wave-like movements help push food down into the stomach.

activities.title: Where Does the Food Go?
activities.prompt: The wave-like movement pushes food down into the ______.
options: stomach
mouth
tongue
small intestine
activities.explanation: The moving pipe walls push the food down into the stomach.

activities.title: Jobs in the Stomach
activities.prompt: Match each stomach part or substance with its job.
activities.explanation: The stomach has several parts and substances that work together.

activities.title: Breaking Down Proteins
activities.prompt: What does stomach digestive juice break proteins into?
options: Simpler components
Bigger pieces
A dry powder
A solid shell
activities.explanation: Stomach digestive juice breaks proteins into simpler components.

activities.title: The Small Intestine
activities.prompt: How long is the small intestine?
options: Almost 6 centimetres
Almost 6 kilometres
Almost 6 metres
Almost 6 millimetres
activities.explanation: The small intestine is almost 6 metres long.

activities.title: The Longest Part
activities.prompt: Which part is the longest part of the alimentary canal?
options: Small intestine
Food pipe
Stomach
Mouth
activities.explanation: The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal.

activities.prompt: A swallowed bite is inside the food pipe. What might happen if the pipe walls stopped moving?
options: The food might not be pushed down into the stomach.
The food might be pushed up back into the mouth instead.
The food might stay mixed with saliva inside the mouth.
The food might become a semi-liquid mass even sooner.

why.The food might be pushed up back into th: This wrongly assumes that stopping the walls reverses their movement.
why.The food might stay mixed with saliva in: This wrongly puts the food back in the mouth after it entered the pipe.
why.The food might become a semi-liquid mass: This wrongly moves stomach digestion into the food pipe.

activities.explanation: Without wave-like wall movement, food may not reach the stomach.

lessons.sceneAlt: A labelled diagram of the human digestive system, including the food pipe leading from the mouth to the stomach.
lessons.sceneCaption: A diagram of the human digestive system, including the oesophagus and stomach.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Absorption, Waste Removal and Other Digestive Systems

activities.prompt: What happens to the food we eat after it leaves the stomach?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Body Uses Food
activities.body: Absorption means taking nutrients into the blood. The small intestine receives digestive secretions from three sources. Bile neutralises acids. Pancreatic juice is basic and breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Digestive juice further breaks down partly digested food. Thousands of finger-like projections help nutrient absorption. The large intestine absorbs water and some salts. Egestion means removing solid waste from the body. Ruminants and birds use special methods for food breakdown.
keyPoints: Absorption moves digested nutrients into the blood.
The large intestine absorbs water and some salts.
Egestion removes solid waste from the body.
activities.explanation: These points connect digestion, absorption and waste removal.

activities.prompt: How do three digestive secretions help food change inside the small intestine?
steps: Food from the stomach can contain acids, so bile neutralises them.
Pancreatic juice is basic and breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Small-intestine digestive juice further breaks down the partly digested food.
Together, the three sources help digestion inside the small intestine.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does bile do to food coming from the stomach?
options: It neutralises acids.
It breaks down proteins.
It absorbs water.
It stores solid waste.
activities.explanation: Bile neutralises the acids in food arriving from the stomach.

activities.prompt: Pancreatic juice breaks down carbohydrates, ______ and fats.
activities.hint: Think of the three food groups named in your book.
activities.explanation: Pancreatic juice breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

activities.prompt: Match each part or substance with its action.
activities.explanation: Each part or substance has a different job in digestion.

activities.prompt: Put the waste-removal steps in order.
items: The large intestine absorbs water and some salts.
Stool is stored in the lower part of the large intestine.
The body removes solid waste through egestion.
activities.explanation: The large intestine takes in water and salts before stool is stored and removed.

activities.prompt: What do ruminants do with partly digested food?
options: They bring it back to the mouth for gradual chewing.
They swallow grit to break down food in the gizzard.
They absorb water and salts in the large intestine.
They pass digested nutrients from the small intestine.
activities.explanation: Ruminants return partly digested food to the mouth for gradual chewing.

activities.prompt: Birds swallow small stones called ______ to help break down food in the gizzard.
activities.hint: This word names the small stones that birds swallow.
activities.explanation: Birds swallow grit to help break down food in the gizzard.

activities.prompt: A small-intestine model has thousands of finger-like projections. What happens if the model loses them?
options: Nutrient absorption falls because the projections help absorb nutrients.
Nutrient absorption rises because the projections block nutrients.
Stool storage falls because the projections store solid waste.
Food digestion stops because the projections make bile.

why.Nutrient absorption rises because the pr: This reverses the role of projections, which help rather than block absorption.
why.Stool storage falls because the projecti: This mistakes projections for the large intestine's stool storage area.
why.Food digestion stops because the project: This mistakes projections for the source of bile.

activities.explanation: The projections help absorb nutrients, so losing them reduces absorption.

activities.prompt: Stool is stored in the lower large intestine. A child says nutrient absorption removes it. Why is this claim wrong?
options: Egestion removes solid waste, while nutrients enter the blood.
Absorption removes solid waste, while nutrients enter the blood.
Egestion stores solid waste, while nutrients enter the blood.
Chewing removes solid waste, while nutrients enter the blood.

why.Absorption removes solid waste, while nu: This swaps the jobs of egestion and nutrient absorption.
why.Egestion stores solid waste, while nutri: This confuses removing solid waste with storing it in the large intestine.
why.Chewing removes solid waste, while nutri: This confuses egestion with the gradual chewing of ruminants.

activities.explanation: Egestion removes solid waste, while absorption sends nutrients into blood.

activities.prompt: A bird swallows small stones called grit. A ruminant brings partly digested food back to its mouth. What do both actions help?
options: Both actions help break down food during digestion.
Both actions help absorb water and salts from food.
Both actions help remove solid waste through egestion.
Both actions help pass digested nutrients into blood.

why.Both actions help absorb water and salts: This confuses food breakdown with water and salt absorption.
why.Both actions help remove solid waste thr: This confuses food breakdown with solid-waste removal.
why.Both actions help pass digested nutrient: This confuses food breakdown with nutrient absorption.

activities.explanation: Grit breaks food down, while ruminants chew partly digested food gradually.

lessons.sceneAlt: A medical illustration showing the organs and structures of the human digestive system.
lessons.sceneCaption: A clear medical illustration of the complete human digestive system.
