funFacts: The large intestine contains various small living organisms, such as bacteria, that help in digestion. They help in keeping our digestive system healthy. They break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: How Humans Breathe

activities.prompt: What happens inside our bodies when we take a deep breath?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How humans breathe
activities.body: Breathing is the process of inhaling and exhaling air. When you inhale, you take in oxygen. When you exhale, you release carbon dioxide. Air enters through your nostrils and moves through nasal passages. Tiny hair and mucus trap dust and dirt. The passages branch and end in tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli. Your respiratory system helps your body breathe. The rib cage protects your lungs.
keyPoints: Breathing is inhaling and exhaling air.
Humans take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
Nostrils and nasal passages lead towards tiny alveoli, while the rib cage protects the lungs.
activities.explanation: You now know the main parts and gases involved in breathing.

activities.prompt: A child breathes dusty air through the nose. What happens to the dust?
steps: The respiratory system begins at the nostrils, so inhaled air enters there.
It next follows the nasal passages because inhaled air passes through them.
Tiny hair and mucus trap the dust because they catch dirt in the air.
Therefore, the dust is stopped in the nasal passages.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What do you take in?
activities.prompt: What do humans take in while breathing?
options: oxygen
carbon dioxide
dust
mucus
activities.explanation: Humans take in oxygen while breathing. Carbon dioxide is released.

activities.prompt: Humans release carbon dioxide while breathing.
activities.explanation: Humans take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide while breathing.

activities.title: Match each part
activities.prompt: Match each breathing part with its description.
activities.explanation: Nostrils are nasal openings. Nasal passages are small passages. Alveoli are tiny balloon-like sacs. The rib cage protects the lungs.

activities.title: Fill in the gas
activities.prompt: Humans ______ in oxygen and release carbon dioxide while breathing.
activities.hint: Choose the short word before 'in'.
activities.explanation: The complete sentence says that humans take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

activities.title: Where does it begin?
activities.prompt: Where does the respiratory system begin?
options: nostrils
alveoli
rib cage
nasal passages
activities.explanation: The respiratory system begins with a pair of nasal openings called nostrils.

activities.prompt: The branches end in large balloon-like sacs.
activities.explanation: The branches end in tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli.

activities.prompt: A child breathes dusty air through the nose. What will happen to the dust?
options: The dust will be trapped in the nasal passages.
The dust will reach the tiny balloon-like sacs.
The dust will leave through the nostrils at once.
The dust will change into oxygen inside the body.

why.The dust will reach the tiny balloon-lik: This ignores the trapping done by tiny hair and mucus.
why.The dust will leave through the nostrils: This assumes trapped dust is breathed out at once.
why.The dust will change into oxygen inside: This confuses taking in oxygen with trapping dust.

activities.explanation: Tiny hair and mucus in the nasal passages trap the dust.

activities.prompt: Which test best shows that tiny hair and mucus trap dust?
options: Use same dust in two tubes; add hair and mucus to one.
Use dust in one tube and clean air, without hair or mucus.
Use dust in one tube but clean air in the other.
Give one tube more air, but keep every tube part the same.

why.Use dust in one tube and clean air, with: This changes the dust instead of testing hair and mucus.
why.Use dust in one tube but clean air in th: Both dust and air change, so the test cannot show the cause.
why.Give one tube more air, but keep every t: This changes the amount of air instead of testing hair and mucus.

activities.explanation: The dust stays the same while hair and mucus are changed.

activities.prompt: People breathe in a closed room. What gas change should happen?
options: Oxygen should decrease, and carbon dioxide should increase.
Oxygen should increase, and carbon dioxide should decrease.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide should both stay unchanged.
Oxygen should turn into dust inside the nasal passages.

why.Oxygen should increase, and carbon dioxi: This reverses the gas changes caused by breathing.
why.Oxygen and carbon dioxide should both st: This ignores that breathing changes the two gases.
why.Oxygen should turn into dust inside the: This confuses oxygen with dust and ignores the released gas.

activities.explanation: Breathing takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Gas Exchange, Respiration and Circulation

activities.prompt: How does your body get and use the oxygen it needs?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Your Body Uses Oxygen
activities.body: Breathing takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Respiration is a chemical process. It uses oxygen to break down food, such as glucose, and release energy. Your blood carries oxygen to every part of your body. The circulatory system includes your heart, blood and blood vessels.
keyPoints: Breathing brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
Respiration breaks down glucose and releases energy.
Blood carries oxygen around the body.
activities.explanation: This links breathing, respiration and blood transport.

activities.prompt: A child eats glucose and releases energy. How do breathing and respiration help?
steps: Breathing brings oxygen into the body because respiration needs it.
The blood carries oxygen to every body part so respiration can work.
Respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy.
Therefore, breathing supports respiration, while respiration releases energy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does breathing bring into your body?
options: Oxygen
Glucose
Carbon dioxide
Energy
activities.explanation: Breathing brings oxygen into your body and removes carbon dioxide.

activities.prompt: Respiration uses oxygen to break down ______ and release energy.
activities.hint: This is the food used during respiration.
activities.explanation: Respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy.

activities.prompt: Which statement about breathing and respiration is correct?
options: Breathing is physical; respiration is physical.
Breathing is chemical; respiration is physical.
Breathing is physical; respiration is chemical.
Breathing is chemical; respiration is chemical.
activities.explanation: Breathing is physical, while respiration is chemical.

activities.prompt: Match each part or process to its correct job.
activities.explanation: Each item has the job shown by the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which set lists all parts of the circulatory system?
options: Heart, oxygen and energy
Heart, glucose and oxygen
Heart, blood and vessels
Heart, blood and breathing
activities.explanation: The circulatory system includes the heart, blood and blood vessels.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: Blood carries oxygen to your body
activities.explanation: Breathing brings in oxygen. Blood carries it, and respiration then releases energy.

activities.prompt: The blood carries oxygen to every body part. What if it cannot?
options: Respiration cannot use oxygen to release energy from food.
Breathing will bring oxygen directly into every body part.
The body can still release energy without any oxygen.
Carbon dioxide will take over the job of carrying oxygen.

why.Breathing will bring oxygen directly int: This mistake confuses breathing with blood transport.
why.The body can still release energy withou: This mistake thinks respiration does not need oxygen.
why.Carbon dioxide will take over the job of: This mistake treats carbon dioxide as if it carried oxygen.

activities.explanation: This is right because respiration needs oxygen to release energy.

activities.prompt: A child wants to compare breathing before and after a game. What should be measured?
options: The amount of air breathed in and out.
The amount of glucose broken down inside the body.
The amount of oxygen carried by the blood.
The amount of energy released during respiration.

why.The amount of glucose broken down inside: This mistake measures respiration instead of breathing.
why.The amount of oxygen carried by the bloo: This mistake measures blood transport instead of breathing.
why.The amount of energy released during res: This mistake measures respiration instead of breathing.

activities.explanation: This is right because breathing moves air into and out of the body.

activities.prompt: Blood vessels carrying blood around the body are damaged. What may happen to oxygen transport?
options: Oxygen may reach fewer body parts through the blood.
Breathing may stop bringing oxygen into the body.
Respiration may become a physical process instead of chemical.
Carbon dioxide may carry oxygen around the body instead.

why.Breathing may stop bringing oxygen into: This mistake confuses damaged vessels with the breathing process.
why.Respiration may become a physical proces: This mistake confuses physical and chemical processes.
why.Carbon dioxide may carry oxygen around t: This mistake treats carbon dioxide as if it carried oxygen.

activities.explanation: This is right because damaged blood vessels may reduce blood transport.

lessons.sceneCaption: Blood follows a pathway through the human heart, illustrating how the circulatory system works.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Breathing in Different Animals

activities.prompt: How do animals breathe in so many different ways?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different ways of breathing
activities.body: Some animals breathe through lungs. This includes elephants, lions, cows, goats, lizards and snakes. Their lung structures are different. Tadpoles breathe through gills, but adult frogs use lungs. Earthworms use their moist skin to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide. Gas exchange means oxygen enters the body while carbon dioxide leaves it.
keyPoints: Elephants, lions, cows, goats, lizards and snakes use lungs.
Tadpoles use gills, while adult frogs use lungs.
Earthworms exchange gases through moist skin.
activities.explanation: Different animals and life stages use different breathing structures.

activities.prompt: A child watches a tadpole grow into an adult frog. Why can it breathe in water and on land?
steps: A tadpole uses gills, so it can breathe while young.
An adult frog uses lungs, so its breathing changes as it grows.
In water, the adult frog can also use its skin for gas exchange.
These adaptations help amphibians survive both on land and in water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Animals with lungs
activities.prompt: Which group contains only animals that breathe through lungs?
options: Cows, tadpoles and snakes
Elephants, lions and cows
Goats, earthworms and lizards
Lions, tadpoles and goats
activities.explanation: Elephants, lions and cows all breathe through lungs. Tadpoles and earthworms use other structures.

activities.title: A changing frog
activities.prompt: A tadpole breathes through ______, while an adult frog uses lungs.
activities.hint: This breathing structure belongs to tadpoles.
activities.explanation: Tadpoles use gills. Adult frogs use lungs.

activities.title: Life on land and in water
activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how frogs use different breathing structures?
options: Tadpoles use lungs, while skin helps on land.
Earthworms use lungs, while skin helps in water.
Adult frogs use lungs, while skin helps in water.
Adult frogs use gills, while skin helps on land.
activities.explanation: Adult frogs use lungs. They also use their skin for gas exchange when they stay in water.

activities.title: Check the matches
activities.prompt: Which option correctly matches animals with their breathing structures?
options: Earthworms use gills; adult frogs use lungs.
Tadpoles use moist skin; lizards use gills.
Adult frogs use gills; cows use moist skin.
Elephants use lungs; tadpoles use gills.
activities.explanation: Elephants breathe through lungs. Tadpoles breathe through gills.

activities.prompt: Gill surfaces have many blood vessels. Why does this help gas exchange?
options: Blood can flow close to the gill surface.
Gills can grow blood vessels after breathing.
Blood vessels can make the gill surface dry.
Gills can work well without any blood.

why.Gills can grow blood vessels after breat: This wrongly treats vessels as something made only during breathing.
why.Blood vessels can make the gill surface: This wrongly connects blood vessels with drying the gill surface.
This wrongly says blood is unnecessary, although gills have many vessels.

activities.explanation: This is right because rich blood vessels supply the gill surfaces.

activities.prompt: Earthworms exchange gases through moist skin. Which test is fairest?
options: Compare gas exchange with moist skin and dry skin.
Compare earthworms with animals that have lungs.
Compare gill surfaces with lungs in one animal.
Compare skin colour with the amount of breathing.

why.Compare earthworms with animals that hav: This compares different animals instead of moist and dry skin.
why.Compare gill surfaces with lungs in one: This compares gills and lungs, not the earthworm's skin.
why.Compare skin colour with the amount of b: This checks colour instead of the breathing surface.

activities.explanation: This is right because it changes skin moisture while checking gas exchange.

activities.prompt: A child claims all listed animals have identical lungs. What is the best reply?
options: Their lung structures differ among the animals.
Their lung structures are all made from skin.
Their lung structures are always exactly the same.
Their lung structures are found only in water animals.

why.Their lung structures are all made from: This confuses lungs with skin, used by some amphibians.
why.Their lung structures are always exactly: This repeats the mistaken idea that all lung structures are identical.
why.Their lung structures are found only in: This wrongly limits lung structures to animals living only in water.

activities.explanation: This is right because lung structure differs among these animals.

activities.prompt: An elephant breathes with lungs. An adult frog can use skin in water. What does this show?
options: Different body systems work together to sustain life.
One body system must work alone to sustain life.
Only lungs can help every animal sustain life.
Every animal uses skin and lungs together.

why.One body system must work alone to susta: This wrongly says one body system must work alone.
why.Only lungs can help every animal sustain: This wrongly treats lungs as the only helpful breathing organ.
why.Every animal uses skin and lungs togethe: This wrongly says every animal uses skin and lungs together.

activities.explanation: This is right because lungs and skin work together in the examples.

activities.context: While an infant feeds on its mother's milk, a child eats a meal containing starch, proteins and fats. The child recalls a favourite dish and releases more saliva. Teeth crush and chew the food into smaller pieces, while a digestive juice in saliva helps break starch into sugar. Digestion begins in the mouth, inside the long tube called the alimentary canal, and ends at the anus.
activities.prompt: If the child's teeth could no longer crush and chew the food, which result would be most likely?
options: The food would remain in larger pieces, so mechanical digestion would be reduced.
The food would be crushed more finely because saliva would take over the teeth's work.
Starch would be changed into sugar without any digestive juice.
Proteins and fats would be crushed into smaller pieces by the digestive juice.

why.The food would be crushed more finely be: Incorrect: saliva does not take over the crushing work of teeth.
why.Starch would be changed into sugar witho: Incorrect: a digestive juice in saliva helps break starch into sugar.
why.Proteins and fats would be crushed into: Incorrect: the digestive juice helps with starch, not with crushing proteins and fats.

activities.explanation: Correct: teeth break food into smaller pieces during mechanical digestion.

activities.context: While an infant feeds on its mother's milk, a child eats a meal containing starch, proteins and fats. The child recalls a favourite dish and releases more saliva. Teeth crush and chew the food into smaller pieces, while a digestive juice in saliva helps break starch into sugar. Digestion begins in the mouth, inside the long tube called the alimentary canal, and ends at the anus.
activities.prompt: If the child's saliva contained no digestive juice that helps break starch into sugar, which result would be most likely?
options: Starch would not be changed into sugar by saliva, but the teeth could still crush the food.
Starch would still be changed into sugar by saliva, but more slowly.
Proteins and fats would be crushed into smaller pieces by the digestive juice.
Starch would be changed into sugar by the teeth alone, without help from saliva.

why.Starch would still be changed into sugar: Incorrect: without that digestive juice, saliva would not help break starch into sugar.
why.Proteins and fats would be crushed into: Incorrect: the digestive juice does not crush proteins and fats into pieces.
why.Starch would be changed into sugar by th: Incorrect: teeth crush and chew food rather than change starch into sugar.

activities.explanation: Correct: the missing digestive juice could not help change starch into sugar.

activities.prompt: Explain why complex food components must be broken down into simpler forms.
activities.answer: Animals obtain energy from the food they eat. Food contains complex components such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats. These components must be broken into simpler forms so that the energy in food can be used by the body.
points: Animals obtain energy from food.
Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are complex components.
Complex components must become simpler forms.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After eating, the student chewed each bite and swallowed it. The tongue mixed the food with saliva and pushed it towards the oesophagus. The food pipe’s walls then contracted and relaxed in a wave-like motion, pushing the meal down into the stomach. Inside, the stomach churned the food while digestive juice, acid and mucus acted on it. The meal became a semi-liquid mass of partly digested food.
activities.prompt: Immediately after the student swallows, which process will move the meal down towards the stomach?
options: A tightening-and-loosening movement along the food pipe
Continued mixing of the food with saliva
Churning of the food by the stomach
Movement of the food through the small intestine

why.Continued mixing of the food with saliva: The tongue mixes food with saliva before it is swallowed.
why.Churning of the food by the stomach: Stomach churning happens after the food reaches the stomach.
why.Movement of the food through the small i: The small intestine comes later than the stomach in the journey.

activities.explanation: The wave-like movement of the food pipe pushes food towards the stomach.

activities.context: After eating, the student chewed each bite and swallowed it. The tongue mixed the food with saliva and pushed it towards the oesophagus. The food pipe’s walls then contracted and relaxed in a wave-like motion, pushing the meal down into the stomach. Inside, the stomach churned the food while digestive juice, acid and mucus acted on it. The meal became a semi-liquid mass of partly digested food.
activities.prompt: The meal is now in the student’s stomach. Which option correctly explains how the stomach lining is protected?
options: A layer of mucus shields the lining from acid damage
The acid creates a barrier that protects the lining
The churning action spreads mucus over the lining
The digestive juice changes the lining into a simpler substance

why.The acid creates a barrier that protects: The acid kills harmful bacteria rather than protecting the lining.
why.The churning action spreads mucus over t: Churning mixes and churns the food in the stomach.
why.The digestive juice changes the lining i: Digestive juice breaks proteins into simpler components rather than protecting the lining.

activities.explanation: Mucus protects the stomach lining from damage caused by acid.

activities.prompt: Explain how food moves from the mouth to the stomach and what happens to it there.
activities.answer: After chewing, the tongue mixes food with saliva and pushes it towards the oesophagus. The food pipe’s walls contract and relax in a wave-like motion, moving it down into the stomach. The stomach churns the food, secretes digestive juice, acid and mucus, and turns it into a semi-liquid mass.
points: The tongue mixes food with saliva and pushes it towards the oesophagus.
Wave-like movements of the food pipe push food down.
The stomach contracts and relaxes to churn the food.
Digestive juice, acid and mucus act as the food becomes a semi-liquid mass.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After a meal, partly digested food moves into the small intestine. Bile neutralises acids arriving from the stomach, while basic pancreatic juice helps digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Digestive juice from the small intestine continues breaking the food down. Nutrients then pass into the blood through thousands of finger-like projections. Undigested material travels to the large intestine, where water and some salts are absorbed before the remaining solid waste is stored and removed.
activities.prompt: In the case, what would happen next if bile stopped neutralising the acids arriving from the stomach?
options: The acids in the food would not be neutralised by bile.
The pancreatic juice would lose its basic nature.
The large intestine would begin digesting carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
The finger-like projections would return partly digested food to the mouth.

why.The pancreatic juice would lose its basi: Incorrect: pancreatic juice remains basic; bile’s action does not change it.
why.The large intestine would begin digestin: Incorrect: the large intestine absorbs water and salts rather than digesting food components.
why.The finger-like projections would return: Incorrect: projections help absorb nutrients; returning food to the mouth is not their role.

activities.explanation: Correct: bile is responsible for neutralising these acids.

activities.context: After a meal, partly digested food moves into the small intestine. Bile neutralises acids arriving from the stomach, while basic pancreatic juice helps digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Digestive juice from the small intestine continues breaking the food down. Nutrients then pass into the blood through thousands of finger-like projections. Undigested material travels to the large intestine, where water and some salts are absorbed before the remaining solid waste is stored and removed.
activities.prompt: If the large intestine stopped absorbing water and some salts in the case, what would happen to the undigested food?
options: More water and some salts would remain in it as solid waste is stored and removed.
Less water and some salts would remain in it before egestion.
Digested nutrients in the blood would immediately leave the small intestine.
Partly digested food would return to the mouth for more chewing.

why.Less water and some salts would remain i: Incorrect: stopping absorption would leave more water and salts, not less.
why.Digested nutrients in the blood would im: Incorrect: nutrient movement into the blood is not the large intestine’s role.
why.Partly digested food would return to the: Incorrect: returning food to the mouth describes the action of ruminants, not this process.

activities.explanation: Correct: without absorption, more water and salts would remain in the waste.

activities.prompt: Explain how bile and pancreatic juice help digestion in the small intestine.
activities.answer: Bile neutralises acids in food arriving from the stomach. Pancreatic juice is basic in nature and breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Together, they help digestion continue in the small intestine, where digestive juice further breaks down partly digested food and nutrients pass into the blood.
points: Bile neutralises acids from the stomach.
Pancreatic juice is basic.
Pancreatic juice breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Small-intestinal digestive juice continues the breakdown.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a walk near a dusty road, Meena breathed through her nose. Air entered her nostrils and moved along her nasal passages. Tiny hair and mucus trapped some dust and dirt. The inhaled air continued into branches that ended in tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli. Meena's rib cage protected her lungs, and the respiratory system helped her body breathe and respire.
activities.prompt: As Meena breathes near the dusty road, what happens to dust and dirt in her nasal passages?
options: Some particles are stopped before the air goes farther inward.
Every particle passes unchanged into the alveoli.
The particles are released as carbon dioxide.
The rib cage stops the particles before they reach the nasal passages.

why.Every particle passes unchanged into the: This wrongly suggests that the air is not cleaned.
why.The particles are released as carbon dio: This confuses trapped dirt with a released gas.
why.The rib cage stops the particles before: The rib cage protects the lungs rather than filtering air.

activities.explanation: Tiny hair and mucus trap some particles.

activities.context: During a walk near a dusty road, Meena breathed through her nose. Air entered her nostrils and moved along her nasal passages. Tiny hair and mucus trapped some dust and dirt. The inhaled air continued into branches that ended in tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli. Meena's rib cage protected her lungs, and the respiratory system helped her body breathe and respire.
activities.prompt: Which change happens in Meena's body as she breathes?
options: Oxygen leaves her body, while carbon dioxide enters it.
Both oxygen and carbon dioxide enter her body.
Only oxygen leaves her body.
Oxygen enters her body, and carbon dioxide leaves it.

why.Oxygen leaves her body, while carbon dio: Breathing reverses the correct gas movement.
why.Both oxygen and carbon dioxide enter her: Breathing involves taking in oxygen, not only taking in gases.
Carbon dioxide leaves the body rather than leaving only oxygen.

activities.explanation: Humans take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

activities.prompt: Explain why tiny hair and mucus are useful during breathing.
activities.answer: Tiny hair and mucus trap dust and dirt from inhaled air. This prevents those particles from traveling farther through the nasal passages. As breathing continues, air can move onward toward the branches that end in the alveoli.
points: Tiny hair and mucus are present in the nasal passages.
They trap dust and dirt from inhaled air.
This reduces how far trapped particles travel.
Cleaner air can continue toward the branches ending in the alveoli.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is taking part in a school activity. As the student breathes, oxygen enters the body, and carbon dioxide leaves. The blood transports the oxygen to all parts of the body. Respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy. This is a chemical process, whereas breathing is a physical process. The student's circulatory system includes the heart, blood and blood vessels.
activities.prompt: The student breathes in, bringing oxygen into the body. Which process can use that oxygen next?
options: Chemical energy release from food
Physical movement of gases
Transport through blood vessels
Removal of carbon dioxide

why.Physical movement of gases: Breathing is physical and brings gases into or out of the body.
why.Transport through blood vessels: Blood transport carries oxygen but does not release energy from food.
why.Removal of carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide removal happens during breathing out and does not use oxygen.

activities.explanation: Correct: Respiration uses oxygen to break down food and release energy.

activities.context: A student is taking part in a school activity. As the student breathes, oxygen enters the body, and carbon dioxide leaves. The blood transports the oxygen to all parts of the body. Respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy. This is a chemical process, whereas breathing is a physical process. The student's circulatory system includes the heart, blood and blood vessels.
activities.prompt: If one of the student's blood vessels could no longer carry blood, which effect should be expected?
options: Some body parts would receive less oxygen
Some body parts would receive more oxygen
Some body parts would break down more glucose
Some body parts would receive less carbon dioxide

why.Some body parts would receive more oxyge: A blocked vessel would not carry more blood to body parts.
why.Some body parts would break down more gl: Less oxygen could mean less glucose breakdown, not more.
why.Some body parts would receive less carbo: Less blood reaching a body part would not reduce carbon dioxide there.

activities.explanation: Correct: The blood transports oxygen to all parts of the body.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between breathing and respiration.
activities.answer: Breathing is a physical process that brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. Respiration is a chemical process that uses oxygen to break down food and release energy. The blood transports oxygen to all parts of the body, where respiration can use it.
points: Breathing is a physical process.
Breathing brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
Respiration is a chemical process.
Respiration uses oxygen to release energy from food.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A keeper at an animal centre checks the breathing of several animals. An elephant, a lion, a cow, a goat, a lizard and a snake all breathe using lungs, but their lung structures are not the same. A tadpole uses gills, while an adult frog uses lungs and can exchange gases through its skin when it remains in water. Nearby, an earthworm exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide through its moist skin.
activities.prompt: A tadpole in the centre’s pond is growing into an adult frog. Which combination best describes the breathing structures it will use as an adult?
options: Lungs, with its skin also involved in gas exchange underwater
Gills only, even after it becomes an adult
Lungs only, with no role for its skin in water
Skin only, because it will no longer use lungs

why.Gills only, even after it becomes an adu: This mistake keeps the breathing structure of the tadpole stage.
why.Lungs only, with no role for its skin in: This mistake leaves out the adult frog’s use of skin in water.
why.Skin only, because it will no longer use: This mistake leaves out the adult frog’s use of lungs.

activities.explanation: An adult frog uses lungs and its skin for gas exchange in water.

activities.context: A keeper at an animal centre checks the breathing of several animals. An elephant, a lion, a cow, a goat, a lizard and a snake all breathe using lungs, but their lung structures are not the same. A tadpole uses gills, while an adult frog uses lungs and can exchange gases through its skin when it remains in water. Nearby, an earthworm exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide through its moist skin.
activities.prompt: The keeper notices that an earthworm’s skin is no longer moist. What is the most likely effect on its breathing?
options: Gas exchange through the skin will be less effective
Gas exchange through the skin will be more effective
Only oxygen will be exchanged through the skin
Both gases will be exchanged through the skin more quickly

why.Gas exchange through the skin will be mo: This reverses the likely effect of the skin losing moisture.
why.Only oxygen will be exchanged through th: This wrongly limits gas exchange to oxygen only.
why.Both gases will be exchanged through the: This wrongly suggests that drier skin improves gas exchange.

activities.explanation: Earthworms use moist skin to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.

activities.prompt: Explain how the breathing of a tadpole differs from that of an adult frog.
activities.answer: A tadpole breathes through gills, while an adult frog uses lungs. An adult frog can also carry out gas exchange through its skin when it stays in water. These different adaptations help amphibians survive both on land and in water.
points: Tadpoles use gills
Adult frogs use lungs
Adult frogs use their skin for gas exchange in water
The adaptations help amphibians survive on land and in water
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

Mouth

activities.prompt: Breathing is a physical process, while ______ is a chemical process.
activities.hint: Think about breaking food down to release energy.

activities.prompt: Match each animal to its breathing structure.
activities.explanation: Adult frogs use their skin to exchange gases while in water.

activities.prompt: Which system includes the heart, blood and blood vessels?
options: Food pipe
Respiratory system
Circulatory system

chapters.title: Life Processes in Plants
chapters.summary: In this chapter: how plants grow; leaves are food factories; air and photosynthesis; how leaves exchange gases.

lessons.title: How Plants Grow

activities.prompt: What do plants need to grow strong and healthy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Plants Need
activities.body: As a plant grows, it develops new leaves and branches. Its stem becomes thicker, and the whole plant becomes taller. Regular watering helps plants grow better. Plants need both sunlight and water for growth. Pot A gets direct sunlight and slightly moist soil. Pot B gets sunlight but no water. Pot C gets daily water but stays in the dark.
keyPoints: New leaves and branches develop.
The stem becomes thicker.
Sunlight and water support growth.
activities.explanation: Pot A has both needs. Pot B lacks water, while Pot C lacks sunlight.

activities.prompt: Pot A has sunlight and slightly moist soil. Pot C is dark but watered. Which plant should grow better, and why?
steps: Pot A gets sunlight, so one plant need is met.
Its soil stays slightly moist, so its water need is met.
Pot C gets water, but darkness leaves sunlight missing.
Pot A grows better because it has both sunlight and water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: As a plant grows, it develops new leaves and branches.
activities.explanation: Growing plants develop new leaves and branches.

activities.prompt: Plants grow better when they receive no water.
activities.explanation: Regular watering helps plants grow better.

activities.prompt: Which choice describes Pot A?
options: sunlight and slightly moist soil
sunlight and no watering
darkness and daily watering
darkness and slightly moist soil
activities.explanation: Pot A receives direct sunlight. Its soil is kept slightly moist.

activities.prompt: Plants need ______ sunlight and water for their growth.
activities.hint: This word joins the two needs.
activities.explanation: Plants need both sunlight and water for their growth.

activities.prompt: Which choice explains why Pot A grows better than Pot C?
options: Pot A has sunlight and moist soil
Pot B has sunlight and moist soil
Pot C has sunlight and moist soil
Pot A has sunlight but no water
activities.explanation: Pot C is watered daily, but it stays dark. Pot A gets sunlight and moist soil.

activities.prompt: A plant's soil dries each day. What should you do?
options: Water it regularly, so it can grow better.
Give it more sunlight, because light is enough.
Keep it in the dark, so it can rest.
Stop watering it, so its soil can dry.

why.Give it more sunlight, because light is: This wrongly assumes sunlight alone is enough for good growth.
This wrongly treats darkness as helpful instead of sunlight as needed.
This wrongly assumes a plant does not need regular water.

activities.explanation: Regular watering helps the plant grow better.

activities.prompt: One pot has sunlight and moist soil. Another is dark but watered. Which plant grows better?
options: The sunlit plant, because it gets sunlight and water.
The dark plant, because daily water is enough.
The sunlit plant, because water does not matter.
The dark plant, because darkness helps growth.

why.The dark plant, because daily water is e: This wrongly assumes water alone is enough for good growth.
why.The sunlit plant, because water does not: This wrongly assumes water does not matter to growth.
why.The dark plant, because darkness helps g: This wrongly treats darkness as helpful instead of sunlight as needed.

activities.explanation: This plant has both sunlight and water, which plants need to grow.

activities.prompt: You want to test if watering helps a plant grow. What should you keep the same?
options: Keep the sunlight the same for both plants.
Keep the sunlight different for both plants.
Keep one plant in sunlight and one in darkness.
Give one plant regular water and one plant none.

why.Keep the sunlight different for both pla: Changing sunlight as well makes the test unclear.
why.Keep one plant in sunlight and one in da: Different sunlight and water would test more than one thing.
why.Give one plant regular water and one pla: This changes water correctly, but it does not answer what should stay the same.

activities.explanation: Keeping sunlight the same makes the watering difference the only test change.

activities.prompt: A child says, "My plant grows well because it gets plenty of sunlight." What is missing from the reason?
options: The plant also needs regular water for good growth.
Regular water makes sunlight unnecessary for growth.
Plants need darkness instead of sunlight to grow.
Water makes a plant stop growing and become smaller.

why.Regular water makes sunlight unnecessary: This wrongly says water can replace sunlight.
why.Plants need darkness instead of sunlight: This wrongly treats darkness as a plant need instead of sunlight.
why.Water makes a plant stop growing and bec: This wrongly says water prevents growth.

activities.explanation: Sunlight alone is not enough because plants need both sunlight and water.

lessons.sceneCaption: A girl waters potted plants, showing how regular watering helps plants grow.

lessons.title: Leaves Are Food Factories

activities.prompt: How can a leaf make food without having a mouth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Leaves Make Food
activities.body: Unlike animals, plants do not eat food. Their leaves use chlorophyll to capture sunlight. This helps the leaves produce starch. Plants store food in the form of starch. In a test, we place a softened leaf in alcohol. It becomes colourless. Next, we place diluted iodine solution on it. A blue-black colour shows that starch is present. Decolourising the leaf makes this colour change easier to see.
keyPoints: Plants store food as starch.
Chlorophyll helps leaves capture sunlight.
Blue-black colour shows that starch is present.
activities.explanation: Leaves catch sunlight and help plants make stored food.

activities.prompt: A plant does not eat food. How can its leaves provide food?
steps: Plants do not eat food, so food is made inside them.
Chlorophyll helps leaves capture sunlight, so leaves can produce starch.
Starch is produced in leaves, so leaves make the plant's food.
The plant stores this food as starch, so leaves are food factories.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do plants do instead of eating food?
options: It stores starch as food.
It eats small pieces of soil.
It drinks water through leaves.
It eats pieces of sunlight.
activities.explanation: Plants do not eat food. They store food as starch.

activities.prompt: Chlorophyll helps a leaf capture sunlight.
activities.explanation: Chlorophyll helps a leaf capture sunlight.

activities.prompt: Plants store food in the form of ______.
activities.hint: It is produced in leaves.
activities.explanation: Starch is the form in which plants store food.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its role in the leaf activity.
pairs: makes colour change easier to see
activities.explanation: Each pair links a substance or action with its role.

activities.prompt: What happens after diluted iodine solution is placed on the colourless leaf?
options: It becomes blue-black if starch is present.
It becomes green if chlorophyll is present.
It becomes softer if starch is present.
It becomes starch if iodine is present.
activities.explanation: Blue-black colour shows that the leaf contains starch.

activities.prompt: The leaf becomes colourless before diluted iodine solution is placed on it.
activities.explanation: The softened leaf becomes colourless before iodine is added.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Place the softened leaf in alcohol.
Place diluted iodine solution on the leaf.
activities.explanation: The activity shows this clear sequence of steps.

activities.prompt: Why is the leaf decolourised before the iodine test?
options: It makes the colour change easier to observe.
It creates more sunlight inside the leaf.
It changes starch into chlorophyll.
It changes the diluted iodine solution.
activities.explanation: Decolourising the leaf makes the colour change easier to observe.

activities.prompt: A softened leaf has been kept in alcohol until it is colourless. Diluted iodine is now put on it. What colour should appear?
options: Blue-black, because the leaf contains starch.
Green, because the leaf still contains chlorophyll.
Yellow, because alcohol has changed the starch.
No colour, because iodine cannot test a leaf.

why.Green, because the leaf still contains c: Green would mean chlorophyll is visible, but the leaf became colourless.
why.Yellow, because alcohol has changed the: Alcohol makes the leaf colourless; it does not turn starch yellow.
why.No colour, because iodine cannot test a: This mistakes iodine for a solution that cannot show starch.

activities.explanation: Blue-black shows that the leaf contains starch.

activities.prompt: Leaves are mostly green. A student says starch makes them green. Why is this claim wrong?
options: Green comes from chlorophyll, not from stored starch.
Green comes from iodine, not from stored starch.
Green comes from alcohol, not from stored starch.
Green comes from sunlight, not from stored starch.

why.Green comes from iodine, not from stored: Iodine tests for starch; it does not make leaves green.
why.Green comes from alcohol, not from store: Alcohol is used during the activity, not to make leaves green.
why.Green comes from sunlight, not from stor: Chlorophyll captures sunlight; sunlight does not make leaves green.

activities.explanation: Chlorophyll is what makes leaves mostly green.

lessons.sceneAlt: A photograph of green cassava leaves showing their chlorophyll colour on a bright, sunny day.
lessons.sceneCaption: Green cassava leaves display chlorophyll on a bright, sunny day.

sceneCredit.text: Cassava leaves in kanyanya Kampala Uganda with a green chlorophyll col by Emma Oruk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Emma Oruk

funFacts: Some plant leaves appear red, violet, or brown because they contain more of these coloured pigments than the green-coloured chlorophyll. This hides the green colour. Some of these pigments also help in photosynthesis.

lessons.title: Air and Photosynthesis

activities.prompt: What happens to a leaf when it gets a little help from the air?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Prepare Food
activities.body: Photosynthesis is the process where plants use sunlight and chlorophyll to prepare food. A leaf is the main place where this happens. Other green plant parts can also do it. Air helps in making plant food. Carbon dioxide from air is needed to prepare starch. Plants also release oxygen and make glucose, a simple carbohydrate.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis happens in sunlight with chlorophyll.
Carbon dioxide from air helps prepare starch.
Plants release oxygen and make glucose.
activities.explanation: This card introduces photosynthesis and the parts involved in making plant food.

activities.prompt: A leaf part inside a bottle does not turn blue-black. Why is it different?
steps: The stored starch is removed so only newly made starch is tested.
Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide inside the bottle.
The outside part turns blue-black because carbon dioxide reaches it.
The inside part does not, so carbon dioxide is needed to prepare starch.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What the Experiment Showed
activities.body: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide from air. Before the experiment, stored starch was removed from the plant. The leaf part outside the bottle turned blue-black. The part inside the bottle did not. Carbon dioxide from air is needed to prepare starch, so the outside part could make starch.
keyPoints: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide from air.
Stored starch was removed before the experiment.
The outside leaf part turned blue-black.
activities.explanation: This card explains what the bottle experiment showed.

activities.title: The Main Place
activities.prompt: Where does photosynthesis mainly happen in a plant?
options: In a leaf
In a green stem
Inside stored starch
Inside caustic soda
activities.explanation: A leaf is the main place where photosynthesis happens. Other green parts can also work.

activities.title: A Released Gas
activities.prompt: Plants release ______ during photosynthesis.
activities.hint: This gas comes out during photosynthesis.
activities.explanation: Oxygen is released during photosynthesis.

activities.title: Outside the Bottle
activities.prompt: The leaf part outside the bottle turned blue-black.
activities.explanation: The outside part turned blue-black, while the inside part did not.

activities.title: Why the Colour Changed
activities.prompt: Why did the leaf part outside the bottle turn blue-black?
options: Carbon dioxide from air was available.
Caustic soda released carbon dioxide.
Stored starch stayed outside.
Oxygen stopped starch forming.
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide from air is needed to prepare starch. Caustic soda absorbs it inside the bottle.

activities.title: Join the Clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue to the correct word.
activities.explanation: A leaf is the main place. Glucose is made, and oxygen is released. Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Idea
activities.prompt: Which statement about photosynthesis agrees with the lesson?
options: It needs carbon dioxide but not chlorophyll.
It happens only inside a bottle.
It can happen in other green plant parts.
It makes starch without air.
activities.explanation: Other green plant parts can perform photosynthesis. The process uses chlorophyll. Air supplies carbon dioxide.

activities.prompt: A leaf has no stored starch. It is put in a bottle with caustic soda. What happens?
options: Turns blue-black, because carbon dioxide reached the leaf.
Does not turn blue-black, because carbon dioxide was absorbed.
Turns blue-black, because the leaf still had stored starch.
Does not turn blue-black, because stored starch was removed.

why.Turns blue-black, because carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide was absorbed, so starch could not be prepared.
why.Turns blue-black, because the leaf still: Stored starch was removed before the experiment.
why.Does not turn blue-black, because stored: Removing stored starch allows the test to show newly made starch.

activities.explanation: The outside leaf received carbon dioxide and turned blue-black.

activities.prompt: Two similar leaves are available. Which comparison best tests carbon dioxide's role?
options: Use two similar leaves, with and without caustic soda.
Use two leaves, one in sunlight and one in darkness.
Use two leaves, one green and one not green.
Use two leaves, one with starch and one without.

why.Use two leaves, one in sunlight and one: This changes sunlight instead of carbon dioxide.
why.Use two leaves, one green and one not gr: This changes leaf colour instead of carbon dioxide.
why.Use two leaves, one with starch and one: This changes stored starch instead of carbon dioxide.

activities.explanation: This changes carbon dioxide while keeping the leaves similar.

activities.prompt: A teacher says blue-black proves carbon dioxide made starch. Stored starch was not removed. What is wrong?
options: Stored starch may have caused the blue-black colour.
Caustic soda may have released carbon dioxide.
The leaf may not have received any sunlight.
Carbon dioxide may have been absent from air.

why.Caustic soda may have released carbon di: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide; it does not release it.
why.The leaf may not have received any sunli: Missing sunlight could stop photosynthesis, but it does not explain this flaw.
why.Carbon dioxide may have been absent from: Carbon dioxide is present in air and is needed to prepare starch.

activities.explanation: Stored starch can cause the colour without proving new starch formed.

lessons.sceneAlt: Spring sunlight passes through red and green leaves in Chippenham Park.
lessons.sceneCaption: Sunlight shines through red and green leaves, illustrating how plants use light.

sceneCredit.creator: Roger Jones

lessons.title: How Leaves Exchange Gases

activities.prompt: What helps a leaf take in one gas and let another out?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tiny Pores for Gas Exchange
activities.body: Stomata are tiny pores found on leaves. They help a plant exchange carbon dioxide and oxygen. To see them, carefully peel a thin layer from a leaf's lower surface. Place the peel in water in a watch glass. Add a drop of ink, then cover the peel with a coverslip. Tiny pores can then be seen under observation.
keyPoints: Stomata are tiny pores on leaves.
They help plants exchange carbon dioxide and oxygen.
A thin leaf peel is prepared for observation.
activities.explanation: Good start! Stomata are tiny leaf pores for gas exchange.

activities.prompt: Your watch glass has water. How can you prepare a leaf peel and observe its stomata?
steps: Choose rhoeo, money plant, onion, or hibiscus because these are leaf choices.
Peel thinly from the lower surface because this creates the leaf peel.
Place the peel in the water and add ink because observation follows.
Use a coverslip; stomata can be seen and help a plant exchange gases.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which two gases do stomata help a plant exchange?
options: oxygen and water
carbon dioxide and ink
carbon dioxide and oxygen
oxygen and coverslip
activities.explanation: Yes! Stomata help leaves exchange carbon dioxide and oxygen.

activities.prompt: Tiny pores on leaves are called ______.
activities.hint: These tiny pores help a plant exchange gases.
activities.explanation: Well done! The tiny pores on leaves are called stomata.

activities.prompt: Which action comes first when preparing the leaf peel?
options: Place the peel in water
Peel a thin layer
Add ink to the peel
Cover the peel
activities.explanation: Right! First, peel a thin layer from the leaf's lower surface.

activities.prompt: Match each action to the item used with the leaf peel.
activities.explanation: Great matching! These items are used to prepare the leaf peel.

activities.prompt: Put the leaf-peel preparation steps in the correct order.
items: Peel a thin layer from the lower surface
Place the peel in a watch glass with water
Place a drop of ink on the peel
Cover the peel with a coverslip
activities.explanation: Excellent! You arranged the preparation steps correctly.

activities.prompt: Which list contains only items used to prepare the leaf peel?
options: leaf, carbon dioxide, ink, water
leaf, water, oxygen, coverslip
watch glass, water, ink, coverslip
leaf, carbon dioxide, oxygen, coverslip
activities.explanation: Yes! These four items are used during the leaf-peel preparation.

activities.prompt: You have a leaf peel and a watch glass with water. What comes next?
options: Add ink to the peel and cover it with a coverslip.
Add ink to the watch glass and cover it with a coverslip.
Add water to the peel and cover it with a coverslip.
Add ink to the peel and cover the watch glass with it.

why.Add ink to the watch glass and cover it: This confuses the leaf peel with the watch glass.
why.Add water to the peel and cover it with: This confuses adding ink with placing the peel in water.
why.Add ink to the peel and cover the watch: This covers the watch glass instead of covering the peel.

activities.explanation: This is correct because ink goes on the peel before it is covered.

activities.prompt: A classmate says, “Ink makes the tiny pores easier to see.” Why is this not proved?
options: The facts only say ink was placed on the peel.
The lower surface was peeled before the ink was placed.
The watch glass held water during the ink step.
The coverslip was used after the ink was placed.

why.The lower surface was peeled before the: The order of peeling does not test the effect of ink.
why.The watch glass held water during the in: The water step does not test the effect of ink.
why.The coverslip was used after the ink was: The coverslip step does not test the effect of ink.

activities.explanation: This is correct because placing ink does not prove what ink does.

activities.prompt: You want to compare tiny pores on rhoeo and money plant leaves. Which plan is fair?
options: Peel both leaves and prepare each peel in the same way.
Peel both leaves but prepare only the rhoeo peel with ink.
Peel one leaf twice and prepare both peels in the same way.
Peel only rhoeo and prepare it, then compare it with money plant.

why.Peel both leaves but prepare only the rh: This gives one leaf extra ink, so the comparison is not fair.
why.Peel one leaf twice and prepare both pee: This compares two peels from one leaf instead of two plants.
why.Peel only rhoeo and prepare it, then com: This watches only one leaf peel before making a wide claim.

activities.explanation: This is correct because both leaves get the same preparation before comparison.

activities.prompt: Your group has prepared a leaf peel for observation. Which action should come last?
options: Add a drop of ink to the leaf peel.
Peel a thin layer from the lower leaf surface.
Place the leaf peel in a watch glass with water.
Cover the leaf peel with a coverslip.

Ink is added before the peel is covered for observation.
why.Peel a thin layer from the lower leaf su: The leaf peel is made before it is placed in water.
why.Place the leaf peel in a watch glass wit: The peel is placed in water before ink and the coverslip are added.

activities.explanation: This is correct because covering the peel is the final preparation step.

activities.prompt: A student watches one prepared leaf peel and says, “All leaves have the same pores.” Why is this claim too strong?
options: Only one leaf peel was watched, so other leaves were not checked.
The ink was placed after the leaf peel was prepared.
The leaf peel came from the lower leaf surface.
The coverslip covered the leaf peel during observation.

why.The ink was placed after the leaf peel w: The order of adding ink does not check other leaves.
why.The leaf peel came from the lower leaf s: Using the lower surface does not check other leaves.
why.The coverslip covered the leaf peel duri: Using a coverslip does not check other leaves.

activities.explanation: This is correct because one leaf peel cannot check all other leaves.

lessons.sceneCaption: Stomata in a microscopic print of spring onion leaf epidermis.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants

activities.prompt: How does water travel all the way up a tall plant?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Get Water and Food
activities.body: All living beings need water to grow. Roots take in water and minerals from soil. Minerals are important nutrients for plant growth. Plants use water during photosynthesis, the process in which plants use water. Xylem is a thin tube-like structure in plants. Phloem is a set of thin tube-like structures. Food made in leaves is carried to all parts of a plant.
keyPoints: Roots take in water and minerals from soil.
Plants use water during photosynthesis.
Phloem carries food made in leaves to all plant parts.
activities.explanation: Plants take in water and minerals, and transport food to their parts.

activities.prompt: A plant makes food in its leaves. How can that food reach the roots?
steps: Food made in the leaves is transported to all parts of the plant.
Roots are plant parts, so they also need this food.
Phloem is a set of thin tube-like structures that carries food.
Therefore, food reaches the roots through phloem.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do roots take in from the soil?
options: Water and minerals
Food and red ink
Red ink and minerals
Water and food
activities.explanation: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil. These help the plant grow.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct description.
pairs: take in water and minerals from soil
are important nutrients for plant growth
has a few drops of red ink added
is a set of thin tube-like structures
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a part or thing with the description given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which structure carries food made in leaves?
options: Phloem
Xylem
Roots
Minerals
activities.explanation: Phloem is a set of thin tube-like structures that carries food.

activities.prompt: Xylem is a thin tube-like ______ found in plants.
activities.hint: It is the tube-like part described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Xylem is called a thin tube-like structure found in plants.

activities.prompt: If roots cannot take in water and minerals, which needs of the plant may be affected?
options: Water and minerals for growth
Red ink and food for growth
Food and minerals for transport
Tumbler B and photosynthesis
activities.explanation: Water is needed for growth, and minerals are important nutrients for plant growth.

activities.prompt: Put these plant steps in order.
items: Roots take in water and minerals from soil
Phloem carries food to all parts of a plant
activities.explanation: Roots take in materials first. Plants use water, make food in leaves, and carry it through phloem.

activities.prompt: A houseplant has dry soil. What is most likely to happen?
options: The plant may grow slowly because water is missing.
The plant may grow faster because the soil is dry.
The plant may grow well because roots take in less water.
The plant may grow well because minerals stay in the soil.

why.The plant may grow faster because the so: Dry soil reduces the water roots can take in.
why.The plant may grow well because roots ta: Less water does not help growth because water is needed.
why.The plant may grow well because minerals: Minerals help growth, but dry soil limits available water.

activities.explanation: Water is needed for growth, so dry soil can slow growth.

activities.prompt: Two same plants get equal water. Only one pot has more minerals. What should happen?
options: The plant with more minerals should grow better.
The plant with less minerals should grow better.
Both plants should grow at exactly the same rate.
Both plants should stop growing and lose their food.

why.The plant with less minerals should grow: This reverses the role of important nutrients in plant growth.
why.Both plants should grow at exactly the s: Equal water does not remove the difference in minerals.
why.Both plants should stop growing and lose: The facts do not say minerals stop food transport.

activities.explanation: Minerals are important nutrients, so more minerals can support better growth.

activities.prompt: A plant uses water while making food in its leaves. Why does this matter for growth?
options: Water helps both food making and plant growth.
Food can be made only when the soil has no water.
Minerals replace water while the plant makes food.
Food becomes water after it reaches the roots.

why.Food can be made only when the soil has: No water prevents food making because photosynthesis uses water.
why.Minerals replace water while the plant m: Minerals are nutrients, not substitutes for water in photosynthesis.
why.Food becomes water after it reaches the: Food is transported to roots; it does not become their water.

activities.explanation: Water helps both food making and plant growth.

activities.prompt: Leaves make food. Which observation would show food reached the roots?
options: Food is found in phloem tubes near the roots.
Food is found in xylem tubes near the roots.
Minerals are found in leaves after roots take them from soil.
Water is found in leaves after roots take it from soil.

why.Food is found in xylem tubes near the ro: Xylem is tube-like, but it is not stated to carry food.
why.Minerals are found in leaves after roots: Roots take water and minerals from soil, not food from soil.
why.Water is found in leaves after roots tak: This confuses water transport with food transport.

activities.explanation: Phloem carries food, and food made in leaves reaches all plant parts.

activities.prompt: A child says, "Xylem carries food because it is tube-like." What is the best reply?
options: Tubes may look alike, but phloem is the food pathway.
Xylem does carry food because all tubes move food.
Phloem only carries water, so roots get no food.
Food travels through soil, not through any plant tubes.

why.Xylem does carry food because all tubes: Being tube-like does not make xylem the food-carrying pathway.
why.Phloem only carries water, so roots get: This swaps the roles of xylem and phloem.
why.Food travels through soil, not through a: The facts say food moves through phloem inside the plant.

activities.explanation: Xylem and phloem both look tube-like, but phloem carries food.

activities.prompt: A plant stands in tumbler B. A few drops of red ink are added. A child says this proves food reaches the roots. What is the best reply?
options: Adding ink to B does not prove that food moves to roots.
The ink proves phloem carries food because it has colour.
The ink proves roots make food from water and minerals.
The ink proves xylem turns minerals into leaf food.

why.The ink proves phloem carries food becau: This mistakes colour for proof of food transport.
why.The ink proves roots make food from wate: This mistakes root absorption for food making.
why.The ink proves xylem turns minerals into: This gives xylem a food-making job not given.

activities.explanation: The fact says ink was added to B, not that food moved.

lessons.sceneAlt: A circular plant diagram shows water and minerals travelling through xylem and organic foods travelling separately through phloem.
lessons.sceneCaption: Xylem carries water and minerals, while phloem carries food made in the leaves to other plant parts.

sceneCredit.text: Xylem and phloem diagram ku by Nefronus, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Nefronus

lessons.title: Respiration in Plants

activities.prompt: How do plants breathe without lungs?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Respire
activities.body: Plants respire, just like other living beings. During respiration, glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen. This releases energy, which helps plants grow and develop. Every part of a plant respires, whether it is green or non-green. In an experiment, moong bean seeds are soaked overnight and kept in the dark. Germinating seeds produce extra carbon dioxide. The lime water may turn milky in both test tubes.
keyPoints: Plants respire like all living beings.
Respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen and releases energy.
Every part of a plant respires, even non-green parts.
activities.explanation: Respiration gives plants energy for growth and development.

activities.prompt: Why might the lime water change during the moong bean seed experiment?
steps: Soak moong bean seeds overnight because the experiment starts with soaked seeds.
Keep the cotton moist with water because it must remain wet.
Leave the seeds undisturbed and dark for 24 hours so respiration can occur.
Seeds release extra carbon dioxide, so both test tubes may turn milky.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Respires?
activities.prompt: Which statement is true about living beings and plants?
options: All living beings, including plants, respire.
Only green plant parts respire.
Plants respire only at night.
Plants stop respiration while growing.
activities.explanation: All living beings respire. Every part of a plant does this too.

activities.prompt: During respiration, glucose is broken down in the presence of ______.
activities.hint: Name the gas used during respiration.
activities.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose when oxygen is present.

activities.title: Prepare the Experiment
activities.prompt: Match each material with its preparation.
activities.explanation: These preparations help show the effects of respiration in germinating seeds.

activities.title: What May Happen?
activities.prompt: What may happen in both test tubes?
options: The water may become salty.
The seeds may turn blue.
The cotton may become dry.
The lime water may turn milky.
activities.explanation: The lime water may turn milky in both test tubes.

activities.title: Why Is Extra Carbon Dioxide Produced?
activities.prompt: Why do germinating seeds produce additional carbon dioxide?
options: They absorb sunlight.
They store more water.
They make their own food.
They respire.
activities.explanation: Germinating seeds respire, so they produce additional carbon dioxide.

activities.title: Respiration and Plant Growth
activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order during plant respiration.
items: Glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen
The energy helps plants grow and develop
activities.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose, releases energy, and supports plant growth.

activities.prompt: Both tubes have germinating seeds and lime water. What may happen?
options: Both may turn milky because seeds release extra carbon dioxide.
Only one may turn milky because only one seed can respire.
Both may stay clear because darkness stops all respiration.
Both may turn milky because seeds absorb extra carbon dioxide.

why.Only one may turn milky because only one: This wrongly thinks only one germinating seed can respire.
why.Both may stay clear because darkness sto: This wrongly thinks darkness prevents the living seeds from respiring.
why.Both may turn milky because seeds absorb: This confuses taking in oxygen with releasing extra carbon dioxide.

activities.explanation: Extra carbon dioxide from germinating seeds may make both tubes milky.

activities.prompt: Both tubes have lime water and moist cotton. What should differ?
options: Add soaked germinating seeds to one tube only.
Add seeds and extra water to one tube only.
Add seeds and keep one tube in the light.
Add seeds and use dry cotton in one tube.

why.Add seeds and extra water to one tube on: Adding extra water changes two things, so we cannot know the cause.
why.Add seeds and keep one tube in the light: Changing light adds another difference, so the comparison is not fair.
why.Add seeds and use dry cotton in one tube: Using dry cotton changes moisture as well as the seeds.

activities.explanation: Changing only seeds makes the lime water comparison fair.

activities.prompt: Lime water stays clear. Why is the seeds’ no-respiration claim weak?
options: Germinating seeds respire even when lime water may stay clear.
Clear lime water proves that the seeds never respired.
Clear lime water means the seeds released no glucose.
Clear lime water shows that the seeds stayed asleep.

why.Clear lime water proves that the seeds n: This wrongly treats one possible result as proof of no respiration.
why.Clear lime water means the seeds release: This wrongly connects clear lime water with glucose release.
why.Clear lime water shows that the seeds st: This wrongly treats unclear lime water as proof that life stopped.

activities.explanation: Germinating seeds respire, while lime water only may turn milky.

lessons.sceneAlt: A young girl uses a blue watering can to water potted plants beside an outdoor fountain.
lessons.sceneCaption: A girl waters potted plants, showing how regular watering helps plants grow.
