activities.context: A person is caring for three potted plants. Pot A is placed in direct sunlight, and the soil in Pot A is kept slightly moist. Pot B receives sunlight but no water. Pot C is placed in the dark, while its soil is watered every day. The plant in Pot A grows better than the plant in Pot C. The plant in Pot B may die because it receives no water.
activities.prompt: If Pot C is moved into direct sunlight and its soil is still watered every day, what would be the most reasonable expectation?
options: Pot C may grow better because it would now receive both sunlight and water.
Pot C may grow better because water is more important than sunlight.
Pot C will grow exactly the same because watering has no effect.
Pot C will certainly grow better than Pot A in every way.

why.Pot C may grow better because water is m: This wrongly treats water as more important than sunlight.
why.Pot C will grow exactly the same because: Different conditions do not guarantee unchanged growth.
why.Pot C will certainly grow better than Po: Nothing proves that Pot C would grow better than Pot A.

activities.explanation: Sunlight would add the other condition plants need.

activities.context: A person is caring for three potted plants. Pot A is placed in direct sunlight, and the soil in Pot A is kept slightly moist. Pot B receives sunlight but no water. Pot C is placed in the dark, while its soil is watered every day. The plant in Pot A grows better than the plant in Pot C. The plant in Pot B may die because it receives no water.
activities.prompt: Why does the plant in Pot A grow better than the plant in Pot C?
options: Pot A receives sunlight as well as water, while Pot C receives water without sunlight.
Pot A receives sunlight without water, while Pot C receives sunlight and water.
Pot A receives water without sunlight, while Pot C receives sunlight without water.
Both pots give their plants the same amount of sunlight and water.

why.Pot A receives sunlight without water, w: This reverses the conditions of the two pots.
why.Pot A receives water without sunlight, w: This also reverses the conditions of the two pots.
why.Both pots give their plants the same amo: This ignores the difference between sunlight and darkness.

activities.explanation: Pot A has both conditions needed for growth.

activities.context: A person is caring for three potted plants. Pot A is placed in direct sunlight, and the soil in Pot A is kept slightly moist. Pot B receives sunlight but no water. Pot C is placed in the dark, while its soil is watered every day. The plant in Pot A grows better than the plant in Pot C. The plant in Pot B may die because it receives no water.
activities.prompt: What should the person do to give the plant in Pot C better conditions for growth?
options: Move Pot C into sunlight and keep watering its soil.
Move Pot C into sunlight and stop watering its soil.
Keep Pot C in the dark and keep watering its soil.
Move Pot C into sunlight and water its soil less often.

why.Move Pot C into sunlight and stop wateri: This removes water, which plants need for growth.
why.Keep Pot C in the dark and keep watering: This leaves Pot C without sunlight.
why.Move Pot C into sunlight and water its s: This reduces the regular watering that supports growth.

activities.explanation: This gives Pot C both sunlight and water.

activities.prompt: Explain why the plant in Pot A grows better than the plant in Pot C.
activities.answer: Pot A receives direct sunlight, and its soil is kept slightly moist, so it gets both sunlight and water. Pot C is watered every day, but it is placed in the dark. Because plants need both sunlight and water for growth, Pot A has the more suitable conditions.
points: Mentions that Pot A receives sunlight.
Mentions that Pot A receives water.
Explains that Pot C lacks sunlight.
Links both requirements to better growth.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is investigating a leaf in a science activity. First, the leaf is softened and placed in a test tube containing alcohol. It becomes colourless. Next, diluted iodine solution is put on the leaf, and a blue-black colour appears. The student concludes that the leaf contains starch. They explain that leaves capture sunlight with chlorophyll and produce starch, which plants store as food.
activities.prompt: After the diluted iodine solution is placed on the colourless leaf, what should the student expect to see?
options: A blue-black colour will appear on the leaf.
The leaf will remain colourless.
The leaf will become green again.
A blue-black colour will appear only after more sunlight is added.

The colourless leaf still contains the starch made in the leaf.
A green colour is not the stated result of adding iodine.
why.A blue-black colour will appear only aft: Sunlight is not stated to be needed for the colour test.

activities.explanation: A blue-black colour shows that starch is present.

activities.context: A student is investigating a leaf in a science activity. First, the leaf is softened and placed in a test tube containing alcohol. It becomes colourless. Next, diluted iodine solution is put on the leaf, and a blue-black colour appears. The student concludes that the leaf contains starch. They explain that leaves capture sunlight with chlorophyll and produce starch, which plants store as food.
activities.prompt: What would be the likely result if the student skipped the alcohol step?
options: A blue-black colour may still show if starch is present, but it would be harder to observe.
No blue-black colour could appear, even if the leaf contained starch.
The leaf would remain green and could not be tested.
The blue-black colour would become easier to see without decolourising the leaf.

why.No blue-black colour could appear, even: Skipping decolourising does not mean that the leaf cannot contain starch.
why.The leaf would remain green and could no: The activity does not state that alcohol is essential for starch to be present.
why.The blue-black colour would become easie: Without decolourising, the green leaf would make the colour change harder to see.

activities.explanation: Decolourising only makes the colour change easier to observe.

activities.prompt: Explain why leaves are called food factories.
activities.answer: Leaves are called food factories because they contain chlorophyll, which helps them capture sunlight. Using this sunlight, leaves produce starch. Plants store food in the form of starch, so the leaves make food that the plant can store.
points: Leaves contain chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll helps the leaf capture sunlight.
Starch is produced in the leaves.
Plants store food in the form of starch.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student placed a green leaf so that part of it was inside a bottle containing caustic soda, while the rest remained outside. Before the experiment, stored starch had been removed from the leaf. The leaf was then kept in sunlight. The part outside the bottle later turned blue-black, but the part inside did not. The student knew that plants prepare food by photosynthesis.
activities.prompt: If the caustic soda stopped absorbing carbon dioxide and everything else stayed the same, what result would most likely occur?
options: Both parts would turn blue-black because carbon dioxide could reach both.
Only the exposed part would turn blue-black because it receives sunlight.
Neither part would turn blue-black because the stored starch had been removed.
Only the enclosed part would turn blue-black because the bottle supplies carbon dioxide.

why.Only the exposed part would turn blue-bl: Sunlight alone is not enough because carbon dioxide is also needed.
why.Neither part would turn blue-black becau: Removing stored starch does not stop new starch being prepared during photosynthesis.
why.Only the enclosed part would turn blue-b: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide rather than supplying it.

activities.explanation: Without absorption, carbon dioxide could reach both parts from the air.

activities.context: A student placed a green leaf so that part of it was inside a bottle containing caustic soda, while the rest remained outside. Before the experiment, stored starch had been removed from the leaf. The leaf was then kept in sunlight. The part outside the bottle later turned blue-black, but the part inside did not. The student knew that plants prepare food by photosynthesis.
activities.prompt: If the leaf had been kept in darkness instead of sunlight, what result would most likely have been expected?
options: Neither part would turn blue-black, because photosynthesis requires sunlight.
Both parts would turn blue-black, because carbon dioxide was available to both.
Only the exposed part would turn blue-black, because carbon dioxide makes starch without sunlight.
Only the enclosed part would turn blue-black, because trapped oxygen would let photosynthesis continue.

why.Both parts would turn blue-black, becaus: Carbon dioxide alone cannot replace the need for sunlight.
why.Only the exposed part would turn blue-bl: Carbon dioxide is needed for starch formation, but sunlight is also required.
why.Only the enclosed part would turn blue-b: Oxygen is released during photosynthesis; it is not the condition that starts it.

activities.explanation: Photosynthesis is the sunlight-and-chlorophyll process by which plants prepare food.

activities.prompt: Explain why the part of the leaf outside the bottle turned blue-black while the part inside did not.
activities.answer: Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide from the air, sunlight and chlorophyll. Caustic soda absorbed the carbon dioxide around the leaf part inside the bottle, so that part could not prepare starch and did not turn blue-black. The exposed part received carbon dioxide, prepared starch during photosynthesis, and turned blue-black.
points: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, sunlight and chlorophyll.
Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
The enclosed part could not receive enough carbon dioxide to prepare starch.
The exposed part formed starch and turned blue-black.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is preparing a leaf peel to observe the tiny pores found on leaves. The student selects a rhoeo leaf, carefully removes a thin layer from its lower surface, and puts the peel into a watch glass containing water. Next, the student adds a drop of ink and covers the peel with a coverslip so the prepared leaf can be observed.
activities.prompt: After observing the prepared rhoeo peel, the student sees many tiny pores. What should the student call them?
options: stomata
carbon dioxide
oxygen
ink

why.carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is one of the gases exchanged through stomata.
why.oxygen: Oxygen is the other gas exchanged through stomata.
why.ink: Ink is the drop placed on the leaf peel.

activities.explanation: The tiny pores on leaves are called stomata.

activities.context: A student is preparing a leaf peel to observe the tiny pores found on leaves. The student selects a rhoeo leaf, carefully removes a thin layer from its lower surface, and puts the peel into a watch glass containing water. Next, the student adds a drop of ink and covers the peel with a coverslip so the prepared leaf can be observed.
activities.prompt: The student has prepared the watch glass with water but has not yet put the leaf peel into it. What is the correct next sequence?
options: Place the peel in the water, add ink, and then cover the peel.
Place the peel in the water, cover it, and then add ink.
Add ink to the water, place the peel in it, and then cover it.
Cover the empty watch glass, and then place the peel in the water.

why.Place the peel in the water, cover it, a: The coverslip is added after the drop of ink.
why.Add ink to the water, place the peel in: The ink is placed on the peel, not into the water beforehand.
why.Cover the empty watch glass, and then pl: The coverslip covers the peel after the other preparation steps.

activities.explanation: The peel is placed in water before ink is added and the coverslip is used.

activities.prompt: Explain how the student uses the leaf peel to observe and identify the tiny pores.
activities.answer: The student peels a thin layer from a leaf’s lower surface and puts it in water in a watch glass. A drop of ink is added, and the peel is covered with a coverslip. Tiny pores can then be seen on the peel, and the student identifies them as stomata.
points: A thin layer is taken from the lower surface.
The peel is placed in water in a watch glass.
Ink is added before the peel is covered with a coverslip.
The tiny pores are called stomata.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student keeps a leafy plant in tumbler B, with its roots in the soil, and adds a few drops of red ink to the water. The plant needs water to grow and uses water during photosynthesis. Its roots take in water and minerals from the soil. The student knows that xylem is a thin tube-like structure, while phloem carries food made in leaves to all plant parts.
activities.prompt: If the soil in tumbler B contains fewer minerals, what is most likely to happen next?
options: The plant's growth slows because it receives fewer nutrients.
The plant's growth speeds up because minerals are important nutrients.
The plant's growth stays the same because water alone supports it.
The plant makes more food because it receives fewer minerals.

why.The plant's growth speeds up because min: Fewer minerals can reduce the nutrients available to the plant.
why.The plant's growth stays the same becaus: More minerals would support growth rather than reduce it.
why.The plant makes more food because it rec: Water is needed for growth, but minerals also matter.

activities.explanation: Minerals are important nutrients for plant growth.

activities.context: A student keeps a leafy plant in tumbler B, with its roots in the soil, and adds a few drops of red ink to the water. The plant needs water to grow and uses water during photosynthesis. Its roots take in water and minerals from the soil. The student knows that xylem is a thin tube-like structure, while phloem carries food made in leaves to all plant parts.
activities.prompt: If the roots are damaged and cannot take in water and minerals from the soil, what would most likely happen?
options: The plant's growth would slow.
The plant's growth would speed up.
The plant's growth would stay exactly the same.
The plant would grow normally because its leaves make food.

Water is needed for growth and photosynthesis.
why.The plant's growth would stay exactly th: Damage to roots would reduce these supplies.
why.The plant would grow normally because it: The plant would not need fewer water and minerals.

activities.explanation: Roots supply the plant with water and minerals.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between xylem and phloem.
activities.answer: Xylem is a thin, tube-like structure found in plants. Phloem is a set of thin, tube-like structures that carries food. Both have tube-like shapes, but phloem has the stated job of carrying food made in the leaves to all parts of the plant.
points: Describes xylem as a thin tube-like structure.
Describes phloem as a set of thin tube-like structures.
Explains that phloem carries food.
Mentions transport to all plant parts.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student set up two test tubes for an investigation of respiration in plants. One test tube contained moong bean seeds that had been soaked in water overnight. The other contained cotton moistened with water and kept wet. Both were left undisturbed for 24 hours in the dark. After the waiting period, the student observed that the lime water in both test tubes had turned milky. The student then thought about the growing seeds and their need for energy.
activities.prompt: The cotton has dried during the investigation. What should the student do next?
options: Wet the cotton again.
Leave the cotton dry for the rest of the investigation.
Add lime water to the cotton.
Move the cotton to a different test tube.

why.Leave the cotton dry for the rest of the: Keeping it dry would change the stated setup.
Lime water is not a substitute for wetting the cotton.
why.Move the cotton to a different test tube: Moving it would not restore the wet condition.

activities.explanation: The cotton must be kept wet.

activities.context: A student set up two test tubes for an investigation of respiration in plants. One test tube contained moong bean seeds that had been soaked in water overnight. The other contained cotton moistened with water and kept wet. Both were left undisturbed for 24 hours in the dark. After the waiting period, the student observed that the lime water in both test tubes had turned milky. The student then thought about the growing seeds and their need for energy.
activities.prompt: What would happen if oxygen were not available to the germinating seeds?
options: Respiration would stop as described, and additional carbon dioxide would not be produced.
Respiration would speed up, causing more additional carbon dioxide.
Glucose would still be broken down in the same way.
The seeds would release more energy and grow more quickly.

why.Respiration would speed up, causing more: Removing oxygen would not increase respiration.
why.Glucose would still be broken down in th: Breaking down glucose during respiration requires oxygen.
why.The seeds would release more energy and: More energy and faster growth would not result from removing oxygen.

activities.explanation: The stated respiration process requires oxygen.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Life Processes in Plants

activities.title: Growing well
activities.prompt: Which setup helps Pot A's plant grow better than Pot C's plant?
options: Pot A stays in darkness
Pot A has sunlight and moist soil
Pot C receives dry soil
Pot C gets direct sunlight
activities.explanation: Pot A has sunlight and slightly moist soil. Pot C is dark but receives water.

activities.title: Plant food
activities.prompt: Unlike animals, plants do not eat food.
activities.explanation: Plants prepare food instead of eating it. This process is called photosynthesis.

activities.title: Stored food
activities.prompt: Plants store food in the form of ______.
activities.hint: This food is made in the leaves.
activities.explanation: Plants store food as starch. Starch is produced in their leaves.

activities.title: Match the plant parts
activities.prompt: Match each plant part or substance with its correct job.
activities.explanation: Chlorophyll captures sunlight. Leaves make starch, stomata exchange gases, and roots absorb water.

activities.title: Testing for starch
activities.prompt: Put the starch-testing steps in the correct order.
items: The softened leaf is placed in alcohol
Diluted iodine is placed on the leaf
The leaf shows a blue-black colour
activities.explanation: Alcohol makes the leaf colourless. Iodine then shows a blue-black colour when starch is present.

activities.title: Making plant food
activities.prompt: Which process prepares food in sunlight using chlorophyll?
options: Respiration
Photosynthesis
Decolourising
Soaking
activities.explanation: Photosynthesis uses sunlight and chlorophyll. It mainly happens in leaves.

activities.title: Air and plant food
activities.prompt: The part of the leaf inside the bottle turns blue-black.
activities.explanation: The part inside the bottle does not turn blue-black. Caustic soda absorbs the carbon dioxide needed to prepare starch.

activities.title: Carrying food
activities.prompt: The set of thin tube-like structures that carries food is called ______.
activities.hint: It transports food made in the leaves.
activities.explanation: Phloem carries food from the leaves to all plant parts. Xylem is another tube-like plant structure.

activities.title: Match the processes
activities.prompt: Match each item with the correct statement.
activities.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose and releases energy. Every plant part respires, and stomata exchange gases.

activities.title: Observing stomata
activities.prompt: Put the leaf-peel observation steps in the correct order.
items: A thin layer is peeled from the leaf
The peel is placed in water
A drop of ink is placed on the peel
A coverslip is placed over the peel
activities.explanation: The lower leaf peel is placed in water. Ink and a coverslip help you observe the tiny pores.

chapters.title: Light: Shadows and Reflections
chapters.summary: In this chapter: light sources and luminous objects; light travels in a straight line; light through materials and shadow formation; reflection of light and plane mirrors.

lessons.title: Light Sources and Luminous Objects

activities.prompt: Why do fireflies glow, and why does the Moon shine at night?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Objects that make their own light
activities.body: Luminous objects give out their own light. These include the Sun, stars, lightning, natural fire and some animals. Non-luminous objects do not. The Moon reflects sunlight, so it is non-luminous. The Sun is Earth's main natural light source. Human-made lighting began with fire. Later, people used animal fat, oil, wax and gas. Electric lighting now meets most lighting needs. LED lamps use less power, shine brighter and last longer.
keyPoints: Luminous objects give out their own light.
The Moon reflects sunlight instead of making its own light.
Fire and electric lighting are human-made light sources.
activities.explanation: Luminous means giving out your own light rather than reflecting it.

activities.prompt: A child sees the Moon shining at night and thinks it makes its own light. How can we explain the Moon's light?
steps: The Moon is non-luminous, so it cannot make its own light.
The Sun gives out its own light, and some sunlight falls on the Moon.
The Moon reflects that sunlight, so we see the Moon.
Therefore, the visible Moon shows reflected sunlight, not its own light.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Fireflies and human-made light
activities.body: Fireflies are seasonal insects that use light to communicate. Their numbers are decreasing. One reason for this is light pollution. Human-made lighting began when humans first created fire. People later used animal fat, oil, wax and gas to make fire. Electric lighting now meets most people's lighting needs.
keyPoints: Fireflies use light to communicate.
Light pollution is one reason fireflies are decreasing.
People first used fire for human-made lighting.
activities.explanation: Fireflies show how living things can use light for communication.

activities.prompt: What does the Moon do with sunlight that falls on it?
options: It gives out its own light.
It reflects the sunlight.
It lights the fireflies.
It powers LED lamps.
activities.explanation: The Moon is non-luminous because it reflects sunlight that falls on it.

activities.prompt: Match each object with its correct description.
pairs: Main natural light source on Earth
Reflects sunlight that falls on it
activities.explanation: Each matching pair shows how its light source works.

activities.prompt: LED lamps use less ______, shine brighter and last longer than traditional lamps.
activities.hint: Think about what an electric lamp needs to work.
activities.explanation: LED lamps use less power than traditional lamps.

activities.prompt: Put these lighting developments in the order described in the lesson.
items: People use animal fat, oil, wax and gas
Electric lighting meets most lighting needs
activities.explanation: People first created fire. They later used other fuels before electric lighting.

activities.prompt: A child sees fewer fireflies than before. Which reason is given in the lesson?
options: The problem of light pollution
The reflection of moonlight
The lower power of LED lamps
The brightness of electric lamps
activities.explanation: Light pollution is one reason for the decreasing number of fireflies.

activities.prompt: Which statement about these light sources is correct?
options: The Sun reflects moonlight.
Fireflies give out moonlight.
The Moon reflects sunlight.
Fireflies use moonlight to communicate.
activities.explanation: The Moon is non-luminous because it reflects sunlight that falls on it.

activities.prompt: A garden has many fireflies. Bright lights are then put near it. What may happen?
options: Bright lights can reduce the fireflies.
Fireflies may make more light.
Fireflies may stop using light.
Fireflies may change their color.

This assumes extra light makes fireflies produce more light.
This confuses communication light with a reason for change.
This assumes fireflies can change their light color.

activities.explanation: Light pollution is one reason fireflies decrease.

activities.prompt: A bright Moon is seen on a night. Which chain explains the light?
options: Sunlight falls on the Moon, and the Moon reflects it.
The Moon makes light, and the Sun reflects it.
Fireflies send light to the Moon, and the Moon reflects it.
Electric lamps send light to the Moon, and the Moon reflects it.

why.The Moon makes light, and the Sun reflec: This reverses the light because the Sun gives out its own light.
why.Fireflies send light to the Moon, and th: This wrongly makes fireflies the source of the Moon's light.
why.Electric lamps send light to the Moon, a: This wrongly makes electric lamps the source of the Moon's light.

activities.explanation: The Sun gives out light that falls on the Moon and is reflected.

activities.prompt: A child wants light without using sunlight. Which object can give out its own light?
options: An electric lamp that is on.
The Moon reflecting sunlight.
A metal spoon in sunlight.
A wooden chair beside sunlight.

The Moon reflects sunlight, so it does not make its own light.
A spoon reflects light from a source.
A chair reflects light from a source.

activities.explanation: A lit electric lamp gives out its own light.

activities.prompt: To test whether bright lights affect firefly numbers, what should the child do?
options: Compare numbers in brighter and darker places.
Count fireflies in one bright place.
Change the lights, then count only once.
Guess the numbers without watching fireflies.

Counting in one place cannot show the effect of different lights.
One count after changing lights cannot provide a fair comparison.
why.Guess the numbers without watching firef: A guess does not provide evidence about firefly numbers.

activities.explanation: Comparing brighter and darker places gives a fair comparison.

activities.prompt: A child says, “The Moon is luminous because we can see it.” What is the flaw?
options: Seeing it does not show it makes light.
The Moon is visible only on sunny nights.
The Moon shines more brightly than the Sun.
Fireflies cannot give out their own light.

why.The Moon is visible only on sunny nights: This wrongly limits moonlight to one kind of weather.
why.The Moon shines more brightly than the S: This wrongly compares the Moon's reflected light with the Sun's own light.
why.Fireflies cannot give out their own ligh: This denies the light that fireflies use to communicate.

activities.explanation: The Moon is visible because it reflects sunlight, not because it makes light.

lessons.title: Light Travels in a Straight Line

activities.prompt: Can we make light reveal the path it takes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How light travels
activities.body: Light travels in a straight line. You can test this with three matchboxes, three holes, a torch and a screen. When the holes are in one line and at the same height, the torch lamp gives a bright spot on the screen. If the holes are not in one line, no light spot appears. A candle flame is visible through a straight pipe, but not a bent pipe.
keyPoints: Light travels in a straight line.
Holes must be in one line at the same height.
A candle flame is visible through a straight pipe.
activities.explanation: These observations help you see that light follows a straight path.

activities.title: Explore shadows and straight-line light

tasks.say: Move the object closer to the lamp than it starts.
tasks.then: The shadow becomes bigger because light travels in straight lines.

tasks.say: Now move the object farther from the lamp than it starts.
tasks.then: The shadow becomes smaller as the object moves farther away.

activities.takeaway: Light travels in straight lines, so an object blocks the light and forms a shadow.
activities.explanation: Light travels in straight lines, so an object blocks the light and forms a shadow.

activities.prompt: Three matchboxes have holes at different heights. Can the screen show a bright spot?
steps: The three holes are not in one straight line.
Therefore, the screen does not show a light spot.
Level holes and a level torch make the setup correct.
The bright spot then shows that light travels in a straight line.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which setup should you use to receive a bright spot on the screen?
options: Three holes in one line, with the torch at their height.
Three holes at different heights, with the torch nearby.
Three holes in a bent line, with the torch at their height.
activities.explanation: Keep the three holes in one line at the same height as the torch lamp. This setup makes the screen receive a bright spot.

activities.prompt: When the three holes are not in one line, the screen does not show a light ______.
activities.hint: This bright mark appears when the setup is correct.
activities.explanation: The screen does not show the light spot when the holes are not in line.

activities.prompt: Match each observation with its result.
pairs: A bright spot on the screen
No light spot on the screen
The holes are not in one line
activities.explanation: Each result follows from the straight-line test in your book.

activities.prompt: Put the investigation steps and result in order.
items: Arrange the three matchboxes in a straight line
Keep all three holes at the same height
Place the torch lamp at the same height
The screen receives a bright spot
activities.explanation: The boxes, holes and torch are aligned before the bright spot appears.

activities.prompt: Which pipe lets you see a candle flame?
options: A bent pipe
A straight pipe
A pipe bent twice
activities.explanation: A candle flame can be seen through a straight pipe. It cannot be seen through a bent pipe.

activities.prompt: Which statement about light is correct?
options: A laser beam in water can be seen on a straight path.
Light always bends around corners.
A candle flame can be seen through a bent pipe.
activities.explanation: A laser beam in water follows a straight path. Light can sometimes bend around corners, but this is studied in higher grades.

activities.prompt: Three holes are level, but one sits aside. What appears on the screen?
options: A bright light spot appears on the screen.
A faint crooked light spot appears.
No light spot appears on the screen.
Three separate light spots appear.

why.A bright light spot appears on the scree: This assumes the three holes are in one line.
This assumes light can pass along a crooked path.
This assumes each hole sends its own spot to the screen.

activities.explanation: The holes are not in one line, so no light spot appears.

activities.prompt: The three holes are in one line. The torch is below them. What will the screen show?
options: A bright light spot on the screen.
A crooked light spot on the screen.
A light spot above the torch lamp.
No light spot on the screen.

This assumes the torch height does not matter.
This assumes light can follow a crooked path.
This assumes light turns upward before passing through the holes.

activities.explanation: The torch must be at the same height as the holes.

activities.prompt: One test uses level holes and a level torch. Which change makes a fair test?
options: Move one hole sideways, keeping every height the same.
Move one hole sideways and raise the torch.
Raise one hole and lower the torch.
Raise the torch and keep every hole level.

why.Move one hole sideways and raise the tor: This changes both hole alignment and torch height.
This changes both hole alignment and torch height.
why.Raise the torch and keep every hole leve: This changes only torch height, not the straight-line arrangement.

activities.explanation: Only straight-line alignment changes; all heights stay the same.

lessons.title: Light through Materials and Shadow Formation

activities.prompt: What happens to light when it meets different materials?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Materials Make Shadows
activities.body: Transparent materials let light pass almost completely through. Translucent materials let light pass partly through. Opaque materials stop light. An opaque object blocks light and creates a dark patch called a shadow. A shadow needs a light source, an opaque object and a screen. Shape, size and sharpness depend on the object's position. Opaque objects make darker shadows; translucent objects make lighter shadows. Some transparent objects create faint shadows.
keyPoints: Transparent materials let light pass almost completely.
Translucent materials let light pass partly.
An opaque object in light's path creates a shadow.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you work out how different materials make shadows.

activities.title: Change a shadow

tasks.say: Move the object close to the lamp.
tasks.then: The shadow grows large.

tasks.say: Move it far from the lamp.
tasks.then: The shadow shrinks towards the size of the object.

activities.takeaway: Light travels in straight lines, and an object blocks it to make a shadow.
activities.explanation: Light travels in straight lines, and an object blocks it to make a shadow.

activities.prompt: A clear sheet makes a faint shadow. An opaque card makes a darker shadow. Why?
steps: The clear sheet lets almost all light through, blocking only a little.
The opaque card blocks light, so less light reaches the wall.
Where light does not reach, a dark patch called a shadow forms.
Little blocked light makes a faint shadow; the card's is darker.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which type of material lets light pass almost completely through?
options: Translucent
Opaque
Transparent
activities.explanation: Transparent materials let light pass almost completely through them.

activities.prompt: Match each material to what happens to light.
pairs: Light passes almost completely through it
Light does not pass through it
activities.explanation: Transparent and translucent materials pass different amounts of light. Opaque materials stop light.

activities.prompt: The dark patch where light does not reach is called a ______.
activities.hint: It forms behind an opaque object.
activities.explanation: This dark patch is called a shadow.

activities.prompt: Which one is given as an example of a shadow screen?
options: A shadow
A wall
A light source
activities.explanation: Walls, floors, ground and other surfaces can act as screens.

activities.prompt: Put the shadow-forming events in order.
items: The opaque object blocks the light.
A dark patch forms on the screen.
activities.explanation: The opaque object blocks light. The dark patch then forms on the screen.

activities.prompt: Which object forms a darker shadow?
options: Translucent object
Opaque object
Transparent object
activities.explanation: Opaque objects form darker shadows. Translucent objects make lighter shadows. Some transparent objects create faint shadows.

activities.prompt:
A clear sheet stands between a lamp and a wall.
What should the wall show?
options: Some light and a faint shadow.
All light and no shadow.
No light and a dark shadow.
All light and a dark shadow.

It treats the clear sheet as an opaque object.
It thinks almost passing light means none is blocked.
It thinks a clear sheet must make a dark shadow.

activities.explanation: A transparent sheet can block a little light, making a faint shadow.

activities.prompt:
A translucent sheet is held in front of a wall.
What should the wall show?
options: Some light and a lighter shadow.
All light and no shadow.
No light and a darker shadow.
Some light and a darker shadow.

It treats a translucent sheet as fully transparent.
It treats a translucent sheet as an opaque object.
It thinks a partly passing sheet still makes an opaque-style shadow.

activities.explanation: Some light passes through, so the sheet makes a lighter shadow.

activities.prompt:
An opaque toy block is put in a lamp's path.
What appears on a wall behind it?
options: A dark patch where light is blocked.
A bright patch where light is blocked.
A clear picture of the lamp.
No patch on the wall.

It confuses a shadow with a bright area.
It thinks the lamp's shape appears on the wall.
It thinks blocked light still reaches the wall.

activities.explanation: An opaque block stops light, leaving a dark patch called a shadow.

activities.prompt:
A lamp and an opaque block make a shadow on a screen.
The screen is taken away. What happens next?
options: No shadow can form.
A darker shadow will form.
A lighter shadow will form.
The shadow stays behind the block.

It thinks removing the screen makes the shadow darker.
It thinks removing the screen makes the shadow lighter.
It thinks a shadow can remain without a screen.

activities.explanation: A shadow needs a screen, so none can form without one.

lessons.title: Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors

activities.prompt: What can we learn about light by watching our reflections?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Light and Plane Mirrors
activities.body: Light travels in a straight line. When it meets a shiny surface or mirror, its direction changes. This is reflection. A plane mirror makes an image that is erect, the same size as its object, and cannot be obtained on a screen. Stand close to a mirror, and its image appears close. Stand far away, and it appears far away. Left and right appear reversed. This is lateral inversion.
keyPoints: A shiny surface changes the direction of light.
A plane mirror forms an erect image of the same size.
Left and right appear reversed in a mirror image.
activities.explanation: A shiny surface changes light's direction, and a plane mirror forms an erect image.

activities.title: Bounce light off a mirror

tasks.say: Make the ray come in at 60 degrees.
tasks.then: It leaves at 60 degrees too.

tasks.say: Shine it straight down the normal.
tasks.then: It comes straight back.

activities.takeaway: The angle going out always equals the angle coming in.
activities.explanation: The angle going out always equals the angle coming in.

activities.prompt: Why does your image look close when you stand close to a plane mirror?
steps: Light travels straight until it reaches the shiny mirror.
The shiny mirror changes the direction of the light.
When you stand close, the image also appears close.
So the image appears close because your position is close.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Light Meets a Mirror
activities.prompt: What happens when light meets a shiny surface?
options: It changes direction.
It keeps the same direction.
It stops at the surface.
It travels in a circle.
activities.explanation: A shiny surface or mirror changes the direction of light.

activities.title: The Upright Image
activities.prompt: A plane mirror forms an ______ image.
activities.hint: This word means upright.
activities.explanation: An upright image is called erect. A plane mirror forms an erect image.

activities.title: Your Mirror Image
activities.prompt: You stand close to a plane mirror. How does its image appear?
options: It appears close.
It appears far away.
It appears much larger.
It appears much smaller.
activities.explanation: When you stand close to a plane mirror, the image also appears close.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct name or description.
pairs: A face seen in a mirror
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an idea and its matching description from the lesson.

activities.title: How Reflection Happens
activities.prompt: Put the steps of reflection in the correct order.
items: Light travels in a straight line.
Light changes direction at the surface.
activities.explanation: Light travels straight until it changes direction at a shiny surface.

activities.title: Describe the Image
activities.prompt: Which words describe the image formed by a plane mirror?
options: Erect and a smaller size
Inverted and a smaller size
Erect and the same size
Upright but a smaller size
activities.explanation: A plane mirror forms an erect image. That image is the same size as its object.

activities.prompt: A child holds a puppet in front of a plane mirror. What does the image look like?
options: It is the same size and upright.
It is the same size and upside down.
It is smaller and upside down.
It is larger and upright.

This confuses an erect image with an upside-down one.
This wrongly thinks the image becomes smaller.
This wrongly thinks the image becomes larger.

activities.explanation: Plane mirror images are the same size and erect.

activities.prompt: What test shows if a plane mirror image appears on a screen?
options: Place a screen where the image appears.
Place a screen behind the mirror.
Look at the image without a screen.
Touch the mirror where the image appears.

This thinks the image forms behind the mirror.
Looking without a screen cannot test screen capture.
why.Touch the mirror where the image appears: Touching the mirror does not test screen capture.

activities.explanation: This checks the screen because plane mirror images cannot be obtained there.

activities.prompt: A child stands far from a plane mirror. What does the child see?
options: A faraway image with the same size.
A faraway image that is much smaller.
A close image with the same size.
A close image that is much larger.

This wrongly assumes distance changes the image size.
This reverses the far image position.
This changes both the position and size wrongly.

activities.explanation: A far position gives a faraway image, and the size stays the same.

lessons.title: The Pinhole Camera

activities.prompt: How can a tiny opening show us the world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How a Pinhole Camera Works
activities.body: A pinhole camera forms an image when light rays pass through a tiny hole. Two cardboard boxes slide together. Make a small hole in the larger box's opposite face. Use thin paper that lets light through as the screen, facing inside. Cover your head and camera with a dark cloth. Move the smaller box until an image appears. The image is upside-down.
keyPoints: Light rays pass through a tiny hole.
Thin translucent paper is the screen.
The image is upside-down.
activities.explanation: You can make a simple camera that forms an upside-down image.

activities.prompt: How can two boxes make an outdoor scene appear on paper?
steps: Slide the small box inside; make a hole opposite it for rays.
Face translucent paper inward in the large box to form the screen.
Cover your head and camera; the dark cloth blocks extra light.
Move the small box so an upside-down image appears on the paper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Forms the Image?
activities.prompt: What helps a pinhole camera form an image?
options: A dark cloth covering the camera
Light rays passing through a tiny hole
Two boxes sliding together
Paper facing outside the box
activities.explanation: Light rays pass through the tiny hole and form an image.

activities.title: Using the Camera Outdoors
activities.prompt: A pinhole camera can be used outdoors.
activities.explanation: Yes, you can use your pinhole camera outdoors.

activities.title: The Small Opening
activities.prompt: Light rays pass through a ______ hole to form an image.
activities.hint: The hole is very small.
activities.explanation: A tiny hole lets light rays pass through it.

activities.title: Parts and Jobs
activities.prompt: Match each camera part with its job.
pairs: Move it until an image appears
activities.explanation: The hole admits light rays, while the screen shows the image.

activities.title: Moving the Inner Box
activities.prompt: What happens when you move the smaller box correctly?
options: The screen changes colour.
The small hole closes.
An image appears on the tracing paper.
The boxes become one box.
activities.explanation: Move the smaller box until an image appears on the tracing paper.

activities.title: Make and Use the Camera
activities.prompt: Put these actions in the correct order.
items: Make two cardboard boxes slide together
Make a small hole in the larger box
Cover your head and camera with a dark cloth
Move the smaller box until an image appears
activities.explanation: These actions prepare the camera and help an image appear.

activities.prompt: Outdoor light reaches the camera's paper screen. What must happen first?
options: The light rays must pass through a tiny hole.
The light rays must pass through the translucent paper.
The light rays must bounce from a mirror.
The light rays must enter through an open box top.

why.The light rays must pass through the tra: The paper receives the image; it is not the opening.
why.The light rays must bounce from a mirror: The camera forms images by rays passing through a hole.
why.The light rays must enter through an ope: An open top is not the tiny opening used by this camera.

activities.explanation: This lets the camera form an image on its screen.

activities.prompt: Extra light reaches the camera. How can you improve the screen image?
options: Cover your head and camera with tracing paper.
Cover your head and camera with a dark cloth.
Cover only the tiny hole with tracing paper.
Cover the camera with the larger cardboard box.

why.Cover your head and camera with tracing: Tracing paper is translucent, not a dark cloth.
why.Cover only the tiny hole with tracing pa: The cloth covers the whole camera, not only the tiny hole.
why.Cover the camera with the larger cardboa: The larger box is part of the camera, not a covering cloth.

activities.explanation: A dark cloth covers the head and camera to block extra light.

activities.prompt: How does a mirror image differ from a pinhole-camera image?
options: The mirror has lateral inversion, but the pinhole image is upside down.
The mirror turns top and bottom, but the pinhole image stays upright.
Both images reverse left-right and turn upside down together.
Neither image reverses left-right or turns upside down.

why.The mirror turns top and bottom, but the: This confuses the mirror's lateral inversion with the pinhole's inversion.
why.Both images reverse left-right and turn: The pinhole image is upside down, but a mirror image is not.
why.Neither image reverses left-right or tur: This wrongly makes both images reverse left-right and top-bottom.

activities.explanation: A mirror has lateral inversion, while the pinhole image is upside down.

lessons.title: Making Useful Items from Light

activities.prompt: How can we use light to make surprising tools for seeing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Useful Mirror Items
activities.body: A periscope uses two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box. Reflection from the mirrors lets you see objects that are not directly visible. A kaleidoscope uses three rectangular plane-mirror strips of equal width. The strips join in a triangle inside a circular tube. Looking through the open end shows a beautiful pattern. Turning it gives a different pattern each time.
keyPoints: A periscope uses two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box.
Reflection helps you see objects that are not directly visible.
A kaleidoscope makes changing patterns using three mirror strips.
activities.explanation: Mirrors reflect light to make useful viewing items.

activities.prompt: A child cannot see a toy behind a screen. What should they make?
steps: Use two plane mirrors because a Z-shaped box makes a simple periscope.
Use two reflections because they show objects that are not directly visible.
Look through the periscope because the mirrors show the hidden toy.
So the child can see what the screen hides from direct view.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which item uses two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box?
options: A periscope
A kaleidoscope
A tracing sheet
A bangle
activities.explanation: A periscope is made with two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box.

activities.prompt: A periscope lets us see an object that is not directly visible.
activities.explanation: Reflection from two mirrors lets us see objects that are not directly visible.

activities.prompt: A kaleidoscope uses ______ rectangular plane-mirror strips of equal width.
activities.hint: Count the mirror strips used in a kaleidoscope.
activities.explanation: The kaleidoscope uses three rectangular plane-mirror strips of equal width.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its description.
pairs: Two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box
Covers the other end of the kaleidoscope
activities.explanation: Each description shows a part or feature of a periscope or kaleidoscope.

activities.prompt: What covers the other end of a kaleidoscope?
options: Thick reflective paper
A transparent plastic sheet
Tracing paper
A coloured bangle
activities.explanation: The other end of the kaleidoscope is covered with tracing paper.

activities.prompt: Put these kaleidoscope-making steps in order.
items: Join the mirror strips in a triangle.
Fix the mirror strips inside a circular tube.
Fix a transparent plastic sheet at one end.
Place coloured bangles or beads on the plastic sheet.
Cover the other end with tracing paper.
activities.explanation: This order places the strips, sheet, coloured pieces and tracing paper correctly.

activities.prompt: Turning a kaleidoscope shows the same pattern every time.
activities.explanation: Turning the kaleidoscope gives a different pattern each time.

activities.prompt: Which answer uses two true facts about periscopes?
options: It uses three mirror strips and makes coloured patterns.
It uses tracing paper and covers a circular tube.
It uses thick reflective paper and joins strips in a triangle.
It uses two plane mirrors and shows objects that are not directly visible.
activities.explanation: A periscope uses two plane mirrors, which let us see objects that are not directly visible.

activities.prompt: Two plane mirrors sit in a Z-shaped box. What can the child see?
options: An object that is not directly visible.
Only the empty inside of the box.
A direct and unchanged view outside.
The two mirrors clearly seen without reflection.

This mistake thinks the box works without reflecting a view.
This mistake assumes the view is direct, not shown by two reflections.
why.The two mirrors clearly seen without ref: This mistake thinks the mirrors show no reflection.

activities.explanation: This is right because two reflections show objects not directly visible.

activities.prompt: Three mirror strips form a triangle. One is narrower. What should change?
options: Make all three strips have equal width.
Make the narrow mirror strip even narrower.
Cover the mirror strips with tracing paper.
Move the mirror strips outside the tube.

why.Make the narrow mirror strip even narrow: This mistake thinks equal width does not matter.
why.Cover the mirror strips with tracing pap: This mistake puts a tube cover around the mirror strips.
This mistake forgets that the strips stay inside the tube.

activities.explanation: This is right because all three strips must have equal width.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between luminous and non-luminous objects, using the Sun and Moon as examples.
activities.answer: Luminous objects give out their own light, while non-luminous objects do not. The Sun and stars are luminous because they give out their own light. The Moon is non-luminous; it looks bright because it reflects sunlight that falls on it.
points: Defines luminous objects.
Defines non-luminous objects.
Identifies the Sun as luminous.
Explains that the Moon reflects sunlight.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Three matchboxes were arranged in a line, with all three holes at the same height. A torch lamp was placed at the same height as the holes, and a bright spot appeared on the screen. When one matchbox was moved so the holes were not in one line, no light spot appeared. The student also saw a candle flame through a straight pipe, but not through a bent pipe. A laser beam in water was seen following a straight path.
activities.prompt: After one matchbox has been moved, what would happen on the screen?
options: The screen would remain without a light spot because the three openings no longer form one straight line.
The screen would show a bright spot because the holes are still at equal heights.
The screen would show a bright spot because the torch lamp is still level with the holes.
The screen would show a bright spot because light can always bend around corners.

why.The screen would show a bright spot beca: Equal heights alone do not produce the spot.
Keeping the lamp level is not enough if the holes are misaligned.
Light does not always bend around corners.

activities.explanation: The displaced openings are no longer in one straight line.

activities.context: Three matchboxes were arranged in a line, with all three holes at the same height. A torch lamp was placed at the same height as the holes, and a bright spot appeared on the screen. When one matchbox was moved so the holes were not in one line, no light spot appeared. The student also saw a candle flame through a straight pipe, but not through a bent pipe. A laser beam in water was seen following a straight path.
activities.prompt: What would the student expect to see when looking through the bent pipe at the candle flame?
options: The flame would not be visible through the bend because the light path would no longer be straight.
The flame would be visible because light can turn at the bend.
The flame would be visible because the candle flame is bright enough to overcome the bend.
The flame would be visible because the bent pipe makes the light path straight again.

why.The flame would be visible because light: Light does not freely turn to follow a bent pipe.
why.The flame would be visible because the c: Brightness does not change the straight-line rule.
why.The flame would be visible because the b: A bend makes the path curved rather than straight.

activities.explanation: A bent pipe does not provide a straight path for the light.

activities.context: Three matchboxes were arranged in a line, with all three holes at the same height. A torch lamp was placed at the same height as the holes, and a bright spot appeared on the screen. When one matchbox was moved so the holes were not in one line, no light spot appeared. The student also saw a candle flame through a straight pipe, but not through a bent pipe. A laser beam in water was seen following a straight path.
activities.prompt: What should the student do to restore the bright spot on the screen?
options: Move the matchbox back until all three holes form one straight line.
Raise the torch lamp so that it is no longer at the same height as the holes.
Tilt the moved matchbox while keeping its hole at the same height.
Leave the matchbox where it is because equal heights are sufficient.

why.Raise the torch lamp so that it is no lo: The torch lamp should remain at the same height as the holes.
why.Tilt the moved matchbox while keeping it: Tilting the matchbox would leave the holes out of line.
why.Leave the matchbox where it is because e: Equal heights alone do not restore the spot.

activities.explanation: The three holes must be arranged in one straight line.

activities.prompt: Explain why the light spot disappears when one matchbox is moved.
activities.answer: Moving one matchbox means the three holes are no longer in one straight line. Matching heights alone is therefore not enough for the spot to appear. The observations show that light travels in a straight line, so the screen no longer receives the light spot.
points: One moved matchbox leaves the holes out of one straight line.
Having the holes at the same height is not sufficient by itself.
Light travels in a straight line.
The screen no longer receives the light spot.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child shines light towards a wall. A transparent sheet is first placed in the path, so light still reaches the wall almost completely. A translucent sheet then replaces it, allowing only part of the light through. Finally, an opaque coloured card is placed in the path. The card blocks the light and forms a dark patch on the wall. Moving the card to another position changes the shape, size and sharpness of the patch.
activities.prompt: If the opaque card is replaced by the translucent sheet, what will happen to the patch on the wall?
options: A lighter patch will appear because less light reaches the wall.
The patch will become darker because the sheet blocks all light.
The patch will disappear because light passes through the sheet.
The patch will keep the same darkness because partly passing light still forms a shadow.

why.The patch will become darker because the: A translucent sheet allows part of the light through and does not block all of it.
why.The patch will disappear because light p: The light still reaches the wall, so a patch remains.
why.The patch will keep the same darkness be: The amount of light reaching the wall changes, so the shadow does not stay equally dark.

activities.explanation: Correct: less light reaches the wall, so the shadow is lighter.

activities.context: A child shines light towards a wall. A transparent sheet is first placed in the path, so light still reaches the wall almost completely. A translucent sheet then replaces it, allowing only part of the light through. Finally, an opaque coloured card is placed in the path. The card blocks the light and forms a dark patch on the wall. Moving the card to another position changes the shape, size and sharpness of the patch.
activities.prompt: If the opaque card is painted a different colour, what will happen to the shadow's colour?
options: Its colour will not change when the card is recoloured.
It will take the new colour because the card changes the light.
It will take the old colour because the wall keeps its colour.
It will become colourless because coloured light does not make shadows.

why.It will take the new colour because the: The card blocks the light rather than colouring the shadow.
why.It will take the old colour because the: The wall's colour does not determine the shadow's colour.
why.It will become colourless because colour: The shadow does not lose its colour when the opaque card is recoloured.

activities.explanation: Correct: changing an opaque object's colour does not change its shadow's colour.

activities.prompt: How does the passage compare the effects of transparent, translucent and opaque materials on light and shadows?
activities.answer: Light passes almost completely through a transparent sheet, partly through a translucent sheet, and not at all through an opaque card. Therefore, the transparent sheet allows the wall to receive almost all the light, the translucent sheet allows less, and the opaque card blocks the light and forms a dark patch.
points: Transparent materials allow almost all light through.
Translucent materials allow only part of the light through.
Opaque materials block light.
An opaque material forms a dark patch where light does not reach.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Alia looks into a plane mirror. She raises her left hand and watches the reflected face. Light from her face travels in a straight line until it changes direction at the mirror. Her image is the same size as she is and is erect, although it cannot be obtained on a screen. When she moves closer, the reflected face also appears closer.
activities.prompt: Alia raises her left hand. On which side of her reflected face will the hand appear?
options: On the right side of the reflected face
On the left side of the reflected face
On both sides at the same time
At the bottom of the reflected face

why.On the left side of the reflected face: This left-right reversal is called lateral inversion.
why.On both sides at the same time: The reflection does not reverse left and right in the same way.
why.At the bottom of the reflected face: The hand changes left and right, not top and bottom.

activities.explanation: Her left side appears on the right in a plane mirror image.

activities.context: Alia looks into a plane mirror. She raises her left hand and watches the reflected face. Light from her face travels in a straight line until it changes direction at the mirror. Her image is the same size as she is and is erect, although it cannot be obtained on a screen. When she moves closer, the reflected face also appears closer.
activities.prompt: What will happen to the apparent distance of Alia's image if she moves farther away from the mirror?
options: The image will appear farther from her
The image will appear closer than before
The image will remain at the same apparent distance
The image will appear at the mirror itself

why.The image will appear closer than before: Moving farther away does not make the image seem closer.
why.The image will remain at the same appare: The apparent distance changes when her distance changes.
why.The image will appear at the mirror itse: The image does not move to the mirror itself as she moves away.

activities.explanation: When Alia stands far away, the image also appears far away.

activities.context: Alia looks into a plane mirror. She raises her left hand and watches the reflected face. Light from her face travels in a straight line until it changes direction at the mirror. Her image is the same size as she is and is erect, although it cannot be obtained on a screen. When she moves closer, the reflected face also appears closer.
activities.prompt: If Alia moves closer to the mirror, how will the size of her image compare with her size?
options: The image will be the same size as Alia
The image will be smaller than Alia
The image will be larger than Alia
The image will change size each time she moves

why.The image will be smaller than Alia: Changing distance does not change the image's size.
why.The image will be larger than Alia: The image remains equally large as Alia.
why.The image will change size each time she: The size stays the same even when the apparent distance changes.

activities.explanation: A plane-mirror image is the same size as its object.

activities.prompt: Explain the lateral inversion seen in Alia's reflected face.
activities.answer: Alia's left side appears on the right side of the reflected image. This left-right reversal is called lateral inversion. Because the image reverses left and right, the hand she raises on her left is seen on the right side of the image.
points: Her left side appears on the right
This reversal is called lateral inversion
The left-right position is reversed
The raised left hand appears on the right
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student makes a pinhole camera outdoors using two cardboard boxes that slide into one another. A small hole is made in the opposite face of the larger box, and thin translucent paper serves as the screen with its tracing-paper side facing inside the larger box. The student covers both the head and camera with a dark cloth, then moves the smaller box until an image appears on the tracing paper.
activities.prompt: The tracing-paper screen is facing the wrong way. What should the student do next?
options: Reverse the paper so its screen surface points toward the box interior.
Turn the paper so its screen surface points toward the outdoor light.
Place the paper outside the larger box facing away from the hole.
Leave the paper in place because its direction makes no difference.

why.Turn the paper so its screen surface poi: Turning it toward the outdoor light does not follow the required screen position.
why.Place the paper outside the larger box f: The screen belongs inside the larger box rather than outside it.
why.Leave the paper in place because its dir: Its direction matters, so it should not be left facing the wrong way.

activities.explanation: The tracing-paper screen is correctly positioned toward the inside of the larger box.

activities.context: A student makes a pinhole camera outdoors using two cardboard boxes that slide into one another. A small hole is made in the opposite face of the larger box, and thin translucent paper serves as the screen with its tracing-paper side facing inside the larger box. The student covers both the head and camera with a dark cloth, then moves the smaller box until an image appears on the tracing paper.
activities.prompt: After the smaller box is moved and an image appears, how does the camera's image differ from a mirror image?
options: It is inverted vertically rather than reversed sideways like a mirror.
It is reversed sideways but remains upright like a mirror.
It is both upright and reversed sideways like a mirror.
It matches a mirror image in every way.

why.It is reversed sideways but remains upri: A mirror image has lateral inversion but is not upside down.
why.It is both upright and reversed sideways: An upright, laterally reversed image describes the mirror comparison rather than the camera image.
The camera image and mirror image do not have the same orientation.

activities.explanation: A pinhole camera forms an upside-down image.

activities.prompt: How does a pinhole camera form an image using the two sliding cardboard boxes?
activities.answer: A small hole is made in the opposite face of the larger box. The smaller box slides inside it, and thin translucent paper forms the screen with its tracing-paper side facing inward. Light rays pass through the tiny hole, and moving the smaller box helps bring an upside-down image onto the paper.
points: The boxes slide into one another.
The tiny hole is in the opposite face of the larger box.
Translucent paper faces inward as the screen.
Light rays pass through the hole and form an upside-down image.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a periscope and a kaleidoscope.
activities.answer: A periscope uses two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box to show an object that is not directly visible. A kaleidoscope uses three equal-width mirror strips joined triangularly inside a circular tube. When looked through, it shows a pattern, and turning it gives a different pattern each time.
points: A periscope uses two plane mirrors.
The mirrors are placed in a Z-shaped box.
A kaleidoscope uses three equal-width mirror strips.
A kaleidoscope shows a changing pattern when turned.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Earth, Moon, and the Sun
chapters.summary: In this chapter: how the earth rotates; day, night, and moving lights; revolution and the changing night sky; why seasons happen.

lessons.title: How the Earth Rotates

activities.prompt: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The spinning Earth
activities.body: The Earth turns around itself. This turning is called rotation. Because of this turning, the Sun seems to move. You see the Sun rise in the East and set in the West. The Earth’s axis of rotation is an imaginary line through its North Pole and South Pole. One rotation takes about 24 hours.
keyPoints: The Earth turns around itself.
The Sun rises in the East and sets in the West.
The axis is an imaginary line through both poles.
activities.explanation: Rotation makes the Earth turn and causes the Sun’s apparent movement.

activities.title: Spin the Earth

tasks.say: Go to midnight.
tasks.then: The place faces away from the Sun.

tasks.say: Bring it to sunrise.
tasks.then: It turns into the sunlight.

activities.takeaway: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.
activities.explanation: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.

activities.prompt: A child watches the Sun seem to move and asks why.
steps: The Sun rises in the East and sets in the West.
It seems to move because Earth turns around itself.
Earth turns around an imaginary axis through both poles.
This imaginary line is the axis of rotation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sunrise and Sunset
activities.prompt: In which direction does the Sun rise?
options: North
East
South
West
activities.explanation: The Sun rises in the East. It sets in the West.

activities.title: Why the Sun Seems to Move
activities.prompt: The Sun seems to move because the Earth is turning around ______.
activities.hint: Think about what the Earth is turning around.
activities.explanation: The Earth’s rotation makes the Sun seem to move.

activities.title: Moving in Circles
activities.prompt: During rotation, what do all parts of an object do?
options: Move in circles around an imaginary line.
Stay still around an imaginary line.
Move in one straight line through its centre.
Move in circles around a real pole.
activities.explanation: During rotation, all parts move in circles around an imaginary line.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each clue to its correct name.
pairs: A place the axis passes through
Another place the axis passes through
activities.explanation: Rotation means turning around itself. Its imaginary axis passes through both poles.

activities.title: Connect the Ideas
activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly connects rotation, movement, and the axis?
options: Parts circle a real line beside both poles.
Parts circle a real line through both poles.
Parts stay still beside an imaginary line.
Parts circle an imaginary line through both poles.
activities.explanation: During rotation, parts circle the imaginary axis. This axis passes through both poles.

activities.title: The Sun’s Daily Journey
activities.prompt: Put the cause-and-effect events in the correct order.
items: The Sun rises in the East
The Sun sets in the West
activities.explanation: The Earth’s turning makes the Sun seem to move. Its rising comes before its setting.

activities.prompt: After sunrise in the East, where will the Sun seem to move?
options: Toward the East, because Earth is turning.
Toward the East, because the Sun turns Earth.
Toward the West, because Earth is turning.
Toward the West, because the Sun turns Earth.

why.Toward the East, because Earth is turnin: This reverses the Sun's known rise and set directions.
why.Toward the East, because the Sun turns E: This reverses the direction and wrongly makes the Sun cause Earth's turning.
why.Toward the West, because the Sun turns E: This wrongly makes the Sun cause Earth's turning.

activities.explanation: Earth's turning makes the Sun seem to move toward the West.

activities.prompt: A spinning plate has a point moving straight away. What is wrong?
options: Rotation makes every point circle a nearby fixed point.
Rotation makes every point stay still beside the imaginary line.
Rotation makes the imaginary line circle every moving point.
Rotation makes every point circle the imaginary rotation line.

why.Rotation makes every point circle a near: This wrongly puts the circles around a nearby point.
why.Rotation makes every point stay still be: It wrongly thinks rotating parts stay beside the line.
why.Rotation makes the imaginary line circle: It reverses what moves around the imaginary line.

activities.explanation: During rotation, all parts move in circles around an imaginary line.

activities.prompt: A model axis misses the South Pole. What must be fixed?
options: Add the missing South Pole to the same axis.
Remove the North Pole from the same axis.
Move the axis into a circle around the North Pole.
Let the axis travel between the two poles.

why.Remove the North Pole from the same axis: The North Pole must be on the axis, not removed.
why.Move the axis into a circle around the N: The axis is a line through the poles, not a circle.
why.Let the axis travel between the two pole: Earth turns around the axis, so the axis does not travel.

activities.explanation: Earth's rotation axis passes through the North Pole and South Pole.

activities.prompt: One Earth rotation takes about 24 hours. What should appear during it?
options: The Sun sets in the East and rises in the West.
The Sun rises in the East and sets in the West.
The axis moves from the North Pole to the South Pole.
A nearby tree moves from left to right by itself.

why.The Sun sets in the East and rises in th: This reverses the Sun's known rise and set directions.
why.The axis moves from the North Pole to th: This wrongly treats the rotation line as something that moves.
why.A nearby tree moves from left to right b: A tree's apparent movement is not the Sun's daily path.

activities.explanation: The Sun's apparent daily path is East to West during Earth's rotation.

lessons.title: Day, Night, and Moving Lights

activities.prompt: Why do the Sun and Moon seem to move across the sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Day and Night Happen
activities.body: Day happens on the half of Earth that receives light. Night happens on the dark half. Rotation means turning. As Earth turns from West to East, places move into light or darkness. This causes the cycle of day and night. The Sun appears to rise in the east and cross the sky. The Pole Star looks almost fixed, while other stars seem to move around it.
keyPoints: The half with light has day; the dark half has night.
Earth rotates from West to East.
Sunrise and sunset happen as places enter light and darkness.
activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation brings light and darkness to different places.

activities.title: Spin the Earth

tasks.say: Go to midnight.
tasks.then: The place faces away from the Sun.

tasks.say: Bring it to sunrise.
tasks.then: It turns into the sunlight.

activities.takeaway: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.
activities.explanation: Day and night happen because the Earth spins.

activities.prompt: Why does the Sun seem to rise in the east each morning?
steps: Earth rotates from west to east, so eastern India receives light first.
The globe's turn moves places between the lit half and dark half.
Entering light means sunrise; entering darkness means sunset.
So the Sun appears to rise in the east and cross the sky.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Half with Daytime
activities.prompt: Which part of the globe has daytime?
options: The half with light
The half in darkness
Only eastern India
Only the globe’s centre
activities.explanation: The half receiving light has daytime, while the dark half has night.

activities.prompt: The dark half of the globe has night.
activities.explanation: Darkness marks the half of the globe where night occurs.

activities.prompt: The globe must rotate from ______ to East.
activities.hint: This lets eastern India receive light first.

options: Earth’s rotation from West to East

activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation makes places enter light and darkness.

activities.title: A Place Through Day and Night

activities.title: Why the Pole Star Seems Still
activities.prompt: Why does the Pole Star look nearly stationary from Earth?
options: Earth’s axis points close to it
Sun’s light holds it still
Moon’s motion holds it still
Stars move it across the sky
activities.explanation: The Pole Star appears nearly stationary because Earth’s axis points close to it.

options: The Sun will appear to rise there.
The Sun will set below there.
Day and night will stop there.
The Pole Star will move away.

This forgets that rotation causes the day-night cycle.
This forgets that the Pole Star looks almost fixed.

activities.explanation: Moving into light causes sunrise there.

activities.prompt: As Earth turns, a place enters the dark half. What happens?
options: Sunset happens at that place.
Sunrise happens at that place.
The Sun appears to move across the sky.
The Pole Star appears nearly stationary.

This confuses entering darkness with entering light.
This confuses the Sun's motion with the event happening.
This describes the Pole Star's position, not the place's change.
