lessons.title: Revolution and the Changing Night Sky

activities.prompt: Why does the night sky keep changing throughout the year?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Earth’s Yearly Journey
activities.body: Revolution is the movement of one object around another object. The path followed during this movement is called an orbit. Earth’s orbit around the Sun looks nearly circular from above. Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours to complete one revolution. It revolves around the Sun continuously. The stars seen after sunset gradually change. The Bhil and Pawara used star patterns as signs of monsoon rain.
keyPoints: Revolution means movement around another object.
An orbit is the path followed during revolution.
Earth’s revolution causes the night sky to change gradually.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects Earth’s journey with the changing stars.

activities.prompt: A child compares the stars after sunset in two months. Why are they different?
steps: Earth revolves around the Sun continuously, so its movement does not stop.
During this movement, different groups of stars rise at sunset in different months.
Because these groups differ, the stars seen after sunset gradually change.
Therefore, the changing night sky is connected to Earth's revolution.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Connecting the Night Sky
activities.body: Earth’s movement around the Sun is called revolution. The path followed during this movement is called an orbit. From above, Earth’s orbit looks nearly circular. This movement happens continuously. It takes about 365 days and 6 hours for one revolution. Different groups of stars rise at sunset in different months. The Bhil and Pawara used star patterns as signs of monsoon rain.
keyPoints: Earth revolves continuously around the Sun.
Different star groups rise at sunset in different months.
Star patterns helped the Bhil and Pawara recognise monsoon rain.
activities.explanation: Earth’s revolution helps explain the changing night sky.

activities.prompt: Earth’s orbit around the Sun looks perfectly circular from above.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the orbit looks nearly circular, not perfectly circular.

activities.prompt: What does revolution describe?
options: Movement around another object
The path of an orbit
A change in star patterns
A sign of monsoon rain
activities.explanation: Revolution is the movement of one object around another object. The orbit is its path.

activities.prompt: The stars seen after sunset gradually change.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that stars seen after sunset gradually change.

activities.prompt: Earth takes about ______ days to complete one revolution.
activities.hint: There are also about 6 extra hours.
activities.explanation: Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours to complete one revolution.

activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its meaning.
pairs: Movement of one object around another
Star patterns used by the Bhil and Pawara
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an important word with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which observation is true about stars in the night sky?
options: Different groups rise at sunset in different months.
All groups rise at sunset in every month.
The same group rises at sunset in every month.
Stars appear only during the monsoon season.
activities.explanation: Different groups of stars rise at sunset in different months.

activities.prompt: Earth keeps moving around the Sun. What would show that one revolution is complete?
options: The Earth returns to its starting place.
The Earth reaches the halfway point.
The Earth passes by the Sun once.
The Earth makes one full day.

The halfway point is only part of one revolution.
Passing by the Sun once does not show a complete revolution.
One full day is much shorter than one revolution.

activities.explanation: Returning to the starting place shows one complete revolution, lasting about 365 days and 6 hours.

activities.prompt: The child watches stars after sunset in two different months. What will the child notice?
options: The groups will be different.
The groups will stay the same.
The stars will grow brighter.
The stars will move closer together.

This mistake confuses a changing sky with an unchanged sky.
This mistake confuses changing groups with changing brightness.
This mistake confuses changing groups with changing positions.

activities.explanation: Different months bring different groups of stars at sunset.

activities.prompt: A child wants to compare sunset stars in two months. Which plan is fairest?
options: Look just after sunset in two different months.
Look just after sunset on two nearby nights.
Look just before sunset in two different months.
Look at the stars at noon in two months.

why.Look just after sunset on two nearby nig: Nearby nights do not test the change between months.
why.Look just before sunset in two different: Looking before sunset does not examine the requested view.
Looking at noon does not examine the requested view.

activities.explanation: This compares the same sunset view in different months.

funFacts: Ancient Indian astronomers, including Aryabhata, had also noticed the daily apparent motion of the celestial objects, such as the Sun, Moon, planets and stars. Aryabhata was a famous mathematician and astronomer of ancient India who wrote an important treatise, Aryabhatiya, around the fifth century CE.
The Bhil and Pawara are indigenous communities from the Tapi Valley in western India, who used the appearance of certain patterns of stars in the sky as markers for the arrival of monsoon rain.

lessons.title: Why Seasons Happen

activities.prompt: Why do some places have summer while others have winter?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Earth's Tilted Axis
activities.body: Earth’s axis of rotation is the line around which Earth turns. This line is tilted rather than upright. Earth keeps the tilt while travelling around the Sun. In June, the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun. Sunlight then spreads over a smaller area, and daytime lasts longer than 12 hours. The Northern Hemisphere has summer then, while the Southern Hemisphere has winter.
keyPoints: Earth’s axis is tilted and keeps this tilt.
The Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun in June.
Sunlight spreads over a smaller area in June.
The two hemispheres have opposite seasons in June.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect Earth's tilt with sunlight, daylight, and the seasons.

activities.title: Travel round the Sun

tasks.say: Go to December.
tasks.then: The north leans away from the Sun: winter there.

tasks.say: Go to March.
tasks.then: Neither half leans towards the Sun.

activities.takeaway: The tilt of the Earth makes the seasons.
activities.explanation: The tilt of the Earth makes the seasons.

activities.prompt: In June, why does one hemisphere have summer while the other has winter?
steps: Earth keeps its axis tilted as it travels around the Sun, because the tilt does not change.
In June, the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, so sunlight spreads over a smaller area.
The Northern Hemisphere then gets sunlight for more than 12 hours, giving it summer.
The Southern Hemisphere has winter at the same time, so their seasons are opposite.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Different Seasons
activities.body: June and December show how Earth's tilted axis affects sunlight and daylight. In June, the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun. Sunlight covers a smaller area, and sunshine lasts for more than 12 hours. The Northern Hemisphere has summer then. The Southern Hemisphere has winter then, so the two halves have opposite seasons.
keyPoints: The Northern Hemisphere has summer in June.
The Southern Hemisphere has winter in June.
December has shorter periods of sunlight in the Northern Hemisphere.
The two hemispheres have opposite seasons in June.
activities.explanation: This pattern shows how sunlight and daylight change between the hemispheres.

activities.title: A Steady Tilt
activities.prompt: What happens to Earth's tilt while it travels around the Sun?
options: Earth keeps the same tilt.
Earth becomes upright.
Earth loses its tilt.
Earth changes its tilt each month.
activities.explanation: Earth keeps this tilt while travelling around the Sun.

activities.title: A Smaller Area
activities.prompt: In June, sunlight spreads over a ______ area in the Northern Hemisphere.
activities.hint: Choose the word that means less than the usual area.
activities.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere receives sunlight over a smaller area in June.

activities.title: June Daylight

options: Exactly 12 hours.
More than 12 hours.
Less than 12 hours.
No sunlight at all.
activities.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere receives sunlight for more than 12 hours in June.

activities.title: Seasons and Daylight

activities.prompt: Put these dates in order through the year.
activities.explanation: Around 21 June has the longest day. Around 22 December is the winter solstice.

activities.prompt: The axis stays tilted as Earth travels around the Sun. Why can June be summer in the Northern Hemisphere?
options: The tilt lets sunlight spread over a smaller area there.
The tilt makes sunlight spread over a larger area there.
The tilt keeps all sunlight away from that hemisphere.
The tilt gives that hemisphere exactly 12 hours of sunlight.

why.The tilt makes sunlight spread over a la: This mistake reverses the effect of the tilted axis.
why.The tilt keeps all sunlight away from th: This mistake thinks tilting blocks sunlight from reaching a hemisphere.
why.The tilt gives that hemisphere exactly 1: This mistake confuses June daylight with the equator's pattern.

activities.explanation: The tilt towards the Sun makes the sunlight spread over a smaller area.

activities.prompt: The equator has 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness all year. Which check tests this claim?
options: Compare equator daylight in June and December.
Compare Northern Hemisphere daylight in June and December.
Compare one equator morning with one equator afternoon.
Compare June daylight in two different countries.

why.Compare Northern Hemisphere daylight in: It changes the place, so it does not test the equator.
why.Compare one equator morning with one equ: It compares one day, not changes across the year.
why.Compare June daylight in two different c: It changes places and does not test the whole year.

activities.explanation: It compares the same place at two times of the year.

activities.prompt: Earth keeps its axis tilted as it travels around the Sun. What causes the June summer pattern?
options: Smaller sunlight spread and longer days in the Northern Hemisphere.
Larger sunlight spread and longer days in the Northern Hemisphere.
Smaller sunlight spread and shorter days in the Northern Hemisphere.
Larger sunlight spread and shorter days in the Northern Hemisphere.

why.Larger sunlight spread and longer days i: This mistake gets the sunlight spread wrong.
why.Smaller sunlight spread and shorter days: This mistake gets the daylight length wrong.
why.Larger sunlight spread and shorter days: This mistake reverses both the spread and the daylight length.

activities.explanation: June has smaller sunlight spread and more than 12 hours of daylight.

lessons.title: Solar Eclipses

activities.prompt: How can the Moon hide the Sun’s brilliant light for a few moments?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What happens during a solar eclipse?
activities.body: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth. The Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth. The Moon and Sun have similar apparent sizes from Earth. The Moon is much closer to Earth. It can appear to cover the whole Sun. Its shadow causes total darkness in one area. Daylight becomes dark for a few minutes. Never look directly at a solar eclipse.
keyPoints: The Moon can block sunlight from reaching Earth.
The Moon can appear to cover the whole Sun.
Never look directly at a solar eclipse.
activities.explanation: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks sunlight from Earth.

activities.title: Make a solar eclipse

tasks.say: Put the Moon between the Sun and the Earth.
tasks.then: The shadow of the Moon falls on the Earth: a solar eclipse.

activities.takeaway: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.
activities.explanation: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.

activities.prompt: Why can the Moon seem big enough to cover the whole Sun from Earth?
steps: Because apparent size depends on distance, the Moon’s closeness matters.
The Moon and Sun have similar apparent sizes from Earth.
Therefore, the Moon can appear to cover the whole Sun.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The eclipse arrangement
activities.prompt: Which body comes between the Sun and Earth during a solar eclipse?
options: Moon
Venus
Sun
Earth
activities.explanation: The Moon comes between the Sun and Earth during a solar eclipse.

activities.title: Safe viewing
activities.prompt: Looking directly at a solar eclipse must always be ______.
activities.hint: Think about keeping your eyes safe.
activities.explanation: Looking directly at a solar eclipse must always be avoided.

activities.title: Why can the Moon cover the Sun?
activities.prompt: Why can the Moon appear to cover the whole Sun?
options: The Moon is much closer to Earth than the Sun.
The Sun is much closer to Earth than the Moon.
The Moon and Sun have very different apparent sizes.
The Moon is farther from Earth than the Sun.
activities.explanation: The Moon is much closer to Earth. Its similar apparent size lets it cover the Sun.

activities.title: Eclipse clues
activities.prompt: Match each eclipse clue with its meaning.
pairs: Only some regions of the Sun are covered
Becomes dark for a few minutes
activities.explanation: Each clue matches one important feature of a solar eclipse.

activities.title: The eclipse sequence
activities.prompt: Put these eclipse steps in order.
items: Moon comes between the Sun and Earth
Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth
activities.explanation: The Moon first blocks sunlight, and its shadow covers an area where it is totally dark.

activities.title: Identify a partial eclipse
activities.prompt: Which event describes a partial solar eclipse?
options: The Moon covers only some regions of the Sun.
The Moon covers the whole Sun from Earth.
Venus appears as a tiny black dot.
The Moon’s shadow causes total darkness.
activities.explanation: A partial solar eclipse happens when the Moon covers only some regions of the Sun.

activities.prompt: The Moon and Sun look similar in size. What best explains why?
options: The Moon is closer, so it looks large.
The Sun is closer, so it looks large.
Both objects have the same physical size.
Apparent size depends only on physical size.

This reverses the fact that the Moon is much closer to Earth.
why.Both objects have the same physical size: This wrongly assumes similar apparent size means equal physical size.
why.Apparent size depends only on physical s: This wrongly says distance has no effect on apparent size.

activities.explanation: This is right because distance and physical size both set apparent size.

activities.prompt: A tiny black dot crosses the Sun. The Moon can cover the whole Sun. Why is the coverage different?
options: The dot is Venus, and the Moon can look larger.
The dot is the Moon, and the Moon can look smaller.
The dot is Venus, and Venus can cover everything.
The dot is the Moon, and the Moon can cover everything.

why.The dot is the Moon, and the Moon can lo: This mistakes the tiny black dot for the Moon.
why.The dot is Venus, and Venus can cover ev: This wrongly says Venus can cover the whole Sun.
why.The dot is the Moon, and the Moon can co: This wrongly identifies the tiny black dot as the Moon.

activities.explanation: This is right: Venus looks tiny, while the Moon can cover the whole Sun.

activities.prompt: One place has a partial solar eclipse. Another has a total solar eclipse. Where should full darkness occur?
options: In the second place, inside the Moon’s shadow.
In the first place, inside the Moon’s shadow.
In both places, wherever the Sun is covered.
Nowhere, because blocked light cannot make darkness.

why.In the first place, inside the Moon’s sh: This mistakes partial coverage for the area of total darkness.
why.In both places, wherever the Sun is cove: This wrongly treats every partly covered place as fully dark.
why.Nowhere, because blocked light cannot ma: This wrongly says blocked sunlight cannot create darkness.

activities.explanation: This is right: the fully covered place is inside the Moon’s dark shadow.

lessons.title: Lunar Eclipses and Sky Watching

activities.prompt: Why does the Moon sometimes glow coppery during a lunar eclipse?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When Earth’s Shadow Covers the Moon
activities.body: During a lunar eclipse, Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon. Earth’s shadow falls across the Moon’s full disc, its whole round face. The whole Moon enters the shadow during a total eclipse. Only part enters during a partial eclipse. You can safely watch an eclipsed full Moon with naked eyes. Kodaikanal Solar Observatory supplied Sun data. M. K. Vainu Bappu is called the father of modern Indian astronomy.
keyPoints: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.
Total eclipses place the whole Moon inside Earth’s shadow.
An eclipsed full Moon is safe to watch with naked eyes.
activities.explanation: Lunar eclipses happen when Earth’s shadow reaches the Moon.

activities.title: Make a lunar eclipse

tasks.say: Put the Moon behind the Earth.
tasks.then: The Moon moves into the shadow of the Earth: a lunar eclipse.

activities.takeaway: A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
activities.explanation: A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.

activities.prompt: Your friend says a partial lunar eclipse puts the whole Moon in Earth's shadow. Why is this wrong?
steps: Only part of the Moon is inside Earth's shadow.
Earth's shadow blocks sunlight from reaching the part inside it.
The part outside the shadow can still receive sunlight because it is not inside Earth's shadow.
So the friend's claim is wrong because a partial eclipse affects only part of the Moon.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens during a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching Moon
Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth
Moon changes into Earth’s dark shadow
Stellarium changes the Moon’s sunlight
activities.explanation: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon. This blocking is called a lunar eclipse.

activities.prompt: An eclipsed full Moon can be watched safely with naked eyes.
activities.explanation: You can safely watch an eclipsed full Moon with naked eyes.

activities.prompt: During a lunar eclipse, Earth blocks ______ from reaching the Moon.
activities.hint: It is the light that Earth blocks.
activities.explanation: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct description.
pairs: Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a fact about lunar eclipses or eclipse information.

activities.prompt: Ancient Indian astronomical texts did not predict eclipses.
activities.explanation: Ancient Indian astronomical texts calculated and predicted eclipses.

activities.prompt: Which pair links modern Indian astronomy with the place that supplied Sun data?
options: Kodaikanal Solar Observatory and M. K. Vainu Bappu
The Stellarium app and M. K. Vainu Bappu
The Stellarium app and Kodaikanal Solar Observatory
Ancient Indian texts and the Stellarium app
activities.explanation: M. K. Vainu Bappu is called the father of modern Indian astronomy. Kodaikanal Solar Observatory supplied data about the Sun.

activities.prompt: The whole Moon is inside Earth's shadow. What happens to sunlight?
options: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.
Sunlight still reaches every part of the Moon.
The Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth.
The Sun enters Earth's shadow and grows dark.

why.Sunlight still reaches every part of the: This mistake ignores that Earth's shadow covers the Moon.
why.The Moon blocks sunlight from reaching E: This mistake swaps the blocker and the shadowed body.
why.The Sun enters Earth's shadow and grows: This mistake puts the Sun where the Moon should be.

activities.explanation: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.

activities.prompt: Only part of the Moon enters Earth's shadow. What happens outside it?
options: Sunlight can still reach that part.
No sunlight can reach any part.
That part casts a shadow on the Sun.
That part pulls the Moon away.

This mistake treats a partial eclipse as a total one.
This mistake reverses the body casting the shadow.
This mistake treats the shadow like a pulling force.

activities.explanation: A partial eclipse leaves the rest outside Earth's shadow.

activities.prompt: Earth's shadow crosses the Moon's full disc. Which part is shadowed?
options: The whole visible disc of the Moon.
Only one small part of the Moon.
Only the empty space around the Moon.
Only the shadowed part of the Sun.

This mistake confuses a full-disc shadow with a partial one.
This mistake treats empty sky as part of the Moon.
This mistake swaps the Moon with the Sun.

activities.explanation: The shadow falls across the Moon's full disc.

activities.prompt: Kodaikanal Solar Observatory is called the father of modern Indian astronomy. What is wrong?
options: Vainu Bappu has this title, not the observatory.
The ancient texts have this title, not the observatory.
The Stellarium app has this title, not the observatory.
The Earth's shadow has this title, not the observatory.

why.The ancient texts have this title, not t: The texts calculated and predicted eclipses, but do not have this title.
why.The Stellarium app has this title, not t: Stellarium provides eclipse information, but does not have this title.
why.The Earth's shadow has this title, not t: Earth's shadow causes an eclipse, but does not have this title.

activities.explanation: M. K. Vainu Bappu is called the father of modern Indian astronomy.

funFacts: An eclipse is known as grahan in Sanskrit and in many Indian languages. Many ancient Indian astronomical texts provide calculations to predict eclipses.

The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory is located in the beautiful Palani range of hills in southern India. It was established in 1899 and has provided data about the Sun for over 100 years. It is operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru.

activities.context: A student watches the Sun rise in the East and set in the West. On a merry-go-round, objects seem to move in the opposite direction. A tree seems to move from the left side to the right side. The Sun seems to move because the Earth is turning around itself. The Earth’s axis passes through its North Pole and South Pole. During rotation, parts move in circles around this imaginary line. One rotation takes about 24 hours.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for the student seeing the Sun rise in the East and set in the West?
options: The Earth’s own turning causes the Sun’s apparent movement.
The axis passing through the poles makes the Sun rise and set.
The sideways movement of the tree causes the Sun’s apparent movement.
The opposite movement on the merry-go-round causes the Sun to rise and set.

why.The axis passing through the poles makes: The axis identifies the Earth’s line of rotation but is not given as the cause of the Sun’s apparent movement.
why.The sideways movement of the tree causes: The tree’s movement is a separate example of apparent sideways movement.
why.The opposite movement on the merry-go-ro: The merry-go-round example does not explain the Sun’s rising and setting.

activities.explanation: The Sun seems to move because the Earth is turning around itself.

activities.context: A student watches the Sun rise in the East and set in the West. On a merry-go-round, objects seem to move in the opposite direction. A tree seems to move from the left side to the right side. The Sun seems to move because the Earth is turning around itself. The Earth’s axis passes through its North Pole and South Pole. During rotation, parts move in circles around this imaginary line. One rotation takes about 24 hours.
activities.prompt: How should the student explain why objects seem to move in the opposite direction on the merry-go-round?
options: The rider’s motion makes the objects seem to move the other way.
Each object is turning around itself in the opposite direction.
The Earth’s axis makes the objects reverse their direction.
The tree’s sideways movement makes the objects seem opposite.

why.Each object is turning around itself in: The case describes apparent opposite movement caused by the ride, not each object turning by itself.
why.The Earth’s axis makes the objects rever: The Earth’s axis concerns the Earth’s rotation, not the reversal seen on the merry-go-round.
why.The tree’s sideways movement makes the o: The tree’s movement is separate and does not explain the objects on the merry-go-round.

activities.explanation: Objects seem to move opposite to the rider on a merry-go-round.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Sun seems to move from the East to the West.
activities.answer: The Sun seems to move because the Earth is turning around itself. The Earth completes one rotation in about 24 hours, so the Sun appears at changing positions during that time. Its apparent motion matches the Sun rising in the East and setting in the West.
points: The Earth’s rotation causes the apparent movement of the Sun.
One rotation takes about 24 hours.
The Sun rises in the East and sets in the West.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student in eastern India watches the Sun rise in the east and move across the sky. The globe turns from West to East, so eastern India receives light first. The light half has daytime, while the dark half has night. At night, the student sees the Pole Star looking almost fixed, with the other stars appearing to move around it. The Moon also appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
activities.prompt: Suppose the globe stopped rotating from West to East. What would happen to the cycle of day and night?
options: The normal cycle of light and darkness would stop repeating.
The Sun would begin rising in the west instead.
Eastern India would receive the light even later.
The light and dark halves would disappear, leaving the whole globe lit.

why.The Sun would begin rising in the west i: This mistake treats the Sun's apparent motion as separate from the globe's rotation.
why.Eastern India would receive the light ev: This mistake suggests only a change in timing, rather than the cycle stopping.
why.The light and dark halves would disappea: This mistake forgets that one half receives light while the other half remains dark.

activities.explanation: Correct: Earth's West-to-East rotation causes the repeating cycle of day and night.

activities.context: A student in eastern India watches the Sun rise in the east and move across the sky. The globe turns from West to East, so eastern India receives light first. The light half has daytime, while the dark half has night. At night, the student sees the Pole Star looking almost fixed, with the other stars appearing to move around it. The Moon also appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
activities.prompt: Why does the student see the Pole Star looking almost fixed while the other stars appear to move around it?
options: The Earth's axis points close to the Pole Star, so it appears nearly stationary.
The Moon's movement from east to west makes the other stars circle the Pole Star.
The Sun's movement across the sky causes the Pole Star to remain fixed while all the stars shift.
The light and dark halves of the globe make the stars appear to move around the Pole Star.

why.The Moon's movement from east to west ma: The Moon's apparent movement does not cause the other stars to move around the Pole Star.
why.The Sun's movement across the sky causes: The Sun's apparent path is not the reason for the Pole Star's nearly fixed appearance.
why.The light and dark halves of the globe m: The light and dark halves explain day and night, not the stars' apparent movement.

activities.explanation: Correct: The Earth's axis points close to the Pole Star, making it appear nearly stationary.

activities.prompt: Explain why sunrise and sunset occur as the Earth rotates.
activities.answer: Sunrise occurs when a place moves from the dark half of the globe into the light half. Sunset occurs when it moves out of light and into darkness. Because the Earth rotates from West to East, this movement repeats and produces the cycle of day and night. The Sun therefore appears to rise in the east and move across the sky.
points: Sunrise occurs when a place enters the light.
Sunset occurs when a place enters darkness.
The Earth rotates from West to East.
This rotation causes the cycle of day and night.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student watches the sky after sunset and notices that the stars change little by little. In another month, a different cluster of stars appears at sunset. The student’s family remembers that the Bhil and Pawara treated such star patterns as signs of monsoon rain. They also learn that Earth keeps moving around the Sun and completes one trip in about 365 days and 6 hours. The student wonders how the changing sky could guide them.
activities.prompt: What should the student expect when observing the sky at sunset in another month?
options: The group visible at sunset may change with the month.
The cluster seen now will remain unchanged throughout the year.
Only one group will ever be visible at sunset.
The stars will disappear whenever a new month begins.

why.The cluster seen now will remain unchang: The stated pattern is monthly change, not a fixed yearly view.
why.Only one group will ever be visible at s: This contradicts the fact that different groups rise in different months.
why.The stars will disappear whenever a new: This contradicts the stated gradual change in stars after sunset.

activities.explanation: Different groups rise at sunset in different months.

activities.context: A student watches the sky after sunset and notices that the stars change little by little. In another month, a different cluster of stars appears at sunset. The student’s family remembers that the Bhil and Pawara treated such star patterns as signs of monsoon rain. They also learn that Earth keeps moving around the Sun and completes one trip in about 365 days and 6 hours. The student wonders how the changing sky could guide them.
activities.prompt: The student wants to draw the route Earth follows around the Sun. Which representation should be used?
options: A nearly circular orbit around the Sun.
A straight route with the Sun at one end.
A square route around the Sun.
A spiral route that changes shape each month.

why.A straight route with the Sun at one end: The orbit is not described as a straight route.
The orbit is not described as square.
why.A spiral route that changes shape each m: The stated orbit is nearly circular and does not change shape each month.

activities.explanation: The Earth’s orbit looks nearly circular from above.

activities.prompt: Explain why the stars seen after sunset can be used as signs of monsoon rain.
activities.answer: Earth revolves around the Sun continuously, so the stars seen after sunset gradually change. Different groups of stars rise at sunset in different months. This gives people changing patterns to observe, which the Bhil and Pawara used as signs of monsoon rain.
points: Earth revolves around the Sun continuously.
The stars seen after sunset gradually change.
Different groups rise at sunset in different months.
The Bhil and Pawara used these patterns as signs of monsoon rain.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a June holiday, a class in the Northern Hemisphere notices that daylight lasts for more than 12 hours. The Earth’s axis is tilted, and the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun then. Sunlight is spread over a smaller area there. The class also learns that June is summer in the north but winter in the south. In December, the north will have winter with shorter periods of sunlight.
activities.prompt: Why does the class have longer daylight and summer in June?
options: Because the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, it has longer daylight and summer.
Because the Earth’s axis is upright, it has longer daylight and summer.
Because the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, it has shorter daylight and winter.
Because the Earth’s axis is upright, it has shorter daylight and winter.

why.Because the Earth’s axis is upright, it: An upright axis contradicts the stated tilt of the axis.
why.Because the Northern Hemisphere leans to: The June direction is correct, but daylight and season are reversed.
why.Because the Earth’s axis is upright, it: The axis is tilted, and June has longer daylight and summer.

activities.explanation: This correctly links the June tilt, longer daylight, and northern summer.

activities.context: During a June holiday, a class in the Northern Hemisphere notices that daylight lasts for more than 12 hours. The Earth’s axis is tilted, and the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun then. Sunlight is spread over a smaller area there. The class also learns that June is summer in the north but winter in the south. In December, the north will have winter with shorter periods of sunlight.
activities.prompt: Which date should the class choose for the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere described in the case?
options: Around 21 June
Around 22 December
Around 21 March
Around 23 September

why.Around 22 December: 22 December is around the winter solstice.
why.Around 21 March: 21 March is around one of the dates when daytime lasts 12 hours.
why.Around 23 September: 23 September is around another date when daytime lasts 12 hours.

activities.explanation: The longest northern day occurs around 21 June.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer and longer daylight in June.
activities.answer: June has summer in the Northern Hemisphere because it is tilted towards the Sun. Sunlight is then spread over a smaller area, and the Northern Hemisphere receives sunlight for more than 12 hours. Meanwhile, the Southern Hemisphere has winter.
points: Identifies the Northern Hemisphere’s June tilt towards the Sun.
Explains that sunlight is spread over a smaller area.
States that daylight lasts for more than 12 hours.
Notes that the Southern Hemisphere has winter in June.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a total solar eclipse, Riya sees daylight become dark for a few minutes. The Moon is between the Sun and Earth and blocks sunlight from reaching Earth. From Riya’s view, the Moon appears to cover the whole Sun. She notices that the area under the Moon’s shadow is in total darkness. A friend starts to look directly at the eclipse, so Riya warns him to stop.
activities.prompt: Why does Riya see the daytime become dark during the eclipse?
options: Earth receives less sunlight because the Moon is between it and the Sun.
The Moon becomes smaller because it moves farther from Earth.
The Sun becomes physically smaller because the Moon hides it.
The darkness occurs only because the Moon is closer to Earth than the Sun.

why.The Moon becomes smaller because it move: The Moon does not need to become smaller.
why.The Sun becomes physically smaller becau: The Sun does not physically become smaller.
why.The darkness occurs only because the Moo: Closeness helps explain apparent size, not the sudden darkness by itself.

activities.explanation: Correct: the Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth.

activities.context: During a total solar eclipse, Riya sees daylight become dark for a few minutes. The Moon is between the Sun and Earth and blocks sunlight from reaching Earth. From Riya’s view, the Moon appears to cover the whole Sun. She notices that the area under the Moon’s shadow is in total darkness. A friend starts to look directly at the eclipse, so Riya warns him to stop.
activities.prompt: What should the friend do after Riya warns him?
options: He should turn away rather than continue viewing the Sun directly.
He should keep looking as long as the eclipse remains total.
He should look directly until the Moon begins moving away.
He should look directly only when the darkness makes it seem safe.

why.He should keep looking as long as the ec: Totality does not make direct viewing safe.
why.He should look directly until the Moon b: The danger remains even if the eclipse changes.
why.He should look directly only when the da: Darkness during an eclipse does not make direct viewing safe.

activities.explanation: Correct: looking directly at a solar eclipse must always be avoided.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Moon can appear to cover the whole Sun even though it is much closer to Earth than the Sun.
activities.answer: The Moon and Sun have similar apparent sizes when seen from Earth, even though the Moon is much closer. Apparent size depends on both physical size and distance. Therefore, the Moon can appear large enough to cover the whole Sun, blocking sunlight from reaching the area under its shadow.
points: The Moon and Sun have similar apparent sizes.
The Moon is much closer to Earth.
Apparent size depends on physical size and distance.
The Moon can therefore appear to cover the whole Sun.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is watching a total lunar eclipse and notices that the whole Moon lies within Earth’s shadow. The student knows that an eclipsed full Moon can be watched safely with naked eyes. Before the next event, the student opens the Stellarium app to learn about upcoming eclipses. The student also wonders how people in ancient India planned for such sky events and learns that ancient Indian astronomical texts calculated and predicted them.
activities.prompt: What caused the Moon to enter Earth’s shadow during the eclipse?
options: Earth blocked sunlight from reaching the Moon.
The Moon blocked sunlight from reaching Earth.
The Stellarium app moved the Moon into the shadow.
Ancient Indian astronomical texts created the shadow.

why.The Moon blocked sunlight from reaching: This reverses the positions of Earth and the Moon.
why.The Stellarium app moved the Moon into t: An app provides information but does not cause an eclipse.
why.Ancient Indian astronomical texts create: Historical texts calculated eclipses but did not create shadows.

activities.explanation: Earth’s blocking of sunlight causes a lunar eclipse.

activities.context: A student is watching a total lunar eclipse and notices that the whole Moon lies within Earth’s shadow. The student knows that an eclipsed full Moon can be watched safely with naked eyes. Before the next event, the student opens the Stellarium app to learn about upcoming eclipses. The student also wonders how people in ancient India planned for such sky events and learns that ancient Indian astronomical texts calculated and predicted them.
activities.prompt: What should the student do to obtain advance information about a future lunar eclipse?
options: Open Stellarium and consult its information on future eclipses.
Open Stellarium and read only its information about the Sun.
Use naked-eye viewing to discover an eclipse before it happens.
Use Kodaikanal Solar Observatory’s Sun data as an eclipse forecast.

why.Open Stellarium and read only its inform: Its Sun information is not the required eclipse information.
why.Use naked-eye viewing to discover an ecl: Naked-eye viewing is used to watch an eclipsed full Moon safely.
why.Use Kodaikanal Solar Observatory’s Sun d: The observatory supplied Sun data, not eclipse forecasts.

activities.explanation: Stellarium can provide information about upcoming eclipses.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a total lunar eclipse and a partial lunar eclipse.
activities.answer: A total lunar eclipse occurs when the entire Moon enters Earth’s shadow, so all of the Moon is affected. A partial lunar eclipse occurs when only some of the Moon enters that shadow, so part of the Moon remains outside it.
points: Total eclipse: the whole Moon enters the shadow.
Partial eclipse: only part of the Moon enters.
Both are caused by Earth blocking sunlight.
The difference is how much of the Moon enters the shadow.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Earth, Moon, and the Sun

activities.prompt: What do nearby objects seem to do while you ride a merry-go-round?
options: Move in the opposite direction
Move in the same direction
Stay completely still
Move only towards the centre
activities.explanation: The merry-go-round makes nearby objects seem to move in the opposite direction.

activities.prompt: The Sun seems to move because the Earth is turning around itself.
activities.explanation: Earth’s turning makes the Sun seem to rise in the East and set in the West.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct meaning.
pairs: Movement of one object around another
Imaginary line around which an object turns
activities.explanation: These pairs connect each movement term with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of a total solar eclipse in order.
items: The Moon comes between the Sun and Earth
The Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth
The Moon’s shadow area has total darkness
Daylight becomes dark for a few minutes
activities.explanation: The Moon blocks sunlight, creating darkness along its shadow.

activities.prompt: Why does eastern India receive light first?
options: Earth rotates from West to East
Earth rotates from North to South
Earth moves from East to West
The Sun moves towards eastern India
activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation from West to East brings light to eastern India first.

activities.prompt: The path followed during revolution is called the ______.
activities.hint: This is the path of an object around another object.
activities.explanation: The Earth’s orbit is the path it follows while revolving around the Sun.

activities.prompt: What happens in the Northern Hemisphere in June?
options: It has summer and longer sunlight
It has winter and shorter sunlight
It has summer and shorter sunlight
It has winter and longer sunlight
activities.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere has summer in June and receives sunlight for more than 12 hours.

activities.prompt: During a total lunar eclipse, the whole Moon enters the Earth’s shadow.
activities.explanation: A total lunar eclipse happens when the whole Moon enters Earth’s shadow.

activities.prompt: Match each eclipse with its correct description.
pairs: Moon blocks sunlight from reaching Earth
Moon covers the whole Sun from Earth
Only part of the Moon enters Earth’s shadow
activities.explanation: A solar eclipse involves the Moon, while a lunar eclipse involves Earth’s shadow.

activities.prompt: Why does the Pole Star appear nearly stationary in the sky?
options: Earth’s axis points close to it
The Moon always stays near it
The Sun moves close to it
Earth’s orbit circles around it
activities.explanation: The Pole Star looks almost fixed because Earth’s axis points close to it.
